https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: When Government Fails, Working People Pick Up the Slack
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
This is happening in every working-class and poor community across the country.

“I am so proud of us,” my neighbor says to the room, her hand on her heart. She swallows the last word like she’s about to cry.

It’s fall but still hot in North Carolina. I’ve abandoned my usual T-shirt for a dressy sweater, and I’m regretting it. We are packed into a school cafeteria. Young couples, a few teenagers, grandparents towing their grandchildren behind them, filling in for caretakers while parents work second shift.

My neighbor takes her seat as applause echoes off the cinderblock walls and out the door into the warm evening air.

We’ve invited the Greensboro City Council to the cafeteria to explain why we want 40-some low-income senior housing units at the heart of our neighborhood. We’ve turned out in spades. Neighbor after neighbor stands up to explain: A father holding his infant daughter says the boardinghouse next to him houses mostly elderly people who are frequently evicted when they fall behind on weekly rent; a nurse describes the substandard housing conditions he sees walking the neighborhood; a teacher explains how some people are renting porches and sheds just to have a roof over their heads.

I think of the family around the corner from me: four generations piled together in a dilapidated three-bedroom house. About a year ago, someone from the overpacked house began to sleep in a car parked out front, towels draped over the windows for privacy.

I’m proud of us, too. So many neighborhoods would resist more affordable housing; they say it decreases property values and invites riffraff. Given Greensboro’s desperate need for more affordable units, it’s wild to me that we’ve had to spend months pressuring the City Council to choose affordable senior housing over privately owned market-rate apartments that even I couldn’t afford.

But as nice as my neighbors are, we aren’t saints. Our campaign to have affordable housing built here isn’t about altruism but about protecting ourselves.

We are a low-income neighborhood; most of us work in the trades, the service industry, or in jobs that require degrees like teaching and social work but still pay very little. The economy looms over us; when it falters, we feel it first. Even if we, personally, are still OK, the impact brushes up against our lives. When our neighbors fall behind on rent and get evicted, they move into our spare rooms. When gas prices go up, we leave the house early to carpool to help a friend save money. Over the years, I’ve shared food with a neighbor out of work, watched children for people who can’t afford childcare, and loaned my car a million times.

I should be grateful for the opportunity to care for others—and mostly, I am. But I also feel tired and nervous when it seems like it’s all on us. When our government doesn’t step up, poor and working-class people are not just the ones hurt but are also left trying to make things right.

Michaela Merz, of Chaves County, New Mexico, insists she isn’t “a bleeding heart liberal.” But when I met her, she was sitting in the corner of a Salvation Army pancake breakfast with her medevac kit. First trained in search and rescue to find people lost in the desert, Michaela noticed that people in town had similar medical needs: dehydration, heat exhaustion, minor injuries that, if left untreated, could worsen. They also lacked primary care doctors or insurance. So Michaela created Pecos Valley Public Services, an all-volunteer, free EMT service for low-acuity medical needs.

Recently, a Facebook post caught my eye: PVPS carefully and diplomatically alerted its followers that Medicaid changes on October 1 would affect thousands of New Mexicans. While the post was written as a PSA, encouraging residents to check their paperwork to confirm their status, I read between the lines: Michaela is bracing to absorb the fallout.

Hours away in Tucson, Arizona, a teacher (who asked to be called just “Mrs. B”) told me that she now collects food donations for her students on her front porch. Her state is the first to roll out the new SNAP requirements mandated through the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act, cutting over 180,000 Arizona children off the nutrition program. “Of course I feel for these children and families,” says Mrs. B. “But if I’m being honest, having hungry kids in my classroom also just makes my job harder. They can’t focus and they can’t learn. Now I’m spending my weekends collecting donations for them, sure, but also to help me.”

Shifting the burden. This is what happens when the government falls down on the job and fails—or refuses—to ensure a basic standard of living for its citizenry. Working people pick up the slack. Sometimes that means volunteering and figuring out solutions like Michaela’s, or going above and beyond at work like Mrs. B; often, it happens within families.

Last month in Slatington, Pennsylvania, I met a retired truck driver who told me that two of his twentysomething-year-old grandsons recently moved in with him.

“Costs have gone up. My home insurance has gone up. I’m retired on Social Security—my Social Security didn’t go up,” Rick tells me. “And food, home insurance, it’s all gone up. I garden, but I still am spending 600 to 700 on food every month. Everything just keeps going up.” But his grandsons can’t even get a foot in the door; they can’t find work with decent wages or afford current housing prices, so now they live with him. He clearly cares about them deeply, but it’s hard on all of them.

Working people do a tremendous amount of charitable work: showing up after long days at work to help staff food pantries and community centers, watching one another’s kids as parents work odd shifts, repairing a neighbor’s alternator so they don’t lose their job come Monday. Some of it is just good neighborliness, but much of it is because we know that keeping the people around us up and running makes life better for all of us.

I don’t know what the calculus is like if you live six to 10 paychecks away from crisis, but I do know what it looks like to do the math at one to five: Our well-being is tightly tethered to that of our neighbors.

My neighbors and I have spent our summer calling, e-mailing, and pressuring our City Council to build affordable senior housing here. If they don’t, our neighborhood will have to shoulder the situation on our own. And that’s not fair.

We need help. And that help needs to come from our government—our city, our county, our state, and our federal government. We do a lot, but we can’t do it all. In my neighborhood—and in Roswell, Tucson, and Easton—we need our government to step up so we aren’t shouldering this burden alone.

Gwen Frisbie-Fulton is a writer and organizer based in North Carolina who works for the Addition Project. She writes about organizing and working-class issues for Working Class Stories on Substack.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Obviously, the Knicks Should Not Visit the White House. Why Is This Even a Discussion?
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The Knicks shouldn’t let their legacy include genuflecting to Donald Trump, one of the most hated figures in the very city printed on their jersey. New Yorkers deserve better.

New York Knicks fans cheer in the second half of Game Six of the Eastern Conference Second Round NBA Playoffs against the Boston Celtics hosted by the Knicks outside of Madison Square Garden on May 16, 2025, in New York City.

In my lifetime, no sports team has represented the city of New York quite like the 2025–26 NBA champion New York Knicks. Even with a new season about to begin, the city is still buzzing from the euphoria of last June, when the squad secured its first title in 53 years. People still talk excitedly about the performances of Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, OG Anunoby, and the rest of this team of newly minted New York icons.

Now the Knicks are now faced with a choice—and how they decide to act will forever be a part of their legacy. Will they visit Trump’s White House?

Doing so, at the behest of James Dolan, the team’s right-wing, nepo-billionaire owner, would make them the first NBA or WNBA champion to visit Trump while in office.

Knicks coach Mike Brown said that the team needs to come together to decide whether they should go. But this shouldn’t even require a discussion. First, doing so would mean crossing a picket line established in 2017 by NBA and WNBA players who, at the time, made it clear that a president who traffics in racism and attacks politically outspoken players should not be graced with their presence. A decade later, with far fewer outspoken players, the Knicks’ crossing that line would symbolize the death of an era where players didn’t check their politics at the door and being a brand wasn’t more important than being principled.

That’s one reason. The other is that, given what Trump is doing to the city, showing up with a jersey and a ring for the regime leader would be hurtful to New Yorkers. ICE has been marauding through the five boroughs for the past two years; last week, an ICE officer shot and wounded 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in upper Manhattan while his 5-year-old son was in the back seat. In such a climate, to have this team visit the White House would be a gut punch to New Yorkers. It would look like the Knicks are more eager to please the people who paid the tens of thousands of dollars necessary to watch the team during the Finals at Madison Square Garden than the New Yorkers who watched in bars and from ad hoc projectors splashing the game across the walls of buildings, the fans who flooded the streets to dance and climb light poles to celebrate the win, or the millions who feted the team in their championship parade.

Undoubtedly the team is facing pressure from ownership to smile for the Newsmax cameras. Dolan wants them at the White House, bending the knee to his dear friend Donald Trump, to consecrate a friendship rooted in every impropriety that comes with believing that your power and wealth allow you to live under a shield of impunity. Yet what they really have in common is being despised by the city of New York.

The city’s hatred of Trump goes back decades, to his time as a crooked, racist landlord repped by Roy Cohn. Dolan, after years as one of the most detested owners in sports, initially benefited from a reservoir of public goodwill following the championship, but he’s done his damndest since then to fritter it away. He can’t help being unlikable. It’s his nature.

It started even before the confetti fell, with an obnoxious speech that followed Mayor Mandani’s at the big parade, where Dolan said churlishly, “I don’t need your vote.” Since then—and this is far worse than his throwing a snit—he has cried poverty throughout the process of re-signing this beloved squad. First, he refused to offer a fair contract to adored center Mitch Robinson, who, after eight seasons with the Knicks, is now—of all damn things—a Celtic. At present, Dolan is refusing to pay fair contracts to starters Karl-Anthony Towns and Josh Hart, breaking a promise Dolan made to Brunson during his last contract negotiation, in 2024, pledging that if the captain took less money, he would keep the team together.

But Dolan cannot in any way compel or force his team to go to the White House against their wishes. He has no leverage to make this happen. He holds no cards. And yet he is still demanding that the Knicks help rehabilitate Trump’s standing in New York, a city currently enraged over his existence. If the Knicks do go, the only reason that makes sense is that they want to go. That will sting.

The 2025–26 Knicks will always and forever be our team—the city’s team. Visiting the White House won’t change that. This team was ours before it was ever James Dolan’s or, as Dolan seems to want, Donald Trump’s. But it will say something about these players and this historical moment if they bend the knee to someone so roundly loathed by the people of the very city inscribed on their jerseys, a blaring sign that leaders in every cultural sphere—despite Trump’s hellaciously low popularity—are choosing compliance over resistance.

Perhaps the powerful realize that under a fascistic regime popularity matters far less than the ruthless exercise of power itself. But to paraphrase historian Howard Zinn, you can’t be neutral on a moving A train. You are either on the side of the man who was shot in his car in front of his 5-year-old or the person who made the order to pull the trigger. Whichever the Knicks choose, it will become part of their story.

Dave Zirin is the sports editor at The Nation. He is the author of 11 books on the politics of sports. He is the author of a new book, The People's Historian: The Outsized Life of Howard Zinn.

https://www.thenation.com/article/activi.title: An Effective Movement for Palestine Needs Allies Like Zohran Mamdani
https://www.thenation.com/article/activi.text:
In order to build a broad-based coalition, we need to work together—not practice purity politics.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (C) joins anti-war demonstrators during October 7 vigil organized by Israelis for Peace NYC at Union Square in Manhattan, New York City, on October 7, 2026.

“October 7 is a day that is immensely painful for our city and is a day of mourning,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani explained at a press conference last week. “We know that it brings up the most horrific memories for so many in this city. And also for others it is a day that is continuing in the Israeli government’s use of it as a justification for a genocide.”

It came as no surprise that New York City’s first Muslim mayor, and a fierce defender of Palestinian rights, would come under fire by conservative pundits, Zionist organizations, and leaders of the Jewish establishment for “mourning terrorists” or “hijacking” a day meant to honor Israeli victims.

The mayor’s statement on the anniversary of October 7, 2023, was an eloquent defense of all human lives taken that day: more than 1,100 Israelis and 251 abducted by Hamas, and the 74,000 Palestinians, among them over 21,000 children killed by the Israeli military. “Three years later,” the statement read, “we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment. To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity.”

It’s hard to imagine a statement from an American mayor that so unequivocally calls out genocide and apartheid, and along with it our responsibility to end the government’s financial and military support of these war crimes. Yet with equal measure from the right came criticism of the mayor from some corners of the Palestine movement. At the October 7 vigil hosted by Israelis for Peace, protesters chanted things like: “Mayor Mamdani, what do you say, how many kids did you kill today?” and called the mayor a genocide apologist.

But the politics of those protesters are those of purity tests, not of building an effective mass movement capable of encouraging policy change. Those protesters alienate not only allies for a Palestine movement in office but also many more regular people who sympathize with the scores of Palestinians killed in this war that could have made up a broad coalition to affect real change. As Palestinian analyst and writer Muhammad Shehada argued recently on X, “Saying ‘I would only work with comrades who fully agree with me’ is the recipe for dooming your movement to [remain] a tiny ineffective minority. The goal is to unite the many against the few, not the few against the many.”

Social-media activist Abier Khatib, too, sounded off on the platform: “You’re attacking one of the very few politicians actually bringing Palestine into the mainstream and you’re making other politicians who might even consider speaking up think twice.” She continued, “You’re not helping Palestine. You’re fucking scaring people away from it.”

For years in the United States—and particularly so since 2023—popular sentiments regarding Israel and Palestine have undergone a sea change in the right direction. The outpouring of mass outrage to the genocide in Gaza fueled thousands of protests in support of Palestine in every state in the country and many cities outside the country in the months that followed October 7. According to information obtained from the Crowd Counting Consortium, more than a million people participated—from Mennonites occupying congressional buildings to Jewish activists in New York City taking over bridges, to Mothers for Ceasefire gathering weekly on a street corner of Durham, North Carolina, to a wave of student encampments on over 125 college campuses. At those schools, students courageously put their degrees and their bodies on the line to speak up for Palestine. In the early months of this new phase in the movement, echoes of the Vietnam anti-war movement reverberated across the country.

The campaign has since suffered repression and setbacks, as the situation in Gaza has grown ever more dire, and the sea change in consciousness has not resulted in concrete policy outcomes stopping the genocide. But the basis for a mass movement still exists, alongside a growing bloc of pro-Palestine elected officials like Darializa Avila Chevalier, Brad Lander, and hopefully Abdul El-Sayed who can help push legislation to block munitions shipments and to cut military aid to Israel. To turn sympathy into an effective, sustained movement requires ongoing organizing work, political discipline, and strategic alliances.

Mamdani, by virtue of being a longtime champion of Palestinian rights—he organized a hunger strike for Gaza in 2023, and sponsored legislation targeting nonprofits who fund the Israeli military—cannot be above criticism now that he is our leader. There are concrete demands to push for, including stopping the facilitation by some New York synagogues of Palestinian land in illegal settlements, and Mamdani’s own “Not on Our Dime!” Act to prohibit New York–registered charities from financially supporting displacement and war crimes.

But to say Mamdani is complicit in genocide is both factually inaccurate and perpetuates a self-defeating practice by some on the left to prove who is the most radical, at the exclusion of many more entrants to the movement.

The problem for the pro-Palestine campaign was never about mourning the dead of October 7. In fact, the issue for many of us was that we were not allowed time nor space to grieve, because the tragedy was just as soon manipulated into justifying untold horrors in Gaza. To mourn all the lives lost does not equate the power imbalance between the colonizing force and the colonized, nor the scale of the resulting tragedies, which have been completely disproportionate. But the politics of liberation flow from our humanity and the idea that every life is to be cherished.

The mayor’s commitment to mourning the loss of human life, sits alongside his commitment to challenging antisemitism at home while opposing genocide abroad. Days before participating in the October 7 vigil, Mamdani launched a municipal Strategy to Combat Antisemitism. Both commitments are morally and strategically necessary. This is not only because he is the city’s first Muslim mayor and an outspoken supporter of Palestine in a city in which Jews make up approximately 12 percent of the population. More broadly, it also threads a critical needle for the movement: making explicit the difference between antisemitism and anti-Zionism. Doing so helps to convince Jewish New Yorkers that our safety need not come at the expense of any other people, and weakens the hold of mainstream Jewish institutions that have insisted on tying Jewish identity to Israel. On the other hand, protesting a vigil for lives lost on October 7 risks undoing so much hard work that the pro-Palestine movement has done for years in disentangling antisemitism from anti-Zionism, and rebuffing accusations from the right and liberal Zionists that the movement is antisemitic.

In the wake of October 7, crimes committed against millions of innocent Palestinians were time and time again perpetrated in the name of world Jewry. Meanwhile at home, pro-Palestine students and protesters were doxed, harassed, and suspended from their schools in the name of fighting antisemitism. College administrators organized task forces to “combat antisemitism,” but instead condemned protest chants like “from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free.”

The Israeli state’s claim to be acting on behalf of world Jewry has sown confusion and only aided in the rise of antisemitism worldwide. Rather than making Jews safe, every instance in which Israel and its supporters have used the charge of antisemitism to build support for war crimes has made us less so. As so many of us have argued for years, weaponizing antisemitism to shut down criticism of Israel has actually fueled anti-Jewish sentiments. We’ve seen rare but rising cases of vandalism and physical assaults at synagogues (including twice this summer in New York), more commonly the spread of antisemitic tropes in mainstream consciousness, and of course the often-corrosive corners of social media. A Yale Youth poll recently reported, for instance, that about a third of Americans surveyed held at least one belief associated with antisemitic tropes or general antisemitism, including that Jewish people have too much power in the United States. That Israel’s actions have only fueled these ideas does not absolve us from having to address them.

In contrast to bogus task forces who challenged protests rather than antisemitism, the thoughtful call by New York City’s mayor for us to cherish Jewish New Yorkers, and not to do so at the expense of Palestinians abroad, is deeply reassuring.

Most importantly, mourning the dead as well as combating antisemitism can lay the basis for a broader and stronger movement for Palestine. American Jews today are still largely divided on the question of Israel and Palestine, with overall sentiments shifting in favor of Palestinians—and this is particularly so among younger Jews. In 2025, a Washington Post poll found that 61 percent of Jewish adults said Israel had committed war crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and 39 percent said it was guilty of genocide. Another poll conducted last month found that a majority of Jews back cuts to US aid to Israel. At a moment in which increasing numbers of Jewish Americans are critical of Israel, but many are still unsure about whether the Palestine movement has a place for them in it, Mamdani’s approach can do so much to build an ethos of mutual caring, respect, and solidarity on the left. An inclusive movement for Palestine, one in which we debate out our differences in a comradely way, is an effective one. And one that is still possible to build.

Hadas Thier is the author of A People’s Guide to Capitalism: An Introduction to Marxist Economics and Crypto-Capitalism: The New Financial Dystopia (forthcoming 2027)."

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Wendell Berry’s Unrelenting Vision
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The poet wrote for The Nation for decades, always demonstrating conscience and prescience.

The beloved poet and essayist Wendell Berry died this summer at the age of 92. In an essay in The Nation in 2019, Jedediah Britton-Purdy observed that Berry was one of those rare figures who received positive attention in both left-leaning journals like Dissent and right-leaning ones like The American Conservative. He lauded Berry for writing “against all forms of violence and destruction—of land, communities, and human beings.” Through all of Berry’s work, Britton-Purdy wrote, ran a consistent note of “praise for what he admires: the quiet, mostly uncelebrated labor and affection that keep the world whole and might still redeem it.”

Starting in 1961, Berry contributed more than two dozen poems, essays, and book reviews to The Nation. Again and again in his work, Berry observed that a healthy democracy depended on a healthy land, and vice versa. He always made his case in elegant, clear, and compelling language and with homespun common sense. Among his first Nation contributions was a poem that ran in December 1963, a month after John F. Kennedy’s assassination. It began: “We know the winter earth upon the body of the young President, and the early dark falling….”

Two years later, Berry published “Strip-Mine Morality: The Landscaping of Hell,” an essay that chronicled a popular struggle in his native Kentucky to ban strip-mining for coal. Berry was shocked by the coal companies’ arguments, which reflected “the unmistakable implication that anything can be justified by profit,” as well as the “assumption that the steep mountain sides, now being ruined on an almost unbelievable scale and at great speed, are good for nothing else.”

No other writer has so thoroughly probed the consequences of that assumption, both on the land itself and on the national character.

In his tribute, Britton-Purdy called The Unsettling of America Berry’s “most enduring work of nonfiction.” In that book, which began as a Nation essay, Berry argued that American agriculture had traded soil-renewing practices for a strictly extractive model. Even wind or solar energy, he predicted, would not solve the alienation of labor and the emptiness of modern life. “We will not find those answers in Washington, D.C., or in the laboratories of oil companies,” Berry wrote. “In order to find them, we will have to look closer to ourselves.”

Richard Kreitner is a contributing writer and the author of Break It Up: Secession, Division, and the Secret History of America's Imperfect Union. His writings are at richardkreitner.com.

In a country that treats workers as expendable parts, Hurts’s playing through a blood clot is just the highest-profile example of the price workers pay in an oligarchy.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/canada-logis.title: How a Canadian Union Finally Bested Walmart
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/canada-logis.text:
In our hyperpolitical age, when mass protests come and go without much clear sense of what was won or lost, the strategies of social movements can seem quixotic, their benchmarks of success fuzzy. In the union world, however, success or failure can be measured in more cut-and-dried terms: by the ratification of a union contract. A contract between a union and an employer does not simply lay out the terms of employment at a particular worksite. It is also a symbol of the begrudging respect that an employer has for the collective organization of its employees.

Until this year, Walmart had not put pen to paper on a union contract in Canada or the United States. As the largest employer in North America (with a headcount of 1.6 million in the US alone, it is still larger than Amazon) and with annual gross profits last year of $171 billion, Walmart has tremendous resources with which to fight off unions, and has developed a sophisticated playbook for doing so. It is not surprising that the company that labor historian Nelson Lichtenstein has called the “template organization” of neoliberal capitalism should have been, for most of its existence, an impenetrable anti-union fortress.

This is why we should appreciate the weight of some recent news from Canada’s warehousing sector: on May 7, 2026, eight hundred workers at a Walmart Regional Distribution Center in Mississauga, Ontario (in the greater Toronto area), won a two-year contract after certifying their union with Unifor Local 252 in 2024. Though it has received relatively little coverage in the left-labor world, it is a truly historic victory, and a story that ought to be studied for its broader implications. No union gets a contract with a company as imposing as Walmart without there being lessons for organized labor to take from the strategy, tactics, and conditions that enabled the victory. The lumbering corporate retail giant that has for so long set the industry standard for working conditions has finally conceded to the union. Why now?

Before Unifor won in Mississauga in 2024, there had only been two prior union certifications — official government recognition that a group of workers is represented by a given union, creating a legal obligation to bargain — at Walmart facilities in Canada. One was at a store in Windsor, Ontario, in 1996 with the United Steelworkers, and it was only certified by labor board order in 1997 due to Walmart’s serious unfair labor practices during the election. The union never got a contract and was eventually decertified. The other was with the United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) in 2005 at a store in Jonquière, Quebec, which Walmart closed just after the union requested binding arbitration from Quebec’s minister of labor. As will become important in this story, Quebec, the neighboring province to Ontario, has strong enough labor law that certification there will almost always result in a contract. This is the dynamic that led Amazon to shutter its entire operation in the province last year.

In the United States, the only successful election at a Walmart was in 2000, to unionize ten meat cutters at a Supercenter in Jacksonville, Texas. Days later, Walmart responded to what would otherwise have been minor news in rural East Texas by announcing that it was getting rid of all meat cutting in their Supercenters across the nation. In 2011, the UFCW attempted to organize the company as a whole with the multimillion dollar OUR Walmart campaign, organizing workers to engage in a wide variety of actions. Union elections, however, were not part of the mix, reflecting the recognition that the official path to unionization in the United States had been effectively blocked in cases where the employer was a corporation as well-resourced and with as much anti-union animus as Walmart. OUR Walmart had some notable wins, but the UFCW pulled funding from the campaign in 2015 when Marc Perrone assumed the presidency of the union.

I am less familiar with Walmart’s arrangements with unions in Mexico, but it appears that many of the contracts that Walmart has signed there are so-called protection contracts, i.e., a collective bargaining agreement made without the workers’ knowledge or consent. By claiming to represent workers, those contracts, often signed by politically connected unions, “protect” the employer from any efforts by its employees to bargain more aggressively. Many such contracts were targeted by reforms promised by Andrés Manuel López Obrador­­ after he won the presidency in 2018. The next year, when the Revolutionary Confederation of Laborers and Farmworkers (CROC) planned a strike on a number of Walmart facilities, the company averted it with a 5.5 percent annual wage increase. But it is not clear that any new contract was signed between Walmart and CROC as a result of the settlement.

So when Marty Gaouette, a worker in the shipping department at Walmart’s Mississauga Regional Distribution Center (RDC), reached out to Unifor Local 252 in December 2023 about the possibility of starting a union that would secure its gains through a legally binding contract, there was no real template in North America for doing so.

But there were plenty of worker frustrations. At the start of the Covid-19 pandemic, Walmart had temporarily offered a wage bump (“hero pay,” the company called it, as part of the broader pattern of pandemic wage increases in the in-person retail sector) and flexible working hours. As unemployment numbers climbed, however, Walmart understood it had a relatively captive workforce and reversed course, eliminating the wage bump after just six months. “It was like the worst thing that they could have done to us,” explained Rhaddy Que, a utility associate in the maintenance department and eventually a member of the workplace’s bargaining team. “We were committed to work, but [they were] taking those dollars away from us.”

Forced overtime was also a major issue. Unlike Amazon’s “mandatory extended time,” which is mostly enforced around holidays and Prime days, forced overtime became a year-round regularity in Mississauga, leaving workers with little control over their work-life balance. Speedup, in addition to longer hours, was increasingly an irritation. The Mississauga distribution center does what Walmart calls “store replenishment” — filling trucks destined for retail locations — and so has not traditionally been under the same management pressure as Amazon fulfillment centers, with their rapid delivery promises. But competitive pressure from Amazon has led Walmart to invest in its e-commerce capacity, offering last-mile delivery from its stores, and as it has done so, the need for greater and greater efficiency in replenishing inventory at Walmart stores has increased. Rodolfo “Tito” Pilozo, who was also on the Unifor bargaining team and works in receiving, says that the volume increase in the shipping department was what pushed Gaouette to contact the union. Management would say that they would have to process a certain number of cases of goods per hour, when in reality the amount was 10 percent more than announced.

Speed-up, forced overtime, clawed back wages and benefits offered during Covid: these were swirling in the well of worker frustration in late 2023. The organizing work went quickly at first. A number of workers at the facility had been working there more or less since 1994, when Walmart first came to Canada. Back then, the warehouse had been located in Brampton, a neighboring auto manufacturing town also part of the greater Toronto area. It had been owned and operated by a third-party company, Tibbett and Britten, though those working there understood it was a warehouse for Walmart. Many of the workers who would lead the organizing in Mississauga had been previously involved with a unionization effort with the Teamsters at the facility in Brampton in the late 1990s. Tibbett and Britten moved the operation to Mississauga in 2002, according to Pilozo, and Walmart took full control of it in 2014. It was workers like Pilozo, with a great amount of seniority, who formed the core of the organizing team.

Around April 2024, however, the organizing momentum slowed. Walmart’s captive audience meetings began to have an effect. “There was a lot of fear,” Que says about that moment. “They gave us that fear. We would have meetings, and they would just say how it’s not worth having a union. And that the company will do what the union is promising you.” Angela Drew Kimelman and Gary Rumboldt, the Unifor staff organizers assigned to the campaign, met with key worker organizers and they decided they were ready to make the campaign more visible. They formed “Team Red,” a group of workers who were willing to wear Unifor red to work on Wednesdays and who would leaflet outside the warehouse about the union. Unifor got so-called protection letters sent to Walmart on behalf of many of the organizing workers, which reminded the company that it was a violation of the rights of pro-union workers to be treated any differently than other workers. This gave Team Red the cover and confidence to organize publicly rather than in secret, as is often done in the early months of union drives.

Justin Gniposky, Unifor’s organizing director, credits the strength of the team for patiently building strong connections during this time:

We had a really strong inside committee. They spent the time, did the work. . . . Sometimes you don’t have that kind of structure on the inside, but these guys built that structure, they built it to succeed, and it showed. They had the respect of their co-workers, and respect’s one thing, but their co-workers also believed they had their best interests in mind. They had their trust to move through this.

Part of building this trust lay in making sure that all union materials were translated into Punjabi, Tagalog, and Chinese. It also lay in getting workers who spoke these languages to reach out to other workers directly. This proved particularly important for getting the sizable part-time workforce on board with the union program. Most of the part-timers were international workers, some on temporary visas. Que estimated that even though at least 30–40 percent of those workers are no longer with Walmart, most of them supported the union when they were at the warehouse, despite many knowing they would not be around long enough to benefit from a contract.

The Mississauga workers voted for their union from September 10 to September 12, 2024. Participation was high, and the union won with a reported 56 percent majority. Que expressed the disbelief that many felt about the victory:

We weren’t sure at all [that we were going to win]. It was sort of embedded in our heads that Walmart is anti-union. You heard a lot that it was impossible to have a union, and that Walmart will not allow it. That’s what they made us feel. But later on, we started to feel like there was more power in people wanting to have the union than in Walmart not wanting one.

The day after Ontario certified the union to represent the Mississauga warehouse workers, Walmart issued an across-the-board wage increase for every single logistics worker in Canada (warehouse workers and drivers both) — except for the eight hundred workers who had just unionized. As Gniposky summed it up, “Here’s the congratulations on getting a union. You are now making less than every single one of your coworkers.” Walmart also brought in workers from temp agencies to staff the Mississauga facility, signaling to the newly unionized workers that they could be easily replaced.

Meanwhile, Unifor had other battles to fight with the company. In October 2024, the month after the election victory in Ontario, 120 Walmart truck drivers in British Columbia won card check certification. Soon after, 280 Walmart truck drivers in Alberta did the same. Peter Pearce, a driver out of the Nisku, Alberta, depot and member of the bargaining team there, said that it was “favoritism, nepotism, and unfair treatment by certain supervisors” that led the Alberta drivers to organize for union representation. To stem the tide of pro-union sentiment across the company’s Canada operations, Walmart issued yet another across-the-board wage increase. This made for two unprecedented countrywide wage increases in the span of a month and half, but the company made the message of these wage increases clear with the workplaces it excluded — the Mississauga RDC workers and the two units of truck drivers.

Due to the particularities of Canadian labor law, the Mississauga warehouse workers’ and the western Canada truckers’ campaigns were run slightly differently. The warehouse workers petitioned for certification at the provincial level by the government of Ontario, while the drivers petitioned the federal government, as truck drivers crossing provincial or international borders are regulated federally. In Ontario, unions need 40 percent of workers to sign a union card before filing for an election, and a simple majority in an election to be certified. Federal elections are run by “card check,” meaning that a union need only get 50 percent plus one on cards to certify. Canadian labor law also has what is called a “freeze provision,” which prevents employers from altering workers’ terms and conditions during a certification drive, including by withholding standard wage increases. As the wage increases and other retaliatory actions by Walmart clearly violated the freeze provision, Unifor filed unfair labor practice (ULP) charges at both the provincial and federal levels. The Ontario labor board delayed the decision on the union’s charges until after collective bargaining ended, but the federal ULP was settled in November 2025.

In the meantime, in May 2025, Walmart had sold off its Canada fleet service to a third party named Canada Cartage. This meant Unifor had to update its certification, which delayed negotiations, and Canada Cartage began a decertification drive. Pearce, the Alberta truck driver, described those negotiations as “extremely difficult.” The bargaining team pushed for a three-year contract, a 2.5 percent wage increase per year, and a limitation on “lease ops” subcontracting to no more than 10 percent of their work. Even though the federal labor board halted the decertification drive, as decertification is not allowed during active collective bargaining, Canada Cartage management did everything to slow things down. During the negotiations, the bargaining team got word that a sizable group of previously anti-union drivers in Calgary decided they now wanted the union to sign a sweetheart deal: a one-year contract, a 1.5 percent wage increase, and a lease ops limitation to 25 percent. “It made absolutely no sense,” Pearce said. “It scream[ed] of manipulation by management. ‘Please don’t give me extra money.’ I’ve never heard anybody say that.” The Unifor drivers eventually settled on a one-year collective agreement with Canada Cartage that expires in May 2027. But things ended quite differently for workers at the RDC across the country in Ontario.

Collective bargaining in Mississauga finally started in May 2025, eight months after a majority of the warehouse’s workers voted for Unifor representation, and the same month Walmart sold off its Canadian trucking operations to Canada Cartage. As is often the case with intransigent employers, Walmart offered Unifor only a few sporadic dates over the subsequent months when it would be available for negotiations. With longer deadline rules for negotiations than there are in Quebec, Walmart intended to drag out the Ontario process as long as possible.

Unifor’s bargaining team consisted of seven workers as well as Unifor’s national bargaining representative, Shayne Fields, and the longtime president of Local 252, Eamonn Clarke, who the year before had won a strike by four hundred workers at a plant owned by Nestlé. This team brought an intimidating amount of collective experience at Walmart. According to Pilozo,

The good thing about our bargaining committee is that the people chosen were very senior people: twenty-nine, thirty, thirty-one, twenty-eight years with the company, and so on. When we first introduced each other, they [the Walmart negotiators] were very impressed. Their facial expressions showed that, “Wow, these guys have been there for a long time, almost since the beginning.” Even their lawyer was stunned.

To negotiate, Walmart sent a delegation of nine company representatives. There was little indication that the company intended to bargain in good faith. According to a few of my interviewees, company management was actively supporting a decertification campaign, giving some anti-union workers special lockers in the building to hold decertification petitions and anti-union literature. Some workers who spoke out against the union got special treatment. Verbal altercations would break out, and at one point there was a physical fight between two employees, one pro- and the other anti-union, both of whom were suspended and later fired. According to Que, however, on the basis of Team Red’s inside connections, most workers understood these altercations to be a product of Walmart’s actions, not the union’s.

I asked everyone I interviewed for this story if there was ever a moment where it felt like negotiations shifted, where Walmart seemed to turn a corner and begin to negotiate in good faith. That moment never seemed to come for anyone. It seemed more that, unlike in the United States, there was a limit on just how long the company could drag out negotiations because in Ontario, Unifor had the right to apply for an arbitrated settlement if collective bargaining ran aground.

On May 7, 2026, a year after negotiations had officially begun, Walmart and Unifor announced they had reached an agreement. The resulting two-year contract was, by everyone’s account, not the “best” contract they could have gotten, but it was a meaningful one: wage parity with other warehouses; retroactive back pay for violating the freeze provision, in the form of a lump sum payment in the range of $4,000 to $9,000 per worker in July of this year; a “me too” clause preventing Walmart from raising wages elsewhere without raising wages in Mississauga, as they had done in the fall of 2024; planned wage raises in 2027 and 2028; a grievance procedure; and a limit on temporary workers. That last bit, according to Gniposky, got the biggest applause at the contract ratification meetings. The next day, Local 252’s Walmart members ratified the contract by a whopping 93 percent.

Que and Pilozo told me that management is slowly acclimating to the new environment. Pilozo said he corrected a manager the other day who was complaining to workers about “your” contract: “It’s our contract, because it was signed collectively by the employer and us.” The manager apologized on the spot. Que said the new grievance procedure is working well, and that communication between stewards and management has improved to the point where they only invoke it occasionally. When I was interviewing them for this story, the lump sum payment was just days away, and workers were giving knowing nods to each other around the warehouse. In Pilozo’s words, where tension had existed not so long ago, “you’re starting to see smiles.”

“Workers at Walmart in the US and Canada have long made it clear that they want a union,” Nelson Lichtenstein told me. “To actually have a signed contract is a major breakthrough and something genuinely new when it comes to the largest private employer in North America.” Still, this story might seem a bit anticlimactic: big union wins are supposed to end in heroic confrontations before the company concedes. But no dramatic confrontation ensued here. Again, the billion dollar question is: Why was this the moment for Walmart to finally cave and sign a union contract? Are they getting soft in their old age, without Sam Walton’s infamous hatred of unions to guide the way?

I would boil down the key factors in this historic victory to four: location, resources, regulatory constraint, and leadership. First, the fact that this happened in Mississauga was no accident. “Mississauga is a hub for most of Ontario and Quebec,” Gniposky explained. “That facility is important. It’s not as easy for them to move.” The company regularly warned workers that a pro-union vote could lead the facility to shut down, but the threat was a weak one. For one, the facility was an RDC and not a store (unlike the location in Jonquière, which Walmart shut down after they won union certification), and, in the Walmart supply chain, the RDC is in a key staging ground for two of Canada’s major metro markets, Toronto and Montreal. Walmart doesn’t have distribution centers in Quebec — having already closed them allegedy on account of the province’s strong labor law — but that market is easily supplied from Mississauga.

Unlike the largest warehousing area in the United States, the sprawling Inland Empire in southern California, Canada’s primary warehousing cluster is nestled in a narrow corridor of the west Toronto suburbs. Stretching from Mississauga to Brampton, it is constrained on all sides: to the south by Lake Ontario, the east by Toronto, the west by suburban residential development, and the north by lack of infrastructure (and eventually Lake Huron). In other words, it would be a huge pain for Walmart to relocate this RDC. Distribution centers are already more strategic organizing targets than stores, on account of the disruptive impact that labor can theoretically cause through their organization. But distribution centers that can’t easily be moved are ideal targets.

Choke point analysis — based on the idea that organized labor is going to be most successful at points in the production and distribution process where the disruptive impact of labor actions is relatively high — has a mixed reputation in the labor world. In part, this is because it involves the idea that some sites of work are more structurally important to a company’s operation than others, and thus that some workers’ struggles are more strategic or important than others. But when it comes to the contemporary logistical economy, in which the flow of commodities has increased in speed and efficiency but also fragility, and at a moment when labor is limited in the resources it can allocate to any organizing campaign, choke point analysis matters more than ever. Organized labor ignores it at its own peril.

None of this is to say that Walmart will not attempt to move the RDC in Mississauga. Unifor and the RDC workers are well aware of this, which is why Pilozo, Que, and their fellow members of Team Red have been leafleting at other Walmart distribution centers all over the western suburbs of Toronto, aiming to saturate the area with union drives to give Walmart no geographic out. When Mississauga workers had been excluded from the prior wage bumps, their plight served as a cautionary tale for other Walmart workers, who benefited from disengagement. But now that the Mississauga workers have a hefty lump sum of back pay and contractually guaranteed raises set for 2027 and 2028, Unifor can persuasively make the case that the Team Red workers at Mississauga have been setting the standard for warehouse workers throughout the entire region.

Second, this was not simply a scrappy, bottom-up drive. Unifor had invested serious resources into becoming Canada’s warehousing union. Gaouette reached out to Unifor because he had heard of the union’s Warehouse Workers Unite campaign, the fruit of its strategic analysis of the warehousing sector. Unifor was 100 percent committed to seeing the campaign through and leveraged the threat of arbitration, a costly and time-consuming process, as well as the combination of federal and provincial ULPs, to push the Mississauga campaign to the finish line. Note that the federal disclosure from the trucking negotiations hung over the provincial proceedings only because Unifor was willing to pursue Walmart on multiple fronts. This is the story of a committed group of trusted workplace leaders, but it is also one of a union with a long-term strategic vision and the will to back up that vision with resources.

Third, Unifor strategically used the constraints of Canadian labor law to make it so that Walmart ultimately had nowhere to go. This is the big difference between the Canadian and American contexts: especially now, when most of the gains of the Biden-era National Labor Relations Board have been reversed, it’s difficult to imagine even a very skillful union in the United States using ULPs and the lingering possibility of arbitration to push toward a contract, as Unifor did in this case. This is not to say, however, that the question of regulatory constraint is not applicable, simply that it must be asked differently: in New York City, for instance, the Delivery Protection Act under consideration by the city council could upset Amazon’s delivery driver subcontracting model, providing the conditions for major wage gains and organizing drives. In many states, and many more municipalities, ballot initiatives can be used to put such regulatory questions governing employment relationships directly before voters. Looking longingly over the border at Canadian regulatory constraint should be cause not for lamentation, but for creative approaches to improving the odds of union drives in the United States.

Finally, it’s overwhelmingly clear that the Mississauga RDC has a robust layer of trusted workplace leaders who not only bore an intimidating amount of collective work experience at Walmart and were committed to the union but also had the respect and trust of their colleagues to easily weather any storm that the company created. “Walmart saw that they weren’t going to be able to manipulate and turn these workers against each other,” Gniposky said. “Certainly there were anti-union people, as there are in any workplace, but they were a minority, and the majority was clearly on the side of their union. This was the strongest inside committee I’ve seen in my career.”

It’s notable that there were no strikes, walkouts, or even marches on the boss in this story. As Que explained, “We educated all our members and said, ‘Maybe the best thing would be to have a strike.’ But we didn’t have to to get this collective agreement done.” If a strike was what was needed, Team Red was prepared to make it happen, and, by all accounts, it would have had high, if not total, participation. But they were reluctant to go down that road. Most stories of successful first contract fights will not be so free of confrontational workplace actions, but they will certainly feature workplace leaders focused more on the resolution than the conflict — people who want to work, to put in the work, and to proudly wear a union shirt while doing so.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/review-gibne.title: Even Musk Haters Will Hate Sitting Through Musk
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/review-gibne.text:
Always glad to see Elon Musk pummeled, of course, as he is in Alex Gibney’s documentary Musk, now playing in theaters. The film sounds the alarm over this right-wing trillionaire tech bastard, which can’t be done too early or too often. But there’s a problem when even I, a fervent, long-term Musk hater, get exhausted, then irritated, then fed up by this film long before its grueling four-hour running time is over.

For me, the burning question quickly became: Who is this film for? What’s the intended audience for this thing?

Gibney’s huge, heavy-handed disemboweling of Musk, clumsily wielding an axe rather than a scalpel, was immediately identified as “a hit piece that misses, and makes the fatal sin of being boring for 4 hours” by Musk himself, warning off his obsessed fans, who’ll obviously be skipping the film. It’s an indication of Musk’s essential stupidity — his cluelessness about everything except how to generate profits, particularly off his own repeated business failures — that he keeps obsessively commenting on this film on social media, thus doing its publicity work for the PR team presumably getting paid to do the same job. Some curiosity-seekers with time to kill might head to the multiplex, thanks to the many free, self-defeating, Elon Musk–generated promo tweets.

The obvious audience for the film would seem to be the many who despise Musk. That’s a vast number of sane people: political leftists; the legions screwed over by him in business deals or working for him in thankless, underpaid jobs; those fired by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and those infuriated by the firings; the hapless car enthusiasts suckered into driving malfunctioning Teslas; and anyone who keeps up at all with Musk’s role in the latest sinister predations of the high-tech industry in league with right-wing governments around the world.

But consider that these are the people in the know, already aware of Musk’s harrowing South African childhood, early business failures that nevertheless made him huge profits, insidious credit-stealing takeover of the Tesla car company, SpaceX ventures, self-driving car and Twitter/X and DOGE debacles, appalling personal life, including the fathering of at least fourteen children by many different women in order to spread Musk seed around the world, and all the rest of it. These potential spectators are perhaps the least likely to feel the need to torture themselves with even more intimate knowledge of a man famous for the widespread repugnance inspired by his ideas, his rhetoric, his practices, and his bizarre physical self-presentation.

I personally feel I deserve a medal for having sat through Musk. Or at least a care package full of soothing home-spa products from a concerned citizens group.

That leaves, as potential audience members, those who don’t know much about Elon Musk or are totally indifferent to him. And obviously those lucky, oblivious citizens aren’t going to create a rush of ticket-buying either.

Oh, and one other tiny group of possible Musk-watchers includes cinephiles who are always interested in what’s being done in the documentary form. They’re all flocking to see the other documentary that opened last week, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything, a total wow of a film that’s drawing in crowds far beyond the size of the usual audience for documentaries. It took in about $15 million its first weekend; Musk made about $315,000 on more than four hundred screens.

But if some of those spectators go above and beyond the call of cinephile duty and watch Musk too, they’ll be depressed at best, and appalled at worst. It’s a sloppy job, Musk, reflecting a juvenile sensibility. It’s constantly presenting slapdash footage and recorded voices that aren’t identified or attributed to any source, and it’s loaded with what I guess must be Alex Gibney’s idea of infotainment stylings intended to make documentaries popular with the masses. Because Musk wouldn’t sit for an interview, for example, Gibney mined his interviews with other filmmakers and journalists and podcasters to digitally generate an AI avatar of Elon Musk who speaks as he might speak if he could be persuaded to speak to the filmmaker.

This is clearly Gibney’s idea of a big “gotcha” triumph, cleverly turning Musk’s massive AI investment against him. But really all it accomplishes is more misery for the half-dozen spectators in the theater, getting forcibly returned over and over to the bizarrely big-headed Musk avatar, made unaccountably handsomer than the actual golem-like real-life Musk, tricked out in leathers and enthroned in a gaming chair to deliver further inane commentary, such as musings on the possibility that we’re living in a simulation or that humans might turn out to be nothing more than “the biological bootloader” for digital superintelligence.

In general, Alex Gibney seems to have made an attempt at form-follows-function in creating a documentary that’s extremely Musk-like, resulting in an overall sense of slovenly gigantism that’s nevertheless unimpressive: a film as crude, outsize, erratic, and shambling as the man himself. For example, Gibney resorts to endless comic book and video game effects, favorite Musk pastimes, in order to present Musk’s rampage through the world. The first time we see a lengthy sequence involving first-person-shooter-style animation to represent Musk’s takeover of Twitter, blasting thousands of employees who actually know how the business runs, mass firings that help Musk turn a sometimes profitable company into a free-falling flop called X, it’s barely endurable. But then we have to watch the same extensive pew-pew-pew gamer massacres a second time, now with Musk’s notorious chainsaw repurposed as a firing weapon, to represent DOGE’s rampage through various US government buildings. It stands for the firing of legions of highly competent officials early in Donald Trump’s second term, before Musk had a spat with Trump and DOGE was shut down. By this point, it’s merely infuriating on too many levels to count.

The message of Musk, just to save you the trouble of actually sitting through the film, especially if you’re a leftist thinking that you really ought to go see it, is that it’s hopeless to resist Elon Musk’s fascist takeover. It’s already too late. Musk has amassed so much wealth, accrued so much political influence among the worst of the worst of global leaders, and created such extensive surveillance systems worldwide, the only thing to do is wait for him to officially declare himself as a comic-book supervillain come to life, having finally achieved world dominance, and probably called something stupid like GreatX, Overlord of the Galaxy.

And the attitude Gibney adopts — gloating over our guaranteed collective doom — serves the lunatic right, the fascist Musk-lovers of the world, very well. Why bother organizing when we’re all going to die?

Musk starts and ends with the sublime imagery of outer space, which is promptly despoiled by Elon Musk and his imagined colonization of all of it (“I want to die on Mars,” he once mused), which began with SpaceX, represented in Musk as his most successful company in spite of all those crashing rockets. If the film succeeds in its mission to induce widespread cynical despair, you’ll be thinking the human race needs to end if only to prevent Musk from getting his big dumb mitts on other planets after he destroys the earth.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/housing-soci.title: Socialize All Housing
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/housing-soci.text:
In 1872, the German socialist newspaper Der Volksstaat ran a series of articles on housing. The breakneck growth of industrial cities had brought overcrowding, squalor, and soaring rents for workers. Their author, Arthur Mülberger, drawing on the ideas of the French anarchist Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, offered a simple solution — tenants should become owners.

In the scheme, rental payments would be transformed into something like a mortgage payment. Eventually, every worker would hold the title to their own home.

Friedrich Engels was unimpressed. In a series of replies later collected as The Housing Question, the cofounder of Marxism dismissed Mülberger’s plan as both impractical and political malpractice. Elsewhere in the same work, criticizing the reformer Emil Sax, he warned: “Give them their own houses, chain them once again to the soil and you break their power of resistance to the wage cutting of the factory owners.” For Engels, the answers to the housing question would only be made possible through the abolition of the capitalist mode of production.

A century and a half later, the Left is still battling over housing. In a certain populist sense, Mülberger won the argument with Engels. Across the world, homeownership has become a defining ambition of working-class life, and the housing crisis is often framed as a crisis of access to it.

Meanwhile, much of the debate on the Left today is framed as a fight between YIMBYs and NIMBYs. One divide is between those who seek to impede market-rate construction, arguing that it can fuel displacement and offers too little to low-income renters, and those who support construction with fewer caveats to boost supply and the bargaining power of renters along with it. We can all agree on building social housing, but so far that hasn’t materialized into a program on the scale of the crisis.

However, it’s worth stepping back from these fights and asking what ultimate vision we are fighting for. In what follows, we set aside the thorny problems of transition — how we get from here to there and who will fight for it — and sketch out a maximalist vision of socialist housing.

Our answer builds on Engels’s critique of Mülberger while putting aside his reluctance to offer details about the possible shape of a socialist future. We advocate the abolition of private ownership of housing and a fully socialized housing system.

A home of your own — one you can shape to your tastes and needs, and that you feel secure in — is a genuine good worth preserving. But capitalist homeownership binds together choices about your home with choices about finance and wealth that inevitably come with risks, and the dynamics of the housing market are prone to generate arbitrary inequalities.

In a socialist economy, we could preserve that security and freedom while socializing the financial risks and gains of housing. Engels warned that “to speculate as to how a future society would organize the distribution of food and dwellings leads directly to utopia.” But given the “capitalist realism” we seem stuck in today, we think the effort is worth it.

In a capitalist society, housing inequality is more than a symptom of broader income and wealth inequality. Homes are both places to live in and vehicles of wealth. In fact, owner-occupied housing alone accounts for about half of gross household wealth in most of the twenty-nine Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries covered in a 2022 study. Individuals often hold business wealth through shares, investment funds, and pensions, but they tend to own dwellings directly, whether they live in them or rent them to others as a landlord. Housing wealth is very unevenly distributed, but owning a home is a widespread experience and ambition, and the fact that it is such a personal form of wealth for owner-occupiers complicates the politics of inequality in contemporary capitalism. Housing makes up most middle-class assets in most OECD countries, and accumulating that wealth is often a lifetime project involving paying off a mortgage over many years.

Many of the features that make housing unusual as a consumer need would persist under socialism, so it calls for special consideration. Housing stock is expensive to produce and very long-lasting if maintained. It occupies space in particular locations. People care about where they live — in terms both of their home’s position relative to other places that matter to them and of the character of the natural and built environment around it. There is an ineradicable element of scarcity to desirable locations. A given patch of land can be used more or less densely, modifying the supply of dwellings in an area, but density and type of housing are themselves aspects of a location that people care about.

Households deciding whether to meet their housing needs by renting or by taking out a mortgage can compare expected interest, maintenance, tax, and insurance costs, along with transaction costs and the opportunity cost of the money tied up in the home, with the rent on an equivalent property. Some households may be willing to pay a premium for the security of ownership and the freedom of renovating; on the other hand, the illiquidity and risks of ownership may lead others to prefer to rent. For some, there is no choice: since mortgage borrowing generally requires a deposit and the lender’s confidence in the borrower’s ability to repay, many of those on low or insecure incomes are unable to finance a purchase.

Then there are capital gains. Even gains driven by rising incomes and population can be arbitrary — windfalls unrelated to anything the homeowner has done. Such gains can widen a wealth gap between homeowners (and their descendants) who got in early and those stuck renting or only “getting on the property ladder” later in life.

There are a number of ways a socialist society might structure the provision of housing. We suggest a simple approach. In our model, the land and housing stock are publicly owned, but households have secure tenure in the dwelling they live in and the capacity to renovate to their taste. People make regular rental payments for housing, rather than being involved in a financial relationship paying off a large asset purchase over decades. Households take neither the property-price risks nor the capital gains that come with ownership — these are socialized — while the system aims to preserve the security and freedom of a place to call their own.

Rents are set by a housing authority, generally aiming to match demand to supply. A household’s rent may shift over time according to changes in supply and demand for dwellings that are similar in location and type. In other words, rents adjust in response to market conditions and are not simply set forever at the beginning of tenure, though movements can be smoothed to avoid sudden shifts. The housing authority is tasked with developing supply in response to projected demand, so that significant general increases in rent would be considered a policy failure to be remedied. Urban planning and development are in public hands and engage worker-managed construction firms to do the building.

This system aims to allow each household to make its own housing choices, each bearing the appropriate cost, within a wider system of guaranteed minimum incomes and needs-based transfers that support those who could not otherwise afford adequate housing. Some may prefer a modest apartment so as to have more to spend on other things, while others put more of their budget into spacious villas. Many people will make different choices at different stages of life. The system can accommodate experiments in self-managed collective living for those who want it — as well as handling the traditional family home.

Residents are custodians rather than full owners of their homes, but they can use and adapt them to their needs within agreed rules. They can initiate renovations in partnership with the housing authority or its associated bank. Instead of paying up front, the costs of renovations are factored into rents and paid over time. Because maintenance costs and depreciation are already baked into the rent of all dwellings, each comes with a budget and schedule for renovations. Households only need to pay extra for modifications that are idiosyncratic or costlier than the standard.

The housing authority could adjust the pace of renovation to help smooth activity for the construction sector, which is notoriously cyclical in capitalism. If a lot of new construction is going on, renovation can be made temporarily more expensive or limited with a waiting list. When new construction slows, this can be reversed. The pace of renovation can also potentially be varied to help with macroeconomic stabilization beyond the sector.

Because capitalist housing markets are riddled with externalities, housing is an excellent place to reduce the role of markets and open up a considerable role for public planning. Our model of socialist housing aims to accommodate the diversity of household preferences and needs and preserve the central features of “a home of one’s own” — without the individual property-price risks and windfalls that come with the capitalist model of ownership. A century and a half after Engels, that remains the answer to the housing question.
