The SNS grip on national media is meanwhile evident everywhere. A CRTA survey in September found that 69% of air time on Serbian television channels was dedicated to the ruling majority. Of the remaining coverage of the opposition, 42% was negative in tone and 53% neutral.

The student movement has sought to sidestep government domination of the media by, it says, going door to door, including sending a canvasser “to every village”, in the hope of making inroads into Vučić’s solid base in the Serbian countryside. The outcome could hinge on whether these student emissaries can change rural minds.

No SNS officials responded to a request for comment. Gordana Čomić, a former member of the opposition Democratic party who served as a minister in the SNS government, said the students were exaggerating the extent of their rural campaign and were deluded if they thought they could win.

“They are not in the field. It’s propaganda. They have no clue who their voters are,” Čomić said, predicting that the Student List would win about 80 of the 250 seats in the national assembly and then dissipate.

“They won’t have a clue what’s their role there. How will they work when they don’t want to talk with anyone from the ruling parties? They will just dissolve.”

Radivoje Grujić, a Serbian electoral consultant based in Warsaw, was also sceptical that the Student List could make gains in the countryside and argued the students’ only path to victory would be if the Novi Sad disaster mobilised Serbians who had previously stayed away from politics.

“These people were saying: I’m not involved in politics, and then politics got them killed,” he said. “This definitely triggered a lot of people to get involved and obviously those people will not vote for Vučić. I think that’s the only chance for a change – that reservoir of votes of people who never voted.”

In a close race, other factors are expected to come into play. Minority parties representing ethnic Hungarians, Bosniaks and Albanians could emerge as kingmakers.

Previous elections have seen multiple allegations of various forms of rigging, including vote-buying, voter intimidation and ballot box stuffing, so the Student List is planning to deploy an unprecedented number of opposition monitors on Sunday.

That could in turn raise the prospect of election day clashes. Attacks on opposition representatives by gangs of anonymous, black-clad burly men has been a frequent feature of SNS rule. In the days before the elections, one of those hired thugs has turned whistleblower.

“My role was to lead a group of guys to the riskiest and most critical places, to any gatherings where students or the opposition were on the other side,” Momcilo Marjanovic told the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network, saying that he was covertly paid through a fictitious job at a public utility.

“It was our job, as a last resort of course, to use force, although it often happened not as a last resort.”

Diplomats in Belgrade thought that Vučić’s plans to host a major international event, EXPO 2027, next year, could constrain any violence. If his hold on power is threatened, Vučić also has the option of forcing repeated recounts in the hope that the students’ momentum may eventually dissipate.

The movement is determined that will not happen and has focused its planning in recent weeks on post-election street tactics to defend any victory.

“I think there is a strong feeling of now or never,” Jelena Kleut, an associate professor of media studies, said at a recent demonstration outside the education ministry in Belgrade.

“I think that people have really felt in their skin what the regime is capable of and there is a sense you still need to stay strong because the job is not finished.”
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Julian Borger in Belgrade

https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oc.title: Veggie Thursdays and vegan surprises! How Ghent became a plant-based paradise
https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oc.text:
In 2014, 13% of the population of this Belgian city described themselves as flexitarian. This year, 83% did. Here is how everyone was convinced to eat their greens – and love them

Sixty bowls of slime-green soup sit waiting for the children to arrive. Pupils rush in from their morning lessons, grab the bowls by the handles and start slurping. No complaints, no refusals. (OK, maybe a few “bleurgh” faces.) Chicory soup dispatched, they get stuck into the main course: falafel, Mediterranean vegetable tagine and couscous. Some ask for seconds; most grab a piece of fruit for dessert and run out to play.

This is a typical Thursday lunchtime in BS De Stadspoort primary school in Ghent, Belgium. Similar meat-free menus are being eaten in other schools and nurseries across the city, plus community centres, care homes and assisted living facilities, not to mention many work canteens and restaurants. Thursday in Ghent is officially “Veggie Day”, with residents encouraged to eschew any meat or fish. So how did a city get its children – and everyone else – to eat their greens?

It didn’t happen overnight. “The success story of Ghent is one where we had an amazing grassroots movement, with people asking for more climate action. But the magic happened when politicians actually listened and implemented policy to introduce the Thursday Veggie Day in 2009,” says Vanessa Debruyne, the head of communications for the nonprofit organisation ProVeg Belgium, who is showing me around town. “It got the ball rolling, companies and restaurants joined, the population got used to it, and more entrepreneurs made the move to plant-based. We’ve been unstoppable ever since! Ghent is the best town in Belgium for plant-based food.”

Veggie day was just the start, agrees Hafsa El-Bazioui, the Green deputy mayor of Ghent, who has cycled over to join us (the city centre has been largely car-free since 2017). “A few years ago, we changed to prioritise plant-based protein,” she says. In 2021, the Flemish government launched the Green Deal Protein Shift – a commitment to switch the ratio of animal to plant proteins consumed from 60:40 to 40:60 by 2030. Ghent has already reached the target.

As well as vegetarian Thursdays and vegetarian options every day, school caterers have turned traditional meat dishes such as burgers, sausages and meatballs into hybrids, cutting out at least half the beef or pork and replacing them with, say, lentils. Stews might combine meat with chickpeas or beans. An incredible amount of effort is put in to making each dish taste good: they are screened by a “taste panel” made up of dietitians, chefs, childcare professionals and people with sensitivities to flavour, bitterness, texture and mouthfeel. Recipes are constantly modified and improved after feedback from children, parents and school staff. As a result, children get to eat the food they know and like, but the dishes are healthier and better for the planet – Ghent has reduced the carbon footprint of its school meals by 38% since 2018.

Although she is a vegan herself, El-Bazioui believes reducing meat consumption across the board is the most effective and achievable policy, rather than trying to convince people to cut it out altogether. “When you approach a lot of people, the impact is more than if you focus on a small group of vegans,” she says. “That’s my philosophy in food, in politics, in life.”

This stealth approach is echoed all over the city. I pop in to the Viernulvier art centre, AKA De Vooruit, for a chat with Tom De Vleesschauwer, its kitchen coordinator – De Vooruit is as popular for its large art deco cafe as for its programme of theatre, dance, film and music. “A few years ago, we made oat milk the default: if you don’t ask for cow’s milk, you get oat,” says De Vleesschauwer. “About 90% of customers now have oat milk. If we had a sign saying you can choose, it would only be 10-20%.”

There have been other changes in De Vooruit’s cafe, too. The soup is now always vegan; the dish of the day is vegetarian; the staff and performers are served a daily “Ottolenghi-style vegetarian buffet” instead of cheese and charcuterie. And, as in the school canteens, the few meat dishes on the menu – today just spaghetti bolognese and meatballs in tomato sauce – have been hybridised. “We cut down the meat by 70% and increased the carrots, cutting them to the same size – 30% still gives the flavour and the idea of meat, and carrots give sweetness,” says De Vleesschauwer. “People say plant-based is niche, but we have a very wide audience.”

There are plenty of fully vegan businesses in the city, too, such as Madam Bakster, where I drink coffee with homemade hazelnut milk and devour rich, chewy chocolate-chip cookies fresh from the oven. Laura Verhulst, the founder, sees her cafe as more, not less, inclusive. “I wanted to make desserts that everyone could enjoy: vegan, allergen-free, non-refined sugar,” she says. At Knol & Kool, a vegan restaurant-cum-minimart, 85% of customers aren’t even vegetarian. The owner, Stijn Sprengers, says: “Our vibe is not, ‘Fuck you, meat-eaters’. We try to be as hospitable as possible and make everyone feel welcome.”

Oh!Ma is a restaurant specialising in plant-based Belgian comfort food. “We serve meals that feel like home: stew, vol-au-vent, meatballs,” says Hannah, a student and waitress. “We introduce it to people’s lifestyles in a non-pushy, non-in-your-face way. A lot of people are shocked the food is vegan. Most walk-ins don’t realise.” The restaurant makes all its own plant-based meat alternatives and condiments, such as Belgium’s beloved sauce andalouse, essential with fries. It says each plant-based dish saves up to 5kg of CO₂and 2,000 litres of water compared with its animal-based equivalent.

Hannah isn’t a vegetarian herself, but Oh!Ma’s “chicken” and mushroom vol-au-vent and “cheezy bacon” loaded fries have won her over. “I prefer the betterballs [a vegan take on the bar snack bitterballen] to the originals,” she says. “I’m looking for plant-based more often. I thought it wasn’t going to taste good – working here has changed that.”

As well as these sorts of independent businesses, Ghent also has a proud tradition of affordable “social restaurants”, where all are welcome – tourists included – and prices for residents vary according to their ability to pay. I have lunch at Parnassus, a social restaurant in a beautiful former Franciscan church, where a two-course meal is €16 [£13.50] full price, or €7/€3.50 for those receiving certain social welfare benefits. Last year, 67% of customers paid a discounted rate. The cost includes a vegetable soup (today courgette) and a choice of two main courses. As it is Thursday, the two mains are vegetarian (a big wedge of cheesy pumpkin quiche) and vegan (seitan and mushroom stew with roast potatoes), both served with salad. There is a meat option twice a week and a fish dish on Fridays, meaning 70% of the menu is vegetarian or vegan.

Nicholas, the head chef, explains his cooking style. “We believe in pure enjoyment with a minimal impact on the planet,” he says. “We cook as natural as possible: fresh, healthy and without heavy cream or fats. We also actively fight food waste.” He and his team feed about 180 people a day, sometimes as many as 250, and produce almost zero waste. Lunch is winding down when I arrive, but the church is still half full of people of all ages: alone, in couples, with family or groups of friends.

Parnassus is one of four restaurants operated by Ateljee, a company that runs employment projects in Ghent; other initiatives include secondhand shops, a bike shop, city gardening and digital skills hubs. Tom Wauters, Ateljee’s general manager, says: “The restaurants employ people who have been long-term unemployed, to help them get back into the labour market. We strongly believe that everyone has talents.” The chefs at Parnassus are certainly talented – my stew is delicious – and the daily changing menus are full of creative plant-based dishes.

After lunch, I head to a biotech lab on a science park that is part of Ghent University. This is the home of Those Vegan Cowboys, a new venture by the founders of The Vegetarian Butcher, an alternative-meat brand now owned by the Dutch company Vivera. Ghent has a history of fostering plant-based innovation: the dairy-free brand Alpro was founded here in 1980, and is still headquartered in the city.

Those Vegan Cowboys are at the cutting edge of the protein transition. They are producing casein – the animal protein used in cheese production – from microorganisms instead of cows, sheep and goats. Steven Geysens, the head of molecular biology, explains why. “Cheese is one of the main things people crave when they go vegan. It is the holy grail of animal-free products.”

Why is vegan cheese still, by and large, so bad? “No plant protein has the same effect as casein. It is important for gelation, stretchiness, meltability, nutritional value, taste …” Geysens says that alternative cheese makes up just 1% of total global cheese purchases, whereas dairy-free milks now constitute 14% of milk sales. He shows me around various rooms in the lab, where white-coated technicians are busily working away. I feel humbled that so many brilliant minds are devoted to giving vegans a tastier cheeseboard, but Geysens corrects me – Those Vegan Cowboys have a far bigger vision. They see this as the cheese of the future.

“This is something that can be durable, sustainable and help feed everyone on the planet. It will have less saturated fat and be lactose-, antibiotic- and hormone-free.” He shows me figures that demonstrate dairy cheese’s environmental impact: it is the worst food in terms of water use, and worse than pork for land use and greenhouse gas emissions. Farmers will still be needed to make animal-free cheese, he says, to grow lower-impact crops such as sugar beet to be used in the fermentation process. “It’s good for farmers to have an opportunity to diversify,” he says.

Two cheese scientists, Hannes Decadt and Mathilde Blin, proudly show me some of their creations: gouda, camembert, mozzarella and feta. They look exactly like the real thing and I’m desperate to try them, but sadly they are still going through the EU’s stringent food safety regulations. I’ll have to rely on the scientists’ verdicts: “We know we’re not completely there yet,” says Decadt. “It’s much closer to real cheese than all the vegan cheeses on the market because of the casein. It’s the same texture. Now we’re focusing on ripening.” Blin will know they’ve cracked it when she is happy to serve her camembert to her parents: “My family are French and they’re really harsh, so they’re the best critics,” she says.

What else does the future hold for Ghent? ProVeg is now focusing on higher education. Next month, it is running a campaign in 15 universities and colleges, taking plant-based chefs into student restaurants to run cooking and tasting sessions. It is also looking at healthcare, having already helped one psychiatric hospital to double the number of plant-based meals, and linked up other hospitals with local organic vegetable farmers.

I wonder why Ghent’s protein transition has proved so successful. Debruyne thinks it is due to a “unique combination” of public pressure and policy. Verhulst, the baker, believes the change is linked to Ghent’s strongly socialist history and the energy from its large student population. “It is anchored in the identity of the Ghent spirit. In Antwerp, for example, everything is perfect and symmetrical. Ghent is more alternative.”

Whatever the reason, it is working. “Twelve years ago, 13% of the population described themselves as flexitarians. This year, a whopping 83% did,” says Debruyne. “It’s a silent revolution.”
https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oc.author: Rachel Dixon

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: World must cut emissions by 18% in four years ‘to find our way back’, UN says
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Action needed to avoid disastrous overshoot of climate targets, according to organisation’s environment body

The world needs to cut carbon emissions by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin.

Although the “window has closed” on holding temperature rises to 1.5C, in line with scientific advice, limiting the “overshoot” of that target is still possible, according to the UN Environment Programme (Unep).

But countries are failing to translate their long-term targets on reducing emissions into short-term actions, a report on the “emissions gap” between climate goals and policies has found.

Global carbon output appears to have stalled: the emission levels in 2025 were broadly similar to those of the previous year. But Unep analysts were wary of calling it a peak or plateau, given the vast uncertainties of geopolitics and an increased reliance on fossil fuels, despite strong growth in renewable energy.

Cutting greenhouse gases by 18% by 2030, and by 45% by 2045, would yield a good chance of limiting temperature rises to 1.7C above preindustrial levels. This would still allow events such as the record heatwaves of the last few months to become frequent and common, but could help prevent them from getting drastically worse.

Governments were warned for years that time was running out, said Inger Andersen, the executive director of Unep. “[We used to say] there’s still an opportunity if we make this herculean effort [to stay within the 1.5C limit],” she said. “It’s now clear the herculean effort was not made. We procrastinated, and now we are saying this window has closed.”

Nevertheless, she urged countries to keep the 1.5C goal – the centrepiece of the Paris climate agreement. “We can make the overshoot as brief and as short as possible. It’s not time to throw in the towel and give up. This is about how to find our way back, as shortly and quickly as possible.”

Under Donald Trump, the US – the world’s second biggest emitter, after China – has withdrawn from the Paris climate agreement and is threatening to reverse its longstanding trend of falling greenhouse gas emissions.

Bill Hare, the chief executive of the Climate Analytics thinktank, said: “All governments have a job to do, but in particular it is time for major fossil fuel producers such as the US and Saudi Arabia, which produce 20-25% of fossil fuels globally, to stop playing politics and face the scientific reality. Right now they are looking at the fire, denying it exists and pouring more petrol on it, while their own citizens increasingly face searing heat, wildfires and other impacts.”

Other countries appear to have been affected by US intransigence – pledges made last year on greenhouse gases were noticeably weak, according to UNEP analysis. At the Cop30 climate summit in Brazil last November, governments were supposed to make fresh commitments under the Paris agreement to cut emissions. But the commitments made were nowhere near strong enough.

Even if all of those updated pledges were fulfilled, temperatures would still rise to 2.6C above preindustrial levels, according to Unep’s projections, endangering life across swathes of the globe. Policy has also not kept up with pledges: on current policies around the world, temperatures would rise to 2.8C. Every five years of greenhouse gas emissions at current levels pushes up forecasts of global heating by 0.1C. Scientists also fear that the greater the margin by which we exceed 1.5C, the greater the likelihood of triggering tipping points in the climate system.

Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, said: “The tragedy is that we have the solutions within our grasp. Solar and wind power are growing far faster than anyone expected, yet governments are still failing to move away from fossil fuels quickly enough. The technology is racing ahead while political leadership is dragging its feet.”

The shortfall in countries’ commitments is supposed to be corrected under a Paris agreement mechanism called the “global stocktake”, an assessment of emissions targets next scheduled for 2028. But that has also been thrown into doubt: this week, the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change failed to set a timetable to publish its latest report before the global stocktake, which would prevent governments from assessing their progress against the latest science.

Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and one of the world’s leading climate scientists, said rows over the timing of IPCC reports must not be allowed to stall government action. “If all current national commitments are implemented, global emissions are projected to reach approximately 50 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent annually by 2035, when they should be below 35 gigatonnes. The science is already clear. Closing that gap is a question of political action, not a lack of scientific evidence,” he said.

One way identified by Unep to limit warming quickly would be to cut methane, a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide.
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensifies days before Brazil presidential runoff
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Lula’s supporters suspect tech firm meddling on behalf of US president Donald Trump, who has close ties to Bolsonaro family

Five days after his defeat in the first round of the Brazilian presidential election, leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spent almost 24 hours unable to boost his Instagram posts, while his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, could.

Lula’s lawyers included the episode in a list of incidents that they submitted to the electoral court and international observers as “evidence” that Meta, Instagram’s owner, was actively trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour.

Reports from Lula supporters saying their content had been removed or its reach restricted flooded social media in Brazil, while about a dozen watchdogs and research groups published reports describing what they called “indications” that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign.

Meta called Lula’s allegations “false and unfounded”, saying there had been “technical incidents” that affected campaigns from “different parts of the political spectrum”.

The controversy fuelled the electoral battle between Lula and Bolsonaro just days before next Sunday’s runoff and gained further traction after the electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”.

Late last week, justice Marco Aurélio Bellizze said he had found no evidence of deliberate action by the company, which would require further investigation, but he gave Meta 24 hours to prove that the problems affecting Lula had been fixed and would not happen again.

On Monday, after saying the company had failed to do so, Bellizze gave Meta a further 24 hours. The company responded on Tuesday, again denying any favouritism and saying it had introduced human review to prevent any automated restrictions.

Meta’s oversight board, a quasi-independent body whose decisions are binding, issued a statement saying it was “concerned by recurring enforcement failures in Meta’s election integrity efforts”, citing both Brazil’s election and the suspension of the anti-Trump No Kings movement’s account in the US for several hours last Saturday, during demonstrations aimed at encouraging early voting in the midterm elections.

The company said it suspended the No Kings account after its anti-fraud systems wrongly flagged what they believed was bot traffic, and apologised.

The board said it had seen the same pattern in Brazil, where there had been an “over-enforcement of Meta’s fraud policies against Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s ad accounts” on 23 September, when his campaign advertising account was disabled for more than an hour. Meta said this had happened “by mistake … and not for political reasons” after an anti-fraud review wrongly classified an ad as an attempt to impersonate a government social programme.

The board said: “From the removal of political activist accounts during protests in the US ahead of the midterm elections to technical restrictions that hit the accounts of a presidential candidate in Brazil leading to allegations of electoral interference, it’s clear that Meta must do more to ensure that its enforcement practices during elections are transparent and consistent, and that political speech is protected rather than stifled”.

João Victor Archegas, the coordinator at the thinktank Institute for Technology and Society, said it was “almost impossible” to prove any interference by Meta in Brazilian elections because only the company has access to its internal data, meaning there is no real external scrutiny, either from the electoral court or from the watchdogs producing reports on it.

“What we have so far is a collection of cases that perhaps one day we can piece together and reach some conclusion one way or the other. But today, because of the lack of information, unfortunately we cannot be certain,” he said.

Platforms such as Google and TikTok are not allowing political advertising in this election, leaving Meta’s services as the only large-scale channels for paid digital campaigning, which so far has earned the company £43m, 85% more than it made during the last presidential election.

A report by the watchdog CTRL+Z, founded by a former executive at Meta’s WhatsApp, catalogued 1,121 reports of lost or suppressed reach, restrictions on reposting, and account bans and blocks affecting mostly leftwing profiles. Meta dismissed it as a catalogue of anecdotes and users’ perceptions.

Media outlets posted examples of an experiment in which WhatsApp’s AI assistant refused to generate artwork featuring “Lula” and his ballot number, but did so for “Flávio” – Brazilians widely refer to the senator by his first name, reserving the surname for his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The company said this reflected “a specific gap in our safeguards, not political bias” and that AI artwork could be generated using Lula’s first name, Luiz, with his ballot number.

Many Lula supporters raised suspicions that Meta was allegedly acting on behalf of the US president, Donald Trump, who has close ties to the Bolsonaro family and whom Lula has accused of trying to interfere in Brazil’s election.

Lula’s lawyers appeared to embrace that argument, describing Meta in their filing to the electoral court as a “foreign company aligned with the Trump administration” that was acting as a “vector of external pressure on the [Brazilian] electorate”, without, however, offering any evidence of possible US involvement.

In the 9 October episode in which Lula’s campaign was temporarily unable to boost posts on Instagram, which 70% of Brazilian adults say they use as their primary source of information, his lawyers said that “silencing” the incumbent’s social media while his opponent’s continued operating normally created an unfair advantage for Bolsonaro.

The company said the problem affected only new posts, while older ones could still be promoted, and that it had been a “global outage” affecting “thousands of advertisers in different countries”, though Bolsonaro’s campaign was not among them.

Meta added: “We apply the same rules to all candidates, parties and political viewpoints in Brazil, just as we do in elections around the world. We do not suppress content to harm one side or give preferential treatment to any side.”

NetLab, a research laboratory on the internet and social media at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, produced a report showing that Meta allowed at least 1,600 election ads to be boosted from outside Brazil, something prohibited under Brazilian law.

Débora Salles, NetLab’s general coordinator, said they had not identified political bias towards either side, but that the failure “shows how the company repeatedly fails to ensure safety and compliance with electoral law”.

On the eve of the vote, NetLab identified paid ads that posed as official posts from the electoral court and contained false information that encouraged abstention, claiming that if it was raining, voters could cast their ballots online, which is not possible in Brazil.

“Regardless of whether a candidacy is being helped or harmed, what we see is that the company has difficulty complying with Brazilian electoral law and ends up undermining the integrity of the electoral process,” said Salles.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Troubled waters: life during wartime for Iranians on the strait of Hormuz
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
Despite US-Israeli airstrikes and Tehran’s attacks on shipping, the waterway still has to provide a lifeline for those that live and work there

Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance.

In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz.

He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home

Farouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home.

Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different.

Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation.

Even with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped.

According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired.

Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait. In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel.

With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes.

But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan.

Fishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety.

Anvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult.

“Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks.

“This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk.

Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night.

Hormuz Island has long been known as a kind of “hippy paradise”, a place Iranians have come to regard as “free”. Artists and creatives moved here from bigger cities in search of peace; women swim in bathing suits, writers and painters find space to work, and life moves slower. There is “love and magic” here, as Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer, puts it, “a different rhythm”.

Life here has changed little, Yashar says, although the war has brought some new restrictions, and a handful of attacks, mostly on infrastructure. The roughly 8,000 residents are trying to support each other, and to preserve the sense of freedom that has set the island apart, he adds.

The government has closed off parts of Hormuz Island’s north, but beyond the now restricted areas, life has continued, he explains. “As long as you don’t go north, they leave you alone,” he says of the army.

Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide – the tourism sector has been hit by the conflict

The Majara hotel, also known as Rainbow accommodation, is one of Hormuz’s attractions. It has been closed since the beginning of the war

“The tourism sector has taken the biggest hit,” says Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide, adding that he prefers to go by his first name only. “Guesthouses and homestays remain closed, as do restaurants and many cafes.” Visitors have largely stopped coming since the war, dealing a heavy blow to an island whose economy depends on tourism and fishing, both of which have been disrupted.

From the higher parts of the island, Omran says, it is possible to see deep into the strait on clear days, when the haze lifts and the humid air clears, all the way to the mountains of Khasab in Oman.

Residents have climbed up these barren mountains of red and white stone, at times watching the war unfold in the distance. Tankers remain stranded in the strait, explosions can be heard regularly. Yet residents also say the war has not driven them from the island.

Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter who was born and raised on Hormuz, laughs when asked whether she had considered leaving in February, at the start of the war.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: ‘This petrol station is my home now’: Malawi’s fuel crisis forces desperate drivers to queue for days
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Shortages caused by the country’s lack of hard currency have escalated into a national emergency, with drivers waiting for a fuel tanker that may never arrive

From the driver’s seat of his rusted minibus, Sido Sombeja stares out at a stationary sea of rear lights stretching for almost a mile down the road. It is 3am in Zomba, the old capital of Malawi, and cold night air comes through the cracked windscreen. For eight consecutive days and nights, the 40-year-old father of four has lived out of this vehicle, waiting for a fuel tanker that may never arrive.

Sombeja chews on a cold piece of fried mandazi – a doughy snack that has been the only food available. The Meru petrol station is no longer just a place of transit; it has transformed into a makeshift village of drivers in parked vehicles. In these queues, strangers form uneasy alliances. Motorists group together to guard one another’s vehicles during rare bathroom breaks, and coordinate to aggressively block any queue-jumpers. Men sleep under the bellies of trucks. They wash their faces with bottled water on the kerbside and gather around charcoal braziers (mbaula) at night.

“This is not a petrol station any more,” Sombeja says, gesturing at the hundreds of dark chassis surrounding him. “It is my home now. It is like I have two families – the one back home waiting for me to bring back money, and this second family of strangers on the road where I must buy snacks just to survive the night.”

Malawi has experienced intermittent shortages since late 2022 but in the past four weeks the problem has escalated into a national emergency. Urban hubs are adjusting to a new reality: a queue economy where the boundaries of labour, community and patience are pushed to their limits.

The roots of this societal paralysis lie in an economic bottleneck. The National Oil Company of Malawi attributes the persistent shortages directly to the country’s lack of hard currency. In briefings before the parliamentary committee on budget on 2 October, oil officials revealed that a surge in domestic vehicle usage meant Malawi now burned through 2m litres of fuel daily, requiring $49m (£37.5m) every month in foreign exchange.

It is a financial burden that the impoverished nation cannot sustain as agricultural exports have collapsed. According to Joan Thaundi, a spokesperson for Malawi’s energy ministry, the petroleum sector must compete with other goods for limited US dollars. As a result, international banks repeatedly leave local letters of credit unhonoured, halting fuel tankers at regional African ports before they can even cross into Malawi.

To manage the escalating panic, the state is taking extraordinary measures. Fitina Khonje, a public relations manager at the Malawi Energy Regulatory Authority, says that while fuel procurement is heavily prioritised by the government, the national cash deficit remains an obstacle. The government has liquidated millions in gold reserves to secure short-term credit from international lenders, while withdrawing non-essential state vehicles from the roads to preserve what little fuel remains for core operations.

At the petrol stations, such explanations do little to soothe a frustrated public. The crisis is turning patience into hostility.

At the Petroda petrol station in the capital, Lilongwe, WillKens Chimwaza, a 26-year-old attendant, says that the station’s normal daily operating capacity of 30,000 litres has dropped to 5,000. When that runs dry, usually within an hour of a tanker’s arrival, the mood among waiting drivers turns ugly.

Chimwaza describes being routinely surrounded and threatened by angry motorists, facing a barrage of verbal abuse for a national shortage he has no power to fix. To keep the peace, attendants are told to ration the amount each customer can buy. “It is terrifying,” Chimwaza says. “People are desperate, and they look at us as the gatekeepers who are actively denying them their livelihoods.”

Gift Ngala, a 34-year-old taxi driver operating out of the business district of Mzuzu city, says the scarcity has hit him hard. Ngala has to buy illicit fuel from roadside dealers at inflated prices to keep his vehicle on the road. “The shortages are hitting us hard, and our customers are paying far more than the normal fare because we are forced to source fuel from the black market just to remain in business,” he says. For low-income commuters, fare increases drain household budgets meant for food and basic necessities.

Back in Zomba, the psychological toll of the prolonged crisis weighs on drivers such as Sombeja. His daily minibus routes used to provide a modest but steady income for his family. Now, his earning capacity is frozen.

He urges the authorities to stop politicising the distribution of resources and to stabilise the supply chain. “We are struggling to meet our basic needs,” he says. “They must ensure the fuel is stabilised so we can go back to work.”

As the sun rises over Meru petrol station, it casts an unforgiving light on the exhausted faces of hundreds of drivers stepping out of their vehicles to stretch. No tanker has arrived. Sombeja turns his key, checking his empty dashboard gauge one more time, before settling back into the driver’s seat to begin his ninth day of queueing.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: ‘A difficult line’: meet the editors tackling Wikipedia’s arms trade pages
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Volunteers and new recruits come together for ‘wikithon’ to put more detail about industry into public domain

“Anyone can edit Wikipedia,” the adage goes. But, it turns out, a relatively small number actually do.

What is worthy of a digital page in the world’s largest and most-read encyclopedia is decided by roughly 270,000 active volunteers, enthusiasts who populate the online resource with information on anything from 19th-century medicine to TikTok trends. Inevitably, some subjects are sidelined – the global south, notable women – but a new batch of Wikipedian recruits are waging war on one neglected topic: the arms industry. Last week, in a classroom in central London, two dozen volunteers huddled around laptops and free servings of vegan Ethiopian food for what is known as a “wikithon”, an event of collective and in-person Wikipedia editing. Some were veteran editors in their 70s, others young students who had never registered an account before. But their targets include subjects such as Palantir, Project Maven and Nitro-Chem.

“Wikipedia pages about the arms industry, in general, are not always super-detailed,” said the group’s co-founder Agnes Cameron. The intention of the wikithon, started by fellows from the n-Space programme at Somerset House Studios, was “to put better quality and more well organised information on the arms industry in the public domain”, the specialist technician said.

Attenders at the monthly event are trained in how to add to the internet’s most popular reference site. But while editing Wikipedia is surprisingly simple – just a few clicks to publish a change – ethical complications quickly bubble up.

“The interesting thing about Wikipedia editing is that you’re encouraged to edit things you care about,” Cameron said. “What it looks like to have a conflict of interest is an interesting question.”

Although Cameron enjoys editing pages about food in her spare time, her interests are also political. “We’re toeing quite a difficult line,” she said. “Difficult lines are important to toe.”

Despite personal and political reasons for wanting to spread information on arms manufacturers and sellers, finding journalistic balance means using Wikipedia in good faith. Cameron said attenders’ chosen subject matter meant that it was “really important” that they followed Wikipedia’s standards to the letter. “This is not an anti-arms industry campaigning event. This is an event really about factual information on Wikipedia,” she said.

When it comes to information, Wikipedia’s rules demand that no original research is included on its pages and conclusions are not drawn. The main goal of the arms industry wikithon, then, was to pull together publicly available information from other sources into one place.

Wikipedia has been repeatedly criticised for its lack of diversity in editors and its coverage. It has been accused of geographical bias towards the west, with most articles focused on the US and western Europe. Similarly, just 19% of the site’s biography entries are for women. In 2018, the female Nobel prize winner Donna Strickland, a physicist, was deemed “not important enough” for a Wikipedia entry.

With a wider range of ages, genders and racial backgrounds at the wikithon, the trainee editors were helping to rebalance the scale, said Hannah Cobb, a co-founder of the event. “There’s a very specific idea of who edits Wikipedia … that doesn’t tend to be the demographic of who shows up,” she said. “There’s a really broad interest in Wikipedia in general. Everyone remembers that at school you were taught not to trust it because anyone could write it.”

Previous arms industry wikithons organised by Cameron and Cobb in Manchester and London have drawn in more than 60 would-be Wikipedians at a time, including activists, journalists, Quaker members – and even Cameron’s own mother.

Newcomers to the group were interested in how Wikipedia could be used to broaden public knowledge of confusing geopolitics, said Cobb. “There is a sense of powerlessness when it comes to countering the narrative by big tech, by governments, by the military industrial complex at large,” she said.

But for the arms industry page editors, those feelings can disappear over a few hours: “When you write something on Wikipedia, it appears immediately on the internet. I think that experience alone is quite empowering for people.”

Cobb spoke of a sense of wonder “when people realise how easy it is to actually contribute”, but attenders have a respect for Wikipedia’s commitment to rigour and quality control. And though dedicated to accuracy, the group prefers to not advertise the details of its edits over concerns that the work could be undone by other editors in bad faith. Cameron said it was unclear if Wikipedia’s wider editorial culture would take offence over how the event was run. While wikithons are not new, the blurry line between activism and accurate dissemination of information stress-tests the platform’s rules.

Real-world politics often spill on to Wikipedia, and editors often disagree publicly about changes. The site has also been covertly used as an informational battleground. The seasoned editor Ksenia Coffman made extensive edits to remove what she found to be flattering and sympathetic entries about Nazi party officials across Wikipedia, and in 2021, the Croatian-language version of Wikipedia was found to have been commandeered by nationalist, far-right organisers who made ideologically motivated edits.

Cameron hopes that the regular meetings can be formalised into a WikiProject, when organised groups of editors collaborate to improve certain topic pages. She hoped her group could be adopted by WikiProject Military history, which she called “far and away the most active project on Wikipedia by miles. It’s amazingly well run.”

The London wikithon is to continue for another session in the winter, and Cameron and Cobb’s faith in encyclopedia editing as a political tool is steadfast. As Cameron said: “Wikipedia is fundamentally anti-fascist.”
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: George Francis Lee

https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.title: The Secret Terms of Trump’s Venezuelan Oil Deal
https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.text:
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

In late August, President Donald Trump announced what he called the “biggest oil deal in world history.” Since then, the full text of the accord — which grants the U.S. sweeping access to Venezuela’s oil reserves — has been one of the most sought-after secrets in Washington, D.C.

ProPublica has reviewed a copy of the 18-page strategic partnership agreement signed for the United States by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The document reveals carefully constructed terms that favor U.S. interests at every turn and cements the power of a small group of people handpicked by the Trump administration to govern and profit from the deal. The role of the Venezuelan government and the potential benefits to its people are largely absent from the text.

One of the most criticized aspects of Trump’s announcement has been his choice of a partner: Alejandro Betancourt, a globe-trotting Venezuelan oligarch who has faced money-laundering investigations in three countries.

The Trump administration is taking a 35% stake in Betancourt’s firm, North American Blue Energy Partners, by acquiring shares in a Barbados-registered parent company. The deal document provides little information about the owners and investors behind the parent company, who could receive enormous wealth from the arrangement.

The agreement also safeguards Betancourt’s position as chief executive of NABEP and says the U.S. government will work with the parent company to appoint a powerful seven-member board to govern the venture for an initial 15-year term. Those aspects of the deal, according to people with knowledge of how it came together, were designed to prevent future U.S. and Venezuelan leaders from dismantling the enterprise.

Orlando Alvarado, a name not disclosed by the Trump administration as a party to the accord, signed the agreement on behalf of the parent company, alongside Betancourt, Hegseth and Rubio. Alvarado has held senior roles in multiple Betancourt businesses, including as chief financial officer of an energy firm that became embroiled in scandals a decade ago. According to the Miami Herald, federal prosecutors identified Alvarado as an unindicted co-conspirator in a scheme to embezzle money from Venezuela’s national oil company.

NABEP spokesperson Terry Wade said that “neither Mr. Betancourt nor Mr. Alvarado has ever been charged with any crime in any country, and any claims against them are baseless.”

We’re still reporting. If you know more about this topic, please contact our reporting team.

I’m interested in talking to people who understand how members of the Trump administration, or their family members, are doing business, at home or abroad.

Key aspects of the plan differ from the Trump administration’s public pronouncements. Trump has said the deal will secure America’s energy dominance for the next century. But the text indicates that U.S. purchasing rights expire in half that time and that the underlying operating rights appear to run afoul of Venezuelan laws limiting oil concessions to 25 years.

The agreement does ensure the United States a deep discount from fair-market value on 20% of NABEP’s oil, as Trump has said. It does not, however, explicitly guarantee that Betancourt’s company is obligated to pay the estimated $200 billion in royalties and tax payments to Venezuela that the White House has said would benefit the country.

There are also significant caveats related to Trump’s central selling point to Americans — that the deal will bring a gusher of low-cost oil imports.

The agreement gives the U.S. the right to purchase 20% of NABEP’s oil at a discounted rate of $30 a barrel, or less than a third of what oil has sold for in recent months, according to one of three supporting documents reviewed by ProPublica.

But this fee does not account for the cost of getting Venezuela’s oil out of the country. Much of Venezuela’s raw crude is so thick that it won’t flow through pipelines unless it is first blended with 20% or more of oil thinner products. Under the deal, the potentially significant cost of importing millions of barrels of those blending materials is not included in the price.

The White House, the State Department, the Pentagon and the energy company NABEP all defended the agreement, saying in statements that their new public-private venture will provide meaningful and lasting economic benefits to both countries that cannot be captured in a legal document.

“This historic deal marks a major step toward stabilizing Venezuela’s economy after years of hyperinflation and almost no new investment, while more than doubling the United States’ oil reserves,” said White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers.

Wade emphasized that NABEP was chosen because of its track record of expanding oil production in Venezuela in recent years and that the agreement was between the company and the U.S. government, not Venezuela.

“Thanks in large part to the agreement,” Wade said, “there is a surge in confidence about the future of Venezuela’s oil industry and, as a direct result, substantial new investments are flowing into the country.”

He added that much of NABEP’s oil comes from fields that require little or no blending materials and that blending costs would not meaningfully impact the price of production. “Our barrel economics are strong.”

The newly revealed details of the agreement are nonetheless likely to raise more questions about whether the unorthodox marriage of the United States and a foreign energy baron can bring lasting benefits to either country — and which private parties might benefit along the way. Trump’s oil deal is likely to face scrutiny in both the United States and Venezuela, especially if Democrats win one or both chambers in the midterm elections, according to former U.S. diplomats and congressional staff.

“Question number one in a new U.S. Congress will be: Why Betancourt?” said former Ambassador James Story, who served as the top U.S. diplomat in Caracas from 2018 to 2023, in an interview. “Why did he get this deal? And was he involved in criminality? It seems reasonable to have a congressional hearing about those questions.”

In public comments, Delcy Rodríguez, who won the backing of the Trump administration to serve as Venezuela’s interim president, praised the accord as “historic.” She has asserted that Venezuela will retain sovereignty over its natural resources and defended the choice of Betancourt.

People with knowledge of the Trump administration’s behind-the-scenes decision-making and negotiations with Betancourt spoke to ProPublica on condition of anonymity because they were either not authorized to do so or were fearful of retribution.

One reason that the precise terms of the deal have remained hidden until now is that the signed agreement is marked as a “sensitive” government document. That classification is commonly used to shield a variety of federal records from public release, including those containing personnel information, details about ongoing law enforcement operations and matters protected by attorney-client privilege. The document also contains a confidentiality clause barring Betancourt’s company from disclosing the “existence and terms” of the U.S. government agreement.

One person familiar with the deliberations said that people close to the Trump administration seemed keen to partner with Betancourt’s company because of the privacy and flexibility it offered. That appeared to give NABEP an advantage over publicly traded oil companies, which would be obligated to shareholder reporting requirements.

“For example,” the person said, “Chevron couldn’t give 35% of their shares to the Pentagon.”

The oil deal is sensitive partly because of likely resistance in Venezuela, where critics have already described it as a U.S. takeover of the country’s precious natural resources.

A ProPublica analysis shows that its terms favor American interests at nearly every turn and try to enshrine the Trump administration’s imprint indefinitely.

The document states that a majority of the seven-member board must be U.S. citizens at all times, and the U.S. government can appoint one “non-voting observer” to join the group. Betancourt, who will serve as the chief executive, is the only board member named by the agreement. The initial board will establish the process for choosing new members.

“Throughout the evolution of the deal, it was clear that the governing structure was intended to ensure maximum control by the people making the deal and to insulate them from future administrations seeking to reverse the agreement or call it into question,” a person familiar with the negotiations said.

There is no requirement for any Venezuelan government participation in the board.

The agreement also offers long-lasting protections for Betancourt and unnamed investors. It requires a supermajority vote of five to oust Betancourt as CEO, change the board composition or execute any transactions with a shareholder that isn’t the U.S. government, an indirect equity holder, director, affiliate or “immediate family members.”

The board will determine compensation for Betancourt in his role as chief executive, the document says. As structured, the deal does not appear to require any public disclosures about pay or distribution of shares to executives.

The agreement does not say which shareholders, affiliates or family members have been approved to transact with Betancourt’s company. Under Barbados corporate law, there is almost nothing that can force those interests to be revealed publicly.

The agreement does, however, require the company to maintain “anti-money laundering controls,” submit to external audits and inspections of its records by the U.S. government, and provide the U.S. government with an annual budget and quarterly unaudited financial statements. It is unclear if these reports will ever be made public.

It could be some time before the company produces enough oil to fulfill a significant share of U.S. demand. Betancourt’s company currently produces about 200,000 barrels per day — or about as much over the course of a year as the United States uses in three days.

NABEP aims to increase its production to 500,000 barrels per day by the end of 2028, according to recent reports.

In addition to securing a discount on 20% of NABEP’s oil, Washington also has “first priority” to purchase all of the company’s remaining oil production for the next 50 years, including an irrevocable right to buy its entire oil supply in the event the U.S. declares a national emergency.

The U.S. also receives a “most favored nation” status that requires Betancourt’s firm to disclose any other business agreements it signs, and, if they are favorable, to grant the Washington matching terms.

One person who reviewed parts of the contract was surprised at the tangible benefits for the U.S. compared with the lack of binding commitments to Venezuela: “I gave you 20% of my production at ‘cost plus,’ fine. I gave you all of my production if there’s a national emergency, OK. … So what do I get in exchange?”

A U.S. official said Rodriguez had granted NABEP 100-year oil concessions to operate there, although this figure is not referenced in the accord and appears to contradict Venezuelan law.

In the event of a dispute, Venezuela can’t challenge the deal in its own courts. The agreement dictates that any conflict between the company and the United States must be settled under U.S. law, not Venezuela’s. The two sides even spelled out that any civil case or arbitration must be argued before the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas, where Trump’s Justice Department has turned, time and again, for favorable rulings.

Where U.S. law does not apply, Texas state law governs, the agreement states.

A Pentagon office has been tasked with someday executing the financial transaction to capitalize on the U.S. government’s 35% share in the venture. The document shows that the U.S. will pay nothing upfront but plans to acquire its stake in Betancourt’s company by paying $0.01 per warrant share. Those terms are set to expire on the 75th anniversary of the closing date.

In a White House statement last month, Trump touted those shares as potentially worth “hundreds of billions,” plus dividends. But Democrats on the Senate Armed Services Committee said they believe the Pentagon office does not have the legal authority to execute an agreement with a foreign entity operating in a country under U.S. sanctions.

Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson said that the Defense Department conducts “extensive due diligence” before extending capital assistance. Wilson declined to comment on any of the legal considerations or further technical aspects of the deal “to protect the integrity of the process.”

Several other detailed aspects of how the company will operate are currently under negotiation among the Trump administration, Betancourt and the parent company, the partnership documents show. The agreement repeatedly cites a set of “Implementation Documents” that will finalize the U.S. ownership stake and the rights of unnamed investors.

The full force of the deal will not take effect until both parties have complied with its closing conditions, which the agreement indicates could happen within months.

Last month, Senate Democrats blasted what was known of the oil accord and demanded details in a letter to Rubio, Hegseth and Secretary of Energy Chris Wright.

“It is unclear why the American public should support this attempt to entangle the United States with a relatively unknown foreign oil company that lacks the capacity or credibility to develop oil fields of the magnitude described and whose leadership has faced international criminal investigations,” four ranking senators said in the letter.

They asserted that most of the “oil fields are nowhere near ready for production” and that it could “take up to a decade before global oil markets are meaningfully impacted and the American people see any tangible benefit.”

Almost immediately after U.S. special operations forces seized President Nicolás Maduro in January and airlifted him out of Venezuela, Trump left little doubt that his larger goal was to restore American access to Venezuela’s oil reserves two decades after most U.S. firms had been ejected from the country.

By early spring, an obscure cast of energy officials, lawyers and lobbyists had started to craft plans to deliver on Trump’s America First energy agenda. One person familiar with the deliberations said that U.S. officials had considered backing an idea for publicly held American oil companies like Chevron, Exxon and Conoco to carve up and rehabilitate Venezuela’s aging oil sector. Another potential route went through Betancourt’s company, which is the second largest private oil firm operating in Venezuela. Working with the Venezuelan state company, Petróleos de Venezuela, SA, was never really an option due to its underlying debt and history of corruption, the person said.

The option of turning to large multinational oil companies quickly stalled. In some cases, oil executives balked at jumping back into the complexity of the Venezuelan market; in others, firms struggled to get more than “lip service” meetings in Washington and Caracas, according to media reports and people familiar with the deal.

“NABEP was given priority,” one person said. “Exxon, Conoco and the others were treated as second class.”

Betancourt’s star was rising in the Trump administration. He had served as an interlocutor for Washington with the Maduro government and had ties to some leaders of the Venezuelan opposition, according to current and former U.S. officials. He had also provided information that helped the U.S. forces seize Venezuelan oil tankers and that aided strategy and planning before the capture of Maduro, Reuters reported.

In addition, Betancourt had developed a good relationship with Rodríguez, whom Trump had backed as the country’s interim president. And Betancourt had done so despite the fact that her influential brother, National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez, had accused him of corruption in a televised speech in 2020, according to former U.S. officials and press reports.

U.S. officials also saw practical reasons to partner with Betancourt, several people said. He and his then-business partner in the U.S., Harry Sargeant, a Trump supporter, appeared to be a rare success story in a battered industry, operating some of the only active oil fields in the country.

“The main thing I found promising is that the fields are producing in Venezuela,” said a former State Department official who analyzed the company’s activities. “I think it’s particularly important that you buy into fields that are producing. … If your policy goal is to raise production quickly, this makes sense.”

For starters, the 46-year-old billionaire was confined to house arrest on his 300-acre Oxfordshire estate in England, fighting off a Swiss extradition request tied to an international money-laundering probe. Betancourt could fly to his $46 million London residence by private helicopter — but his Venezuelan and Italian passports were locked down, and British authorities had barred him from driving on public roads, according to media reports about the special bail arrangement.

Betancourt’s legal problems stemmed from his role in troubled Venezuelan energy projects during the corrupt rule of former President Hugo Chávez. Several of Betancourt’s known or alleged associates were charged or convicted in a major U.S. money-laundering investigation known as Operation Money Flight. Betancourt surfaced as a suspect in the U.S. case and is still under investigation for suspected money laundering by authorities in Spain, according to former U.S. and European officials and press reports.

The most popular leader of the Venezuelan opposition in exile, María Corina Machado, recently described Betancourt as having been involved in “obscene corruption” that caused great suffering for the Venezuelan people, according to a recent New York Times interview.

Betancourt has not been charged in any country. His lawyer has maintained his client’s innocence, saying Betancourt has been unfairly maligned because people associate him with a group of wealthy young Venezuelans, some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing, according to press reports.

Many Venezuelans see Betancourt as a “totemic, emblematic, corrupt figure,” said Brian Naranjo, a former senior U.S. diplomat in Venezuela, in an interview.

“He is not really an oil man,” Naranjo said. “The talent he brings is that he’s a new person in a long line of Venezuelan businesspeople who deal in influence. Their big lever is connections and influence. It is know-who, not know-how.”

In a recent interview with Spanish language media, Rubio defended Betancourt, praising his oil company’s work in Venezuela and his support for factions of the Venezuelan opposition in exile.

Rubio downplayed the legal scrutiny Betancourt has faced, saying a review conducted with U.S. law enforcement agencies indicated “there were no investigations of him in our system.”

“The talent he brings is that he’s a new person in a long line of Venezuelan businesspeople who deal in influence. … It is know-who, not know-how.”

It remains unclear exactly how Betancourt shed the travel restrictions imposed by European authorities. But The Washington Post reported that senior Trump administration officials, including Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, former Attorney General Pam Bondi and then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, petitioned their foreign counterparts to allow Betancourt to travel freely and to close their investigations into him and his business ventures.

The Trump administration’s next hurdle to working with Betancourt was figuring out how to legally invest. The government’s $200 billion investment agency, the International Development Finance Corporation, was created to do just that but is currently barred by U.S. law from operating in Venezuela.

At different points through the summer, aides to Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought stepped in, pressing Defense and State department officials to consider alternate financing paths, according to one person familiar with the deal’s progression.

By July, the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital, headed by David Lorch, emerged as a potential solution.

Lorch, who had moved to the Pentagon from Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg’s private equity firm, Cerberus Capital, quickly embraced the idea, according to people familiar with the deal. Lorch and other Pentagon and State Department officials flew to Caracas in the final days of that month and agreed in principle to a deal. The details would be hammered out back in Washington, the people said.

On Aug. 5, Betancourt strode into a conference room behind the art deco facade of the old Greyhound Bus Terminal in downtown Washington that houses an auxiliary Pentagon office. The assembled Defense Department officials gave the Venezuelan billionaire the red carpet treatment, lining up to shake his hand, according to people familiar with the meeting. But some in the room were stunned to discover that the U.S. government was preparing to do business with Betancourt, the people familiar with the meeting said.

Betancourt was accompanied by Jacob Hirshman, the chief executive and co-founder of Erebor Bank, the first new bank chartered after Trump returned to office, according to people familiar with the meeting. The bank, backed by Trump supporters and investors Peter Thiel and Palmer Luckey, has vowed to reconnect Venezuela to the world economy.

Lorch told the group, which included dozens of former Wall Street associates he’d hired into the office, that the alliance with Betancourt was a major “opportunity” to fulfill one of the Trump administration’s top goals, securing benefits to the United States and Venezuela for decades to come.

The meeting touched off a month of around-the-clock calls and video conferences.People familiar with the deal’s progression said Lorch soon became involved in structuring key aspects of the deal beyond its financing, including how the board would sit for 15 years and choose its successors. One said he put an explicit premium on setting up the venture in a way that it could not be undone by Trump’s successor.The months of work on the deal burst into public view on Aug. 28 with a Trump announcement on Truth Social.

“The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” Trump posted on a Friday night.

Your support today will directly fund investigations that shine a light on urgent issues: corporations prioritizing profits over public safety, health insurers denying coverage to patients, unintended consequences of new laws and more.
