https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US extreme weather survivors are a growing group – now they want to be a political force
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
At a gathering in Texas, near where floods killed 136 people last year, survivors are united on the need for urgent action

It may be a club none of its members actually want to be in, but the growing number of people in the US affected by extreme weather disasters are starting to organize into a political force.

Severe wildfires, floods storms and other calamities now touch the lives of huge numbers of Americans – about half of all people in the US by one estimate – as the climate crisis supercharges extreme events. Some survivors are now coalescing to push for improved disaster response and even action on the politically contentious issue of global heating.

“The group has grown, sadly, quite rapidly,” said Sierra Kos, a film-maker who co-founded Extreme Weather Survivors after being caught in a pall of toxic smoke from wildfires in rural Oregon in 2020 as she attempted to take her son to receive medical care.

“I am positive though that survivors of extreme weather will not just shape political outcomes and policies moving forward but also look to run for office,” said Kos. “This is going to be a constituency that policymakers and politicians need to listen to.”

The shock of extreme weather help bonds people in an unusually bipartisan way, Kos said, with politically diverse delegations of survivors making several trips to press lawmakers in Washington.

Survivors overwhelmingly feel that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) should be more responsive but also that disaster aid should not be politicized, Kos said. Donald Trump has enacted deep cuts to Fema, stressing that states should take more responsibility for disaster relief, and has been accused of withholding resources from states that did not vote for him.

“I think you’d be hard pressed to find a group of people that are more united on the core issues,” Kos said of her organization’s survivor network, which now spans around 2,500 people across the US.

A meeting of survivors this month in Texas, though, suggests that politicians don’t yet feel overwhelming political pressure to engage with those affected by extreme weather.

In a community hall in Kerrville, near where flash floods killed 136 people in 2025, all of the Texas gubernatorial and senate candidates were invited to speak to survivors but only one, Vikki Goodwin, Democratic candidate for lieutenant-governor, showed up.

“We are seeing more extreme weather in Texas and we need to do more for survivors,” Goodwin told the group.

Several of those who spoke at the event expressed surprise at how they had been thrust into the role of advocate. “I just didn’t care about politics. I never thought I’d be doing this,” said Kylie Nidever, a former pre-school teacher whose childhood home in Hunt, Texas, was one of the few in the neighborhood to survive inundation from the floods.

“It radicalized me to see my community devastated, and there was some survivors’ guilt, too. So that was initially how I dealt with the trauma,” said Nidever, who has spoken to a committee of Texas lawmakers and expressed shock at the lack of Fema response to similar, less deadly, floods that hit the region again this year.

“We need more authority, we need more guidance, we need more support,” she said. “And seeing that not happen even after this second flood has lit a fire under me. I guess I knew it would flood again, I just didn’t think it would happen so soon.”

Georgia Bishop, whose best friend Felicity Jarmon died in the 2025 floods, said she still finds it difficult to talk about the disaster, which caused “devastating” damage to her own home. But the 19-year-old has got involved with Extreme Weather Survivors events and traveled to Washington in June to speak to members of Congress about the need for better flood warnings, such as sirens, for communities like hers.

The reception she got was mixed, she said, with some lawmakers appearing uninterested while some promised to do more. “My only thing is that you say you’re trying, you say you’re working, and I will believe you on that, but will it be in time before something really is going to happen again?” Bishop said.

“I just want to help make sure that this never happens again, because I never want that to happen again to anybody.”

Survivor groups routinely share tales of frustration when dealing with the labyrinthine and often fruitless process of dealing with insurance companies, Fema and a catalogue of other local, state and federal government agencies to get the resources to piece back together shattered homes and lives.

Several people at the Texas meeting spoke of how they will soon be evicted from temporary housing, with no payments from Fema or other bodies to help make their ruined homes habitable again. Other survivors have been rejected multiple times for Fema assistance, under this and previous administrations.

“Fema is terrible, they are awful, they are so inefficient and antiquated that people give up, it’s not worth your stress,” said Elisabeth Anderson, whose home in Atlanta, Georgia was hit by Hurricane Helene in 2025.

After several rejected applications, Anderson had to take out a loan to cover the $400,000 needed to repair her home from flooding that had forced her, her husband, child and two dogs to sit on the top of their car to escape the rising waters. “It was insane, like something out of a movie,” she said of the floodwater. “I definitely thought we’d die at one point.”

Many survivors complain about the lack of preparation and response to major disasters, Kos said. “There’s this sense of ‘we are American, we should have the best possible evacuation notifications’ – and the fact that all of that funding has been cut really infuriates people,” she added.

These common woes help pull together survivors from different parts of America’s politically fractured landscape, even helping foster a greater appreciation of the role of the climate crisis in disasters among those previously skeptical of such links. Scientists have been clear that global heating likely worsened the floods in Texas and elsewhere, as well as recent heatwaves and wildfires.

“I used to think global warming was just indoctrination, then I lived through a flood where I genuinely thought I was going to die,” said Mike Malcolm, a 70-year-old Republican voter from Leander, Texas, who wrote his social security number on his hands and feet in case his body had to be identified as muddy water from the 2025 floods filled his home.

Malcolm’s children helped him understand the link between the floods and global heating, he said. “We have to be willing to have difficult conversations and look for solutions,” he added. “I keep asking myself: what do we want to teach our children, and what kind of future do we want to leave them?”

Still, the political toxicity around climate change, which Trump has called a “hoax” and “bullshit”, means that the “C” word is not prominent in survivors groups, sporting names such as Extreme Weather Survivors and Rebuild: the National Disaster Survivors Association.

“It’s crazy to me that the term climate change can be divisive, but it can be,” said Nidever. “That’s why we just say extreme weather. We use that instead of going there with climate because it’s more inclusive and it’s not a hot-button term.”

Campaigns for the upcoming midterm elections have barely featured mentions of the climate crisis or major disasters, despite American voters wanting politicians to speak more about these issues in the wake of the hottest summer on record in the US and the onset of one of the strongest ever El Niño events, which is already bringing flooding to the west coast and is set to spur even worse heat next year.

Survivors may not make a major impact at this election but many feel this will change as warping weather continues to raise home insurance rates and other costs and pockmark large chunks of the year with toxic wildfire smoke, flooding and heat.

“More and more people know someone affected by this. I was in shock when this happened to me again but I’m not the only one affected by multiple events,” said Alex Webber, a medical journal illustrator who evacuated New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina hit in 2005, only to relocate to Asheville, North Carolina ahead of Hurricane Helene, which tore through the city two years ago.

“The money for the region from Fema just hasn’t showed up,” said Webber, who said much of Asheville remains moribund two years after the flooding. “A lot of politicians were paraded downtown, it was like disaster tourism and we felt like zoo animals. Then they disappeared and we are just old news now.

“You can’t combat climate change unless you accept it exists; it feels our pigeons are clearly coming home to roost. We can’t keep delaying. We have to solve this, it has to stop being a partisan issue. But there’s nowhere safe now. No-one is immune from this.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Oliver Milman in Kerrville, Texas

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘What are you implying?’: El-Sayed confronts critics head-on as attacks ramp up
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Against a backdrop of rising Islamophobia, Michigan Senate hopeful has challenged premise of repeated questions on Muslim Brotherhood, Israel and faith

As a candidate positioned at the center of what researchers say are the worst Islamophobic attacks seen since the aftermath of 9/11, many would expect Abdul El-Sayed to simply defend himself and move on.

Instead, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan has repeatedly demanded those who question his positions on Israel, the Muslim Brotherhood, and his faith, explain the premise of their enquiry. Rather than let others put his loyalties on trial, he has tried to put their assumptions on trial.

The clearest example is a town hall exchange from this weekend that has been viewed more than 50m times. A man in the crowd demanded he disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. “Sure, yeah, absolutely,” El-Sayed said. Then: “What are you implying? Do you assume that I wouldn’t?”

For five minutes he stayed on it, comparing the question to the doubts people once had about JFK’s Catholicism, and asking the man whether he would disavow reading religious doctrine into American law. The man said he wouldn’t. El-Sayed told him he was the one who needed to understand the constitution. The room cheered.

The man turned out to be Thomas Teepell, a former aide to the Republican senator Josh Hawley. His father’s firm was paid $250,000 by a non-profit for “canvassing and influencer marketing” against El-Sayed, according to an FEC filing, though nothing shows the son was paid. The connection did not establish that the question was coordinated, but it added another dimension to an exchange that showed El-Sayed’s preferred method in action.

His direct approach has yielded a nickname: “Mean Mamdani”, or “Meandami”. While New York City mayor and fellow Muslim Zohran Mamdani wins people over with warmth, El-Sayed goes at his critics head-on. Both have made establishment resistance part of their political identity, but El-Sayed treats confrontation itself as a way to expose what he sees as a rigged political debate.

It is an approach the Democratic establishment doesn’t quite know what to do with.

When Mamdani-backed challengers beat establishment favorites in New York primaries, the party’s minority leader in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, played the wins down. In Michigan, state governor Gretchen Whitmer and senator Gary Peters backed El-Sayed’s rival for the Democratic nomination, Haley Stevens, and more than $60m in outside money, mostly from pro-Israel groups, went her way. El-Sayed won by about a point and a half, after daring the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) to “come for me”.

His victory in the primaries challenged the assumption that a Democrat who confronts powerful donors over Israel must pay a prohibitive price.

During the primary, an interview with CNN’s Kasie Hunt encapsulated the same dynamic. Hunt asked three times whether Israel has a right to exist. “I’m not going to play this gotcha game,” El-Sayed said, adding: “Nobody’s ever asked me whether or not I believe Palestine has a right to exist.”

He challenged why his position on Israel’s existence was being treated as a test of political legitimacy while the equivalent question about Palestine went unasked. The real question was whether Israel has a right to “our tax dollars”, he suggested.

After winning the primary, Fox’s Jesse Watters spent 25 minutes with El-Sayed on Ice, Sharia and transgender issues. “You want to bring up all this culture war,” El-Sayed told him, repeatedly steering back to prices. The strategy is to stop his opponents from defining the election around his identity, and keep it focused on the economy and healthcare.

But the tactic doesn’t always land. On Meet the Press, asked whether he or his family had any ties to the Brotherhood, he said no, twice. The Washington Free Beacon then dug up his half-sister’s 2012 posts about their mother’s activism in the group in the 1970s. There is no evidence El-Sayed took part, and he told NBC: “I wasn’t raised by my mother.” But he also called the questions “not serious” and asked the host if he was “insinuating that somehow I was lying”.

All of this is happening against a hostile backdrop. Islamophobic posts naming him jumped almost 1,900% in the week after his primary win, according to the Center for the Study of Organized Hate. Tuberville called him a terrorist within hours, and Donald Trump has called him a “jihadist”. A Rutgers report released on Tuesday, covering more than 30 cases since 2001, finds the same playbook has been used against Muslim candidates again and again.

The media response to El-Sayed’s viral town hall exchange offered another example of the divide. CBS News chief legal correspondent Jan Crawford praised the questioner and described El-Sayed’s response as a “self-own”, then deleted the post and apologized. The episode raised questions about how a Muslim candidate’s refusal to accept an insinuation can itself be portrayed as evidence against him.

CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss has reportedly encouraged the network’s journalists to pursue story angles related to El-Sayed’s supposed sympathy toward the Muslim Brotherhood. (A spokesperson for CBS News told Semafor: “We’ll let our journalism – not baseless accusations – speak for itself.”)

For Muslim and Middle Eastern candidates, the burden can extend beyond proving they can do the job, to proving their religion, family and foreign policy views do not make them a threat. Legitimate scrutiny of a candidate’s record is necessary; treating Muslim identity as grounds for suspicion is something else.

El-Sayed’s confrontational style is an attempt to force this distinction into the open, even if his instinct to counter-attack can sometimes work against him.

His primary victory suggested that Democratic voters wanted more than a candidate who shared their policy preferences. They wanted one willing to confront the donors and party leaders they believed had ignored their values.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: ‘Hunted like animals’: inside Trump’s war on the people who build America
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was a house framer before he was killed by ICE agents. Countless other Latino builders in Texas live in fear of a similar fate

Every morning long before dawn, while America sleeps, legions of Texas construction workers grab their fluorescent vests and hard hats, sling ladders and tools into their trucks, and head down the highway for another day of grueling labour under the blistering sun.

Elsewhere, before the first flush of daylight settles over Texas’s concrete sprawl, a separate army gets on the move in a fleet of shiny unmarked SUVs. They hover at gas stations, prowl around bodegas, pounce on the highways.

They’re on their way to work too. But the federal agents who form this second army are on a different mission.

Unlike the builders, they are not forging the US’s future one new starter home at a time. Their job is to pursue those who do the building: they follow the framers, track down the roofers, chase the cement masons and concrete finishers.

“In Texas, you go deer hunting in the early morning,” said Jacob Monty, an immigration lawyer in Houston. “That’s what they are doing. They are hunting for construction workers, early in the morning, like you would an animal.”

Texas and its construction workforce are the ground zero of Donald Trump’s latest mass deportation effort, dubbed ICE 2.0. As the US president has pivoted from last year’s militarized “invasions” of Los Angeles and Minneapolis to this year’s less visible but no less devastating stop-and-search tactics, he has found rich pickings in Texas.

Texas is seeing by far the greatest number of ICE arrests in the country. More than 12,000 in July alone, almost double the number in the next most affected states, Florida and California.

Many of the detainees are Hispanic builders. Of every 10 construction workers in Texas, four are foreign born, most of whom are Hispanic and undocumented.

“This is low-hanging fruit,” Monty said. “If you target Texas Hispanics in trucks, you have a good chance of nabbing an undocumented person, and feeding the mass deportation machine.”

But there is a price to pay for ICE casting its dragnet through Texas barrios and building sites as it seeks to meet its new target of 3,000 immigration arrests daily. The street-level apprehensions are roiling the state, distorting its economy, forcing up house prices and the cost of groceries.

Hispanic families are also being torn apart. Hardworking people are being pushed into the shadows, others disappearing as they flee the country or are deported. The foundations of new homes are lying unfinished, building sites empty.

With the midterm elections just days away, and hugely consequential congressional races as well as the gubernatorial contest hanging in the balance, there are also political costs. Trump appears to be digging a hole for himself with Texas’s Hispanic voters.

Latino Texans who were born in the US or have naturalised, and thus can vote, are increasingly angry and confused. Many of them voted for Trump two years ago, attracted by his promise of a stronger economy and a fortified border that would keep out “criminal” immigrants.

They delivered Trump a historic victory, even in majority-Hispanic districts that had been Democratic strongholds for more than a century – voters like Sergio Benavides, 44, the owner of a home-building construction company in the Texas borderlands of the Rio Grande valley.

A naturalised US citizen, he voted for Trump in 2024. He liked his campaign promises that he would lower prices and secure the border. When people warned him it would turn sour, he didn’t listen.

He’s listening now. The prices of homes, food and gas have all gone up. Workers have to be paid more because so many have been deported. One of his subcontractors and his wife have disappeared, picked up by ICE, leaving behind three US-citizen children.

“That makes me sad,” he said. “We are here to protect our families, send our kids to college, to learn and grow. This is not what I thought when I voted for Trump.”

Benavides is part of a backlash that is showing up in the polls. Latino voters are turning against the president on the very issues that drew them to him – the cost of living, and immigration enforcement.

A poll last month from Equis Research found that disapproval of Trump had risen to 63% among Texas Latinos. In the critical US Senate race, which could determine which party holds the upper chamber during Trump’s final two years in office, 58% of likely Latino voters intend to back the Democratic candidate James Talarico, while only 33% support the scandal-ridden Republican, Ken Paxton. This, in a state that last returned a Democrat to the US Senate in 1988.

Latinos make up a third of Texas’s registered voters, the second-highest number in the country. And they know it.

A member of his crew comes to pick him up at his house in Houston. They drive around in their shared white truck gathering other crew, then head off to the site of a new apartment complex where they spend the next 10 hours laying TV and wifi fiber optic cables.

It’s their speciality. They are good at it, and in demand. If only they were left to get on with it.

Around the beginning of the year Osorio, 50, noticed a surge in ICE street activity. “There were so many more sheriff’s vehicles, state troopers, ICE on the highways weaving between cars checking plates.”

As an undocumented Mexican who came to the US in 1993, aged 17, he knew he was vulnerable. But he thought he had some cover. His US-born daughter Gabriela is serving as a marine at Camp Pendleton in California. She has helped him apply for residency, and the paperwork is being processed.

Still, he wasn’t taking chances. He changed his habits. No going out of the house unless for essentials. No nights out at the movies. He couldn’t stop working, or else how would he pay the bills? But now he wears a button-down shirt on the drive to the site rather than his fluorescent yellow vest. No point advertising himself as a construction worker with ICE on the hunt.

He told his company he didn’t want to work outside Houston any more. The freeways to Austin and San Antonio were crawling with cop cars. “The company told me there weren’t any jobs here – either go out of town, or you don’t work.”

So he took a job in Austin. On 10 June, as he was returning home after another 10-hour shift, a sheriff’s car did a U-turn on the freeway and pulled him over. The officer said it was because his truck had a faulty rear light, but Osorio asked himself how they could have known that as they were traveling in opposite directions. More likely, he thought, was that his vehicle has a clear front screen. “They could see we were Hispanic.”

Within two minutes of the traffic stop, ICE SUVs blocked him in, front and back. The speed with which they appeared, Osorio realised, meant it had to be coordinated.

He told them his daughter was a US marine. He showed the officers the receipt for his residency application. An ICE officer replied: “Oh, that doesn’t count.” They took him to a freezing cell, the notorious las hieleras, and from there to an immigration detention facility near the border. He spent 40 days in the wilderness of ICE custody, until Monty got him released for lack of due process.

As he awaits his appeal, Osorio continues to work. Those bills keep coming, his children need feeding. On drives to work sites in Houston, he thinks about his daughter serving the country whose government wants him gone. He worries about his youngest child, an autistic boy, and what will become of him. He imagines returning to Mexico, a place he hasn’t known for 33 years.

As he drives, he spots apartment blocks all over the city that he helped put up. And he’s proud. “See those – I worked there 10 years ago. Or those – we built them 15 years ago.”

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, a Mexican national, had been in the US for 35 years, two longer than Osorio. A house framer, the skilled worker who puts up the wooden skeleton of new houses, he carried out his days with an identical drill. Out the door at 5am, pick up the crew, 10 hours of hard graft, then relax on the balcony of his self-built Houston home listening to tierra caliente music with Ñoño, his beloved dog whom he named after a podgy 1970s Mexican sitcom character.

When ICE began to crank up its street arrests in February, Salgado spotted an opportunity. Many workers were too scared to leave the house, and new homes were standing half finished. A fearless entrepreneur, Salgado began accepting jobs that other undocumented framers like him would not contemplate.

He took precautions. He swapped his construction vest for a suit jacket while driving to work. He removed the jumble of blueprints, invoices and receipts from the dashboard of his white van. It was like his mobile office on wheels, but it branded him as a building professional, so he cleaned it off.

As time passed, and the ICE presence grew more oppressive, his three sons grew concerned. They are all American-born US citizens, and Salgado had high aspirations for them. They weren’t going to be builders like him – they were going to be educated, fulfill their own American dream. Ronaldo Salgado, the eldest, is a history teacher; Lorenzo Salgado Jr studied at the prestigious Tufts University and is now an engineer in Washington DC; and the youngest is at college, also studying engineering.

The sons got together and prepared a plan for their dad. They gave him a phone number that he should call if ever he were stopped, and they made sure he carried a “know your rights” card in his wallet. They made him swear that he would never sign any ICE form, as they feared he would be hoodwinked into self-deporting.

Lorenzo Jr had an additional reason for being worried. On 29 October 2025, he was walking to work in DC. It was early morning, around the time his father would be getting on the road. That day he had a big presentation to make to a government agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

As he was walking down Georgia Avenue in the direction of the White House, he saw two unmarked cars coming towards him. They passed him and then both turned around, stopping on either side of him in a pincer movement. His first thought was that he was about to be mugged. But then he realised they were federal agents. They asked him his name and where he was going. As soon as they heard his perfect English, saw his neatly buttoned shirt, and took on board his FAA destination, they backed off. “OK, go ahead, you’re good to go.”

Lorenzo Jr has no doubts he had been ethnically profiled. He was shaken by the experience. It freaked him out about his dad. If they could stop him, a Tufts-educated engineer on his way to advise the US government in the nation’s capital, what could they do to his father, an undocumented framer?

On 7 July, Lorenzo Jr got a call: his father had been stopped by ICE. He rushed to the airport and got on the first flight to Houston. Onboard the flight he saw a news report of an undocumented person in the city who had been shot by an ICE officer.

As the plane was still mid-air, Lorenzo Jr refreshed the article. The headline had been revised from “shot” to “shot, killed”.

I met Lorenzo Jr and Ronaldo Salgado in a coffee shop about 10 minutes from where their father had been shot through the window of his van after ICE mistook him for a Guatemalan national they were searching for. There was a memorial shrine to their father in a corner of the cafe, with his photo in the center surrounded by lit candles and rosaries, a few of his construction tools, a sombrero and the Mexican flag.

Ronaldo talked about how his father had been hunted down by ICE “because he didn’t look a certain way. He didn’t match what an American is supposed to look like.”

How cruel that was, he mused, considering that his dad had spent his entire life pursuing core American values. Ronaldo rattled them off: “Work hard. Pay your taxes. Have a family. Educate them. Good things will come to you.”

Lorenzo Jr talked about how his father was killed by a government agent three days after the US celebrated its 250th birthday. On the Fourth of July, he himself had attended the fireworks in DC. He felt proud then to be an American. He recalled the history he had studied of Frederick Douglass, WEB Du Bois, Malcolm X, Martin Luther King and his biggest hero, Abraham Lincoln. He felt he was well on the way to achieving his own American dream.

Three days later, he suffered what he describes as “extreme patriotic whiplash”. Now he has only one purpose: to get justice for his dad.

Drive 350 miles south-west from Houston and you come to the border region of the Rio Grande valley. Life down here is a perfect fusion of Mexican and American. Tejano, they call it.

The valley is dusty and hot. Midday temperatures frequently hit 105F (40.5C), rising to 110F. The day I visited a building site in Harlingen, about 10 miles from the border, it was already exceeding 100F, with the sun beating down mercilessly.

Four framers were working under a cloudless sky, erecting the second-floor wooden structure of a duplex house. They were swaddled in loosely fitting clothes to protect them from the sun, with heavy tools slung around their waists. They looked unperturbed by the heat, but then this was a normal working day – 10 hours a day, six days a week.

The oldest of the four, the sombrero-wearing Joaquin, is the age that Salgado was when he was killed by ICE. Two months ago, Joaquin’s wife was taken away. She was hunted down on her way to work at a restaurant, and is now in detention awaiting deportation to Mexico.

“Now I’m scared they will grab me,” Joaquin said in Spanish. “We have three kids, born here, who will take care of them?”

His crewmate, Fortino, 38, his face hidden behind large ski glasses, is also undocumented. Two of his uncles have disappeared. “Right now, nothing is safe,” he said. “In Mexico we were taught to put our trust in God and go to work. But every single day we are looking over our shoulders, thinking that maybe today is the day they catch us.”

The third crew member, Alexis, 33, has a green card. That doesn’t stop him feeling anxious. He drives to the site now only in ordinary civilian cars, never in white vans or trucks and never with tools visible, and he regularly changes the route.

I asked him what he thinks of the argument that Trump made to the American people: that American jobs should be for Americans, not for those unlawfully residing here. Alexis laughed.

“Sure, that’s fine,” he said, also in Spanish. “But most Americans don’t do the work. They won’t do it. This is hard work, under the blazing sun. No shade. Educated Americans, they demand an office job with air-conditioning. So it’s us Latinos who do this work.”

The fourth crew member, 20-year-old Isaias, chimed in. He is a US-born citizen. Americans, he said, were used to having it easy. “Nacen en cuna de oro” – they’re born with a silver spoon in their mouths.

The four framers filled the air with the noise of banging and hammering and sawing. To my untrained ear, it seemed a healthy cacophony: the sound of a new neighbourhood, a new community, being born.

But for Ronnie Cavazos, 49, the manager of the site, the noise is symptomatic of sickness. There isn’t enough of it. It should be decibels louder. The four framers working on the house, there should be three times as many of them. Last week the site was entirely empty, he couldn’t find any crews. All his subcontractors had ceased operating.

“We don’t have enough guys to do the work – they’ve been picked up, or are too scared to leave the house, or they’ve given up and gone back to Mexico.”

Sites that were taking six months to complete are now taking 10 months. Overheads are going up. In the summer he had to pause construction for 60 days; there were no framers to call on.

Cavazos is doing all he can to protect his workers, and encourage them back on site. He has erected a fence right around the 16 duplexes he is building to keep ICE out. He expects it’ll cost him $30,000 in fencing alone, but it will be worth it if it buys some peace of mind.

He led me inside an unfinished duplex and showed me a Murphy door under the stairs. It leads to a space where workers can hide should ICE turn up.

One day his construction manager called Cavazos and alerted him to an ICE agent trying to enter the site. “I told him, ‘Get the fuck off my property!’ A lot of my workers ran away. Some went and hid behind the Murphy door.”

A few months ago he had a crew sleep on site. They were so afraid of being pulled over as they drove to work, they decided to sleep right there on the concrete foundations until the job was done.

“This is America,” Cavazos said, shaking his head. “What the fuck! This is America.”

Cavazos is chair of the South Texas Builders Association (STBA), the largest such alliance in the Rio Grande valley. He and his fellow construction leaders have decided enough is enough.

“It’s time to speak up,” Cavazos said. “A lot of people have been too afraid of what Trump will do to say anything. To stay quiet is not American. If we can’t tell the truth, what the fuck are we doing?”

In July, STBA, with the American Business Immigration Coalition Action that advocates for comprehensive immigration reform, staged what they called a “rally in the valley”. The gathering, close to the border in Pharr, Texas, concluded with a warning for Trump and the Republicans: if you carry on hunting our people, you will feel our wrath.

Benny Melendez, the owner of a small construction company in Weslaco, Texas, handles government relations for STBA. He voted for Trump in 2024, but since then 10 of his workers have been taken by ICE. As a result, his home-building projects are going up at half speed, and completed homes are costing $30,000 or more above the usual price.

As part of his lobbying duties for STBA, Melendez began gathering smartphone footage of ICE raids and posting them on social media. They show masked police and ICE agents swarming over building sites, without a warrant, apprehending workers. In one video, a framer can be seen running off the site with agents in hot pursuit, like a fox and hounds.

In another a police officer escorts several workers, hands cuffed behind their backs, from a site. “We’ll be back for the guys on the roof,” the officer threatens, adding: “It’s hot up there.” “We’re used to it, it’s what we do,” one of the workers replies. “We probably built your house.”

Melendez made his own video to add to the collection, in which he vents his fury as a one-time Trump voter. At the start of the video we see Melendez fully masked, dressed in a black tactical utility uniform. He pulls off the mask and throws it to the ground. “Only cowards hide under a mask,” he exclaims. Next he discards his heavy armor flak jacket and replaces it with an orange construction vest and hard hat. “These are the tools we need to make America great again.”

Melendez told the Guardian that for him, the Trump administration’s assault on the Rio Grande valley amounted to a humanitarian crisis. “The dignity of our community is being walked all over.”

STBA executives decided earlier this year to blast that same message directly at the Trump administration. A delegation of seven STBA leaders, including Melendez and Cavazos and the association’s CEO, Mario Guerrero, demanded a face-to-face meeting with the Department of Homeland Security in Washington.

I wanted to hear about that meeting, so I visited Guerrero at the hub of his construction company in Edinburg, Texas. There was no mistaking his loyalties: the stars and stripes and flag of Texas dominated his office.

Guerrero describes himself as a fourth-generation Mexican-American, and a proud patriot, who voted for Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024. “I’m probably more American than JD Vance. More American than Marco Rubio. Definitely more American than that damn Stephen Miller,” he said.

He voted for Trump because he was incensed by the record number of undocumented immigrants who crossed the border under Joe Biden, and because he thought Trump, as a businessman, would strengthen the valley’s economy.

But he has been dismayed since Trump’s return by the soaring prices, and by the number of hardworking, law-abiding immigrants that the administration has detained.

Guerrero told me what happened when he joined the STBA delegation to DC. They were given just 15 minutes to address top DHS officials, who sat impassively along one side of a long mahogany table.

ICE was spreading fear throughout the valley, the Texans, lined up on the other side, began. Agents were storming on to building sites without warrants, arresting people with work permits, using unmarked SUVs to hunt concrete trucks, then carting off all the workers as they poured foundations.

Shortly before the allotted time was up, the Texans were invited to give closing words. Guerrero took this as his cue. He locked eyes with the top ICE official right across the table from him. He informed him that he had voted for Trump every time he was on the ballot.

“You know what you guys are doing is fucked up. If you carry on like this, your administration is going to lose.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Scream review – Wes Craven meta horror remains super smart and scary 30 years on
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Self-aware romp through the genre is redolent of the 90s but its ghost-masked killer is as alarming as ever

The 30th anniversary re-release of the original Scream, from screenwriter Kevin Williamson and director Wes Craven, brings us to a locus classicus of the 90s: a self-aware romp through the horror genre. It features Skeet Ulrich’s high schooler Billy Loomis announcing that reality is “all one big movie – but you can’t pick your genre”, which is the meta-slasher equivalent of Jacques Derrida’s belief that there is nothing outside the text.

A ghost-masked killer is murdering and terrorising the bland Californian town of Woodsboro, and we begin with his gruesome assault on Casey (Drew Barrymore); he makes chilling calls to people’s landline phones, in an era where that meant you more or less had them pinned them down to a certain location. (The existence of “cellular” phones was still an exotic novelty.) The mother of teen Sidney (Neve Campbell) had been brutally killed previously, a crime pinned on local man Cotton Weary (a cameo for Liev Schreiber) who is now in jail. But was he really guilty? Now Sidney is at risk like everyone else.

Yet as one of the local horror fans points out: you’re safe as long as you stick to the three scary-movie rules: stay a virgin, avoid drink and drugs, and don’t utter the hubristic phrase “I’ll be right back”. (Perhaps someone could also have pointed out the difference in vulnerability-level between blondes and non-blondes.) So when Sidney has sex, she puts herself in mortal danger. Meanwhile, brash local TV reporter Gale Weathers (played by Courteney Cox, already a star from Friends) figures she can crack this case wide open, and she has a tendresse for the goofy young cop deputy Dewey Riley, played by Cox’s future husband, David Arquette.

The self-aware references are many, and the action of Scream is often wittily juxtaposed with narrative sequences from a classic such as Halloween. What comes across from watching the original Scream 30 years on is that there is one horror classic that could be an influence but isn’t referenced, perhaps because it isn’t canonical in the purist slasher-film sense: Truman Capote’s reportage history In Cold Blood. (I think of this, when one character here dismisses the idea of “motive”.)

What also emerges, perhaps not entirely intentionally, is how very obnoxious, and very possibly sadistic, male movie fandom can often seem in itself. It’s very apparent when the killer smugly challenges his victim with a trick question about who the killer is in the first Friday the 13th. This film is brash and smart in that distinctive 90s way – and the title sounds like an order.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Usha Vance is a closed book – but her Goodreads account is surprisingly revealing | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
From Roman-era political potboilers to stories of Catholic priests struggling to impose their authority, what could the reading list of vice-president JD Vance’s wife be trying to tell us?

Usha Vance, a very clever woman with dubious taste in men, likes to keep herself busy. While lesser mortals (me) waste their one wild and precious life watching Love Is Blind, the second lady has various self-improvement projects on the go. She’s brushing up on her German! She’s hosting a literacy podcast! She’s rereading the classics! And, of course, she’s juggling four young children and the demands of being the vice-president’s spouse.

How does she do it all? With the help of taxpayer dollars, I suspect. Easier to get some reading done when you’re being helicoptered everywhere and, as JD Vance has boasted: “People go to the grocery store for me.”

But I’m not here to moan about how much the Vance family is costing the taxpayer. I am here to share an important, and only slightly unhinged, theory. The second lady is notoriously private; people are constantly trying to understand what she’s thinking. Now, I think I’ve figured it out. While Usha herself is not an open book, I reckon her bookshelf – or, rather, her Goodreads account – is trying to tell us something. Either that or she’s trolling us.

Remember, for example, when JD was trying to mansplain Catholicism to the pope back in April? (Pope Leo XIV, to be clear; pope Francis died the year before, one day after meeting Vance.) As all that was happening, Usha picked up Death Comes for the Archbishop by Willa Cather. Which, to be wildly simplistic, is a book about a French missionary priest tasked with imposing order and Catholic norms on a church in New Mexico, where some other naughty priests have gone a bit rogue. Make of that what you will.

Then there’s all the recent chatter about whether JD Vance is going to be Trump’s heir. Per her Goodreads account, Usha has just finished reading I, Claudius by Robert Graves. That book is about a member of Rome’s imperial family who survives vicious palace politics because everyone underestimates him. All the infighting and murder means he’s the last man standing and becomes emperor almost by accident. Is that a reflection on her husband’s political future? Perhaps! Now that Usha is done with Graves, she’s reading the nonfiction book Medieval People by Eileen Power. Perhaps to prepare for the dark ages her husband is helping drag the country back to.

“Arwa,” you might say, “you’re reading way too much into this!” Of course I am. I have a degree in English literature: that’s three years of explaining how doorknobs in Jane Austen novels represent the hollowness of colonialism. Nevertheless, I think I may be on to something. Let’s just hope that Usha’s next choice of reading material isn’t Annie Jacobsen’s Nuclear War: A Scenario.

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/21/trum.title: Trump’s Obsession With Somalia Isn’t Just Racist. It’s Been Lethal.
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/21/trum.text:
The Trump administration is waging a multi-pronged war on Somali people, painting them as criminals, murderers, and terrorists and using multiple federal agencies to target them at home and abroad. The campaign includes military attacks in Somalia, as well as arrests, deportations, and the weaponization of federal law enforcement agencies against immigrants and the Somali American community in the United States, including the recent use of Homeland Security agents as a goon squad to target Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar.

In his second term, President Donald Trump has routinely cast Somalia as lawless and Somalis as violent. Meanwhile, his administration has, largely without public knowledge, killed hundreds of people in Somalia, claiming they belong to terror groups. Trump personally ordered the death of a Somali man within days of regaining the White House, according to his counterterrorism czar Sebastian Gorka. The administration claimed, without offering any evidence, that the man was connected with the Islamic State terror group. Trump has sought to do the same with Omar.

Homeland Security agents raided Omar’s Washington, D.C., home last Monday, three weeks before the midterms, in which she is seeking reelection. The Trump administration reportedly launched the investigation to build a case to strip Omar of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her. (Omar fled war in Somalia with her family when she was 8 years old, later immigrated to the U.S. as a refugee, and became a citizen in 2000.) The administration has also issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to some of Omar’s relatives. On Monday, conservative media outlets reported that federal prosecutors obtained Omar’s DNA as part of their investigation.

“This is what happens in a dictatorship. The leader identifies his political, ethnic and religious enemies, and his agents scramble to do his bidding and make him happy,” Zaynab Mohamed, a Somali immigrant who represents Minneapolis in Minnesota’s state Senate, told The Intercept. “Representative Omar is the latest subject where Trump identifies the target and his minions go looking for a crime. The cases always fall apart, and this one will, too.”

Trump claimed not to have ordered the raid, but throughout his second term, his Justice Department has repeatedly targeted his political enemies — from New York’s attorney general, to the former head of the FBI, to members of the Federal Reserve. “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ,” Trump said to reporters. “I have nothing to do with it.”

Omar called it “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” She added: “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.” Omar’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment from The Intercept.

With the Somali community, Trump found a target that he could attack with Islamophobic, racist, and xenophobic rhetoric, without incurring much mainstream backlash, said Jaylani Hussein, the executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.

“As immigrants, Muslims, and — most importantly — Black people, it’s the trifecta,” he told The Intercept. “None of us expected the scale and level of the vitriol. But despite this, it’s at the point that the traditional media almost ignore the attacks on the Somali-American community because it’s not a large constituency. Trump says these things, and people just move on.”

Most Read Inside ICE, Officials Question String of Trump Admin “Midterm Panic Moves” Karl Loftus Lockheed Martin Showered Susan Collins With Cash as F-35 Program Hit Turbulence Noah Hurowitz President Apocalypse Tom Engelhardt

Over the last decade, Trump has overseen the killing of as many as 1,500 Somalis in more than 400 attacks, according to a count by New America, a D.C.-based think tank. During his second term alone, the Trump administration has conducted more than 200 airstrikes in Somalia, including close to 90 this year, claiming to target terrorists.

The U.S. military has been at war in Somalia for almost a quarter-century, conducting air attacks and commando raids aimed at the terrorist group al-Shabab as well as the Islamic State group, while the CIA and special operators created local proxy forces to conduct low-profile operations on behalf of America. At the same time, the U.S. has provided Somalia with billions of dollars in counterterrorism assistance.

U.S. attacks in Somalia have skyrocketed during Trump’s terms in office. From 2007 to 2017, under the administrations of George W. Bush and Barack Obama, the U.S. military carried out 59 declared airstrikes in Somalia. The Biden administration conducted 51 declared strikes over four years. During Trump’s six years in office, the U.S. has launched more than 400 attacks against purported militants.

The U.S. rarely offers any evidence that those killed are members of terrorist groups, much less leaders. A New America analysis found militant leaders comprised just 1.7 percent of those killed. Africa Command refused to provide requested evidence that any of those killed in airstrikes in Somalia this year were militants. “All U.S. strikes in Somalia are conducted in close coordination partners [sic] against designated terror groups,” an AFRICOM spokesperson told The Intercept by email.

“Trump has conducted more drone strikes in Somalia than Bush, Obama, and Biden combined. And so many civilians have died,” historian Elizabeth Schmidt, the author of “Foreign Intervention in Africa After the Cold War: Sovereignty, Responsibility, and the War on Terror,” told The Intercept. “They were often just young men living in an area where it was easy to label them jihadis. And it turns out they had nothing to do with terrorism.”

The U.S. claims that it has only killed six civilians over almost two decades of war in Somalia. A count by the airstrike monitoring group Airwars put the number at as much as 2,600 percent higher. A 2023 investigation by The Intercept determined, for example, that a drone attack in Somalia during Trump’s first term killed at least three, and possibly five, civilians, including 22-year-old Luul Dahir Mohamed and her 4-year-old daughter Mariam Shilow Muse. At the time of the attack, the U.S. announced it had killed “five terrorists” and that “no civilians were killed in this airstrike.”

Trump calls Somalia a “third-world” or “fourth-world nation,” says that it “stinks,” and disparaged Somalis who come to the U.S., saying “we’re going to go the wrong way if we keep taking in garbage into our country.”

His most xenophobic consigliere also claims Somalia is responsible for violence that has caused people to flee the country. “The entire Somali refugee program is predicated on a lie,” wrote Trump’s deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, Stephen Miller, late last year. “Destroying your own country does not give you the right to become a citizen in ours.” But this faux history disregards America’s decadeslong role in fomenting violence in Somalia and destabilizing the country.

“The presence of Somalis in the U.S. has a lot to do with U.S. wars in Somalia.”

A casualty of the Cold War geopolitics that led to widespread conflict, political repression, and millions of deaths across the developing world, Somalia has experienced persistent political instability and strife since the late 1960s. In recent decades, the country has suffered civil war, famine, droughts, a longtime al-Shabab insurgency, and persistent humanitarian crises.

Over the last quarter century, the U.S. has intensified conflict in Somalia through direct attacks; training, funding, and running proxy forces; and funneling in weapons and other military assistance to one side of a civil war. As early as 2007, the Pentagon was aware that there were fundamental flaws with U.S. military operations in the Horn of Africa, and Somalia devolved into another forever war stalemate. This has continued, despite the record number of airstrikes in Somalia under Trump.

Before Trump took office, in 2016, Islamist militants in Somalia killed 4,281 people, according to the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, a Pentagon research institution. By August, this year’s total hit 6,731 deaths, a 57 percent increase. An analysis by the Costs of War project at Brown University found that instead of eliminating militant groups, the U.S. counterterrorism campaign in Somalia was “ensuring that the conflict continues in perpetuity.” An AFRICOM spokesperson said the command’s “operational focus remains on working with partners to degrade terrorist organizations to create the space required for Somali-led governance and stability.” But Trump claims Somalia has no government, no military, and is “not even a country.”

“ They weren’t coming because they wanted a better job. It’s because they feared for their lives and their children’s lives.”

The Intercept interviewed people displaced by the forever war in a camp on the outskirts of Somalia’s capital, Mogadishu, in 2023. “We had to leave because of the drought and the conflict,” a mother of seven told this reporter. She was one of more than a dozen women from the Lower Shabelle region of southwest Somalia who spoke to The Intercept after fleeing the front lines of an offensive by the U.S.-backed Somali government against al-Shabab. Since Trump first took office, the number of Somalis forced from their homes has almost doubled from 2.4 million to 4.4 million.

“I don’t think most Americans realize that the presence of Somalis in the U.S. has a lot to do with U.S. wars in Somalia. U.S. military intervention made a bad situation worse. This led to a surge of refugees and asylum-seekers to the U.S.,” said Schmidt. “They weren’t coming because they wanted a better job. It’s because they feared for their lives and their children’s lives.”

During Trump’s first term, his administration acknowledged “the ongoing armed conflict” as a reason to extend temporary protected status — which grants legal status, work authorization, and protection from deportation — to Somalis in the U.S., noting the security situation was “fragile and volatile, with ongoing armed conflict among government forces, clan militias, African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) troops, and al-Shabaab.”

Original reporting. Fearless journalism. Delivered to you. Will you take the next step to support our independent journalism by becoming a member of The Intercept?

By signing up, I agree to receive emails from The Intercept and to the Privacy Policy and Terms of Use.

Despite the increase in violence, according to Pentagon statistics, the administration terminated Somalia’s TPS designation earlier this year. More than 1,000 Somali asylum-seekers have been ordered deported since February; more than half the deportation orders involve Somalis living in Minnesota, a nearly tenfold increase from 2025, according to a Minnesota Star Tribune investigation.

About 84,000 of the 260,000 people of Somali descent in the U.S. live in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area, according to the Census Bureau’s annual American Community Survey. The overwhelming majority are American citizens. Almost 58 percent were born in the U.S. and 87 percent of foreign-born Somalis are naturalized citizens.

The administration targeted that Somali community during a violent immigration crackdown in and around Minneapolis known as “Operation Metro Surge” during late 2025 and early 2026. “I don’t want them in our country,” Trump said in December 2025. The next month, he said: “Every one of them should be forced to leave this country, including Ilhan Omar.”

During Metro Surge, federal agents shot and killed protesters Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti. They, like Omar and hundreds of drone strike victims in Somalia, were labeled as terrorists by the administration without providing evidence.

“If the president can threaten to denaturalize and deport a member of Congress, no one is safe.”

During Trump’s second term, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have also arrested hundreds of Somali people, with reports of assault and mistreatment at the hands of federal agents.

Trump recently seemed to call for vigilante violence and threatened to back it with federal force. “The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants,” Trump posted on Truth Social earlier this month. “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Hussein, of CAIR-MN, said Trump’s rhetoric was endangering the Somali community. “Every few weeks, he’s literally going on a tirade. And I don’t think he’s ever spoken about other people the same way. He literally put out the message saying, ‘go fight them. I’ll come and help’ on social media,” he told The Intercept. “We’ve seen bullying. We’ve dealt with harassment. We’ve have some assaults.”

Trump has routinely demonized Somalis by tying the broader community to a high-profile fraud case: the alleged theft of $250 million from a pandemic-era program that provided food for children. The former leader of Feeding Our Future, the nonprofit at the center of the case, is white, although most of the defendants in the related cases are of Somali descent. “The Somalians, they’re crooked as hell,” Trump ranted at a Cabinet meeting in May, with the administration offering escalating and unverified claims, including reference to a “$19 billion Somali fraud scandal.”

The Trump administration’s effort to denaturalize and deport Omar is part of a broader push to strip naturalized Americans of their citizenship, with those of Somali descent specifically singled out. “I would do it in a heartbeat if they were dishonest,” Trump said in an Oval Office interview earlier this year. “I think that many of the people that came in from Somalia, they hate our country.”

Trump’s border czar Tom Homan said on Saturday that he had been “told they have a strong case” against Omar. “Of course, if you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody. We’ve done it before,” he told Fox News. The rarely used denaturalization statute has been most famously employed to strip citizenship from Nazi war criminals, like John Demjanjuk, a former death camp guard and retired U.S. autoworker convicted on 28,060 counts of being an accessory to murder.

Mohamed, who in 2022 became the first Somali woman elected to the Minnesota Senate, called out Trump’s push to expel Omar as a grave threat to the country. “If the president can threaten to denaturalize and deport a member of Congress, no one is safe,” she told The Intercept. “This is a test of our democracy, and even Republicans should be speaking out about it. If we don’t defend the rights of Ilhan Omar, Somali-Americans, immigrants, and Trump’s political targets, we lose everything.”

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

I’M BEN MUESSIG, The Intercept’s editor-in-chief. It’s been a devastating year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

Mississippi has yet to release any support for its claim that a “thorough and impartial” review showed the shooting was “justified.”

At least 10 patients with kidney failure near Taiz, a city under a Houthi siege, died because they were unable to get to their dialysis treatments.

The Republican running for Senate in Michigan is directing campaign funds toward chartered flights, a Miami car service, and BMW repairs.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: ‘Sham tribunal’: one family’s battle with Louisiana’s ‘feudal’ eviction courts
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
In rural Louisiana, eviction hearings are held at kitchen tables and other unorthodox venues – and many justices have little legal training

The eviction notice stuck to Lesley Wilson’s door, with two streaks of green tape and a hand scrawled note, was left at a precise moment of crisis in her life.

It was April 2025 and Wilson, a 54-year-old mother of six, was living with her partner and her 11-year-old granddaughter named Kat in a stilted bungalow, surrounded by sugar cane fields and a small trailer park. She loved the peace and quiet of the place, about 10 miles from the rural city of New Iberia in southern Louisiana. A crawfish pond was a short walk away.

But the night before the notice was stuck to the door, her partner became abusive again, she told police. She called 911 multiple times, and she and her granddaughter cowered inside a locked room, according to interviews and her statement to police.

“It kept escalating and escalating,” she recalled. “And I don’t handle conflict well. My brain just shuts down.”

He eventually agreed to leave their home, a police report confirms. The following morning she obtained a temporary protective order to keep him away. As she returned from court, she was met with the eviction notice that Kat plucked from the door.

The handwritten note cited the reason as “disturbing the neighbors + fighting”.

Louisiana’s Violence Against Women Act, passed in 2015, limits landlords’ ability to evict victims of domestic violence, mirroring similar protections in federal law. But, Wilson said, despite her presenting the temporary order to her landlord, he made clear he wanted her gone.

“He told me he knew the justice of the peace,” she recalled. “And that: ‘All I’ve got to do is tell him what I want, and that’s the result I’ll get’.”

Three weeks later, Wilson arrived for her eviction hearing in Justice Patrick Broussard’s courtroom – the backroom of a small public library.

Across rural Louisiana, dozens of justices of the peace courts operate on the fringes of judicial formality. These elected justices, who are required only to hold a high school education and be of “good moral character”, are allowed by law to hold court in unconventional venues. They are required to complete 16 hours of training every two years. Many do not even comply with this basic requirement, a Guardian investigation has found.

Because operating expenses for these low-profile courts are paid with court fees, hearings can be held in almost any venue, except for those that sell alcohol. Living rooms. A spare bedroom. An old jailhouse. A small office next to a roadside daiquiri bar. A cellphone repair store. All have been used to hold eviction proceedings in Louisiana justice of the peace courts, according to interviews with 10 housing attorneys who have practiced within them.

The use of such venues “gives the signal to both parties that evictions are unimportant and uncomplicated legal proceedings”, argued Hannah Adams, a senior attorney at the National Housing Law Project. “But the stakes are so extreme for a tenant and these are often complicated cases.”

Adams is a former legal aid attorney in Louisiana and has fought evictions in venues including a pool house and a kitchen table. She described the process as “a real holdover from the feudal era”.

Documents released under a public records request reveal that dozens of justices mostly in these rural locations are failing to comply with their mandatory minimum training requirements.

For the past nine months the Guardian has been examining evictions in Louisiana’s justice of the peace system, which operates in every parish of the state except the city of New Orleans.

A handful of these justices earn hundreds of thousands of dollars a year via revenue from court filing fees. Critics argue the system is plagued with potential conflicts of interest and routinely denies tenants their rights to due process under the US constitution.

The majority of these courts sit in rural settings with lower populations, so most generate little income. A Guardian review found that 52% of Louisiana’s 390 justices declared less than $10,000 in fee revenue over the past decade.

Still, experts say, the conflicts of interest are baked-in to the system – they exist no matter how much money is made.

“Whether it’s a high-volume court or a low-volume court, the more landlords that file evictions, the more dollars go into the justice of the peace’s pocket,” Adams said. “It’s still extra money for the person who is supposed to be a neutral arbiter of these cases.”

She had found pro-bono legal assistance after the eviction notice was stuck to her door, a civil rights attorney named Donald Hodge.

She arrived at her local public library 20 minutes early and headed to the backroom that served as the courtroom. The corridor was daubed with canvases decorated with self-help quotes: “be humble & gentle”, “be patient & kind”. A librarian could be heard scanning books around the corner.

“It all felt illegal,” Wilson recalled. “I don’t know how else to describe it.”

As she waited inside, she spotted her landlord, named Steven Freyou, and Justice Broussard deep in conversation outside, she said.

“That’s not right,” she thought to herself. “That’s not how this should go.”

What followed, Wilson would later claim in legal filings, was a “sham tribunal”.

Justice Broussard sat behind a gray library table near a large US flag. “All rise,” his constable instructed the almost empty room. Wilson’s attorney, Hodge, listened in over the phone.

The justice first announced it was his intention to “wrap this up quick”, according to Wilson and Hodge’s recollection. It was his birthday and he had plans. It was also, the justice remarked, the first time he had ever presided over an eviction hearing where a tenant had secured a lawyer.

The grounds for Wilson’s eviction had now multiplied. Along with claiming she was “disturbing the neighbors”, her landlord was now also arguing that she had not paid her rent on time. This, Wilson said, was untrue. The cash in hand payments had always been delivered correctly, she claimed. Documents supported her: a petition of eviction signed by her landlord on 21 April recorded that “$00.00” rent was due.

The petition also stated her landlord was seeking eviction because her lease had expired.

To her horror, the court then called a witness. It was her ex-partner, who she now had a full restraining order against. He was invited to testify over the phone and supported the landlord’s claims that she and her ex-partner were behind on their rent, Wilson and Hodge recalled. His evidence was not sworn testimony, according to a lawsuit Wilson is currently pursuing in federal court.

“I was in shock,” she remembered. “Like, you’re really going to let him testify over the phone?”

At the hearing Wilson and her attorney also argued that her lease contained an unlawful clause that permitted eviction if law enforcement was called to the home.

But, as proceedings progressed, the lawsuit claims, Broussard “threatened” to charge Wilson three months’ rent as a bond if she appealed his decision and delayed the eviction. It was an amount she had no means to pay. She felt as though she was being bullied into submission.

After a few minutes weighing up her options she decided it would be impossible to stay in the house at this point, and asked Hodge to try and negotiate a deal. She was adamant she would not pay another penny in rent. After a 40 minute hearing, Wilson signed a “judgment of compromise” that compelled her to leave in a month’s time and forfeit her deposit.

It would not constitute a formal eviction, “but I was still being forced out,” she said.

The federal lawsuit that Wilson filed alleges she was harmed by violations of due process and seeks damages against Broussard and her landlord. It claims the agreement was “extracted by duress, by the threat of an unpayable appeal bond … by the admission of ex parte hearsay from her abuser, and by the deprivation of every procedural safeguard to which a litigant before a court of law is entitled.”

Hodge recalled in an interview: “There was no order. No rules. No procedure. No law.”

“It speaks to why the justice of the peace system needs to be reformed,” he said. “Lesley is just one example of who this is happening to every day across the state. And most people don’t know their rights and can’t afford an attorney.”

Justice Broussard and the landlord, Freyou, did not respond to detailed questions from the Guardian.

In legal filings, Broussard laid out a lengthy list of defenses, including judicial immunity, and denied any unlawful conduct. He also claimed a lack of sufficient information to assess Wilson’s status as a survivor of domestic violence. His motions, which seek to have the lawsuit thrown out of court, were written by Louisiana’s attorney general’s office, which was representing him.

The landlord denied he violated any state or federal law in terminating Wilson’s lease, according to recent legal filings, which also seek to have the case thrown out. One document states Wilson’s lease was not ended “because she contacted law enforcement, obtained a protective order, experienced domestic violence or possessed any protected characteristic”.

Louisiana is among 17 states that allow judges, including magistrates, with no law license to preside over eviction hearings, according to research. The state mandates that all justices must attend a minimum of 16 hours of training every two years. Legal experts and housing advocates argue these basic training requirements are not enough to prepare many of the state’s justices to handle often complex areas of housing law.

A separate lawsuit being pursued as a class-action in federal court in Louisiana argues the system routinely violates tenants due process rights. The case, which was filed by the Southern Poverty Law Center and the National Housing Law Project, notes that the state’s justice of the peace training manual contains just 10 pages on evictions “and does not include any relevant or even binding case law governing evictions”.

Justice Steven Sanders of East Baton Rouge, the named defendant in that litigation, acknowledged under sworn deposition that the training courses contain roughly “an hour and half of discussion” on evictions.

Despite these basic requirements, documents obtained by the Guardian under a public records request revealed that over a quarter of the state’s justices failed to comply with even these standards. An analysis by the Louisiana attorney general’s office, covering the years 2024 and 2025 showed that 98 justices and 142 constables had failed to complete mandatory training. The documents revealed that 37 of these justices and 52 constables had completed no training at all during that time period.

Broussard, a retired engineer who indicates online that he does not hold a law license, was among those listed as non-compliant, having attended only nine hours of training in two years.

“These courts are acting like their own fiefdoms, where they get to act with impunity and do not do the training they are required to,” said Micah West, a senior supervising attorney at the Southern Poverty Law Center.

The Louisiana attorney general’s office did not respond to detailed questions from the Guardian.

In the month after her case was in heard in eviction court, Lesley Wilson scrambled to find a solution to impending homelessness.

She had been unhoused once before in her life, at the beginning of her last marriage when her partner lost his job and they lived together with their children in a tent for three months.

She always prided herself on being resourceful and working to solve problems in her life. Her only available option this time was to move with her granddaughter to the small, unincorporated town of Harwood in Texas and live with a friend, about 400 miles away from the rest of her close family. She borrowed money to rent a U-Haul, and put all of her belongings into storage: mattresses, bed frames, the balls of yarn for her crochet business, and her late daughter Kelsea’s ashes.

Wilson had become her granddaughter Kat’s legal guardian shortly after she was born. Kelsea, Kat’s biological mother, had died in 2018 after a fentanyl overdose at the age of 21. Kat had only been told about her birth mother two months before the eviction ordeal. She still calls Wilson “mom”.

They arrived in Harwood, a dusty railway town with a population of less than 200 people, and moved into a travel trailer that sat in the front yard. There was no running water. Electricity ran via a cable plugged into an outdoor shed, which frequently short circuited. It had only one bed.

She was able to get a job at a local Buc’ees, working a night shift at the bakery. The pay was decent, but the living situation became untenable within a month. They decided Kat would have to move in with relatives in New Mexico. Wilson would stay behind. It was the first time they had been apart in all of Kat’s life.

“I already felt alone,” Wilson recalled. “But now even more so. I just couldn’t see the way out. Every single thing that has happened in my life since is tied to that eviction proceeding.”

In 2009 a justice of the peace named Keith Bardwell from the rural parish of Tangipahoa caused outrage after he refused to conduct an interracial marriage, over four decades after the landmark US supreme court decision Loving v Virginia ended legal restrictions against people of different races being married. In a referral to the state’s judiciary commission, the ACLU of Louisiana argued that Bardwell’s “blatant bigotry poses a substantial threat of serious harm to the administration of justice” and highlighted he was “persistently failing to follow the law”.

The case was extreme, but Louisiana’s justice of the peace courts have faced recurring criticism for over a century. Ahead of a state constitutional convention in 1921 a local legal scholar named Edmond Bourgeois argued for complete abolition of the system, citing concerns over justices’ lack of legal training. In an article for the Loyola Law Journal, he wrote: “The procedure is a farce; the courts’ dignity a myth; justice is frequently absent; attorneys hold the courts in virtual contempt, and in some instances indignantly refuse to practice before them.”

Nonetheless, accounts from the time indicate that while the issue was considered, the lobbying in support of them “was too strong”.

The convention occurred at the height of Jim Crow segregation in the south, and was attended by only white delegates, who passed further laws to suppress black citizens from voting in the state.

The pro-justice of the peace lobby remains strong in Louisiana today. Along with voting earlier this year to expand the territorial jurisdiction of some high-earning justices, the Republican dominated legislature passed a law in 2020 that exempted justices of the peace from mandatory retirement. While all other judges in the state must leave the bench when they turn 70, Louisiana’s justices of the peace can continue holding court at any age from 18 onward. A November “Peace Talk” newsletter published by the Justices of the Peace & Constables Association, announced the news under the headline “Mission Accomplished!”.

Last month, the state’s rightwing attorney general attended the annual justice of the peace convention and described their “vital role in serving our communities and upholding the rule of law”.

Part of Lesley Wilson’s salvation came in the form of a garden ornament. While scrolling online one evening earlier this year, she discovered a resurgence in the popularity of a beloved porch goose statuette and in particular the tiny custom stitched sweaters people were dressing their porch geese in. She put her crochet skills back into use, and started posting images of her unique goose sweater designs. They came in many colors and were selling for $50 a piece.

Wilson had spent eight months living in the travel trailer in her friend’s yard. But with the Texas winter setting in and no heating inside, the cold had begun to bite. She moved again to live with another friend in Colorado, hauling many of her belongings with her.

Two months later, Kat left New Mexico and rejoined Wilson in Colorado. They had been apart for more than seven months.

The funds from her increasingly popular porch goose knits had helped make it possible to think about moving back to Louisiana. She found a small place with two bedrooms and told Kat it was time to come home.

In May of this year they got the keys to their new rental unit, and spent two full days cleaning it out front to back. Wilson’s possessions were split between storage units in Texas and Colorado. Some items had been destroyed or damaged after a leak in one of the units; an antique mirror passed down between generations, a bedroom set now covered in mould.

“Unless you’ve lost everything, you just don’t know what it’s like,” she said.

After moving in, both were still sleeping on air mattresses as they waited for a final large delivery to arrive from Colorado amid persistent delays. The shifting timelines compounded her worry and triggered diverticulitis, a painful inflammation of the digestive system linked to stress.

One day in late August, the delivery arrived. There was one item she had thought about more than any other: Kelsea’s ashes, which she had left behind in Colorado.

She found them days later nestled in an unmarked box. She placed them on the kitchen counter and felt a moment of relief.

Additional reporting by Tom Richards, Rachel Shur, Sophie Sullivan, Cameron Armstrong, Mahesh Makani, Georges Lebreton, Izzy Kiff, Frederick O’Brien and Aliya Uteuova
