I have tested consumer products ranging from automatic coffee makers to Xbox peripherals for publications including PC World, Reviewed.com, CNET and many others. For all of those publications, I bring an objective scientific eye to testing products and helping consumers make better buying decisions. For the Filter US, I’ve tested the best gadgets if you live with back pain, the Kiziks hands-free shoes and an eco-friendly mattress.

A good pair of slip-on shoes should be comfortable, cool looking and ridiculously easy to put on. So, I wore each pair for dog walks and ambles around town, logging how comfortable they felt on the move and around the house. I asked friends, family and strangers on the street to tell me what they thought of the look of the shoes, talking to sneakerheads, comfort fans and all those in between. To test the slip-on feature, I looked at how easy it was to step into the shoes and put them on, when paying attention and without looking down: imagine leaving a shoe-free friend’s house encumbered with leftovers and stepping into them by the door. A good pair of slip-ons should guide your feet into place, with a clean action to the heel mechanism that makes them work. A bad pair will need you to move your feet in a certain way, or, God forbid, reach down and move the shoes to get them on.

After this review was completed, I donated all of the slip-on shoes to Goodwill.

For more, check out our guide to tech neck fixes, the best seat cushions and products that offer help with back pain.

While most of the shoes from Swiss manufacturer On are for runners, hikers and other athletic types, the Cloud 6 are an all-day casual wear pair, made with the same hi-tech materials. Translation: they are incredibly light on the feet – just 9.4oz – but slip on easily and feel very tough and resilient. They’re also the only pair I tested that included a second pair of longer faux laces and extended eyelet loops that allow you to lace them further down the top of the foot, more like a pair of running or hiking boots, which disperses the pressure for those with sensitive feet. The fit of the 8.5 men’s pair I tried was good: tight without being restrictive.

I found the step-in mechanism to be darn near perfect: just step into the shoe, slide your foot forward and the heel pops back up without catching, hitching or any excess pressure. In use, the fit is tight but comfortable, with enough give for all-day use and enough ventilation to avoid stinky feet. Taking them off is easy too: just hold down the heel with the other foot and step out. Plus, as someone who loathes heavy branding, the On logo is small and easily mistaken for a bit of abstract stitching.

It’s a shame that … they are so expensive and are only water resistant, not waterproof: to be able to walk in the rain, you’ll need to go up to the Cloud 6 waterproof, which adds a waterproof membrane and another 1oz (28g) of weight and another $20.

At about $65 the HeyDude (or, as they put it, HEYDUDE) Men’s Wally Stretch Sox Slip-on Loafers are about half the price of our top pick, but they are much more than half as good. This low price gets you a solid pair of comfortable, cool-looking loafers with a decent step-in design, good traction and a comfortable fit. The 8.5 men’s size I tried came in a denim-like blue fabric material that felt breathable.

The fit on these shoes is comfy but much looser than the others: they don’t feel loose enough to slip off, but they are a lot looser on the heel and across the top of the foot. The laces are adjustable, but it isn’t easy. The shoes are also machine washable once you remove the laces and insoles: HeyDude recommends a minimal amount of liquid detergent and a gentle cycle followed by air drying. The step-in design is fine: I found that the heel back bent over easily and popped up without problems when I stepped in and pushed my foot forward, but that’s partly due to the looser fit and more, erm, loafing design of these loafers. The fit of the 8.5 men’s pair that I tried was OK, although the loose design of these shoes makes it a little difficult to judge: they feel large by design.

It’s a shame that … they lack the more refined fit and finish of other pairs I tested. Without socks, a couple of rough seams by the tongue rubbed against my bare foot, especially as the shoes moved around while I was walking. Adjusting the laces requires unpicking a tight knot inside the decorative tassel, then tightening and retying the knot without losing your spot. HeyDude is also not a name I’d relish telling someone who liked the shoes and asked me what brand they are. But, then again, I am an old fart, so if it’s hip with you kids, go for it. You be you, you wacky funsters.

Stepping into a pair of Kizik Madrid 2 shoes feels like stepping into an old, familiar and very comfortable pair: they just feel right straight out of the box, zero breaking-in required. The stretchy upper knit material gives them plenty of flexibility, so you don’t need to adjust the laces, although you can undo and retie the knot if you want. The standard lace and knot also makes them look more like normal casual shoes than some, which have a more running-shoe-like design.

The arch foam insole is quite bouncy, which gives you a certain spring in your step, but not enough to make you feel like a kangaroo. There is plenty of toe space, and Kizik offers an extra wide version for those with wider feet. The fit of the 8.5 men’s pair I tested was spot-on: comfortable without being tight, with room for the toes to wiggle.

The step-in mechanism (which Kizik refers to as the Internal Cage) is easy: step into the shoes and the heel top bends over under the ball of your foot. Push your foot forward and the heel top pops back without catching or scraping, so you don’t have to brace the shoes or lean on the heel, as the friction of the sole is enough to stop the shoe slipping forwards.

It’s a shame that … you can’t machine wash them: they are spot-clean only. The insoles can be machine washed and air dried, though, which is a plus for kids with stinky feet.

If your travels take you from beach to boardroom via barbecue and family bonding in a single day, the OluKai Nohea Moku has your back. Well, your feet, anyway: these breathable slip-on, no-lace boat shoes can be worn with or without socks and includes rain holes and quick-drying materials. That means you can go from skipping through the surf to slouching poolside without stopping to dry your shoes or worrying about the stank of damp socks.

Personally, I think that all sounds completely exhausting, but my experience with the Nohea Mokus (translation: handsome in Hawaiian apparently) while dog walking and gardening was great: the 8.5 men’s size pair I tested were instantly comfortable and the tension of the laces and the stretchy design held the shoes on without pinching. (Which is good, because the laces can’t be adjusted.) When I wore them without socks, I had no issues with rubbing or pinching on my feet.

It’s a shame that … the slip-in design is rather rudimentary compared with others: the heel back of the shoe is made of a more flexible material than the sides, so it bends under the ball of your foot when you step in, but doesn’t always pop back up around your heel when you move it forward. I found I had to shuffle my foot around or even, heaven forbid, lean over and pull the heel back up to get them on.

Like most deck shoes, they have minimal cushioning or bounce, which makes for a different feel when walking that might not suit those with foot pain or who have to stand for long periods at work. The thin breathable design does mean your feet get a bit chilly in colder climates: a quick dog walk on a chilly New England fall morning led to rather chilly toes for me, even with socks on.

Instant comfort: the Glover Peaks slip on like a glove and fit tightly, but without pinching. The thick memory foam insole and rubber soles provide a bouncy, boing-y feeling that feels like it is pushing you to run. Skechers refers to this design as Glide Step, but it’s more of a push step – there’s a forward tilt and push from the structure that makes you feel like stepping forward. If you are inspired to go out for a jog (or even a long walk), your feet will stay cool and dry as these shoes have great ventilation. You’ll also stay firmly on the sidewalk: the rubber soles have excellent grip for navigating the obstacle course of daily life, and the memory foam insole provides comfortable cushioning.

The step-in system is the best of the ones we tested: even though the back of the shoes is high, it bends easily under your foot, then pops right back behind the heel when you push your foot forward without catching or pulling on your sock.

Kudos also goes to Skechers for providing the widest range of shoe sizes available, from a diminutive size 6.5 up to a Bigfoot-esque size 16. There is no wide fit version, though. I found the fit of the 8.5 men’s pair I tested to be just right, with a comfortable fit for the heel and toes. The shoes are also machine washable.

It’s a shame that … the branding on the shoe is a bit vulgar, with a giant logo that is obvious even with black thread on black fabric. The rubber soles provide plenty of grip, but can also be rather squeaky on wooden floors.

The ridiculously named Skechers Slip-ins: Max Cushioning Glide-Step are our top pick for those of us who have to work for a living: they offer the same comfortable, bouncy insole as our casual pick, with the same Glide-Step design that feels like it’s pushing you onwards. That also helps if you are on your feet all day: the cushioning means you can shift your feet easier and keep the circulation in your feet going. That’s joined with a few work-related innovations, such as a Goodyear rubber nonslip insole and ASTM-F2892-rated electrical hazard insulation, which means they won’t provide an easy path for electricity if you happen to touch something live. That’s not just important for electricians: retail and other commercial workers are regularly around electrical devices that can kill.

The slip-on design is excellent, with the apex of the shoe’s back bending over under your foot, then smartly snapping back behind your heel with a slight forward motion once your foot is all the way in. It’s an impressively smooth design that just works. Plus, the shoes are machine washable.

It’s a shame that … the huge white logo branding is a bit much and seems inappropriate for a pair of work shoes. (Unless you work for Skechers, I guess.) I also found that the 8.5 men’s pair I tested felt a little tight in the toes and across the top of the foot: you might want to go up a half size from your usual.

The Ravello Penny Loafers are a comfortable, stylish pair of loafers for, well, loafing about. The design is clean and simple, and the suede-like ReVelvet material is plush and soft on bare feet. It’s made from recycled bottles (one pair takes 13 bottles, apparently) and the rubber insoles are nice and grippy for the dancefloor. The penny part of the name comes from the diamond cut in the strap over the top, supposedly allowing you to store an old penny in it so you can get home after a night on the town. (A credit card doesn’t fit, unfortunately.)

It didn’t make the final cut because … they aren’t true slip-ons: although the loose fit means you can usually slip them on and off without reaching down, there’s no structure to push the heel top back up around your feet.

The Lima 2 are quite similar to the Madrid 2, but with a cleaner design, slightly wider foot entry and tongue shape that I found more comfortable on longer walks.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the Lima 2s are a great pair of shoes, but the Madrid 2s were my preference in the end.

Magic. Well, sort of: these shoes rely on a combination of clever design and flexible materials, all covered with a tasty sauce of patent law. The specifics vary, but the gist is that a precisely formed piece of plastic in the heel provides a specific mixture of flexibility and rigidity. This makes the heel flexible enough to bend under your foot when you put your heel into the shoe, but rigid enough to snap back into its initial shape when you move your foot forward, pushing the heel back around the ball of your feet without you having to pull on it.

The real fun starts when the lawyers get involved. Kizik, for instance, has several hundred patents on what it describes as “rapid entry footwear”, while rival Skechers has their own portfolio of patents covering what they describe as their “hands-free slip-in” shoes. Kizik is now suing Skechers in the US and Europe, claiming that Skechers has used their patent designs without a license. Skechers have denied this. This case is continuing, but it hasn’t yet reached a point where either company has stopped making shoes. The winners? The lawyers, as the case is likely to drag on for some time.

Yes. Although older slip-on shoes and slippers have a reputation for loose fits and slipping off when you move your foot, none of these modern shoes have this problem. No matter how vigorously I shook a leg, danced or gyrated, they all stayed on. (Oh, the things I do for the sake of journalism.)

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.title: Musk pledges $10bn in SpaceX shares for US children: Who really gains?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.author: Nils Adler
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.text:
Elon Musk has pledged to give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States next year – a gift that could be worth more than $10bn.

“This will be the first of many,” the world’s richest man wrote on X on Monday.

About 73 million children under 18 live in the US, according to US Census Bureau data.

At Friday’s closing price of $146.03, the pledge would be worth about $10.7bn.

President Donald Trump thanked Musk on his Truth Social platform, and claimed the shares would be given to children “through TRUMP ACCOUNTS”, the tax-friendly investment accounts for children created under his signature tax and spending law last year.

Musk is the biggest known donor in the run-up to those elections, having given more than $276m to Republican groups since July.

Musk has not said which children will qualify, when the shares will be handed over, or how.

SpaceX, the world’s seventh-largest company, began trading on the Nasdaq in June at an initial public offering price of $135 per share. That price has been volatile. SpaceX shares have fallen 35.3 percent since peaking days after the listing.

The shares are currently trading at around $146 a share. Every $1 move in the share price will change the gift’s value by about $73m.

Musk owns 4.8 billion shares in SpaceX outright, according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in August.

Including unvested awards and stock options, his stake rises to about 6.4 billion shares, or 48.4 percent of the company.

Giving away 73 million shares would reduce his outright holding by about 1.5 percent, barely affecting his control of the company. That’s because his voting power, which is currently about 82 percent because SpaceX has two classes of shares, would fall by only 0.1 percentage points, according to a Bloomberg Opinion calculation.

Trump said the shares would be held in Trump accounts, and Musk thanked Brad Gerstner, the tech investor behind the accounts, for “helping enable this”.

Nearly 70 million Trump accounts have been opened, one for every child under 18 with a Social Security number, according to the White House. Investments held in Trump accounts can roll up with tax deferred until they are withdrawn when a child turns 18. Alternatively, they can be rolled into a tax-friendly IRA – a retirement account for adults – and continue with the tax-friendly status.

Under Treasury rules published on September 30, donors can now gift individual company stock to children via the accounts. Families and friends making regular contributions to a child’s Trump account are limited to investing low-risk index funds.

Families cannot refuse the shares on behalf of their children and generally cannot sell them for five years, or until the end of the year the child turns 17 if that comes sooner.

Musk cannot sell or trade most of his SpaceX shares until June 2027, the Wall Street Journal reported.

The accounts carry the president’s name, and Trump has tied himself closely to the gift.

He thanked Musk on Truth Social, saying the pledge was “exactly what was envisioned when we created TRUMP ACCOUNTS”.

The White House has presented the accounts as a signature achievement of Trump’s tax law, noting that “every single Democrat voted against” the legislation.

The pledge also marks a public reconciliation. Musk and Trump fell out in 2025 over Trump’s tax-and-spending bill, a rift Trump later called a “little dispute”.

Children will be gaining a share for free, but the gift could also save Musk money.

Donors who give appreciated stock to charity avoid capital gains tax and can usually claim a deduction, the US broadcaster CNBC reported.

As SpaceX’s founder, Musk paid very little for his shares, and selling $10.7bn of them could mean a tax bill of up to about $2.5bn.

It is “a popular practice for particularly high-income taxpayers that would otherwise be paying a high rate”, Will McBride, chief economist at the Tax Foundation, told the broadcaster in May.

Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Boulder, told Inc. magazine that millions of shareholders unable to sell would also have an interest in SpaceX’s success and in “minimising its regulatory burdens”.

For Mitchell Downey, an economist at Stockholm University’s Institute for International Economic Studies who studies political influence in the US, the more striking part of the pledge is what he called “the horseshoe aspect of this” – the idea that right-wing and left-wing policies can curve around and meet.

For decades, progressives have backed the concept of Child Development Accounts, investment accounts for every newborn designed to reduce inequality in wealth, he said. The idea was associated with groups such as the Democracy Collaborative but struggled to gain federal support. Now the idea may become more mainstream as a result of Musk’s gift and Trump accounts.

“It always felt like it might be out of reach,” Downey said. “But I don’t see how Musk’s proposal would be possible without building some infrastructure like this.”

The pledge comes just two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the two houses of Congress. All seats in the House of Representatives and one-third of the Senate are up for re-election.

Trump’s approval rating has meanwhile fallen to a record low of 33 percent, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, with many political observers expecting to see the Republicans lose seats to the Democratic Party as a result.

Musk, who campaigned with Trump in 2024 and spearheaded the president’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative to reduce the size of the federal workforce, has contributed heavily to Republican candidates in advance of the midterm elections.

“Individuals are allowed to spend their money in support of a politician,” he told Al Jazeera. “The law only gets violated when either it isn’t publicly reported, or it is part of an explicit and documented quid-pro-quo.”

But he said it does raise ethical concerns, though not ones unique to Musk’s approach.

Those concerns relate to “the outsized role that external donors play in US elections”, Downey said. In his view, they apply much like when someone spends heavily on television advertisements for a candidate.

Because Musk is the richest person in modern history, he said, it is perhaps unsurprising that he is “doing something that involves more money than other very rich people have done”.

He pointed to the Gates Foundation’s spending over the past three decades as “a different type of ‘gift to the public’”. The difference, he said, is that the Gates Foundation focuses funding on health crises in countries in Africa and South Asia – not on voters in the US.

Last year, Gates pledged to “give away virtually all my wealth through the Gates Foundation over the next 20 years to the cause of saving and improving lives around the world”.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: New prize launches for books co-written with AI
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Ella Creamer
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMs

The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA invites submissions of manuscripts co-written with AI tools, with the winner promised publication.

Entrants are asked to submit an unpublished manuscript of between 10,000 and 50,000 words, along with information about which AI model and prompt were used to generate the text. All major language models are allowed, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA. Entrants can be based anywhere, but entries must be submitted in French.

The Prix Pascal is named after Blaise Pascal, a French polymath who helped invent one of the first mechanical calculators and also wrote theological texts, including Pensées, which Pope Francis praised for its “philosophical depth and literary charm”.

While the terms and conditions ask for a work of fiction, the prize also states that submitted texts should help solve an ethical, social or ecological problem threatening humanity. The prize was founded by Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré, all of whom are technology entrepreneurs.

Rodriguez is a founding partner at the mergers and acquisitions advisory firm Avolta, and is described as a “leading figure in the European crypto and blockchain industry” on the company’s website. Serviant is a digital media entrepreneur and former chair of the LGBTQ+ magazine Têtu. Meanwhile, Mentré is a former civil servant with a PhD in philosophy who teaches at Harvard and the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. Mentré also co-founded Electis, an online voting platform.

The Prix Pascal is launching after months of controversy over the possible use of AI by finalists and winners for a number of literary prizes this year, including the Commonwealth short story prize, the Caine prize and the Prix Goncourt, France’s most prestigious literary prize.

Applications for the Prix Pascal opened on Tuesday, with entrants invited to submit via the prize’s website, and are set to close at the end of November. A shortlist of 10 will be drawn up before the winner is announced in early December. The jury will be made up of a panel of five or six writers, critics, journalists, philosophers and publishers, to be announced early November.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: ‘I’m always being real’: what on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in?
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Henry Roberts
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?

In You Can See Everything, convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes invites film-makers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into her home in a supposed act of “radical transparency”. Holmes is filmed, along with her partner, Billy Evans, and their two young children, in the weeks before starting a prison sentence for defrauding Theranos investors. “The best way for people to see who she is,” Evans says, “is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”. It may also be the best way to market “Theranos 2.0”, which the couple are working on during filming. But the documentary questions whether Holmes is presenting her authentic self or a manufactured persona. Fielder speaks for the audience when he asks Holmes in a tense exchange whether she’s “being real” with him. “I’m always being real,” she says.

That question of authenticity is at the heart of documentary film-making. You Can See Everything is as much about the ambiguous relationship between film-maker and subject as it is about Holmes herself. There is often a power struggle over narrative control in documentaries, with both sides of the dynamic wanting different outcomes from the final film. Watching You Can See Everything inevitably prompts the question: why would Holmes, days before she heads to jail, invite the scrutiny of a film crew?

Some people, like Holmes, think a documentary will help rebuild their reputation after public disgrace. When Anthony Weiner, who resigned from Congress after tweeting a photo of his bulging groin, tried to stage a professional comeback with a New York mayoral bid, he allowed cameras to film the journey. Only, he had more to hide: when further sex scandals emerged, his campaign went from a story of public redemption to innuendo-laden humiliation. And all the while, the cameras kept rolling. Weiner is a prime example of a subject losing control of the narrative.

Weiner may have wanted a sympathetic portrayal, but he should have known that film-makers always have their own agendas. In the book The Journalist and the Murderer, Janet Malcolm reflects on the relationship between journalists and their subjects: “The subject becomes a kind of child of the writer, regarding him as a permissive, all-accepting, all-forgiving mother, and expecting the book to be written by her. Of course, the book is written by the strict, all-noticing, unforgiving father.” The same is surely true of the documentarian.

When Jackie and David Siegel allowed Lauren Greenfield to film their attempt to build a modern-day Versailles in Florida, the director wasn’t giving them free PR. Rather, with The Queen of Versailles, Greenfield was interested in the corrosive effects of extreme wealth. The Siegels agreed to be filmed because they were proud of their success. When their dream collapsed following the 2008 financial crash, The Queen of Versailles turned from a story of Xanadu-like grandeur to one of hubristic overreach. David later sued Lauren – unsuccessfully – for defamation, but he should have known from the beginning: it may have been his story, but it was never his film.

A few years after Versailles, Greenfield made The Kingmaker, about former first lady of the Philippines Imelda Marcos and her attempt to return the family to power. From the beginning of the film, Greenfield said, there was a power struggle over who was telling the story. Marcos, known for her lavish lifestyle during her husband’s brutal rule, understood the power of optics. In a children’s cancer ward, she hands out money to children in a public display of compassion. “Perception is real,” Marcos says in the film, “and the truth is not.”

Some people agree to projects believing they will have editorial control. Idi Amin gave Barbet Schroeder unprecedented access after the director essentially promised that they would make the film together. But Amin was unhappy with General Idi Amin Dada: A Self Portrait and demanded some footage be cut, rounding up more than 100 French residents in Uganda and holding them hostage until his demands were met. Schroeder agreed. It helps to be as ruthless as Amin if you want final cut.

Documentaries are often about the past, but some of cinema’s most memorable moments show people acting violently in the present, fully aware that they are being filmed. Frederick Wiseman’s austere films show abuse in psychiatric institutions (Titicut Follies) and horrific police violence (Law and Order). Why did people do unspeakable things in front of a camera? “People basically go about their business,” Wiseman told an interviewer, “and the presence of the camera doesn’t have much, if any effect on their behaviour.”

But cameras did have an effect on the subjects of Joshua Oppenheimer’s The Act of Killing, probably the most morally complex example of the film-maker-subject relationship in cinema history. Perpetrators of Indonesia’s mass killings gleefully re-enact their crimes, restaging their violent memories in the style of Hollywood movies. They do not profess their innocence. Rather, they agree to be filmed because they are proud of what they did. They really do want us to see everything.

Perhaps the most interesting case of someone willingly putting themselves under scrutiny is Lance Armstrong. Alex Gibney’s documentary on Armstrong was expected to be a puff piece. When the full extent of Armstrong’s doping was revealed, however, Gibney’s film changed direction, becoming a documentary not on a cyclist’s triumph but on a master manipulator who lied to everyone, including the film-maker. In The Armstrong Lie, Armstrong admits that he “was prepared to say anything” to keep his lie going.

Some people are simply arrogant enough to think they can get away with their lies. But others become so invested in their skewed version of reality that to refuse a documentary crew would be like admitting their deception. So they welcome the cameras, often doing more damage than if they had simply retreated from public view. But unlike Armstrong, Holmes still insists she has done nothing wrong. As she says in You Can See Everything: “I have nothing to hide.”

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: ‘He had this electrical charge’: the short life and long legacy of Jason Molina, master of Americana
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Daniel Dylan Wray
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
As a documentary celebrates the late US musician, friends and collaborators describe an incomparable storyteller who brought ‘myth and magic to everyday life’

Jason Molina grew up in a trailer in the working-class city of Lorain, Ohio. The city’s skyline once flickered with blue flames and a warm orange glow emanated from clattering steel mills, but by Molina’s teenage years, Lorain was in a tailspin. “Things were really on the economic decline,” says Tommy Nickoloff, Molina’s childhood friend and director of a new documentary: You Fuckers Figure It Out: A Jason Molina Story. “Nobody had any money and we were encouraged to get out. It’s a place where the American dream was born and died. And we watched it die.”

Molina did indeed get out: the singer-songwriter released almost 20 studio albums and numerous EPs, primarily under the monikers Songs: Ohia and Magnolia Electric Co, spanning lo-fi to slowcore via polished Americana and alt-country. By 2009, he estimated he had written thousands of songs. But he died in 2013, aged 39, after years of alcoholism.

The documentary is a warm and intimate look back on Molina’s early life and how his rust belt upbringing, along with notions of home, place and landscape, became recurring themes in his bountiful songs. The audience for them has kept growing after his death: there’s been a biography, cover albums, a touring tribute band titled Magnolia & Johnson Electric Co made up of ex-bandmates, and he’s got a new generation of fans in Phoebe Bridgers, MJ Lenderman, Clairo, Kevin Morby, Waxahatchee and hyped young singer-songwriters such as Greg Freeman. “You have a moment with a handful of artists in your life where you hear their music and it clicks and you immediately fall in love,” says Freeman. “That happened with Jason’s music.”

But this wasn’t always the case. “It still shocks me how few people are aware of Jason and his legacy, especially around home,” says Nickoloff, recalling a 2006 show in nearby Cleveland that drew just 70 people.

When Songs: Ohia started in the mid-1990s, it was via lo-fi skeletal songs recorded to tape that were tender yet raw and delivered with a quivering high tenor reminiscent of Neil Young and soon-to-be collaborator Will Oldham. As grunge and alt-rock boomed, Molina went against the grain. “There was nothing less cool than a ukulele in 1994,” laughs his former bandmate Max Winter in the film. “Holy shit, he may as well have been playing bagpipes.”

But Molina was unique from a young age. A voracious reader as a child, he consumed everything from instruction manuals to foreign language poetry. His teenage years were spent as a metalhead and by the time he was at college, his fervent, enthusiastic – sometimes annoying – energy earned him the nickname “sparky”. Now writing a song a day, he would sometimes play impromptu 5am shows on a roof or porch to show them off. “I’ve never met anyone like him,” says Nickoloff. “He’s like a 20-sided die in Dungeons and Dragons. Most people are lucky if they have six sides.”

Chris Swanson, co-founder of record label Secretly Canadian, heard Molina’s first single, Nor Cease Thou Never Now, and was besotted. “We obsessively played it and drove 19 hours to New York to go see him,” he says. Songs: Ohia was the label’s second ever signing and a lifelong relationship began. “Without him there would be no us – plain and simple,” the label said after his death. A pattern of releasing at least an album a year followed, including 2000’s The Lioness, in which he decamped to Scotland to work with Alasdair Roberts and members of Arab Strap on a ghostly yet beautiful record of post-rock-folk-blues.

Emma Niblett, who performs as Scout Niblett, was a friend, collaborator and touring partner of Molina’s. “He had this electrical charge around him, which matched his nickname,” she recalls. “And he had this ability to bring myth and magic to everyday life as a master of storytelling. You never quite knew if his stories were true or fantasy or a bit of both.”

The late producer Steve Albini, who worked with Molina, also recalled this blurring of truths. “He was a big bullshitter,” Albini said in 2014. “A lot of the things that he said were fantastic and it seemed like he wanted things to be magical and awesome, and that he needed to create fables for himself to inhabit in order to do that.” Swanson describes this unusual quirk as “the elephant in every room with Jason”, adding: “He was just a consummate storyteller and if that meant him saying he was bitten by a tarantula which ended up quasi-paralysing him, then that’s the story.”

This seeped into his songwriting too: Molina’s obsession with ghosts and hauntings added an otherworldly element to his work. “The songs belong in his own secret world,” says Freeman. “There’s an internal logic and language to his songwriting, the way motifs reappear and build this imaginary psychic place. Like he’s painting a dream.” Niblett describes him as “a magician”, “incomparable” and “a one-off, playing in a major league by himself”.

In 2003, Molina released his magnum opus, Songs: Ohia’s The Magnolia Electric Co (confusingly, the name of the album then became the name of the band afterwards). Mike Brenner’s stunning, shimmering lap steel is all over the record. “When I was sent the demos, I was stunned by how much of a quantum leap it was,” he says of the progress from the previous record. “It sounded like a whole different game.” Swanson felt similarly. “You can hear it in the demos but when they made the album, it just became effervescent,” he says. “The songs had stepped up by a full magnitude of order and they just sounded timeless. It was like, holy shit! These are all-time country songs.”

Produced by Albini, with a full band, it was a lightning in a bottle moment for all involved. “The most otherworldly experience I’ve ever had in a studio,” says Niblett. “It felt like some supernatural powers were present. His writing felt like pure channelling. It was so clear, vulnerable, yet insightful, and undeniable. We all knew that something special was occurring.”

However, changing your name halfway through your career is not an ideal scenario to help boost your profile. “It was very tricky,” says Swanson. “And this was also during the era when he’d go on tour and not play any songs from the album he’d just released, and only play ones that no one’s heard before.” Molina was driven, prolific, and at times stubborn and impatient: “He wasn’t super interested in doing things twice,” says Brenner.

He was also capricious, says Brenner, which Swanson also recalls. “Very generous, sometimes to his own detriment,” he says. “He’d be like, ‘I just gave away our guarantee [fee] for the show to someone on the street who looked hungry.’ He would do very irrational things out of a generous impulse.”

Molina continued to release albums and EPs at a remarkable pace but by the end of the 2000s things slowed down. “The later it got in the story, the more stressful and darker the touring became,” says Brenner. “It became less enjoyable and I don’t think the quality of the shows were at the forefront of his mind.” Niblett recalls seeing a change when watching him perform. “He seemed to slowly disappear,” she says. “Although he was present on stage, his presence diminished. He started leaning on the band to take the weight, so his powerful, unique, and nuanced way of carrying a song was fading. I could hear and see he had lost himself. He was literally hiding behind his band in the later years.”

Unbeknown to many, Molina had begun to drink heavily. “He was a very light drinker in his 20s,” says Swanson. “But in his 30s, he went whole hog.” This eventually led to debilitating alcoholism that meant he retreated and stopped releasing music in 2009. The last four years of his life are described by his family as “pure chaos” in the documentary. For those who knew the young Molina, “it was unbelievable,” says Nickoloff. “It made zero sense. To the degree it was like: I don’t know anybody else named Jason Molina but they have to be talking about that person.”

Swanson recalls visiting him a few months before his death in Indianapolis. “He had given away all his belongings, which was something he would do routinely,” he says. “So he was living in a shell. We made the decision to move him to Bloomington, where he had more of a community, as his community was with street people in Indianapolis around the projects he was living in.”

But a week after that decision was made, Molina died of organ failure related to his alcoholism. “I honestly wouldn’t have believed it if you’d have told me years earlier that’s how his life would end,” says Niblett. “I don’t think the shock ever leaves.”

Despite being a heartache of enormous magnitude, for Nickoloff it ended up changing his life in numerous ways. “Jason’s death saved my life,” he says. “I was in a terrible spot emotionally and psychologically. He’d always been this beacon for me, and then he’s gone. But as a kid he was the only voice that was encouraging and believed in me to do something. So, in that spirit, we made this film and what a tremendous pleasure it is to be a small vehicle in helping make people more familiar with him, his work and his life. He was my homeboy.”

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Seth Meyers on Elon Musk: ‘Nobody likes him’
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
Late-night hosts discussed Donald Trump’s praise for Elon Musk as well as the physical appearance of several male US Senate candidates

Late-night hosts recapped Donald Trump’s recent comments on Elon Musk and the physical attractiveness of numerous male candidates in the upcoming US midterms.

Seth Meyers opened Tuesday’s Late Night with a nod to the world champion New York Knicks, who kicked off their season that evening with a ceremony to raise their NBA championship banner at Madison Square Garden. “Meanwhile, over at the Brooklyn Nets stadium, they raised a ‘help wanted’ sign,” Meyers quipped.

The president, meanwhile, said in a post on Truth Social that the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool was repaired, 70% filled with water and “looking good”.

“Oh man, well, you keep us posted,” Meyers laughed. “I think Trump missed his calling as a condo board president. ‘The koi pond is almost filled and the new mailbox keys are in, come find me when you can.’”

Similarly, at an executive order signing ceremony at the White House, Trump praised the Rose Garden and said “that stone is so beautiful”.

In other White House news, according to numerous reports, Trump is considering several replacements for former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, including the New York Yankees president, Randy Levine. “Because any time someone goes 17 years without winning a championship, you gotta capture that magic,” Meyers joked.

And at a recent White House science summit, Trump praised Elon Musk and said “quite honestly, there’s nobody like him”.

And on the Daily Show, Michael Kosta checked in with Trump’s efforts on the midterm campaign trail. “As we all know, he has a very important day job looking for things on the map to rename,” he joked. “But with the midterms in the home stretch, he’s also been holding daily rallies in support of embattled Republican candidates. And lately, he’s hit upon a very interesting observation about many of these men.”

Kosta then played several recent clips of Trump referring to the physical appearance of male candidates, calling them “good looking”, “beautiful looking”, or in the case of Ohio Senate candidate John Husted, “I started examining his body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete … I looked at his ass.”

“Yes, you live your truth, Donald!” Kosta joked. “It doesn’t matter what anyone says! You find a man with a nice tight ass and take him dancing in your big gay ballroom.

“And Maga, if you’re upset by this, you are the ones who love Trump because he ‘says whatever he’s thinking’,” he added. “But that’s a double-edged sword. Because sometimes you get ‘I hate immigrants’, and sometimes you get ‘reincarnate me as a desk chair so this guy can sit on my face all day’.

“But if Donald Trump is not secretly gay, what he definitely is, is an 80-year-old man,” Kosta continued. “That’s the age where the filter starts to slip and grandpa just says out loud anything that pops into his head.”

Kosta made sure to caveat, there’s “nothing wrong with being an ass guy, OK? But Trump has now spent more time thinking about this guy’s butt than how to end the Iran war,” so he had some advice: “Mr President, rub one out and get back to work!”

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: Popcorn with your Puccini: can opera on screen ever work?
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Tom Service
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
Composers have harnessed TV and cinema since Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors pulled in five million viewers 75 years ago but for my money Kombat Opera’s satire showed us how to do it best

It’s not even Halloween, but here’s an operatic Christmas story for you. This is the 75th anniversary of the first opera made for television: Gian Carlo Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors, broadcast at Yuletide in 1951 and watched by five million people across the US in a production sponsored by Hallmark. You can watch the original broadcast on YouTube: it was introduced with wit, self-deprecation and early 50s elegance by Menotti himself (vastly less charmingly, the role of King Balthazar was played by a singer in blackface). Chet Allen’s performance as the boy, Amahl, is staggering, and even more moving is Rosemary Kuhlmann’s Mother, especially in her aria, All That gold!.

Amahl is “an opera for children because it tries to recapture my own childhood”, Menotti said. It was played on US TV every Christmastime throughout the 50s, and was recorded and remade in new productions the next decade, while the BBC picked it up in 1953, and there was even an Australian TV version. Less than an hour long, Menotti’s festive fable works because of the intimacy of its story, and its refusal to patronise its intended audience.

But Amahl was a high-water mark. Another opera-made for-telly anniversary this year is Benjamin Britten’s Owen Wingrave, composed for the BBC and first broadcast 55 years ago. Britten’s piece definitely wasn’t made for children. Based on a gothic novella by Henry James, it’s the story of the pacifist Owen Wingrave’s struggles against his military forebears and his fiancee who is ashamed of him. Britten’s opera is uncompromisingly claustrophobic and intense, one of his most underrated scores – but it’s a piece that wasn’t designed to capture Amahl’s popularity on screen.

The later story of operas made for TV in Britain is more about exploration of the possibilities of the medium rather than following in Menotti’s audience-first footsteps: in the 90s and 00s there are pieces composed for TV including Judith Weir’s Armida or Jonathan Dove’s When She Died …, written on the fifth anniversary of the death of Princess Diana, and there were filmed productions of existing operas especially remade for television, such as the director Margaret Williams’s scintillating versions of Thomas Adès’s Powder Her Face or her version of Britten’s Owen Wingrave, produced for Channel 4 in 2001 to mark the opera’s 30th anniversary.

These days, opera is more often found on the big screen: cinemas all over the world can take you to a night at the opera, and here’s another anniversary for you – this autumn marks 20 years since the Metropolitan Opera started streaming its productions to cinemas, an innovation that the Royal Opera House in London quickly followed, finding new audiences, as well as a parallel stream of income and impact.

The Met: Live in HD has been controversial: Peter Gelb, the Met’s general manager suggested in 2013 that the cinema audiences were “cannibalising” the audience for live shows; but surely, from Japan to Brazil, and here in the UK, these broadcasts reach opera-lovers who are unable to go to the Met in person.

On cinema screens there are huge gains in seeing close up what the singers are doing as actors, subtleties of facial expression and the relationships between the characters on stage that you can’t pick up when you are sitting at the back of the gallery. But the essential problem with broadcasting live opera on any screen remains the same as it was in 1951. We are watching performers who are projecting through the acoustic miracles of their voices into an auditorium that seats thousands.

The intimacy of film, and especially TV, requires precisely the opposite mode of delivery. In drama on TV or film, the wonder and the illusion lies in sharing an intimacy of space and feeling with the actors, whereas the mechanics of opera work through the other end of the telescope, zooming out from their voices towards us in the audience, rather than zooming us in to be with them in each scene. Opera and film are essentially made for entirely different purposes.

But if you do want to see what happens when opera is made for television from the ground up, there’s another anniversary to tell you about: it has been 19 years since Richard Thomas’s Kombat Opera Presents, half-hour shows broadcast in 2007 that sent up TV staples from The Apprentice to the South Bank – Bragg! – Show. Thomas was hot on the heels of the success of his theatre show with Stewart Lee - Jerry Springer: The Opera, but the origins of Kombat Opera also go back to sketches in Simon Munnery’s Attention Scum series that aired on the BBC in 2001, with the soprano and contemporary music catalyst Loré Lixenberg, who made a new art-form dressed as a gothic uber-diva, filmed on the white cliffs of Kent.

Lixenberg, and trained singers including Leigh Melrose, Janis Kelly and Sophia Ragavelas made every half-hour long episode of Kombat Opera their own, but it’s the way Thomas included parts for actors including Kevin Eldon, Hugh Dennis and Jon Culshaw, and mixed all the media together, that makes these shows so compelling.

The format never feels as if it is selling either medium short: the heightened emotionalising and ridiculousness of opera serves the satire perfectly, joyously and concisely. Seems opera on screen works best when its turns its attention to the screen itself.

Talking of taking the artform into new places, Raymond Gubbay celebrates his 80th birthday with the Choir of King’s College, Cambridge at Wigmore Hall, London tonight. Gubbay’s Classical Spectaculars, his Christmas shows, his operas at the Royal Albert Hall – which included flooding the arena with 65,000 litres water every night for Puccini’s Madame Butterfly, a Turandot at Wembley Arena in collaboration with the Royal Opera House, and even his Savoy Opera venture, a brave but doomed attempt to make repertory opera work in the West End without subsidy, are some of the most brilliant, energetic, and imaginative ways of popularising classical music over the last 60 years.

To make large-scale classical music profitable is a vanishingly rare phenomenon. (Even if, while it’s true to say that as a business, Gubbay never took a penny from any Arts Council, most of the musicians and orchestras he worked with wouldn’t exist without it.) Gubbay’s 80th birthday concert will give its profits to another now Arts Council-free organisation, Wigmore Hall itself. Gubbay’s subsidy-free business model remains an impossible dream for most, but Wigmore Hall is an unlikely contemporary torchbearer for the same spirit of entrepreneurship.

This week Tom has been listening to: Anna Meredith’s Dusky, the single from her new album.

You know that feeling when you’re on the summit of the rollercoaster Stealth at Thorpe Park, and there’s that microsecond where your heart’s in your mouth before the drop? Dusky is like six and a half minutes spent in that place of delirious freefall, as rhythms grind against each other, melodic arcs rising and falling, to make time warp and your stomach pitch and yaw.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I’ve booked my first proper holiday – and it’s pulled me out of winter grimness like a magic spell
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Bim Adewunmi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Anticipating a potential spring in which I am bathed in sun on a Greek island is giving me the kind of glee that makes anything feel possible

Reader, it’s important to tell you that I’ve never been to Greece in my life. Not once. But I might be going, for the very first time, in the spring. And so, for the last week or so, all my dreams have featured fresh fish cooked to flaky perfection, a swimming pool into which I shall venture no deeper than my waist (I can’t swim), and the heat of the sun that not even the climate crisis can make happen in the UK in April.

I don’t come with a history of exotic foreign holidays. Travelling abroad fell under the umbrella of familial duty: “Going Home”, AKA a brief return to the place where my parents were born (and coincidentally more and more foreign to them the longer they lived in the UK) in order to keep the ties of kinship going and remind us of our roots. I should say we didn’t do idyllic UK-based holidays either. I read about caravans in Enid Blyton books and watched Vaseline-lensed ads for CenterParcs and knew neither was in my immediate future. I made peace with it. We just weren’t a “going on holiday” type of family. It didn’t bother me. I harbour no resentment, and honestly, feel largely equanimous when I consider this “gap” in my life experience.

But this potential Greece trip? It’s been on the back burner of my mind for years. A low-level, always-running app on my personal CPU, taking up very little energy but alive and constant. Almost as soon as I found out I was pregnant, I had a full-fledged fantasy. Picture it: somewhere in Europe 2027. A villa, a group of friends, two weeks of deep chats, delicious local cuisine, reading books and afternoon swims (remember, I can’t even swim). Our children? I dunno, somewhere safe and/or soundly asleep. My mind? Unencumbered, dreaming up the outline of my next play. My body? Relaxed but strengthened by the daily yoga session that also magically happens shortly after every sunrise. Before you ask, yes, I can hear myself. I know I sound insane. And I’m fine with it!

My friend, newly a mother of two also, is the planner of this Greece trip. She sees the vision, works at the same foolish bank of romantic illusion where I have my account. But she’s not just a dreamer. She’s done solid, boots-on-the-ground research. She’s checking dates, curating the invite list: who likes cooking? Whose vibe matches our knackered-but-trying-to-be-a-good-friend situation? How many childfree adults can we ethically invite until we have the optimal number of eyes to cover all the children who’ll be around? She’s checking availability, organising the group chat, working to make my dreams a reality. I could kiss her. And perhaps in Crete, with the permission of all affected parties, I shall.

More than the treat of a fortnight somewhere far away and yet in the company of old, dear friends, what I’m feeling most acutely is the pleasure of a promise. Having something to look forward to? A balm in the best of times. But especially so right now. I am re-emerging from beneath the cloud of the fourth (and fifth!) trimester. I read – and finished – a book the other week. I worked out with a kettlebell at some point in the past month. I went to a gig! Things are feeling viable again.

Outside of my little sphere, having something pleasurable on the horizon feels like a magic spell. There is a grimness to reading headlines in the morning that can’t be shaken off. Going on holiday clearly won’t solve these problems but my Cretan dreams give my soul small moments of uncomplicated anticipatory glee that make life worth living despite the horrors of near and far. Spring will come again, as it always does. The human race trudges on.

Perhaps I feel my most human when I am anticipating. Inside of that anticipation is the incredible knowledge that while everything is possible, sometimes I get to imagine only delightful things. It’s an excellent exercise. Like I said, a magic spell.

So here goes: I might be going to Crete with my children. What if we have an amazing time? What if this is the beginning of a new family tradition? What if the baby takes his first steps there? Could I master a couple of new recipes with new ingredients before we return home? Will 2027 be the year I start and finish Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan quartet? In Crete, anything could happen.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/capital-labo.title: Profits Are Soaring. Workers’ Share of Income Is Sinking.
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/capital-labo.author: Conor Lynch
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/capital-labo.text:
Outside periods of recession, the public mood has rarely been as downbeat about the economy as it is today, with consumer confidence at a historic low and polls recording a deep pessimism about where things are headed. Against this backdrop, political and business leaders are touting an economic “golden age,” pointing to solid growth, stable unemployment, record profits, and a stock market that seems to only go up. The vibes on Main Street are gloomy, but on Wall Street they are nearly euphoric.

One way to understand this growing disconnect between everyday people and elites is to examine how today’s celebrated gains are distributed across the economy compared with earlier periods. To do that, economists typically look at the national income and how much of it goes to workers — the “labor share” — versus the portion that flows to capital in profits and rents. (Together labor and profits make up roughly two-thirds of gross domestic income; the remaining third is absorbed by rents, taxes, and a mix of other smaller categories.)

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) tracks the labor share of the nonfarm business sector (the private economy minus agriculture) with quarterly data going back to 1947. For most of the twentieth century, that share was remarkably stable: it rose during recessions, as business income fell, and it declined as companies regained profitability, yet it never dropped below 60 percent and averaged around 63 percent. Labor’s consistent capture of about two-thirds of the national income was, in the words of John Maynard Keynes, “one of the most surprising, yet best-established, facts in the whole range of economic statistics.”

This historical pattern began to shift around the turn of the century. After peaking at 64 percent during the 2001 recession, the labor share began a long slide, falling below 60 percent for the first time in 2004 and staying there ever since. More recently, this long-term decline has accelerated. In September, the BLS announced that the labor share had dropped to its lowest level on record for the fourth quarter in a row.

The labor share now stands at 52.8 percent, more than ten points below its twentieth-century average. The downward trajectory coincides with rising profits across corporate America. As a share of gross domestic income, corporate profits are now the highest they’ve been since the early 1950s — at a time when hourly wage growth has cooled to a five-year low and is now well behind inflation.

Economists have offered many explanations for this trend. In a 2021 paper, Gene M. Grossman and Ezra Oberfield reviewed the vast literature on the subject and compiled the most commonly cited culprits, including technological change and automation, globalization and neoliberal trade policies, deindustrialization, increasing market concentration, the decline of unions, and more.

Beyond these structural causes, others have pointed to shifts in how some business owners and executives report their income. According to research by economists Matthew Smith, Danny Yagan, Owen Zidar, and Eric Zwick, roughly a third of the decline in the corporate sector’s labor share between 1978 and 2017 can be attributed to changes in how business owners pay themselves and how this income is recorded in the national accounts. They largely attribute this change to the Tax Reform Act of 1986, which encouraged firms to organize as “pass-throughs” and their owners to take income as profits rather than wages. Among pass-through firms owned by the top 1 percent, the owners’ share of value added rose from 37 percent to 48 percent between 2001 and 2014, a gain that came at the expense of their employees.

The different theories of labor’s declining share are often framed as rival explanations. In practice, they’re pieces of the same political-economic shift. The neoliberal turn of the late 1970s ushered in a new era of shareholder capitalism, which made maximizing shareholder returns the organizing goal of the corporation. To deliver those returns, America’s business leaders waged a broad assault on the labor movement, using every lever available to curb worker power. Technology, globalization, and union busting all operated through the same channel toward that end.

This reality has led some economists to put forward a more “unified explanation,” one that identifies the decades-long erosion of worker power as the root cause of labor’s dwindling share.

Dramatic as it is, the labor share decline understates how much income has moved away from ordinary workers over the last forty years, because it tells us nothing about the vast inequalities hidden within the labor share itself.

According to research by economists at the Economic Policy Institute (EPI), nearly 80 percent of the productivity-pay gap — the widening gulf between productivity growth and pay gains for nonsupervisory workers — has been driven by inequalities within the labor share, with the shift toward capital accounting for the remaining 20 percent. Before 1979, wage growth for the vast majority of workers tracked closely with productivity gains and with the growing compensation of high-income earners. Since then, most of the gains from productivity have flowed to top earners and shareholders.

EPI’s analysis shows that the bottom 90 percent of workers captured nearly 70 percent of all earnings in 1979, while the top 1 percent of earners took in a little over 7 percent. By 2021, the share of the bottom 90 percent had fallen by more than eleven points to 58.6 percent, while the top 1 percent of earners had doubled their share to nearly 15 percent — the highest point since the data became available in 1937. This trend was even more pronounced for the top 0.1 percent, whose share of earnings more than tripled, from 1.6 percent to 5.9 percent. Subtract the top 1 percent’s earnings, and the labor share falls well below its current historic low, by a much wider margin than in the past.

In an email, EPI Chief Economist Josh Bivens told Jacobin that the fall in the labor share and the growing inequality within it both stem from excess employer power in the labor market and decades of wage suppression. “Basically, I think a set of policies aimed at wage suppression have successfully slowed wage growth for the vast majority of workers,” Bivens said, “and this left a large and growing ‘excess’ wedge of income that went to much more privileged actors in the economy.”

Before 2000, most of this excess wedge showed up as rapid pay growth at the top of the income scale; during that period, as Bivens put it, “there was not a huge shift in the labor/profit shares.” Instead, top executives like General Electric CEO Jack Welch, poster boy of the shareholder revolution and ruthless union-buster, saw their pay explode. Between 1978 and 2000, the CEO-to-worker pay ratio at America’s top companies ballooned from under 25-to-1 to nearly 400-to-1.

Since the turn of the century, the excess has flowed more directly from labor to capital. “Post-2000, you see less of a wedge in pay growth between the very top and typical workers (still a big one, just not as big), but you start to see a noticeable rise in the profit share,” Bivens said. Part of this reflects changes in how business owners and executives report their income. The post-2000 shift away from labor coincided with a time when “a bunch of tax policy and regulatory policy changes made it more advantageous for super-privileged actors (corporate executives mostly) to report their income in forms that don’t show up in the labor share but do show up in the profit share.”

But reclassification explains only part of the shift. Profits also claimed a genuinely larger share of what the economy produced, boosting stock prices along with them.

Whether it flowed to executives or shareholders, this redistribution of income has been a driving force behind the rapid growth of both income and wealth inequality over the last half century. As Bivens and EPI President Heidi Shierholz point out in a recent essay, estimates suggest that “anywhere from 40 percent to nearly 100 percent” of the nominal gains in the stock market since 1989 can be attributed to capital’s growing share of the national income.

The implication, they write, is clear: “The wage suppression of recent decades is not just by far the biggest driver of the rise in income inequality; it is also by far the biggest driver of the rise in wealth inequality.”

The recent acceleration in the labor share’s decline has unfolded alongside an explosion in corporate profits and the strongest stock market bull run since the dot-com era. Yet these surging profits and asset prices have been driven less by genuine productivity gains than by financial speculation and a series of market shocks — from the supply-chain disruptions of the pandemic years to the recent spike in energy costs triggered by the Iran war.

Apart from these disaster-driven profits, the stock market boom has been powered by a handful of superstar companies concentrated in the tech sector. The top ten companies listed on the S&P 500 now make up roughly 40 percent of the index’s total market cap and generate over a third of its earnings, buoyed by the debt-fueled artificial intelligence boom.

These record profits are unlikely to last. If the current AI boom goes bust, as a growing number of market watchers now believe it will, earnings will plummet, and the profit share will decline relative to labor. But workers, not shareholders, invariably bear the brunt of recessions. Labor currently has little to gain and much to lose from the breakneck development of AI, especially if it proves as disruptive to jobs as many economists and AI boosters predict. Yet workers have even less to gain from a recession triggered by the collapse of the AI bubble, which would create ideal conditions for capital to further discipline labor — this time with some of the shiny new AI tools developed over the last several years.

The path to avoiding these outcomes and reversing the long-term decline of the labor share lies in a revitalized labor movement. As long as labor is weak and fragmented, workers will continue to see their share of the economic pie contract as billionaires and CEOs reap the rewards of the new AI economy.

The recently reelected president of the United Auto Workers (UAW), Shawn Fain, wasn’t being hyperbolic this June when he described the development of AI and the push for mass automation as a “profound threat and challenge to our way of life.” The compounding threats that workers now face have, in turn, increased public support and sympathy for labor unions. In September, Gallup’s annual survey on the labor movement showed that more than seven in ten Americans now approve of unions — the highest level since the 1960s — along with a record-high plurality of 47 percent who say that unions should have more influence.

Fain is among a cohort of new labor leaders who have pushed for a bolder and more combative labor movement willing to take the fight to capital. The UAW’s successful “stand-up strike” against the Big Three automakers in 2023 was part of a new wave of labor action in the post-pandemic years. New organizing efforts have also helped to slowly reverse the long-term decline in unionization, with data from the BLS showing the number of workers represented by unions rising to a sixteen-year high in 2025.

Whether the labor movement can sustain its current momentum is far from certain. What is clear is that its strength and influence will need to grow substantially in the years ahead if it is to meaningfully shape the emerging AI economy and shift the balance of power back toward workers. Until then, the economic gains touted by political and industry elites will almost certainly continue flowing straight to the top.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Bush’s brother crosses party lines to vote for James Talarico for Senate
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Republican Neil Bush says he was ‘deeply troubled’ by Ken Paxton’s conduct and ‘enormously impressed’ with Talarico

Neil Bush, a son of former president George HW Bush and a lifelong Republican, announced on Tuesday that he crossed party lines to vote for James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Texas.

In a Facebook post, Neil Bush said he chose to vote early for Talarico over Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate and current Texas attorney general, because he was “deeply troubled” by Paxton’s conduct and was “enormously impressed” by Talarico’s principles.

As a moderate Republican, Neil Bush’s statement on the competitive Senate race in Texas reflects views from a faction of the party that often disagrees with Donald Trump while holding traditional conservative views. It comes just two weeks before the midterms, when Democrats and Republicans are battling for the seat in Texas.

“I have been deeply troubled by Paxton’s conduct as Texas Attorney General, particularly his decision to challenge the results of the 2020 presidential election in other states in an effort to help Donald Trump remain in power,” Neil Bush, 71, wrote.

The former president’s son and brother of George W Bush expressed concern about Paxton’s past controversies, including Paxton’s 2023 Texas state legislature impeachment and acquittal, as well as Paxton’s loyalty to Trump.

“I have been a Republican for most of my life, and I still believe deeply in many traditional Republican principles. But character matters more than party affiliation. Our democracy depends on leaders who respect our institutions, tell the truth, accept accountability, and seek to unite rather than divide,” Neil Bush wrote.

Neil Bush said he sees Talarico as “a principled, pragmatic leader” who has a “willingness to listen to those with whom he disagrees”.

“He speaks with respect, seeks common ground, and seems genuinely interested in bringing people together rather than driving them apart. His faith appears to be a deeply rooted source of humility, compassion, and conviction rather than a political weapon,” Neil Bush wrote.

Talarico, a progressive liberal candidate who uses faith-based messaging, is the Democratic party’s latest hopeful to flip the seat in the deep red state. No Democrat has secured the Senate seat in Texas since the 1980s.

“Today, I voted against a style of politics that I believe has damaged our country. More importantly, I voted for the kind of character and leadership I hope will help heal it.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Woman told Russell Brand he treated her ‘like an animal’, court hears
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Emine Sinmaz
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women

A woman said Russell Brand degraded her and treated her like “a piece of meat” when he raped her at his London townhouse, a court has heard.

She alleged she repeatedly begged the 51-year-old comedian to stop the assault which left her bleeding for days and in pain.

Months later she bumped into Brand who texted her saying: “You’re dirty and I wanna push you further.”

Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

The TV personality listened intently in the dock as the woman gave evidence from behind a screen at Southwark crown court on Wednesday.

Brand is accused of anally raping the woman at his three-storey Victorian townhouse after picking her out from a crowd at one of his stand-up performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009.

The woman told police she was a “massive fan” of Brand and had performed oral sex on him after the gig despite having a boyfriend at the time. Days later, she went to Brand’s home in Hampstead, north-west London, knowing she would have vaginal sex with him. But she alleged Brand anally raped her after consensual vaginal sex.

In tense exchanges with Brand’s barrister Ian Winter KC during cross-examination, the woman denied she had consented to anal sex but later regretted it because she was in pain and feared she had contracted HIV.

The woman told the court that Brand “didn’t act like he’d done something criminal” after the alleged attack, to which Winter replied: “That’s because you consented.”

She insisted she had not, telling the barrister: “We’re not here to discuss my morality.”

“I didn’t consent to what happened to me,” she continued. “I have said that repeatedly in questioning. I made it very clear that I thought I was going to have penetrative vaginal sex with a condom.

“I agree that I haven’t painted myself in a very good light. I did just meet Mr Brand at the Hammersmith Apollo and I did have a partner who I really loved and I made a huge mistake.”

The woman was also questioned about her pre-recorded police interviews which were played to court on Tuesday and Wednesday. She told officers she ran into Brand at the Edinburgh Festival months after the alleged rape, and then received a “random” text from the comedian.

The woman, who was in her early 20s, said she challenged Brand: “Why are you even messaging me?” She claimed he responded: “Because you are dirty and I want to push you further.”

She said she replied saying: “I think you’ve pushed me far enough, you treated me like an animal,” to which Brand responded: “I’m sorry.”

She told police: “I feel how I’d felt at his house, that I felt completely degraded and fucking treated like an animal, like a piece of meat.”

Winter questioned why she had not replied to Brand saying he had raped her. He told the woman: “That’s because he had pushed you and probably had treated you like an animal, but he didn’t rape you.”

Earlier, Winter said the woman was aware of Brand’s reputation, to which she replied: “I had not heard about Mr Brand raping somebody.”

Winter replied: “Of course not. You knew that he was extremely sexually active with multiple women. You knew that he won the Sun newspaper’s Shagger of the Year three years running.”

He went on to describe how Brand’s show at the Hammersmith Apollo was “extremely sexually explicit” and that women were throwing their bras at the comedian and flashing their naked breasts. “I didn’t do that,” the woman replied.

The barrister said that after the show the woman had performed oral sex on Brand “who was effectively a total stranger, because you were obsessed with him at the time”. She replied: “If what you are asking is, would I have met someone … and then perform oral sex on him had he not been the person that he was, the answer is no.”

The barrister said the woman was aware that Brand was interested in “transactional” sex when he persuaded her to go to his house after the gig. “I didn’t think I was going to be his girlfriend,” she replied.

But the woman denied Winter’s suggestion that Brand had told her he wanted to have anal sex with her.

Winter said: “In a way, you went along with what he wanted because you were young and impressionable and obsessed with him. I’m putting to you, you agreed to do that.”

“The reason I made the comment about going there willingly and regretting it afterwards was because I did not consent to that,” she said.

The woman said she had not been able to immediately tell Brand to stop the alleged rape because she was in shock and pain. “In the very first instant I couldn’t speak, I couldn’t breathe,” she said.

She said she carried a lot of guilt and shame about what had happened, saying: “Because I went to his house willingly, because I engaged in a consensual type of sex, I didn’t feel I had as much right to feel as bad about it as I did.”

When Winter pressed her, she replied: “I felt a lot of burden. I carried that feeling of guilt and shame and I felt lots of things but particularly for exactly the reason that you are doing right here, making me feel like I brought it on myself. That just because you go somewhere willingly and the outcome in the end is not consensual – it’s a different scenario.”

Alyssa Wilson, 17, was driving to a party at city zoo when prosecutors say Willie Herndon fired a gun at her car

A Texas husband and wife are facing criminal charges following the fatal shooting of a 17-year-old girl who was driving to a Halloween celebration at the St Louis zoo when gunfire struck her vehicle on a Missouri highway.

St Louis county prosecutor Melissa Price Smith announced on Monday that Willie Herndon, 43, has been charged with first-degree murder and armed criminal action in connection with the death of Alyssa Wilson. His wife, 45-year-old Taiya Herndon, is also facing a charge of hindering prosecution.

The charges follow an investigation into the deadly 14 October shooting along Interstate 170 in Overland, Missouri, a community north-west of St Louis.

Wilson was traveling southbound at about 7pm, heading to meet a friend for the zoo’s Halloween festivities, known as Boo at the Zoo, when the shooting occurred.

Court documents reveal that at least one bullet was fired into the back of the teenager’s vehicle.

The gunfire left Wilson “incapacitated,” according to court records, and her vehicle subsequently slammed into a concrete median barrier. Emergency responders transported the teenager to the Barnes-Jewish hospital, where she was pronounced dead.

Investigators say security footage captured crucial details that helped authorities identify the suspects.

Jack Abell, chief deputy commander of the region’s major case squad, said during a news conference that Wilson had just driven past a white Buick Enclave parked along the highway shoulder when a single gunshot could be heard.

“A person exited the vehicle and stood outside for a short period of time,” he said. “There was a gunshot, got back in the vehicle. The vehicle turned its hazards off and continued on.”

Authorities used surveillance footage and automated license plate readers to trace the Buick, which carried an out-of-state registration, which ultimately led authorities to the Texas couple.

During Monday’s press conference, Wilson’s father, Robert Hickman, spoke about the devastating loss of his daughter and the future she will never get to experience.

“Alyssa was 17, excited about her life, excited about her future,” he said. “She had 60 days until she turned 18, and we were getting ready to take our first family vacation together to go to Disney for her to see her favorite person in the world, Princess Tiana, and unfortunately, she’s not going to get to do that any more. This was a senseless act.”

Investigators did not disclose what may have prompted the deadly encounter. Abell confirmed that Wilson had no relationship with either of the accused individuals.

Willie Herndon now faces first-degree murder and armed criminal action charges, while Taiya Herndon has been charged with hindering prosecution in connection with the teenager’s death.
