It is for that reason that Wells, who is co-president of Boston Korean Adoptees, is reluctant to share hers.

“I feel guilty that I won the adoption Lotto,” she said, “because I learned the stories of hundreds of fellow adoptees where the outcomes were nothing of the sort.”

White-Gydas also has a photo with adoptive parents on her wedding day, but to her it amounts to sugary frosting, hiding rot. There’s no longed-for baby in White-Gydas’s arms, because in 1999, when she was 10, her American adopters left her in a children’s home for failed adoptions. White-Gydas alleges the home’s director put pressure on her to have a surgery that cut out her womb and ovaries when she was 18, sterilising her.

After decades on separate paths, White-Gydas and Wells’ stories have converged again. In March of 2025, South Korea admitted government responsibility for enabling private adoption agencies to “mass export” Korean children for sale abroad, sometimes without the consent of birth families, since the 1950s. Now, more than 100,000 Korean-born adoptees in the US are asking themselves questions like: “Who am I, really? And how did I get here?”

The story told in the US of international adoption is often presented as a holy trinity: a woman struggling in a poor country, a newborn in need of a better life, and a western couple with love and resources in abundance. It is familiar to anyone who watched celebrities such as Mia Farrow and Angelina Jolie popularise foreign adoptions. Katherine Heigl, whose older sister was adopted from South Korea, in turn adopted her daughter Naleigh from the same country in 2009. “It is this gorgeous girl … born of a young woman who could not raise her but could give her the gift of life … that made me a mother,” Heigl posted on Naleigh’s 11th birthday.

Last March, a Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) convened by the South Korean government acknowledged the underhanded role South Korea played in delivering newborns to western couples’ doors.

It began in 1955, when evangelical Oregon couple Bertha and Harry Holt were “led by God” to “save” thousands of mixed-race babies fathered by GIs during the Korean war and left on the streets in economically devastated, conservative South Korea. They adopted eight themselves and set up an adoption agency, Holt Children’s Services, to help other Americans do the same. Arissa Oh, a historian of Asian American immigration at Boston College, said a combination of Red Scare-era thinking, an inclination for white saviourism, and promotion by churches drove customers to the agency’s services. “People who had little interest in adopting brown babies in America went abroad to ‘rescue orphans’ from communism,” Oh said.

The original Korean war babies ran out by around the 1960s. But “orphan fever” had already spread across the US and Europe, where women’s increasing access to welfare, contraception and abortion would lead to shortages of infants to adopt domestically. “That’s when market mechanisms come in,” said Oh, who authored the book To Save the Children of Korea: The Cold War Origins of International Adoption. With the Korean government’s blessing, “competing agencies sprang up to keep the pipeline going”.

According to Oh, the surge in adoptions became a source of wealth, welfare savings and soft power for Korea, now the world’s 15th largest economy. Its blueprint was replicated by Russia, China, Guatemala and Ethiopia, among many, all claiming to struggle with rehoming children domestically due to poverty, medical needs or policies like China’s one-child rule. US politicians – including President Dwight Eisenhower, who the Holts lobbied in the 1950s; Senator John McCain, who adopted from a Bangladesh orphanage in 1993; and Hillary Clinton, who in 2012 called international adoption “an important matter of foreign policy” – have also championed the framework. International adoption to the US peaked in 2004, when 23,000 children landed on American soil. Adopters today pay an estimated $30,000 to $60,000 per foreign child.

Then in December, on the heels of the TRC, South Korea announced international adoption of its children will end by 2029. That means in three years’ time, many of the world’s most prolific “sending countries” will be closed for business: Romania, Guatemala, Nepal, Ethiopia and China have already banned or limited foreign adoptions amid accusations of trafficking children via international adoption.

Months before the announcement, Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, offered a “heartfelt apology” to adoptees and birth parents for the government’s complicity in allowing agencies to dismantle generations of Korean families so white people could make new ones in the west.

According to the TRC, which took three years to consider evidence from 367 adoptions to 11 countries between 1964 and 1999, young, mostly unmarried Korean mothers felt pressure to give up babies due to stigma and poverty. It confirmed fraudulent practices in 56 cases in which children were adopted without valid parental consent or with falsified records claiming they were orphans even if they had living relatives; the cases were handled by multiple adoption agencies, including the one set up by the Holts. Reporting in 2024 by AP/PBS Frontline went further, alleging children were kidnapped off the street and from hospitals to be adopted.

Susan Soonkeum Cox, vice-president of policy and external affairs at Holt International, which split from Holt Children’s Services (South Korea) in the 1970s, acknowledged that some children were improperly separated from their families by Holt and sent on fraudulent documents, but told the Guardian there was “not evil intent” and denied that children were “trafficked”.

She said: “Holt is very concerned about [the Guardian’s reporting] and takes it very seriously. Holt feels strongly that every adoptee has the right to their own story and experience and how they interpret it belongs to them. Anyone who has come forward with experiences that were negative we respect that and we frankly are deeply saddened by it.”

Cox, a Korean-born adoptee to the US in 1956, continued: “Holt has been very determined to provide ethical, professional services. Were mistakes made in the beginning? Of course they were, but we were a very strong proponent of The Hague Convention [on Intercountry Adoption, established in 1993] because there had to be global standards.” Holt Children’s Services (South Korea) did not respond to a request for comment.

The revelations caused a wave of mass awareness among Korean-born adoptees in the US.

Katie Bozek, 45, a Korean-born adoptee and couples therapist in Grand Rapids, Michigan, said “waking up” to the dark reality of Korea’s adoption industry felt like being deprogrammed, or entering a multiverse like in the movie Everything Everywhere All at Once and becoming aware of infinite parallel lives she might have led.

“Thousands of adoptees are popping their heads out of the water, seeing [allegations such as] ‘kidnapping’, ‘trafficked’, and going, ‘where am I?’” Bozek said. “I don’t know how to explain to people that phrases like ‘I just found out my friend was kidnapped,’ ‘I may have been stolen’ or ‘my file is a lie’ are not extreme hypotheticals.”

Bozek’s adoption file claimed she was found near a police station in Korea in 1981. In 1982, she was adopted by a white Michigan family whom she loved. But outside the home, she endured painful, racist bullying, and yearned to be blond.

International adoptees are frequently the only person of color in mostly white families. On the advice of agencies to “not see race”, some families were unprepared to help adopted children deal with intrusive questions like: “where did they get you?” or “why didn’t your real parents want you?” In decades past, white adopters were more likely to downplay racist comments or ignore adoptees’ racial or ethnic backgrounds, leading to incidental promotion of whiteness as “normal” or “better”. Some Asian adoptees reported feeling isolated among Asian people too, who can perceive them as “too white to be Asian and too Asian to be white” – a double rejection.

Growing up, Bozek had few Korean role models to teach her about her birth culture. “It was hard because the dominant adoption narrative says: ‘You went to the best country in the world! You should be grateful we saved you,’” she said. “But I [feel an] ambiguous loss of something … When I’m in Korea I can sense it, I can smell it, I can taste it.”

Bozek started searching for her biological parents aged just 13. While she hasn’t yet found them, in 2019 and 2021 she discovered two first cousins through 23andMe’s DNA testing. They are also US adoptees, and half siblings. It sparked more uncomfortable questions: were agencies plucking multiple children off the streets at the same time?

In 2018 Bozek became the executive director of Korean American Adoptee Adoptive Family Network (KAAN) – the first leader who is an adoptee, not an adopter. Since the initial TRC bombshell, KAAN has welcomed new members seeking support as they process complex feelings of anger, guilt and loss.

Thousands of adoptees, some of whom are in their 60s and 70s, await their turn to be heard by the TRC. In the meantime, many are trying to track down adoption paperwork in Korea. Despite widespread fraud, these files still contain scraps of evidence, making them holy grails to adoptees hoping to piece together clues about their origins, reclaim lost identity, and find family.

US adoptee Oh Myo Kim, 46, a psychologist in Brookline, Massachusetts, who specializes in adoption, was in Seoul on a Fulbright scholarship when the TRC’s report was announced and felt its full force hit the adoptee community. “Just off the top of my head, I know four Korean adoptees who found out they were stolen,” she said.

The mother of two, adopted by a white family in New Jersey in 1981, became an accidental activist when she co-founded Emergency Action for Records Storage (EARS) with other adoptees, after plans were revealed for the Korean government to centralise adoptee files in inadequate storage, possibly delaying access for years and damaging or destroying fragile paperwork. In between school runs and work at Boston College, Kim uses vacation days to fly 7,000 miles to lobby a foreign government to better care for the documents – and identities – of thousands of strangers, in a language she still speaks “like a child”, she joked.

But adoptees are also searching for something files can’t always provide: a sense of belonging. “I feel like adoptees chase fiction. They chase ghosts,” Kim said. “On my paperwork it says my parents were married and gave me up as I was their fourth daughter, but there are no parental signatures. Do I have sisters?”

While the TRC surprised many adoptees, activists had sounded alarms since the 1970s, when the first adult adoptees from Korea found birth families and learned the truth of their adoptions. But the advent of commercial DNA genetic testing in the 2010s was the gamechanger, facilitating more reunions – as well as lawsuits against the Korean government from two birth mothers. One, Han Tae-soon, claimed her four-year-old daughter, Kyung-Ha, went missing while playing outside in 1975. Mother and daughter were reunited in 2019 after Tae-soon signed up to Korean DNA database 325Kamra and matched with Kyung-Ha, now Laurie Bender, a middle-aged nurse in California.

Bender only took the test because her US-born daughter was interested in their mysterious Korean roots. To her shock, Bender discovered Han had been walking the streets for 44 years, looking for her, until all 10 toenails fell off. “It’s like you’ve been living a fake life,” Bender told AP.

Han Tae-soon is suing the Korean government for $445,000, for failing to prevent Bender’s adoption through a children’s home that said she was an orphan despite a missing persons report filed with local police by her mother. A government spokesperson told the BBC in 2025 that it “deeply sympathises with the emotional pain of individuals and families who could not find each other for a long time” and would act based on the trial’s outcome.

While adoption agencies sold the dream of a better life, that wasn’t what awaited everyone.

Lauren White-Gydas, 37, was born in Korea in 1989 and at five months was adopted through Holt Korea by a white couple from Salem, Oregon. Problems started early. White-Gydas felt she wasn’t the “girly Asian” her adoptive mother desired. “I was a very explosive, angry child,” she said. Her therapist believes she was suffering from relinquishment trauma, a term increasingly used to describe anxiety, dysregulation, anger and depression experienced by many adoptees after separation from biological mothers.

“There was a lot of physical and emotional abuse, constantly screaming at me. I screamed back. They were not prepared for how much trauma I had,” White-Gydas said. “By the time I was seven I was completely stripped of everything. I was not allowed to have friends or go out or leave my room apart from school.” She has some happy memories of playing with her adoptive father but felt she had to earn her adoptive mother’s love.

In 1999, just after her 10th birthday, the couple put White-Gydas on a plane to Hope House in Nampa, Idaho, eventually terminating parental rights. “Being possibly abandoned by my biological parents and then abandoned by my adoptive parents pretty much told me … there’s something wrong with me,” White-Gydas said.

Hope House was opened in 1976 by Donna Velvick-Lowry, now in her 80s, as a Christian home and school for children from disrupted US and international adoptions, many of whom had severe mental health issues and were labeled as “incorrigible”. At Hope House, White-Gydas joined abandoned adoptees from Russia, Romania, Ukraine, Haiti, Mongolia, Brazil and China. She claims that during her time there, some staff were physically abusive, “slamming” children to the ground, locking them in solitary, and keeping them “doped up” by a visiting psychiatrist. By age 12, White-Gydas claims she was prescribed, among many medications, birth control to suppress her cycles. Her weight ballooned to 200lbs (90kg), medical records showed, and she developed type 2 diabetes.

White-Gydas said Velvick-Lowry wanted her to stay at Hope House beyond the age of 18 as her adopted daughter, and she felt like Velvick-Lowry belittled her to make her feel like an eternal child.

White-Gydas experienced painful periods and intense mood swings, and from age 12 claims that Velvick-Lowry started to “pressure” her into a hysterectomy, taking her to doctors by age 16: “She said if I didn’t, my hormones would make it so I ended up in jail.” After White-Gydas turned 18, in 2008, she alleges that Velvick-Lowry and the visiting psychiatrist put pressure on her to sign paperwork consenting to the procedure.

The OBGYN who performed the surgery noted on her intake paperwork that the psychiatrist, whose name appears on the surgery referral, diagnosed White-Gydas with “severe premenstrual disorder with anger and violent behavior”. The paperwork says White-Gydas was “absolutely certain that she does not desire any children”. White-Gydas was on Seroquel, the paperwork also notes, an antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia that sedates patients and causes drowsiness.

Medical notes confirm White-Gydas underwent a total hysterectomy in February 2008, with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (removal of fallopian tubes and ovaries), plunging her into menopause at 18 years and five months. “As they wheeled me in, it was the only time Donna wasn’t there,” White-Gydas said. “I told the nurse: ‘I don’t want to do this.’ She looked sad and said: ‘Sorry.’”

White-Gydas added: “Donna knew the one thing I wanted was a family who loved me, and she took that from me.”

Five adults who lived at Hope House as children in the 1990s and 2000s alongside White-Gydas told the Guardian allegations of physical and emotional abuse by Velvick-Lowry and other ex-staff, as well as being given medication that made them feel like “zombies”. Two former Hope House staff, who began working there after White-Gydas’s operation, stated that knowledge of her hysterectomy was “widespread” among staff and students but did not have personal knowledge as to whether she was pressured to have the procedure. The former Hope House residents and staff requested anonymity to protect their privacy.

Cleve Cushing, chair of Hope House’s board of directors, said in a written statement to the Guardian that for 50 years the organization had provided a home for children in need and given them “love and care, a quality education, and a real opportunity to succeed”.

He said: “Hope House takes any concern about the welfare of a child extremely seriously. We are, however, bound by state and federal confidentiality obligations and by our duty to protect the privacy of the children and families we have served. For that reason, we do not discuss any current or former resident or the details of their care. Anyone with a concern about the care of a child at Hope House, past or present, is encouraged to contact the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare or law enforcement.”

Cushing added the nonprofit is subject to Idaho’s licensing standards and oversight and would cooperate with any official review.

Velvick-Lowry no longer operates Hope House, now located in Marsing, but is understood to be living on the property, according to former staffers and students. She confirmed to the Guardian that she had been Gydas-White’s legal guardian, but declined to answer questions about alleged abuse or sterilisation. She said she was consulting a lawyer but did not provide their contact information.

She told the Guardian: “I remember loving [Gydas-White] very much and offering her a full time position after she left.”

White-Gydas left Hope House at age 22, moved to Montana, and started trauma therapy after being diagnosed with complex PTSD. She invited her former adopters to her 2014 wedding, hoping to salvage the only parental relationship she remembered, but it broke down again over their refusal to accept how damaged she was by their actions. She now works with disabled adults and co-owns an animal rescue, but still struggles with her infertility.

“We’re supposed to be grateful we got this ‘better life’ in America,” White-Gydas said. “A lot of us didn’t have a better life.”

Transracial, international adoption in the US is rife with issues that, until the last decade, were underdiscussed and underreported. Generations of children were funnelled for profit into largely white families ill-equipped to support minority kids, oftentimes in monoracial, segregated or racist communities. Even in loving placements, many adoptees had increased likelihood of attachment issues, depression and rage. Some were overmedicated, abused, or illegally “rehomed”.

A recent AP investigation found that, due in part to overdiagnosis of a rare condition called reactive attachment disorder (RAD), adoptees of all backgrounds account for an estimated 25-40% of institutionalised US children even though they are a tiny minority of total children (just 2%). A 2026 report by Winston-Salem State University found that adoptees were 35 times more likely than non-adoptees to attempt suicide.

Issues sometimes follow them into adulthood – and new ones arise. An estimated 35,000 US adoptees lack citizenship, more than half of them Korean-born. Minnesota lawyer and founder of the pro-bono group Adoptee Rights Law Center Gregory Luce says a vast majority of Korean adoptees arrived on visas requiring US adopters to apply for citizenship on their behalf. Some didn’t, which adoptees do not realise until applying for passports or college, or even until retirement. “Some [Korean] adoptees were essentially smuggled into the country,” said Luce, who is a domestic adoptee.

In 2016, US adoptee Adam Crapser was deported to South Korea after a green-card application uncovered old criminal charges, separating him from his children. He became the first Korean adoptee to sue the Korean government and Holt International for not telling his adopters to apply for his citizenship. Crapser won $68,600 in damages in 2023 when the Seoul high court dismissed accusations against the government yet found Holt responsible, but the result was thrown out on appeal. Holt and the government successfully cited a 1976 law that sped up foreign adoptions in part by absolving agencies of responsibilities such as ensuring citizenship for adoptees abroad. Crapser now lives in Mexico.

In September 2025, the Protect Adoptees and American Families Act (PAAF), intended to close citizenship gaps through which adoptees fall, reached US House committee stage; it is at least the sixth attempt since 2015. In light of surging immigration arrests at US airports, international adoptees and groups including Luce’s are urging each other not to fly, even domestically, without a US passport.

Some “receiving countries” are reexamining international adoption. Denmark and the Netherlands – facing scandals over fraudulent adoption paperwork and government complicity in trafficking adoptees – have made moves to end participation in the industry. The UK keeps an updated list of adoption restrictions on sending countries facing allegations of trafficking and fraud.

There have been no such developments in the US, where the likelihood of a ban remains low, Luce said. Despite international adoption to the US plummeting 94% since 2004 and some adopters publicly expressing regret for the role they played in funding its continuation, it is simply too popular.

US families get a $17,000 federal tax break per international or domestic adoptee, and positive international adoption stories permeate social media (as with “reunion porn”) and pop culture (Grey’s Anatomy, Modern Family, Sex and the City and Sesame Street have featured transracial, international adoption). Kim, of EARS, remembers people in the 80s telling her white adoptive mother, “God bless you,” as if she were a saint for adopting Kim. “Adoption as this force for good is very strong in American culture,” she said.

Even politicians who support PAAF, like senator Amy Klobuchar and representative Adam Smith, are “super pro-adoption”, Luce said. “If you criticize adoption as a politician, you’re seen as way outside the norm.”

But two recent legal cases have signalled to adoptees an increasing awareness in the US of the dark side of a system that promised them more.

In one, a Chinese-born adoptee was awarded $30m in damages by a New Hampshire judge in 2024, after her adopted parents pleaded guilty to criminal charges for keeping her tied up in their basement until she escaped in 2018, at age 15.

And just this summer, ex-Kentucky governor Matt Bevin and his ex-wife, Glenna Bevin, were accused of abuse and neglect by their Ethiopian-born adopted son Jonah Bevin, who described being used as a “political puppet” for campaigns and claimed he was sent away to abusive facilities in the US and Jamaica. Matt described Jonah’s claims as “false”, and Glenna testified that Jonah was “aggressive” toward his siblings as a teen. The case is playing out in state family court, with Jonah seeking retroactive child support payments.

South Korea’s TRC relaunched in February, inheriting 2,100 unresolved complaints from the last commission while accepting hundreds of new submissions from adoptees, and, for the first time, birth parents. They include Lee Aeri Rana, whose daughter, Park Mi-ae, was stolen at birth from a hospital in 1993 and sent on allegedly fraudulent documents to the US. Homeless and estranged from her adoptive family, Park died by suicide in 2023 at age 30, the day after legally restoring her Korean surname. “This is a death produced by illegal adoption,” said her grieving mother, who had been told her daughter died as a newborn.

Some activists have called for reparations from the Korean government including restored citizenship, and compensation for travel to South Korea and family searches. But as many adoptees will tell you, you cannot relive a life you lost.

“It’s very draining, the feeling that I don’t know who I am,” White-Gydas said about trying to digest the TRC’s initial findings. “Growing up whenever I saw another Asian person I wanted to ask them where they were from, because I knew so little. I wouldn’t even consider myself Korean.” The one sliver she has held on to is the name in her file: Jung Hee June.

So many questions remain unanswered: “I have done DNA tests and found nothing. I don’t know whether I truly was given up or I was stolen. Do I have a mom in Korea who loved me? How did I get here?”

Wells didn’t escape unscathed either. For years she suffered crushing depression misdiagnosed as bipolar disorder when she was 13, leading to unnecessary medication that caused suicidal thoughts. She met her Korean family, but only after 10 years of her birth mother declining to meet or tell her birth father and brothers about her.

Wells, now pregnant with her second child, was not a stolen baby. It does not lessen how adoption affected her, her birth family and her children, another generation removed from Korea. “I feel truly lucky because of the rare hand I was dealt, but I had to fight like hell for my life,” she said.

Some adoptees are reframing the US’s endorsement of international adoption as part of its long legacy of forced family separation.

“Adoption is an amazing analytic … to look at settler colonialism, white supremacy [and] anti-Black violence,” said Dr Kimberly McKee, a Korean adoptee and critical adoption scholar at Grand Valley State University, Michigan. Her Instagram handle is proudly “@adopteekilljoy”.

Academics like McKee argue that the international slave trade, which split up African families for sale to white people, laid the framework for state-sanctioned separation that disproportionately affects Black and brown US families today. In the 19th and into the 20th century, thousands of Native American children were sent to Indian boarding schools, sterilised, or forcibly adopted by white families. Likewise, McKee says international adoption is “a violent institution” that continues this pattern.

McKee married another Korean adoptee, reunited with her birth family in 2013 and has taken her son to celebrate Chuseok, a major Korean holiday, with them. She told the adoptee activist Haley Radke on the Adoptees On podcast that eating with her appa, or father, felt like a “glimmer” of the life she might have led. But being unable to communicate with this genetic stranger left her feeling a “living grief” – or han, a Korean word for sorrow and rage, resulting from injustice.

“I can order food … get directions … [but] I can’t have that sustained deep conversation,” McKee said. “Even though I am in reunion … there is a grief there and it’s palpable.”

The historian Oh saw a type of han walk into her classrooms at Boston College, as adoptee descendants took her course on adoption, looking for their own answers about why their line was cut, and who wielded the knife. She wonders if one day people will talk about international adoption the way they talk about slavery: “a historical phenomena, with a beginning and an end, thought to be firmly in the past”.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: In You Can See Everything, it’s Elizabeth Holmes’s partner who makes for 2026’s timeliest villain
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Jesse Hassenger
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Nathan Fielder’s conversation-igniting film on the Theranos founder finds its darkest moments in her deceptive, Charlie Kirk-loving fiance Billy Evans

Secrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the year

‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth Holmes

It’s likely that most audiences going into the surprise documentary smash You Can See Everything are familiar with either its nominal subject (and literal poster gal with an intense stare) Elizabeth Holmes, the tech founder serving a prison sentence for defrauding investors; or the film’s on-camera co-director Nathan Fielder. Holmes, as the movie points out, was all over the media as her company Theranos was hyped to the moon and then spectacularly imploded; she was also played by Amanda Seyfried in the well-regarded Hulu miniseries The Dropout. Fielder, meanwhile, may not have graced as many magazine covers, but is similarly familiar to prestige-TV acolytes from his comedy-reality series Nathan for You and its successor, the more reality-bending series The Rehearsal. A third figure not included in the film’s ad campaign becomes a key part of the film in the second half, and will also be familiar to many viewers.

This should leave Billy Evans as the odd man out. Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’s partner (she has said they’re not legally married, though they did get engaged in 2018, have two children and seem to treat each other as spouses), is a not-particularly-famous guy whose screen time competes with the other three well-known faces in what is essentially a four-character drama. But while Evans isn’t boxed out in terms of screen time or memorability, he does remain the odd man out in the sense that in all the discussion You Can See Everything has prompted about manipulation, shifting sympathies and who can or cannot be trusted, everyone seems to agree on one crucial point: Billy Evans sucks.

Well, everyone except Holmes, who never indicates so much as a moment of doubt or hesitation toward her common-law husband, at least so far as Fielder or co-director Lance Oppenheim show us. But the movie does show Fielder appearing baffled by Holmes – her absurd claims to have never lied in her adult life; her tautological and nonsensical explanation of how her blood-testing device does actually work (which basically amounts to “if everything about it worked, it would work”); her inability to understand Abbott and Costello’s most famous comedy routine – to the point of having trouble discerning whether she’s consciously scamming him or just, let’s say, reality-divergent. By comparison, Evans comes across as more of a slightly puzzling but recognizable nuisance.

When he calls a meeting to demand a percentage of the film’s profits – the kind of arrangement that might be typically reserved for a promotional piece commissioned by a musician, not a nonfiction film extensively interviewing a notorious subject – Fielder and Oppenheim zero in on the question of whether Holmes knew about this request and what became of it. But Evans is the one who violates documentary norms by asking for profit participation (and getting it, at least temporarily). Earlier on, he demands privacy when he grows visibly uncomfortable with questions asked of Holmes while also appearing fully, frontally nude in the film. In a small but underlined moment, he casually relieves Holmes of egg-scrambling duty because he believes she’s not stirring vigorously enough.

And those are just some of his antics before the film’s two year time-jump, after which Evans seems to exert even more control over his partner. Given Holmes’s reputation as a Silicon Valley scam artist, it would make sense enough to categorize Evans as a real-life version of Hollywood’s favorite go-to villain: the evil tech bro. The film even refers to Holmes’s turn in that particular hot seat as the subject of The Dropout, which is not a story of heroes and villains, exactly, but certainly exists adjacent to narratives about tech-forward monsters.

Evans has plenty of grimly hilarious signifiers, before and after his partner’s incarceration. Beforehand, he can be seen listening to podcasts at double speed like a true #content consumer/wannabe timemaxxer. Afterward, he shows repeated signs (uncommented upon by Oppenheim or Fielder) of posturing but increasingly intense post-“woke” radicalization: he spends time at a shooting range, claims to carry a gun everywhere, volunteers that he’s a fan of Charlie Kirk and brags about his own supposed vindictiveness. He uses his sketchy control of Holmes’s social media to engage in petty clapbacks that seem entirely out of character for her; he uses his sketchy control of her AI likeness to side-boast about how much healthier she looks as a prisoner than she did immediately postpartum.

With paranoia, delusions of grandeur, lofty-sounding projects that don’t amount to anything and a seeming possessiveness of the woman in his life, Evans checks plenty of tech-bro boxes – only without even a modicum of demonstrated tech expertise, seemingly not even in his fevered imaginings. Yes, Elon Musk propped himself up as a genius on the basis of other people’s companies and his vast fortune, Mark Zuckerberg is a dead-eyed egomaniac whose famous invention is a Friendster clone that bought up a bunch of other already-successful websites and Sam Altman’s career is littered with failures that in no way qualify him to order us all to treat AI as the future. But even if you see these guys as scammers nearly on par with Holmes, they have the distinction of having successfully made money and, in the case of Musk and Zuckerberg, placing some of their might behind products that people do actually use (in some cases, whether they really want to or not). One reason they’re villainized in fictionalized true stories like those powering The Social Reckoning (with Jeremy Strong as Zuck) or the upcoming Artificial (with Andrew Garfield as Altman and Ike Barinholtz as Musk) is that they have actually accrued power in the first place. There are stakes to their existence.

Evans has no such claims to fame or even big-canvas notoriety that could inspire something like the four-hour Musk documentary by Alex Gibney, released concurrently with You Can See Everything. It seems notable, too, that the similarly lengthy You Can See Everything has seemingly stolen focus from the more traditionally rigorous piece on Musk, a far more influential individual compared to either Holmes or Evans. Holmes was certainly a destructive force for the cancer patients whose hopes she raised, and Evans comes across like a restless creep, but it feels telling, and a little discomfiting, that the gossipy nervous laughter provoked by You Can See Everything is proving a vastly more headline-grabbing draw than a movie laying out the case against a maniacal on-again, off-again trillionaire who has done genuine damage to the world, and is poised to do plenty more. Does someone need to be as petty, strange and blatantly unsuccessful as Evans to be truly finished off in public?

Then again, Evans does make a compelling villain for precisely that restless lack of achievement. He will never be as influential as someone like Musk or Zuckerberg, but apparently aspires to that kind of overlord-level bravado (why else would you use your wife’s social media to pick fights?). He’s a fake-it-til-you-make-it-and-then-keeping-faking-it type, more akin to erstwhile reality star turned pretend mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt or any number of filibustering podcasters. Instead of Facebook or Tesla or a portfolio of Donald Trump-style scams, he can simply puppeteer the damaged brand that is Elizabeth Holmes – near-literally, when he shows off his AI version. Holmes is clearly manipulative (and based on available information about Theranos, an unambiguous liar), yet Fielder does locate, or maybe even manufacture, some kind of humanity through her inscrutability. There’s something haunting about her, sometimes in spite of herself. Evans is the odd man out in You Can See Everything because he seems to lack that kind of turmoil. He’s hustle-and-grind culture in its final dehumanizing form. The world is just something for him to absorb and scan for advantages at 2x speed.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Welcome to the trap: swaggering Atlanta Dream turn WNBA finals into a hometown spectacle
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Andrew Lawrence at State Farm Arena
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Atlanta’s long-suffering sports fans know better than to get carried away. But the Dream’s first WNBA finals game in 13 years showed this might finally be a team worth falling for

The Atlanta Dream were exactly where they wanted to be on Wednesday night, comfortably ensconced inside their downtown arena for Game 3 of the WNBA finals against the Golden State Valkyries. Kerry Washington, Ludacris and Cam Newton led the courtside celebrity delegation. Quavo and TI headlined the halftime show, while two more hugely popular Atlanta rappers performed during other extended play stoppages – a mini-spectacle that speaks to the city’s deep bench of hip-hop talent.

But it was the crowd that really made State Farm Arena a house of horrors for Golden State. They didn’t just fill the 20,000-seat venue. They donned matching sky-blue T-shirts and waved rally towels. They sang along with their favorite emcees and lived and died with every point. They were so loud in the first quarter that I couldn’t hear the referee’s whistle from my 100-level press seat. They stayed to the end – well, two minutes from the buzzer anyway (gotta beat traffic) – and, with the 97-71 win sealed and DJ Khaled’s All I Do Is Win blasting through the arena speakers, serenaded the departing Valkyries with the unofficial Atlanta battle cry: “ATL hoe!”

Angel Reese never knew basketball could be like this. “When you can have at the end of the quarter a performance,” she gushed after a 21-point, 12-rebound effort. “And at the timeout, another performance. You smell the chicken, you smell the fish. It’s a blue-out in here. I didn’t even get to see Kerry. You don’t know who you gonna see in the A.”

In the US, the series will air on NBC, USA Network and CNBC, with all games streaming on Peacock. In the UK, it will be carried by Sky Sports. In Australia, fans can watch through WNBA League Pass, with selected coverage also available through ESPN.

Atlanta has always been a strange sports town – one where fans learn not to fall too hard, lest they get burned by teams that either get ahead of themselves, self-destruct or wear out your patience with their underachieving. So fans proceed with apprehension. They find out-of-town teams to insulate themselves from disappointment, leave games early when defeat seems imminent and convince themselves they’re just beating traffic. They enjoy the music, the invitations to sing along and swag surf.

The last time a playoff basketball game was played at State Farm Arena, the Knicks routed the Hawks to seal their Eastern Conference first-round series – and by the end, the New York fans had cleared out most of the Atlanta supporters and glitterati. With the Hawks down some 40 points, rappers Young Joc and Lil Boosie performed their hits for a crowd that half-bobbed along. It was hard to imagine the Atlanta sports scene getting more unserious.

Then the Dream reached the WNBA finals, only to learn they wouldn’t be able to play at State Farm Arena – their occasional home court. The Hawks, State Farm’s main tenant, were opening their season, while rising emo-pop artist Sombr had a gig scheduled. The Dream faced the possibility of hosting their first WNBA finals game in 13 years at the 3,500-seat airport arena where they played most of their home games, with neither the local college arenas nor the 13,000-seat suburban concert venue available. Gateway would have made for a jarring contrast with Chase Center – the NBA arena where the Valkyries’ passionate, violet-clad fans have created Ballhalla, one of the WNBA’s toughest places to play. The racial and economic makeup of the Atlanta and Golden State crowds would have surely added another dimension. But a combined effort by the teams, the league and the arena to bring the games to State Farm spared us that discourse.

It allowed Dream fans to show they can match that home-court advantage when Atlanta has a team worth believing in and the right venue. Three previous times the Dream have reached the finals, only for all three appearances to end in sweeps. But no one was thinking much about that on Wednesday night. Not with the Dream holding the Valkyries scoreless for the first five minutes before picking up where they left off in Game 2 and smothering them with their defense. Not with Reese jawing at the Valkyries bench after tough layups and, for good measure, setting off the crowd with a pair of open threes as her college coach, LSU’s Kim Mulkey, looked on in her blued-out pantsuit. Not with the Dream’s length and speed throwing a spanner into the Valkyries’ carefully choreographed offense, forcing Golden State to heave away at the basket late in the shot clock.

Only thanks to three-point shooting from Cecilia Zandalasini and Gabby Williams did Golden State cut the deficit to six by halftime, then pulled level at 48 in the third quarter, with Zandalasini perfect beyond the arc to that point. Otherwise, a Valkyries team that prides itself on depth and balance was mostly caught off guard by a Dream team beating them at their own game while also doing what they do best: short-circuiting the pick-and-roll, winning extra possessions on steals and rebounds and scoring in transition.

Rhyne Howard, one of three Dream players named to the WNBA’s all-defensive team last week, became the first player to record five or more steals in consecutive finals games. Reese, the newly crowned defensive player of the year, became the youngest player in WNBA history to record a double-double in three straight finals games and joined A’ja Wilson as the only players to record at least 20 points and 10 rebounds in consecutive finals games. The Valkyries bench was a major factor again, outscoring the Dream reserves 38-27. But that advantage counted for little with Atlanta neutralizing Golden State starters Kiah Stokes, Veronica Burton and Kayla Thornton, who combined for five points on 2-of-11 shooting.

When the final buzzer sounded, the Valkyries slinked off the court in defeat, while the Dream gathered at midcourt to drink in the atmosphere and toss mini balls into the stands, hard-won souvenirs for the sixth man who showed up and showed out. Hardly a Sombr crowd. And to think: if it hadn’t been for a sloppy final two minutes in Game 1, Atlanta would still have a perfect playoff record and be looking at a chance to clinch a title in Game 4 on Saturday afternoon in front of their fans. Instead, they’ll look to exploit their fearsome new home-court advantage for a shot at closing it out on Monday. If Golden State have Ballhalla, beware Atlanta: home of the trap.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Super Bowl contenders: are the NFL’s unbeaten teams as perfect as they seem?
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Graham Searles
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The early standouts have emerged. But even the best teams have flaws that can be exposed by their opponents

Who would have thought the 49ers would be here after a rough old offseason? Head coach Kyle Shanahan’s participation in training camp was limited due to a serious car crash, team owner Jed York’s visit to an Ohio trailer park did not end well, and one player after another endured serious injuries. Despite all this, San Francisco are full of positive vibes. They are top of a tough division and their immense defense, led by the intensity of players such as safety Malik Mustapha and Fred Warner, is complemented by an equally impressive offense.

Brock Purdy’s record-setting quarterback rating has grabbed the headlines – and rightly so, as his laser accuracy on aggressive downfield throws sets the 49ers offense apart. But there are warnings Purdy’s offensive surge may not last. Pablo Torre pretty much debunked the 49ers’ electrical substation conspiracy theory, but injuries are piling up in the receiving corps. The team have four wide receivers on injured reserve, plus Brandon Aiyuk, who is in self-imposed exile. Purdy had found relief in the form of future Hall of Famer Mike Evans, but the 33-year-old left Monday’s win over the Washington Commanders with achilles pain and is also dealing with fractured ribs. And when Evans is off the field, Purdy struggles. On Monday, Evans caught three passes for 94 yards as the Niners appeared to be cruising at half-time. Without him, the offense went three and out three times, and only just hung on to beat the Commanders.

The three-game lead the 49ers have in the NFC West should see them walk into the playoffs. But if Purdy can’t find healthy, reliable targets, the Niners will see another promising campaign end against the big boys in the postseason.

The Chiefs are back. After they limped to a 6-11 finish last season, their record is spotless, and the AFC West – thanks in part to the Los Angeles Chargers’ implosion – already looks sewn up. Patrick Mahomes is back from the ACL tear he suffered in 2025, and the offense is no longer solely relying on the quarterback to paper over the cracks: the acquisition of running back Kenneth Walker III looks to be the move of the offseason. It was likely that last season’s Super Bowl MVP would be a solid get for a Chiefs rushing attack that averaged a sluggish 4.2 yards per carry last season. But Walker’s production has made the Seattle Seahawks look a little foolish to let him go.

Kansas City picked him up for $14.35m a year, making him only the ninth-most expensive running back in the league. Did the Chiefs think Walker would be the NFL’s leading rusher coming into Week 7? Unlikely, especially as the Chiefs have already had their bye week. His 665 rushing yards still top the charts, as do the team’s 5.5 yards per carry. Walker’s penchant for explosive big plays has been the biggest transformation for Kansas City. He already has seven carries of more than 20 yards. The Chiefs managed just three all of last year.

The knock on Kansas City is that Walker’s rampage has come amid a soft schedule to start the season. But if he overpowers his former employers – and their formidable defense – on Sunday night the rest of the league should be very worried.

The Vikings have an important talent when it comes to going the distance: the ability to win ugly. The Seahawks pulled off the same trick last season on the way to winning the Super Bowl. Now Minnesota are doing the same thing with a similarly dominant defense leading the charge. How important is the defense to the Vikings? They are the first team to go 4-0 while not scoring an offensive touchdown in multiple games (wins over Miami and Chicago) since the Detroit Lions in 1934.

Perhaps more importantly for the Vikings’ championship hopes: their offense has shown signs of waking up. In their last game, a 23-13 victory over the Saints before the bye week, Kyler Murray had his best day in purple and gold. He looked reliable as the team’s starting quarterback, with an 80% completion rate, 229 passing yards and a highlight-reel touchdown throw that Justin Jefferson caught in triple coverage. As is the case with Evans and the 49ers, Jefferson unlocks a much higher level of production from Murray. The difference for the Vikings is their defense is a cut above the 49ers’ unit. They aren’t one of the best defenses – they are the best. Brian Flores’s blitz-heavy package led by Dallas Turner on the edge and linebacker Blake Cashman has conceded just five touchdowns so far.

OK, the Bills have lost a game, but we’re throwing them in here as they’ve been the best of the rest. You have to admire Josh Allen’s fondness for high drama – and his defense-shredding talent even more. Buffalo lead the league in scoring with four of their five wins coming in box-office shootouts. It’s never dull on the other side of the ball either: Buffalo’s defense has allowed the most yards per game (386.8) of anyone in the league, bar the leaky Lions.

The question is whether having such an abject defense is sustainable for the rest of the season. One key metric – stopping teams on third down – suggests they are in for a rough ride against elite opposition in the playoffs. What’s worse is that they started the season poorly in that category and have gotten progressively worse. The NFL average for stops on third down is about 40%. In Week 2, the Lions were successful on third down 36% of the time against the Bills. Last Sunday the Raiders had 58% success in the same scenario. With Allen at the controls, the Bills will always have a shot; it’s just a shame he can’t play both ways. Buffalo need to function at a higher level on defense in fundamental areas to win it all.

The Jets have a few shots at “glory”. Their three first-round picks are owned by 2-4 teams: the Colts, Cowboys and the Jets themselves. However, that trio are part of a bunch of franchises with two wins. Many would have been surprised to see the Philadelphia Eagles among those nine teams, but they could sink further. The ongoing saga over Jalen Hurts’s blood clots means the untested Tanner McKee is now the team’s starting quarterback and the Eagles are dealing with a huge injury list. It’s not impossible to imagine they could be in play for the No 1 pick by the end of the season.

However, much more likely to be picking first in 2027 are the winless Chargers and Dolphins. Miami are the solid choice to pick first. Their offense has been abysmal, except for one quarter of fluency under zero pressure from the Cincinnati Bengals. Sunday’s matchup will probably highlight the huge gulf in class between the merely bad Jets and the pit of despair that is the Dolphins.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: John Anderson, five-time US country chart-topper, dies aged 71
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
Florida-born singer-songwriter had major hits with Swingin’, Seminole Wind and Straight Tequila Night

John Anderson, the traditionalist US country singer whose extensive body of work included five No 1 hits on the country charts, has died aged 71.

The news was announced on social media by his family, who said: “To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely and made every ordinary moment feel special.”

So woven into the culture of country music that he once worked as a roofer on the genre’s focal point, Nashville’s Grand Ole Opry, Anderson’s career spanned nearly 50 years and resulted in him being inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2024.

Among those paying tribute to Anderson was country singer and friend Blake Shelton: “I am a very lucky man. I got the opportunity to find out that my hero wasn’t just the guy I hoped he’d be.” Shelton’s wife Gwen Stefani wrote: “We loved him!! His music is part of our family’s hearts for ever!!”

Born and raised in Florida in a music-loving family whose tastes spanned big band jazz to the Rolling Stones, Anderson headed to Nashville after graduating high school to try to make it in the city’s country music scene by playing live sets at night while doing manual labour during the day. “I’d fill up the truck with gravel and take the truck to wherever the order was and drop it off. A lot of odd jobs, but never lost sight of the fact that I really wanted to play,” he said in 2024.

Writing his own material as well as performing that of others, he released his debut single in 1975, but broke through two years later with I’ve Got a Feelin’ (Somebody’s Been Stealin’), and inched his way up the country charts with each subsequent release. He had his first country Top 5 single in 1981, I’m Just an Old Chunk of Coal (But I’m Gonna Be a Diamond Someday), which earned him his only Grammy nomination, for best male vocal country performance – and was a typical showcase of his wry, earnest and pure vocal tone.

It ushered in a number of years of commercial success, with the songs Wild and Blue, Black Sheep and Swingin’ all becoming country chart-toppers – the slick, hard-driving sound of the latter gave it crossover appeal and it became Anderson’s only hit on the US pop chart.

The latter half of the decade was a frustrating time for Anderson as he was dropped by his label Warner Bros and shuttled between others, before finding his groove again with 1992 album Seminole Wind, containing three Top 3 hits; the title track, an ode to his birth state of Florida, and Straight Tequila Night have endured as country radio staples and streaming successes. Follow-up Solid Ground was also a hit, containing the chart-topping Money in the Bank.

Anderson ended up recording 22 studio albums, most recently 2020’s Years, recorded with Dan Auerbach of blues-rockers the Black Keys. That was a proud and hard-fought return for Anderson, who faced illness with a non-cancerous tumour in 2017 that left him hospitalised. “I had been very, very ill,” he told Billboard in 2020. “I had almost 100% hearing loss … that really almost put an end to me. I just started praying and praying harder than I’ve ever prayed in my life and you know what? My hearing started coming back.”

Anderson continued to perform live thereafter, saying in 2024 that since his recovery, “I’ve really been enjoying every day. I live out in the woods and take a lot of lessons from my little wildlife friends. They pretty much live day to day, minute to minute. Enjoying that minute, enjoying this time. I’m very thankful to be able to go out and play any music at all.”

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Big pharma accused of ‘free-riding on nature’ as global fund attracts just $7,000
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Rebecca Ratcliffe
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
The Cali Fund, set up to raise $1bn a year for biodiversity from drug companies, remains near empty

Big pharmaceutical companies have been accused of “free-riding on nature”, after a landmark biodiversity fund that invites businesses to put some of their profits back into conservation was left virtually empty.

The Cali Fund set out to raise $1bn (£750m) annually, by asking companies that profit from nature’s genetics to contribute towards conservation in low-income countries. But more than 18 months after the fund was launched, it remains far below this target.

As of Monday, at the start of the Cop17 biodiversity summit in Armenia, the fund had received just $10,656 in commitments, of which $7,085 had been deposited.

No money has so far been given by major pharmaceutical companies, despite the industry’s reliance on genetic information from organisms around the globe for the development of lucrative new medicines.

The industry’s participation could prove pivotal to the fund’s success. A study by Zero Carbon Analytics (ZCA) found the top 15 pharmaceutical companies could have contributed $756m based on their performance last year, if they had followed guidelines set out by the fund, which suggests companies make a voluntary contribution of 1% of their profits or 0.1% of revenue.

In 2025, the top 15 pharmaceutical companies generated about $161bn in profits, according to ZCA’s research.

“Look at how much profit these pharmaceutical companies are getting – and we’re only asking for a tiny percentage,” said June Rubis of Macquarie University, who is an Indigenous peoples and local communities representative from Asia and sits on the Cali Fund’s steering committee.

“Definitely, they’re free-riding” on nature, said Rubis, who added that businesses did not appear to recognise the importance of protecting nature or of supporting “communities who have been in the frontlines of defending biodiversity conservation and therefore their future profits”.

The Cali Fund is a key issue to be discussed at the UN biodiversity conference – Cop17 – in Yerevan, this week, and is part of wider efforts to plug a $700bn gap in funding for nature conservation.

At least half of the money from the Cali Fund will be directed towards areas identified as priorities by Indigenous peoples and local communities.

“The future of health is written in nature’s DNA,” said Victoria Kalyvas, who authored the Zero Carbon Analytics analysis. “The pharmaceutical industry stands to lose a great deal from its destruction, as do patients.”

According to Zero Carbon Analytics, the total sum given to shareholders by the top 15 companies in 2025 was 175 times more than the suggested contribution to the Cali Fund.

Ensuring that companies pay for their use of nature has become increasingly complex, due to advances in biotechnology that mean large volumes of genetic information, known as digital sequence information (DSI), can now be stored in public databases.

The Cali Fund was designed to plug loopholes that have emerged as research has shifted from a reliance on physical samples to use of DSI.

However, pharmaceutical companies have criticised the fund, saying the blanket amount they are asked to contribute is not appropriate, arguing that not all medicines are built using DSI, and that the fund overlaps with existing laws.

Since its official launch in February 2025, the fund has received just three contributions by small private-sector companies: $5,000 from the UK-based biotech firm Prozomix; $1,000 from TierraViva AI, also based in Britain; and $1,085 from the Belgian firm E-Biom.

“More money has been spent on meetings talking about the Cali Fund than there is in the Cali Fund’s coffers,” said Brian O’Donnell, director of Campaign for Nature, who said it was too optimistic to expect companies to contribute voluntarily and that they should be compelled to do so.

Guilherme Cintra, director of innovation policy at the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations, said the industry was committed to biodiversity but had “ongoing questions about the design and implementation of the mechanism”.

“The current mechanism overlaps with existing law, relies on inaccurate assumptions about how data is used in the discovery of medicines, and asks companies to hand over a share of their total revenue, whether DSI was used to develop a medicine or not,” Cintra said.

A spokesperson for the Cali Fund said the amount raised so far was “disappointing but not entirely surprising”, adding that “comparable financial instruments have generally taken two to three years before contributions began to scale [up]”.

The spokesperson said: “Contributions will likely remain modest while the operational infrastructure is being completed and until the Cali Fund becomes better known.” They added that discussions at Cop17 would give greater information to companies, enabling them to come forward with commitments.

A spokesperson for the French pharmaceutical multinational Sanofi said the company recognised “the critical importance of biodiversity and healthy ecosystems to human health and the long-term resilience of healthcare systems” and that protecting nature was a core component of its environmental sustainability strategy.

A spokesperson for the British biopharmaceutical company GSK said open access to DSI was “critical to enable continued medical innovation and rapid response to public health emergencies, including pandemics”.

They added: “We support the intent behind the Cali Fund and will make a decision regarding voluntary contributions when there is more information about how the Cali Fund will work alongside other national and multilateral access and benefit-sharing mechanisms.”

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield on the app for all the latest news and features

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Experts alarmed by ‘less transparent’ CDC as US measles deaths rise
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Melody Schreiber
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Agency declines to reveal in which state latest measles death occurred as it delays reporting other measles deaths

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) added a third measles death to its dashboard on Wednesday, but the agency would not reveal whether the death occurred in Pennsylvania or another state – which is “notable” as the agency delays reporting other measles deaths, experts say.

The CDC cited privacy laws in not sharing the name of the state, but experts say there are no privacy concerns in doing so – and this information is important for the public to have as the outbreak continues accelerating, growing by 8% in one week to 4,410 confirmed cases so far this year, nearly double last year’s count.

“Due to privacy laws and legal restrictions, NCHS [the National Center for Health Statistics] cannot identify a state or provide additional details about the third individual,” a spokesperson with the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) told the Guardian in response to questions about where the death took place.

The spokesperson did not respond to follow-up questions about which laws and restrictions prevented that information from being shared.

“I don’t buy it,” said Dorit Reiss, a professor of law at UC Law San Francisco. “Naming a state won’t be giving personal details, and they give the number of cases in each state,” she said, adding there was “nothing to prevent giving numbers of deaths in each”.

The CDC is not governed by Hipaa as health providers are. The agency is instead guided by the Federal Privacy Act, which usually prohibits disclosing government records about specific individuals, said Lindsay Wiley, professor of law and faculty director of the Health Law and Policy Program at UCLA Law.

“But this general prohibition only applies to information that reveals an individual’s identity,” Wiley said. “It’s hard to see how identifying the state where a death occurred would allow the public to identify the patient.”

At the same time, it’s “not unheard of” for agencies to use an “overly broad, unwarranted interpretation of privacy protections to decline to share information that they prefer not to share anyway, because it may be seen as damaging to their reputation or agenda”, Wiley said.

The CDC switched in September to using NCHS rather than the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS), a system that usually reports deaths quickly and provides the state where a death occurs. The agency has not given a clear reason for the change.

When only a few deaths have occurred, NCHS usually does not say where those deaths are happening, which is one of the weaknesses in using it to report information like this.

“But it’s also in the news, so it already is likely identifiable,” said Debra Houry, former chief medical officer at the CDC. And the agency still has access to other reporting systems, like NNDSS, to know which state has deaths, Houry said.

Pennsylvania has strict privacy laws about not reporting demographic information or medical details, but “that still wouldn’t limit state and deaths”, she said.

Pennsylvania has now reported a total of six deaths, with the most recent case still under investigation by state officials. By carefully tracing the cause of death before reporting it on the state dashboard, officials in Pennsylvania are “doing the right thing”, Houry said.

The CDC dashboard only lists three deaths from measles this year, despite five confirmed deaths in Pennsylvania. The agency has not given a reason for the delay; usually, the NCHS system is updated within days of states sending information.

Reiss said it was “a change from past practice, and not a good one. [The] CDC is being less transparent than in the past.”

Not having a clear picture of what’s happening in each state, including a possible death from measles, makes it hard to understand risk levels, said Paul Offit, an infectious diseases physician at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “You’d like to know what the activity is in your state.”

Offit said he wondered if the secrecy was “coming from the top”, since officials such as Robert F Kennedy Jr, HHS secretary, or Erica Schwartz, CDC director, have reportedly given orders to decrease the measles death count.

It’s also not clear if the public is receiving accurate numbers of cases, Offit said. A 39-year-old woman in Franklin county, Pennsylvania, died of an acute cardiac event, a known but very rare complication of measles infection, Offit pointed out.

“When you see something like that, you’re looking at the tip of a much bigger iceberg,” he said. “Are you really monitoring how many adults are getting infected? I doubt it.”

It’s also harder to reach adults who may be at risk because they’re not vaccinated, because most vaccination requirements happen at the school level, Offit said. “What do you do for adults?”

The decision not to include all deaths from measles is “notable” and will likely have wide-ranging consequences, Offit said. The CDC has offered to send a support team to help Pennsylvania with the outbreak, but state and local officials may be wary of working alongside staff at an agency that is refusing to record accurate data, Offit said. “You wonder, ‘Can you trust them?’ It’s really that bad.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Meta strikes deal with Zuckerberg to protect him from California wealth tax
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Graeme Wearden
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Company says deal will keep its chief executive living in California even if state brings in one-off billionaire tax

Meta has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to protect him from the threat of a California wealth tax targeting billionaires.

The social media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp revealed on Wednesday night that the arrangement would keep its chief executive living in California, where its headquarters are located.

Under the deal, Zuckerberg will receive new shares that could be sold to potentially foot a multibillion-dollar tax bill in the event that California passes a one-off billionaire tax. In return, he is committed to remain a resident of the state, or wherever Meta maintains its base, for eight years

Californians will vote early next month on Proposition 40 – a one-time 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state.

Zuckerberg, worth $239bn according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence elsewhere because Prop 40 could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it.

In response, Meta is creating a new class of non-voting shares via a two-for-one stock split for all existing shareholders.

This will allow Zuckerberg to sell some of this new class C shares to pay a potential tax bill, without diluting his control of the company.

Recent polling has shown that Prop 40 remains short of majority support with voters. Tech billionaires have been spending heavily to fight the measure, including the Google co-founder Sergey Brin, the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

Rohit Khanna, the US congressman representing California’s 17th congressional district, has dubbed Prop 40 as a choice between standing with the working class or the oligarchs.

“Every society is taxed. The only question is who will pay. In Trump’s America, working people pay more than they should, while billionaires are so unburdened that they are becoming trillionaires. In the America we seek, billionaires and trillionaires will pay their fair share, while working people will be unburdened,” Khanna wrote in the Guardian last week.

Meta also reported a 26% rise in revenues for the last quarter to $64.6bn, beating expectations of $63.3bn.

But profits fell by 37% to $13bn, dragged down by a $9.9bn charge related to Meta’s landmark lawsuit over child protection and social media addiction failings.

In a separate case, a judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn on ⁠Wednesday after a trial found the company had misled the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

Meta also revealed it had cut its headcount to 66,775 at the end of September, 15% fewer than a year ago.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Russia bombards Kyiv with missiles – hours after agreeing to resume talks with Ukraine
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Luke Harding and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Experts say Russia is trying to destroy energy infrastructure before winter, showing US ‘appeasement and flattery’ will not achieve peace

Russia has carried out a massive “demonstrative” attack on Ukraine, bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume trilateral negotiations after talks with the US envoy Steve Witkoff.

Overnight, Moscow pounded the Ukrainian capital, killing at least two people and wounding 22, including four children. Targets included the southern bridge over the Dnipro River, civilian houses, energy infrastructure, an ambulance station, office buildings and a monastery.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Thursday that numerous sites across the city had been hit and damaged. Twelve regions across the country were bombed including the southern city of Odesa, where the port was badly hit.

Zelenskyy said the latest devastating strikes showed that Russia was not serious about peace. “Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening,” he said.

During negotiations on Wednesday in St Petersburg, Witkoff lavished praise on Vladimir Putin, who was sitting across the table. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff said.

In a social media post after the strikes in the early hours of Thursday, Zelenskyy issued a sardonic reply. “Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian “humanitarians” since yesterday evening. They used 21 missiles,” he wrote.

Zelenskyy said he was grateful to those among Ukraine’s western partners who saw “the situation for what it is” and “acknowledged the reality” that the Kremlin had little intention of stopping its war. He called for stronger air defences, Patriot interceptors which could bring down enemy missiles and more sanctions against Moscow.

Ukraine’s foreign minister, ⁠Andrii Sybiha, ⁠added that “appeasement, ⁠servility ​and flattery” ‌would ‌not ‌stop Russian aggression.

On Wednesday, Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said Putin had agreed “in principle” to resume three-way negotiations involving Russia, the US and Ukraine after 10 November, a week after the US midterm elections. In reality, Russia’s real intention is to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, leaving millions in the dark and cold, officials in Kyiv believe.

According to Zelenskyy, the US has resumed intelligence warnings of Russian missile attacks. But the White House has so far not reversed the slowdown of Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk’s Starlink internet satellite system, leaving Ukraine unable to intercept enemy drones or carry out mid-range battlefield strikes.

The New York Times reported that when the slowdown was imposed last week, dozens of armed drones heading to Russian military targets fell from the sky. The video feeds streaming their flight paths suddenly went fuzzy as the connection with Starshield was lost, the paper said.

The decision to cripple Ukraine’s successful drone programme came amid the most serious row between Washington and Kyiv since Russia’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. It began after Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, to lower US fuel prices, a move which Zelenskyy branded “weak”.

The Trump administration denies it is deliberately helping the Russians. But European diplomats concede that the US appears to have switched sides. Ukrainian civilians are dying as a result, they say.

Russia, meanwhile, said it had shot down hundreds of Ukrainian drones launched in overnight attacks. One man ⁠was ⁠killed ​and another was ⁠wounded as a ⁠result ​of ‌a Ukrainian aerial strike in Russia’s Belgorod region, local ‌authorities said.

Details also emerged of a Ukrainian counterattack through a tunnel in the north-eastern city of Kupiansk, which Russia partly occupies. As part of Operation Veles, the Khartia corps carried out the world’s first underground counteroffensive, advancing 15km into enemy rear lines.

“We observed how the enemy operates underground and studied their methods. The Russians intended to use gas pipelines to infiltrate the rear of our forces. So, we went underground ourselves,” Khartia’s commander, Brig Gen Ihor Obolenskyi, told Ukrainian media.

The Ukrainian servicemen crawled 15km through tunnels – without communication, GPS, or light – having developed their own navigation and life-support technologies in advance. About 100 Russians were killed in the operation, and 30 taken prisoner, the Khartia corps said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Meet the volunteers who will observe Trump’s election monitors during the midterms
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Fabiola Cineas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Thousands of people are training to be poll observers to look out for any interference or ICE presence on election day

Stevie Lyn is angry at what she’s seen in her Phoenix, Arizona, neighborhood over the past year. Since US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) began conducting raids all across the city, her Latino neighbors on the west side have had to hide in their homes, too scared to grocery shop, work and vote. That’s why she volunteered to become a poll observer.

“I had to take the anger, because it was eating me alive, and direct it towards a constructive activity,” she said.

Lyn was trained by the grassroots non-profit organizations Living United for Change in Arizona (Lucha) and the Arizona Center for Empowerment (Ace), both focused on immigrant rights, to work the primaries in July. Sitting on the back hatch of her SUV 75ft from her local polling place – the legal distance allowed for poll observers in the state – she watched the area for any disorder or disturbances. She only encountered one problem in 10 hours: a campaigner for a local legislative candidate repeatedly walked with voters beyond the legal line. When she reported it, poll workers asked the campaigner to stay back.

Lyn, who has been through observer training three times, called the primary a dress rehearsal. She has taken election day off work to observe again. She hopes she won’t have much to report. “I just want to be bored to death on 3 November,” she said. “That’s my goal.”

Lyn is one of the thousands of volunteers trained by organizations like Lucha and Ace to safeguard the polls against election interference. The US justice department plans to send about 1,000 federal monitors to polling sites, in what it has called the “biggest DOJ election observer effort in history”, claiming the effort will ensure elections are carried out fairly. But critics suing the government over the plan said it could intimidate voters. And the administration hasn’t ruled out sending ICE and other law enforcement officials to the polls. Poll observers want to be prepared to counter any intimidation, even if many expect election day to be business as usual.

“I am not naive about this administration and have my eyes wide open,” said Justin Levitt, a Loyola Law School professor and former Barack Obama justice department official. “But this administration wants to project power that it doesn’t have and finds it in their interest to get the electorate freaked out.”

On a Monday night in late September, about 20 people logged on to learn how to protect voters in Arizona.

First, though, Karime Rodriguez, an organizer with Ace, told volunteers why the job “constitutional observer” exists. As immigration raids began surging in neighborhoods across Arizona earlier this year, Republican state lawmakers introduced a bill to station ICE agents at polling places. That’s when Ace decided to recruit and train volunteers for double duty: to monitor ICE activity in the Phoenix area’s most vulnerable neighborhoods and to keep watch at the polls during the midterms season.

“These aren’t abstract polling places,” Rodriguez told the trainees during the call. “These are our schools, our churches, our community centers where immigration enforcement has already been taking place.”

When Ace started mapping ICE activity in Maricopa and Pima counties, the map showed a pattern that the neighborhoods hit hardest by raids were often the same ones already facing barriers to voting, including polling place closures. In the two weeks before the July primary, the group recorded a spike in reported raids. There was also ICE activity around a few polling places in West Phoenix, a primarily Hispanic neighborhood. That alone discouraged some people from voting, Rodriguez said. Turning Point USA had a presence at a voting center in south Phoenix, and some voters told the groups they felt intimidated.

“ICE is in our neighborhoods and even people who are citizens are afraid that they’ll be taken if they go to vote,” said César Fierros, a spokesperson for Lucha. “We see the trucks driving by, the unmarked vehicles driving by. And we’re scared because we never know who is going to be in that vehicle.”

Organizers said the heat map has become the backbone of their election protection effort, using it to decide where to station observers and deploy its rapid response volunteers on election day. The groups’ plan is to have three or four observers at every polling place who must simply observe; if they see something suspicious, all they have to do is report it back to the leadership team. If ICE agents show up, they should also alert Lucha and Ace leaders, who will then send an alert within the group’s chat, post on social media or call for community members to show up. Volunteers who can’t be at the polls will answer phone calls and texts.

Groups like Lucha and Ace are preparing volunteers for election day all across the country. In Pennsylvania, more than 250 people participated in poll watcher training hosted by the state’s Democratic party on the same Monday night in September. They flooded the chat with questions: Could an ICE officer challenge a voter’s eligibility? Almost certainly not, a party lawyer said. Law enforcement officers can’t come within 100ft of a Pennsylvania polling place unless they are voting or the site is in a police building. The only exception he could imagine was an off-duty agent casting a ballot in his own precinct.

Jack Doyle, the communications director of the Pennsylvania Democratic party, said Democrats are building “an unprecedented voter protection program” that will deploy thousands of volunteer observers to priority locations, backed by volunteer attorneys in every county and a hotline staffed in English, Spanish, Mandarin, Vietnamese and Korean.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has seen a similar surge. Since June, 68,000 new volunteers have signed up to be “democracy defenders”, said Molly McGrath, the ACLU’s director of national democracy campaigns, people who are ready to be called upon to watch polling places or protest in the event of election interference.
