The invasive cyber-surveillance and data-mining in The Audacity are deeply chilling. “We consulted experts but all the information is out there,” says Glatzer. “The Guardian and New York Times do some terrific reporting on AI. It always feels like the journalists secretly want to headline their articles: ‘Wake the fuck up! This is happening!’”

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet faces ecosystem collapse by 2075, UN advisors say
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Assessment finds global heating is endangering 96% of coral reefs across 80 countries – a figure scientists say should serve as a ‘wake-up call’

Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet, including Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, faces a high risk of ecosystem collapse before 2075 because of global heating, according to an assessment by United Nations nature advisers.

About 24% of the planet’s reefs across more than 80 countries are already critically endangered, the assessment said, but when the expected impacts of global heating were added this rose to 96%.

Coral reefs are known as the rainforests of the sea. A quarter of all known marine species are found in and around them and they support hundreds of millions of people with food, as well as protecting shorelines and supporting tourism.

Overfishing, pollution, coastal development and global heating have already caused declines in the ecosystems over the past 50 years, measured by the loss of live coral as well as changes in fish populations, the assessment said.

But the scientists said while the prognosis was dire, the findings should serve as a “wake-up call” because reefs could survive with rapid cuts to fossil fuel use and strong conservation action at local levels.

Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

“The risk is real and very concerning,” said Dr Mishal Gudka, research director at CORDIO (Coral Reef Degradation in the Indian Ocean) East Africa and the scientific lead for the assessment.

“We stand to lose one of the most valuable ecosystems we have – the impacts of which will affect millions of people around the world.”

The assessment analysed the current status and future threat levels of 127 coral reef regions and was coordinated by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), an international group that advises the United Nations.

The assessment assumed greenhouse gas emissions – mainly from burning fossil fuels – would follow a “middle-of-the-road” pathway, causing about 2.7C of global heating by the end of the century when compared with temperatures before the Industrial Revolution.

Current climate policies and targets adopted by countries around the world are likely to cause about 2.6C of global heating, one assessment finds.

The share of coral eco-regions considered critically endangered would likely be even higher, the IUCN said, but four regions did not have enough data to assess them and the coral reefs of the western Galápagos had already collapsed.

The critically endangered classification meant an “extremely high risk” of ecosystem collapse before 2075.

The group considers a coral reef ecosystem to have collapsed if the reef could not maintain itself because of a near or complete loss of living reef-building corals.

The assessment did not fully account for the impacts of the fourth global mass bleaching event from early 2023 to mid-2025 – the most widespread global mass bleaching event on record, the US government’s Coral Reef Watch has confirmed.

That global event was bookended by the worst mass bleaching event on record for reefs in Western Australia where a heatwave killed corals across 1,500 kilometres (930 miles).

Marine heatwaves can cause corals to separate from the symbiotic algae that provides them with colour and nutrient. While not always deadly, bleaching can weaken corals and make them more susceptible to disease.

Gudka said the results were a “wake-up call” and were “alarming, but certainly not hopeless”.

He said: “They should be seen as a call to action – an early warning sign before the worst outcomes eventuate.”

Dr Grethel Aguilar, the director general of the IUCN, said: “It is not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover, but it requires decisive action to tackle climate change and halt further ocean warming.

“We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them.”

Four of Australia’s 17 reef regions were considered critically endangered. Five were endangered and five more were classed as vulnerable.

But all 17 regions, including the Great Barrier Reef, were critically endangered once the expected impacts of climate change were accounted for.

Dr Ben Fitzpatrick of the University of Western Australia Oceans Institute led the Australian assessment. He said even after accounting for the ability of some corals to adapt to warmer water, the rising heat “overwhelmed everything”.

“Reefs are like Picasso paintings underwater,” he said. “They have all these wonderful inhabitants in their millions. You can spend a lifetime trying to understand how all these weird critters go about their daily lives.

“To think we might lose that is devastating. There’s one message. We have to stop burning fossil fuels.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Florida police officer finds man dead and steals his house and identity, authorities allege
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The officer says he took possession of the property and renovated it ‘to prevent criminal activity’ and ‘squatting’

A Florida police officer who discovered a man dead during a welfare check stole his house and identity and spent years renovating the property for himself, authorities said.

Brian Louis Sguros, 35, an officer with the Lauderhill police department near Miami, appeared in court Wednesday on charges including criminal use of a deceased person’s identification.

Sguros was part of a team sent to check on a Lauderhill resident, Dennis West, in July 2022, after the department received a call from a worried neighbor, a press release from the Broward sheriff’s office (BSO) said. West was found deceased in the home of natural causes.

Within weeks, the officer embarked on what BSO said was “a complex scheme to take control of the individual’s home” by involving himself in West’s post-death affairs.

“Sguros represented himself to the Broward county medical examiner’s office as West’s friend, although there is no indication he knew West, and stated that West had no living family, which was untrue,” the press release said.

“The investigation also revealed that Sguros paid the taxes and utilities at the home in West’s name and used West’s identification to make it appear that West was still alive to get the city of Lauderhill to issue a permit to facilitate repairs.”

A 21-page arrest affidavit alleges Sguros forged West’s signature on multiple documents, and between August 2022 and February 2025 spent more than $210,000 of his own money upgrading the property, including replacing doors and windows in 2024.

The affidavit said that Sguros, in sworn statements and civil pleadings, maintained he took possession of the property and worked on it “because it was hazardous and he wanted to prevent criminal activity and people from squatting”, NBC Miami reported.

During that time, Sguros allegedly used law enforcement databases to improperly access West’s driver’s license record, date of birth, social security number, and other personal information.

Then in February 2025, he and his spouse filed a claim with the Broward property appraiser’s office seeking to establish a claim to ownership, the affidavit said.

A neighbor told WSVN TV that Sguros often talked with her, and told her he was renovating the property with a plan to rent it out on Airbnb. She said Sguros told her West was his friend, and had given him the property before he died.

The alleged scam came to light in August 2025 when a real estate company that bought the property legally from West’s heirs sent an employee to take possession and encountered Sguros, NBC reported.

Sguros surrendered the keys, but filed civil litigation against the real estate company demanding compensation for the money he had invested in renovations, the news outlet said.

The officer was placed on administrative leave with pay following his arrest on Tuesday after a months-long investigation by BSO detectives. He appeared in court in Fort Lauderdale on Wednesday on charges including official misconduct and criminal use of deceased person’s identification, and was released on $25,000 bond.

Sguros could not be reached for comment, and it is unclear if he is represented by an attorney.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Robert Booth and Aisha Down
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Problem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch fault

Websites around the world have been hit by millions of attempts to exploit a recently discovered vulnerability in their code, cybersecurity companies have said, as the US National Security Agency warned the flaw could allow attackers to take control of web servers, steal data and disrupt services.

The problem in the PHP programming language, which underpins about 70% of the world’s websites, emerged on Wednesday causing governments and companies to pull their websites off the internet before they could be attacked and so they could patch the fault.

In the UK, 32 government services have been taken offline, the cybersecurity minister, Liz Lloyd, told parliament. She said this “largely resulted from precautionary measures” while updates were applied. Downing Street said no public-facing critical services had been affected and that “some limited services may be temporarily offline” but this did not mean they had been hacked. The website for the BBC’s Traitors was one of those that was down on Thursday. It sparked particular concern about the ongoing vulnerability of systems used by schools, local governments and charities, which may not have dedicated cybersecurity support to execute the fix.

Ciaran Martin, the former chief executive of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, described the flaw as “very bad”, saying that while most internet software vulnerabilities didn’t matter, this was “the most serious vulnerability discovered for five years”.

However, Ryan Austin, a researcher at the cybersecurity company Calif, who was key to discovering the flaw, said: “At the moment it doesn’t look like exploitation has taken off or been widespread.”

The flaw prompted governments into action, with the NSA in the US saying it could allow attackers to seize control of web servers, steal sensitive data, disrupt services and move deeper into a network. Government websites were quickly taken down so the patch could be installed with many coming back on line soon afterwards.

In an update overnight on Wednesday, and into Thursday, Matthew Prince, the chief executive of the cybersecurity business Cloudflare, said the company encountered tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the weakness in the 45 minutes after the problem was announced, rising to “hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now”.

Amazon Threat Intelligence, another cybersecurity company, added that PHP2Shell, as the vulnerability is known, was “now being broadly exploited in the wild” and said it identified several attempts from multiple actors to test ways to capitalise on the vulnerability before the fix was released by the PHP developers on Wednesday.

Cloudflare also said that in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, it saw thousands of attempts to exploit the vulnerability, amid concern over the handling of the alert, with one cybersecurity expert, Prof Alan Woodward, saying the flaw was revealed a day before the patch was released, and that “somebody let the cat out of the bag”.

The PHP vulnerability could allow hostile actors to “grab the resources” of exposed sites, said Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. A website, such as Slack or Wikipedia, has access to computing power, servers, and IP addresses – which locate it on the internet. In many cases, this infrastructure is managed and mediated by PHP.

Criminal groups, state-sponsored hackers, or crypto miners might “nest” themselves into exposed sites using this PHP vulnerability, and then exploit those resources for their own aims. A hacking group could use an exposed site’s IP address to launch attacks that could not then be traced back to it. Crypto miners could use a server’s computing power to run their energy-intensive calculations for free.

It is unclear at what scale this has been done, said Woźniak, and many sites would not even be aware of it.

Wiz, one of the research organisations that uncovered the vulnerabilities, said it was arguably among the most severe software vulnerabilities ever discovered. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” it said in a blogpost. “Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

“Cyber-actors are likely to weaponise PHP2Shell,” the NSA said. “These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across US government departments and agencies.”

The government of South Korea said on Thursday it was activating emergency response measures, raising its private sector cybersecurity alert level and issuing guidance to tens of thousands of companies on how to fix the problem. China’s industry ministry urged organisation to immediately inspect their systems and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP and recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring, changing passwords and keys.

The prime minister of Japan encouraged businesses and organisations to patch the vulnerability – or shut down their sites.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: How tech became the villain of the US midterms
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Nick Robins-Early
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Datacenters, AI and distaste for the billionaires developing it has soured Americans on big tech

How will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questions

The campaign ad begins with a clear, idyllic stream that suddenly turns sludge-brown as two concrete datacenters slam onto its banks. Another facility thuds down on a peaceful suburban park, and two more crush-green pastures as an ominous soundtrack to a disaster movie blares overtop.

“They’re coming for our rivers. Our neighborhoods. Our farmland,” a deep-voiced narrator says. “Because Brent Taylor wrote the law allowing datacenters to take over Tennessee.”

The attack ad, paid for by the Democrat-aligned Three Star Pac and targeting a Tennessee Republican congressional candidate, is one of more than 150 midterm election campaign commercials across the US focused on datacenters or the artificial intelligence industry. At debates and at rallies, in mailers and online ads, the burgeoning AI industry has taken center stage, as both Republican and Democratic candidates try to convince voters that their opponents will put the unpopular facilities in voters’ backyards.

And it’s not only datacenters – the public anxiety over AI and distaste for the billionaires developing it, as well as backlash over encroaching tech like surveillance cameras, has turned the tech industry into a ubiquitous villain this election cycle. As with big pharma before it, candidates are straining to distance themselves from big tech.

The stigma of the tech industry has even forced prominent Republicans to break with Donald Trump’s pro-AI party line, with candidates like Ken Paxton, campaigning for US Senate in Texas, calling for a slowdown. In Tennessee, Taylor’s campaign ran its own television spot that claimed he was tough on tech and datacenters.

The campaign ads focused on tech have sprung up alongside an ecosystem of pro- and anti-AI political action committees, which have collectively spent hundreds of millions of dollars to influence elections and back candidates. The breathtaking amount of spending has pushed tech into the forefront of the midterms, even as polls show issues like the economy, democracy and healthcare still rate as more important among voters.

Super Pacs funded by tech billionaires are among the top spenders in this election cycle. Leading the Future, formed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, has raised more than $75m to back tech-friendly candidates. Elon Musk has sunk $366m into Republican causes, more than he spent on the 2024 presidential election. AI money has also been funneled into pro-regulation Pacs seeking to counteract the influence of deregulation groups.

Including Musk’s contribution to various Republican-aligned Pacs, the tech industry and its leaders have spent more than half a billion dollars to influence elections and ballot proposals in 2026.

The cumulative effect of such vast spending, lobbying and advertising is that tech issues and the tech industry have become far more pervasive in the midterms than previously seen in US elections, marking the first major test of how American voters will react to the AI boom.

Concern over AI’s potential effect on society has grown over the last year, and the backlash has been most intense where there is a physical target for voters’ ire. None of those targets have loomed larger than the sprawling datacenter facilities that are part of the tech industry’s multitrillion-dollar infrastructure build-out. Although campaigns have nodded to AI regulation and fears over the technology’s risks, it is datacenters that candidates have repeatedly and specifically called out as a real, tangible threat to constituents.

“Datacenters are now a campaign question in nearly every race in the nation,” said Brad Carson, the head of a pro-AI-regulation group Public First Action and a former congressman.

The growing animosity toward datacenters has also been reflected in nationwide protests and polling. A Pew Research poll from last month showed that the percentage of US adults who believe that datacenters are bad for the environment, energy costs and quality of life has spiked upwards across demographics since January. Only 4% of respondents believe the facilities will be good for the environment or home energy costs.

Datacenters have become toxic enough that some candidates have even begun using the facilities as an epithet to tar their rivals.

“Data Center Derek gave the billionaires and greedy corporations a $2bn tax break. Driving up our electric bills, destroying Ohio farms,” declared a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee attack ad against Ohio Republican candidate Derek Merrin.

At least 20 candidates for governor across the US are calling for moratoriums on datacenters, according to policy tracking firm MultiState, while fewer than 10 candidates across 36 gubernatorial races are backing the projects without any calls for increased regulations.

Along with datacenters, the public backlash against AI-enabled Flock surveillance cameras that automatically scan license plates has also bled into campaigns, including in key battleground races. In Michigan, Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed ran a Flock-focused ad that accused his Republican opponent Mike Rogers of pushing a surveillance state by backing the cameras. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico has similarly spoken out against the company and its data collection.

“Flock cameras have no place in Texas,” Talarico said last month at a rally. The state’s Republican governor, Greg Abbott, surprisingly agrees with him, blocking state agencies from spending on Flock cameras in August.

Elsewhere, legislation has targeted not just tech infrastructure but the billionaires behind it. In California, voters are considering a ballot measure that would levy a one-time 5% wealth tax on any resident of the state worth more than $1bn. The state’s ultra-rich have feverishly mobilized against it, raising more than $340m and spending more than $1m a day to fight the measure. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone has contributed at least $102m to oppose the tax.

The collective backlash against the tech industry has put its leaders in a bind. Companies are facing internal and external criticism of their products and politics, but accepting more intense government regulation or halting datacenter construction would threaten their growth.

The pushback has caused a shift in at least one company’s calculus – OpenAI has distanced itself from Leading the Future in recent months, and Brockman backed out of a planned $25m donation to the Pac.

Musk, Brin and other tech moguls, however, have doubled down on their efforts to swing votes their way.

“They have never met a problem that they didn’t think they could solve by throwing more money at it,” said Charles Blaettler, political director of pro-AI-regulation Pac Guardrails Alliance. “They’re realizing there’s an intense backlash to their ideas.”

The political landscape of the tech industry is vastly different from the last time the US held midterm elections. Anthropic, now potentially set to go public at a more than $2tn valuation, was just one year old in 2022. OpenAI had not publicly released ChatGPT. Musk had not yet allied himself with Donald Trump’s campaign.

The tech industry has become increasingly entrenched in government and determined to shape regulation in the period since. Tech leaders have simultaneously built up immense campaign finance and lobbying arms that have come into full force in this year’s midterms.

Meanwhile, Americans feel negatively about how AI will affect a range of issues from personal relationships to the economy to elections, multiple polls show, as well as broadly opposing datacenters in their communities. More Americans oppose a datacenter being built in their area than oppose a nuclear power plant, according to a Gallup poll from earlier this year.

The public distaste for the AI industry also extends to its leaders, with polls showing that the US generally views executives such as Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as untrustworthy and unlikeable.

“There’s this very deep-seated sense of anxiety people have about the direction this technology is taking and who’s in control of it,” Blaettler said. “People just feel like they don’t have any agency in their lives anymore.”

The enormous spending from the tech industry has largely flowed to Republicans, but it has also inspired a new category of pro-AI-regulation Pacs that have formed to counter groups like Leading the Future. Some of these pro-regulation Pacs have received money, counterintuitively, from AI companies and workers with different views on how government should oversee the technology. Anthropic contributed more than $40m to Carson’s Public First Action, while the Guardrails Alliance and its associated non-profit have raised more than $11.5m.

One of the early tests for this type of battle was in the Democratic primary for New York’s 12th congressional district in June, where pro- and anti-AI groups, including Carson’s, cumulatively spent $24m on the race – largely targeting candidate Alex Bores, who was running on a pro-regulation platform. The result of all the spending was hard to determine, with Bores coming second in a crowded field and losing to similarly pro-regulation candidate Micah Lasher. After the vote, Lasher sought to distance himself from both Anthropic and OpenAI’s spending.

“I have some news for the two big AI companies who’ve taken such an unusual interest in who won this congressional seat,” Lasher said in June. “I won’t be taking my cues from either of you when it comes to protecting our kids, our jobs, our environment.”

While the spending frenzy on pro- and anti-AI campaigns has helped fund some of the fights over tech in the midterms, leaders of pro-regulation Pacs say these are issues that voters already organically care about and are mobilizing around. The message from the AI industry has for years been that their products will usher in a utopian era of abundance and affluence, but this election cycle has shown there is deep skepticism from everyday voters that they will benefit from the boom.

“It’s now a world where most people on the street have a view about AI,” Carson said. “And it’s mostly negative.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump’s war and tariffs have battered Alaska. A pro-oil Democrat could flip the key Senate seat
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein in Anchorage, Alaska
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Democrats believe circumstances have aligned for them to win a slew of competitive elections in the state

How will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questions

Mary Peltola’s campaign to represent Alaska in the US Senate has taken her to parts of the massive state’s interior that are inaccessible by road and on the frontlines of the cost-of-living crisis she hopes will make her the first Democrat to win the seat in nearly two decades.

She has been to towns where paper towels retail for $40, a half gallon of oat milk goes for $21 and the cost of a new freezer can be quadruple what it is in the state’s largest city, Anchorage, simply because it’s so complicated to get there. Along the Arctic Ocean, she’s heard of communities where power bills have climbed to $1,500 a month because they rely on generators for power and the Iran war has pushed the cost of diesel to new heights.

Alaska, a right-leaning state that’s about twice the size of Texas but the third least-populous in the country, has always been among the more expensive places to live, and the price increases in the state’s rural areas haven’t necessarily been felt to the same degree in the more populous cities and towns.

Yet the state’s Democrats believe circumstances have aligned for them to win a slew of competitive elections in the 3 November midterms. The Senate seat currently held by two-term Republican Dan Sullivan is a top prize.

“In 23 short days, we’re going to be voting both [Republican congressman] Nick Begich and Dan Sullivan out of office, and they richly deserve it,” the chair of the state Democratic party, Eric Croft, said at a press conference last week.

“They are self-serving, self-dealing DC politicians who repeatedly voted to make life harder and more expensive for Alaskans.”

All signs indicate that Republicans are taking seriously the threat posed by Peltola, an Alaska native and former US House lawmaker who supports oil and gas and gun rights. Outside groups have poured in tens of millions of dollars into supporting both candidates, and last week Donald Trump made the long journey from Washington DC to the conservative Matanuska-Susitna valley to rally voters behind Sullivan, who has trailed in some recent polls.

“Here in Alaska, the Democrats are running radical left Mary Peltola for the Senate. If she gets in, you’re screwed,” the president told a packed sports center in Wasilla, which is best known outside the state as being the home town of Sarah Palin, the Republican former vice-presidential nominee.

On the campaign trail, Peltola and Sullivan have dueled over who would do a better job lowering costs for Alaskans, and also representing its vital fishing and oil and gas industries in the US Capitol. There have been mutual accusations of allegiances not to a state known as “the last frontier” but to special interests in the Lower 48, while Sullivan has accused Peltola of denigrating Alaskans after a report that she mistreated her staffers.

The incumbent has his own unique vulnerability in the form of a similarly named Republican challenger who made it through the state’s top-four primary, and could split his support. And while polls open on 3 November, the outcome may not be known for days – Alaska has always taken a long time to count its ballots, and its use of ranked-choice voting in the Senate contest could result in an even lengthier wait for the final result.

Since becoming the 49th state in 1959, Alaska has only once supported a Democratic candidate in a presidential election – Lyndon B Johnson in 1964. But its politics are nuanced – bipartisan majorities currently control the legislature and the frontrunner in the governor’s race is a Democrat. In the race for the state’s lone US House seat, the party has coalesced behind the independent candidate Bill Hill to take on Begich.

“Sixty per cent of Alaskans do not identify with the Republican or the Democratic party. We are a great example in this state of how government should work,” Hill, who is receiving support from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said in an interview.

A former state lawmaker, Peltola rose to prominence in 2022 when she won a special election to replace Don Young, the long-serving Republican congressman who died at 88, and became the first Alaska native in Congress. She was elected to a full term later that year, then lost re-election to Begich in 2024. This year, Peltola is viewed as the best candidate Democrats could field to take on Sullivan.

Centering her campaign on the slogan “fish, family, freedom”, she has added an Alaskan twist to the cost-focused platform many Democrats have adopted nationwide. Visitors to her campaign website can play a video game intended to highlight her views on bycatch, or the accidental netting of other species by trawlers, which has become a major controversy in Alaska as salmon runs have dwindled.

Peltola opposes Trump’s tariff regime, noting it has driven up costs for imports from Canada, which separates Alaska from the rest of the country. She has also condemned his decision to attack Iran and spark a conflict that has driven costs for gasoline and diesel – which typically arrive by barge or ship in the state’s interior and island communities – even higher than usual.

“These really frivolous decisions are just putting Alaskans in a bind, and we’re really paying the price for these weird partisan wars,” Peltola said as she visited a picket line of flight attendants at Anchorage’s main airport. With a laugh, she added: “I don’t know what’s funny about that, but it’s funny.”

Sullivan, her opponent, was first elected in 2014 after ousting a Democratic incumbent. He serves alongside Republican Lisa Murkowski, Alaska’s senior senator who is one of the most outspoken Trump critics in the Senate, but has nonetheless remained a firm ally of of the president, even as his popularity has waned, unlike many vulnerable Republicans who have sought distance. Sullivan has emphasized his advocacy for Alaska’s military installations, as well as the state’s long list of proposed oil developments and major infrastructure projects that he argues will only come to fruition if Republicans are kept in charge.

“Joe Biden, Schumer, their Democratic allies came after Alaska with a barrage of executive orders to shut down our state, kill jobs, drive up the cost of energy, and my opponent, Mary Peltola, not only did nothing to stop it, she enabled it,” Sullivan said as he rallied with Trump.

“They try to kill our jobs and turn us into a national park. Ladies and gentlemen, the conflict in the Middle East is temporary. The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas and our jobs.”

He gained new ammunition against Peltola in September, when the New York Times reported allegations that she had verbally and physically abused her staff and used slurs. “My opponent really doesn’t like her fellow Alaskans. She just doesn’t,” Sullivan told supporters in Wasilla.

Peltola’s campaign has said parts of the report are not true, and noted some of the behavior occurred when she was grieving the death of her husband in a plane crash, and the death of her mother around the same time. When Peltola was asked about the report during a debate with Sullivan last week, she replied: “I do not think that this election is about me on my worst day, and I found so many of these allegations concerning and outright fabrications.”

Alaska is one of the nation’s top oil-producing states, and every year its permanent fund pays each resident a dividend that’s usually upwards of $1,000. But production, which is concentrated on the state’s North Slope, has steadily declined since peaking in the late 1980s, and how to manage the resource is a constant topic in the state’s politics.

Sullivan is all-in on oil production, supporting moves by Trump to open up more protected federal land and waters to drilling, which could offer new revenue opportunities. He cheered the president’s announcement that South Korea would invest $54bn to build a long-discussed natural gas pipeline across the state, although reports have since emerged that Seoul has agreed to no such deal.

Though she was in the House of Representatives for just over two years, Peltola has taken credit for pushing Joe Biden to approve the massive Willow oil project, over the objections of environmentalists. But she also emphasizes the opportunities renewable energy could present to Alaska’s communities, and is cognizant that she is a member of a party that prioritizes fighting the climate crisis, which many believe requires curbing oil and gas production.

“We do need more oil production in our state for our state revenues to pay for our schools, our roads, our public safety,” Peltola said.

But the sky-high prices for gas in parts of Alaska are proof to the candidate that oil is not the solution alone.

“When you’re paying $26 a gallon for gas or diesel, we’re priced out of petroleum,” she said.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Zach Braff: ‘You can be talented and good-looking, but acting success is still like winning the lottery’
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: As told to Rich Pelley
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
The Scrubs and Garden State star answers your questions about working with megastars, getting his hair to look good and being brutally killed on BoJack Horseman

How do you manage not to act starstruck when directing people like Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine and Harrison Ford? TopTramp That’s where my acting comes in – I pretend that I don’t know how famous they are. Every actor really wants a leader. They want someone who knows the script really well, has a plan for how the scene is going to be executed, and – in the case of comedy – knows how to make it funny. The last thing any of those guys wants is someone coming in starstruck and wide-eyed. So I use my acting skills to pretend I’m not starstruck and treat them like normal people.

Your Fake Doctors, Real Friends podcast was a real help through lockdown. You were very emotionally open and personal; it was like catching up with friends. I still think about your line that making it in acting, even if you’re talented and good-looking, is like winning the lottery. Do you think that early 00s Zach Braff would make it in the present day the way you did? KamesJ Back then, the broadcast networks were making so many pilots, at least it was work for people. Now, I think it’s a much harder landscape to break through. I firmly believe that you can be talented and good-looking, but success is still like winning the lottery. I know plenty of brilliant actors whose lottery ticket hasn’t come up yet. I started auditioning at 14 and barely got anything for years, so I’ve always felt very lucky.

And as far as the podcast, that’s so great to hear. We didn’t plan to start it during Covid, but it became a nice sort of warm hug for people who wanted a little bit of nostalgia. Donald [Faison, who plays Dr Turk] and I loved getting together, making each other laugh and reminiscing. So much so that we’re actually bringing it back.

Have you thought about Garden State 2? Haggisneepsnfatties We did an anniversary concert for the soundtrack last year – we got most of the bands together and did a charity show for the Midnight Mission in Los Angeles – and that was really cool. Natalie Portman was there. I had told her that people have come to me about doing a musical of the movie. I love musicals, but I’ve always thought: “I don’t know if that I want to do that.” Then she said: “Why don’t you do it with the songs from the soundtrack?” It’s funny, because I never thought of that. I haven’t taken any steps to make it a reality, but I do daydream of somehow using the music that people love so much from the soundtrack to make it into a musical.

When you agreed to join the cast of BoJack Horseman, how did you feel about your character having such a grisly end? topfoot I love the show, so it was so fun to play a cartoonish version of myself, and I just did whatever they said. I never said: “Don’t kill me that way. Don’t have Jessica Biel feast on my carcass,” or whatever the hell it was.

How much fun was it playing a small role in Arrested Development – to my mind the funniest, cleverest and silliest of all the US sitcoms? Manofthesouth It was amazing, especially because I didn’t know I was going to be a never-nude until I got the script. In the world of Arrested Development, a never-nude is someone – mainly Tobias – who can never be fully naked, even in the shower, so he wears denim short-shorts.

Scrubs and Arrested Development were both doing really well. Jason Bateman and I were at some big event with the heads of both networks – we were NBC, they were Fox. We were laughing, saying: “It’d be fun if we each guested on each other’s show, but the networks would never let us do that.” Then we realised: “They’re all here. Let’s just go ask them.” They said “Sure,” so I guested on Arrested and Jason did an episode of Scrubs as an ostrich farmer.

Who would you most like to cast in Dr Acula: The Movie – JD’s vampire-doctor screenplay in Scrubs? PickleMan Michael B Jordan and Leonardo DiCaprio, if we’re in the fantasy where we’re going to make an amazing, huge-budget version. Remember at the end of Pee-wee’s Big Adventure when they make the movie of his life and cast beautiful movie stars, and Pee-wee ends up as a bellhop? That’s the version of Dr Acula I want: megastars, while Donald and I are just in the background.

You’ve had huge success whether you’re acting, writing or directing. If you were to pick one standout pinch-me moment, what would it be? Turnipsnitzel Morgan Freeman saying yes to my film was one of those great moments. So was standing in the back of the Eccles theatre in Park City when Garden State premiered, thinking: “Holy shit, how did this happen?”

When I got Scrubs, I was waiting tables. I put my Motorola StarTAC phone on the passenger seat as I was driving home from the final callback, and was just eyeing it to see if it was going to ring. Then it rang, I pulled over, called my parents, then I called the manager of the restaurant. She said: “I’m so happy for you, babe, but you got to work tonight still.” I said: “Oh, don’t worry, I’m coming in.” So I worked the whole shift knowing I probably wouldn’t be waiting tables for a couple of years.

If you were on a plane and there was an announcement asking if there’s a doctor on board, would you put your hand up? MrSOBaldrick Absolutely not. I don’t know anything. I really don’t. We have the most amazing consultants on set, including this wonderful nurse who’s just a badass. She shows us what to do and tells us what the hell we’re saying. Anyone who thinks we know anything for real is crazy.

Scrubs taught me a lot about illness, life and death. Did it do the same for you? waydgroods I was so young when we did the original series that I don’t think I had any experience with loss and being in hospitals and grief. In the years since, I’ve lost so many people. I’ve sat in hospital and ICU waiting rooms, waiting with bated breath for the doctor to come in with good or bad news. I’ve seen how the nurses run the whole hospital. I’ve witnessed it first-hand in a way I hadn’t as a young man. So I think now I have even more respect. I feel more like I’m playing a superhero as the guy who’s the chief of medicine at an underfunded hospital who’s meant to be a particularly badass doctor.

Does your hair have its own agent? Dr_J_A_Zoidberg My hair’s agent is that I take a shower at night and then I go to sleep on it and you get magical bedhead.

https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.title: Delays, deodorant and ripped up carpet: how airlines handle mid-flight ‘biological hazards’
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.author: Natasha May
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.text:
When stomach bugs meet turbulence, air travel can become a health hazard for all onboard – and it happens, unfortunately, ‘more regularly than you would think’

A little over an hour into their transatlantic flight, Kate Carson’s daughters had just laid down to sleep when suddenly their Air New Zealand “cuddle class” skycouch became a “nightmare” scene.

A stomach bug that had been troubling their family during the holiday reared its head again: her youngest, three years old, started throwing up. “The first time, she was asleep, and no one saw it coming, and it went all into the seat … down the side and into the crack,” Carson says.

Her daughter did not stop vomiting until an hour before they landed in Los Angeles. “Everyone’s worried about their kid crying on a plane – no, no, no – this is so much worse,” Carson says.

Her husband spent “10 straight hours just trying to catch whatever else she threw up into the barf bag” while Carson cleaned the plane bathroom “top to bottom”. After she’d “nuked” it with what she thought was a cleaning product, supplied by the crew, she realised all she had been given was “deodorising spray”. (When contacted by Guardian Australia, Air New Zealand declined to comment.) Carson and her husband decided to abandon the plan to surprise their daughters with a visit to Disneyland during the layover. Instead, they booked into a hotel to do laundry.

As the other passengers disembarked, ground crew were waiting to take away the family’s chairs, clean around them, then replace them with an entirely new row. “I was so grateful … you come in and you sit on a seat of a plane and you just don’t know who was there, you don’t know what happened,” Carson said.

But some passengers have been left with clues. A Delta passenger sat in the faeces of an ill service animal from the previous flight; a man travelling with Air France found blood and faeces on the floor from a passenger’s hemorrhage two flights before; while Air Canada passengers were threatened with being placed on a no fly list for refusing to sit in vomit-soaked seats. In a statement, Delta said their safety and security protocols are “top customer priorities”; Air Canada said “for any extraordinary situations” the airline “follows the standards as set out by the health authorities to deep clean and disinfect aircraft cabins using professional grade products”; while Air France did not respond to requests for comment.

While these incidents suggest airlines don’t always allow hygiene issues to hinder the schedule, they can also cause major delays. In 2023 a woman’s trail of diarrhoea forced a Delta flight from Atlanta to Barcelona to turn back, while a 2008 flight diverted after several passengers from the same New England tour group were struck with norovirus mid-air – and was the subject of a study by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Travel is a major risk factor for gastrointestinal illnesses, with travellers’ diarrhoea thought to affect between 30% and 70% of travellers during a two-week period. Combined with turbulence increasing nausea and logistical barriers sometimes hindering passengers from making it to the lavatory on time, air travel can become not just messy but a biological hazard.

Flights are delayed due to biological hazards from passengers “unfortunately more regularly than you would think”, says Justin Brownjohn, a former operations manager for Singapore Airlines, Qatar Airways and Virgin Australia.

While there is no publicly available data on the subject, and multiple airlines refused the Guardian’s requests for internal data, Brownjohn says that, from his experiences, an airline would probably be delayed due to a biohazard issue roughly once a week.

The extent of the delay depends on what the substance is, “how bad it is”, where it is on the aircraft and where the flight has landed, says Brownjohn, now manager of the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology’s Aviation Academy.

When an incident happens midflight, cabin crew will attempt to contain the contamination, using biohazard kits they have on board for this purpose, which include an absorbent powder that can turn liquid into clumps so it can be scraped away. Then the area will be sanitised with a spray.

“But depending on the severity of the contamination, the aircraft may need a more thorough cleaning and disinfection by the ground team before it can operate again,” says Leila*, a flight attendant from a low cost carrier airline in the Middle East.

She says that “the really extreme cases”, when body fluids get into carpets, seat cushions or other areas that are difficult to properly clean, can cause a delay. Sometimes whole sections of carpet have to be removed.

Flight attendants may also be able to swap out seat covers, block off a row of seats if the flight isn’t full, or close off a bathroom, says Seth Heiple, a flight attendant for a major US carrier and a safety representative for the Association of Flight Attendants. “Unfortunately, we’ve had faeces all over the walls of a lavatory.”

Flight attendants will notify the pilot, who will warn the ground crew, or other teams who may need to be involved, such as maintenance crews if seatbelts need to be replaced due to contamination, Heiple says.

Most airlines have third-party contractors who provide the ground crew cleaning services. Osman Yılmaz is the managing director of one such service, Çelebi Aviation, which contracts for airlines including Lufthansa, Emirates and Air China at their stations across five countries.

Yilmaz says crews are “well trained” in cleaning up vomit and spills. “But something beyond that, they don’t have to touch it.”

For more extreme cases, especially if there is blood, specialist cleaning companies with training in biological messes are called in. These experts can usually resolve issues fairly quickly in major ports, Brownjohn says.

However, when incidents occur in smaller airports without access to cleaning and engineering support, “the airline quickly runs out of options about what they can do”, Brownjohn says.

“It’s usually one of two: do the best they can – by cordoning off areas, changing seat covers, using air freshener – the other option is usually cancel the flight,” he says.

Heiple says in these situations “if the smell’s really bad, they might be legal to fly, but it’s not something that we want to accept if it’s going to maybe trigger more people to throw up on the next flight”.

The captain has the final authority on whether to accept an aircraft, Heiple says, but the crew will occasionally demand additional cleaning through a consultative process.

These kinds of delays are becoming more common with the advent of low cost carriers who turn planes around in short windows. “The system is not designed to accommodate last-minute problems like this,” says William McGee, who previously worked in airline operations management.

Last century, aircraft spent more time on the ground between flights, while airlines had a much lower rate of seat occupancy (about six in 10) and in-house cleaning staff. This meant “they had more ability to address this stuff”, says McGee, now a senior fellow for aviation at the American Economic Liberties Project.

While long-haul international flights are generally cleaned between flights – because these are the routes that make the most money – domestic short haul routes are often only thoroughly cleaned at the end of the day, McGee says.

Aircraft are typically deep cleaned every two weeks or so – which involves cleaning nooks and crannies and steaming carpets and seats, Brownjohn says.

McGee says: “My best advice is take the first flight of the day because chances are that’s the cleanest that plane is going to be all day.”

Heiple agrees. “Between flights during the day, [a passenger] might not realise that somebody used the tray table to change their baby and now it’s contaminated.

“Anything that can come out of the human body has and does on the aircraft unfortunately.”

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: $950 of beauty products for $150: is Revolve’s advent calendar too good to be true?
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Karen Yuan and Lauren Gould
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
We reviewed Revolve’s 12- and 25-day beauty advent calendars to see if the brand’s offerings provide value for your money

October is too early for Bing Crosby and peppermint cocoa – but if you’re considering a beauty advent calendar, you’re right on time.

We have tested popular calendars from Anthropologie, Lush, Charlotte Tilbury and Amazon’s sold-out edition to see if any live up to the hype – and we math-ed out the true value of each.

Thus far, Revolve’s has had the best cost-to-value ratio of them all. The brand, perhaps best known for its huge catalogue of high-end, trendy clothing, doesn’t offer glitzy dresses or funnel-neck jackets in its calendar, just a ton of the best beauty products packed in a charming pink suitcase.

Its 25-day beauty advent calendar has a listed value of $953, but only costs $150. As we are always on the lookout for truly good deals, we tested it alongside its cheaper 12-day option. Below, we reviewed the de-bloating supplements, body lotions and sleep masks in each calendar. In the end, one came out on top.

Read more: The best beauty advent calendars of 2026 in the US are already here and selling out

Listed value: $953 Filter calculated value: $960 Total items: 25 Full-size items: 13 Bestsellers included: Seven

If you or someone in your life is a beauty obsessive, chances are they have heard of most of the buzzy items in this calendar.

We were impressed with the fairly even ratio of hair, makeup and skincare items, too. The packaging is also the best we have seen – the magenta pink suitcase, complete with metal handle and clasps, is reusable and each product comes in its own pink box, which is perfect for gifting each item separately.

Summer Fridays Dream Lip Oil (full size): My mom introduced me to this lip oil, which feels hydrating and weightless on the lips, and thankfully, not sticky. Lauren Gould

Ilia The Base Face Milk (full size): This milky toner is one of my skincare staples, so I was excited to see it included in the calendar. It leaves my skin refreshed and smooth, without feeling too harsh. LG

Tower 28 SOS Daily Rescue Facial Spray (mini): I recommended this popular spray in my running guide, but I also love it for post-gym sessions or when I come inside from a walk but don’t have the energy for a whole skincare routine. LG

Ouai Detox Shampoo: Most shampoos don’t work for me, so I’ve stayed loyal to this one for years – it actually removes the grease from my scalp and leaves my hair feeling clean and soft. LG

Foreo Mini UFO Device + Call It A Night Mask Pack (full size): An early Christmas gift to my mother, who now uses this combo nightly as a 90-second spa routine. You place the mask pack (ginseng, hawthorn extract) on to the device, then glide it around your face. The heat is soothing, like warming your face with a hot towel, and the LED therapy is doing … something that she hasn’t noticed the effects of yet, but it doesn’t matter when the routine itself is so relaxing. Karen Yuan

Salt & Stone Black Rose & Oud Body Lotion (mini): Out of everything I’ve tried, this is the one item I will be buying again and again because the scent is so rich and fragrant. It smells like reclining on a throne in ancient Greece while being fanned and fed citrus fruit. KY

Abbode Sleep Mask: I gave this to a friend, who said it felt like a cushy pillow for her eyes. She only wished the strap were adjustable. KY

Dr Barbara Sturm Glow Drops (mini): Sort of like a serum and highlighter combined – a few drops brightened my face with a faint shimmer. A nice touch if you’re going for a no-makeup look. KY

Lavender dry shampoo: This did nothing. It was messy to apply and didn’t revive my unfortunately greasy scalp. LG

Lemme Mini Debloat Daily Digestive Gummies: These have an indiscernible fruit flavor and did not affect me at all, positively or negatively. Like the stale gummies you may stumble upon in the back of your pantry. KY

Sometimes the costlier item is worth the splurge. While I would love to say that the 12-day option is just as good as its pricier counterpart, I simply can’t (more below). This $150 calendar is worth it.

Though the 25-day option only costs $60 more, it gets you about $540 more in value in product and has six more full-sized items.

Revolve’s 25 days of beauty advent calendar punches far above its weight, just like Liberty London’s nearly $400 calendar (valued at $1,700) that we also liked. It’s a more affordable way to gift higher-end items to multiple people, a trendy larger gift that looks like you are really in the know when it comes to beauty or something to keep for yourself as you count down to the holidays.

Listed value: $409 Filter calculated value: $435 Full-size items: Six Bestsellers included: Five

The product selection is strong. Nearly half of the items included are bestsellers, such as Sol De Janeiro’s Bum Bum Cream and Ilia’s mascara, which I have used for years. Like the 25-day version, it practically comes gift-wrapped, with an adorable, large gift tag fastened to a light pink reusable suitcase. (And because each item is in its original packaging, you could also dole out each product as individual gifts.)

Ilia Limitless mascara (full size): I have lost count of the number of times I have repurchased this mascara. It doesn’t clump and adds much-needed length to my lashes. LG

Summer Fridays Cloud Dew moisturizer (mini): My slightly oily skin loves this lightweight moisturizer, which hydrates my skin without leaving it feeling like I rubbed grease all over it. LG

Mutha Exfoliating Detox Body Bar (mini): Satisfyingly scratchy on the skin, like those Japanese exfoliating bath towels. A little goes a long way – just a few passes covers your body in a creamy lather. I’ve always preferred body washes, but this may have converted me into a bar soap person. KY

Arrae bloat gummies: These felt a bit diet culture-esque to me (ie useless), and I didn’t notice that my stomach felt less bloated after trying. LG

Compared with the 25-day calendar, no. While nothing in this calendar is bad, only a quarter of the products are ones we would go out of our way to buy individually.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘Former inmates want to come back to visit’: inside Florida’s prison zoo
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Jamie Lee Taete
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
Prisoners look after a kinkajou, zebu and ostrich at Monroe County detention center in the Florida Keys. It is the only correctional facility in the world with its own zoo

At the Monroe County detention center on Stock Island in the Florida Keys, most of the prisoners do the type of work you’d typically imagine people doing in jail. Preparing meals in the kitchens, cleaning the common areas, working in the laundry, and so on.

But for about five prisoners at a time the work looks a little more exotic. They’re working in the jail’s on-site zoo, taking care of animals including a capybara, a kinkajou, a zebu and an ostrich.

The zoo was started in 1994, after a sheriff’s deputy noticed that ducks living near the jail were often getting hit by cars while crossing a highway. He gathered a group of prisoners and relocated the flock to a disused area beneath the jail, which sits on stilts as it is in a hurricane-prone area.

Word of the rescue spread, and people started showing up at the jail to drop off rescued or unwanted animals. “People started bringing in a goat, a pig, a cow, pets they’d gotten that they didn’t want or couldn’t keep,” said Jeanne Selander, the zoo’s supervisor. “We got a blind horse from the Miami area that had been abandoned, and then the sheriff thought, ‘Well, there’s a need for this.’”

The Monroe County detention center is the only correctional facility in the world with its own zoo. There was, briefly, another one. In Venezuela, a gang took over a prison and installed various resort-style amenities for the prisoners, including a pool, night club, and a zoo, with big cats, monkeys and flamingoes. But the Venezuelan government forcefully retook control of that prison a few years ago. Several of the zoo’s animals were reportedly killed in the battle for the prison and the ones that survived were relocated.

Jeanne Selander, the supervisor of the zoo at the Monroe County detention center, with Thunder the Zebu in September 2026

According to Selander, all of the animals in her zoo were either rescued, donated or confiscated. Rocky the fox was rescued from a fur farm in Minnesota. Jack the ostrich was donated as a tax write-off by a breeder that was unable to sell him because he’s blind in one eye. Harriet Houdini, a red-tailed boa constrictor, was donated by a school after the teacher that kept her as a class pet retired. “I had some alligators one time that came from a raid on a crack house,” said Selander.

A prisoner cleans out the fox enclosure at the Monroe County detention center in July 2021

But the zoo doesn’t accept all of the animals it is offered. Selander said she previously declined a camel and a bear as they presented too much of a risk to the residents.

You are unable to see the zoo from the inside as the building’s windows are frosted. Selander said that, when she is upstairs in the jail, the prisoners will ask her about the sounds they can hear coming from outside. She has been told that, from inside the jail, the peacock can sound like a woman screaming.

Peter Faraco looks after a lizard at the zoo back in 2021, when he was serving his sentence.

The prisoners that work on the zoo spend around six hours a day feeding and cleaning the animals, and performing maintenance tasks. Those selected are typically low-level offenders and are not allowed to have charges for violence or animal abuse. “It’s kind of hard to get down [to the zoo] because if you have a high bond or you’re in any way shape or form a risk to run away, they’re not going to let you come outside,” said Peter Faraco, a former inmate who worked on the zoo in 2021.

Inside the jail, prisoners sleep on concrete bunk beds with no pillows. “Stuck in them cells all day, or in the kitchen; it’s not that nice,” said Rodney Cox, who previously worked on the zoo. “There’s no air.”

A then-inmate prepares food for the foxes at the on-site zoo of the Monroe County Detention Center in July 2021

Boredom is also an issue. “It’s a lot of time,” said Nicholas Sheldrake, a current inmate who is working in the zoo. “It’s just very boring. Watching the same TV shows and movies over and over, hoping a football or baseball game or something comes on.”

The zoo offers a respite for the prisoners that get to work there. “I love it down here,” said Sheldrake. “It makes my time go by fast. Nobody bothers me. I love working with the animals and talking to them.”

It is important to Selander that the zoo not look like it is part of a jail, as she hopes to make it appealing to visitors on the zoo’s regular open days. She has planted trees around the property, and had inmates paint murals of animals on the walls and support pillars. “People will come in, they’re like, ‘You don’t even realize you’re at a jail,’” she said.

Selander strokes Kramer the emu in September 2026. The emu is named due to his resemblance to the Seinfeld character

In the 20 years she has worked there, she said, the number of visitors on open days has grown from about a dozen to more than 300.

Studies have shown that access to animals can have a positive effect on incarcerated people, leading to improvements in mental health, as well as a decrease in reoffending after release.

Peter Faraco, a then-inmate in the Monroe County detention center, with several animals in the jail’s on-site zoo in July 2021

There are animal programmes of various kinds in prisons around the world. There are prisoners in Chile living alongside cats, and in New Zealand training service dogs, and in the UK receiving equine therapy, and in South Africa raising birds. Selander said that she believes working on the zoo has had a positive effect on the prisoners she has worked with, and has, over the years, received positive feedback from her workers.

She was recently out for brunch and her server was a man who’d worked at the zoo. “He was like, ‘I wanted to thank you, Miss Jeannie … Being able to be on the farm and have peace while I served my time just made it so much easier,’” she said.

Selander said that it’s not uncommon for former incarcerated zoo workers to come back and visit during open days to see the animals. Some will bring their family members. “One of the greatest compliments is that the inmates want to come back to visit,” she said. “What a compliment. Who wants to come back to jail?”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Prepare for more website shutdowns in the age of AI – but human inaction is the real culprit | Chris Stokel-Walker
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Chris Stokel-Walker
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
I’ve been banging the drum about these vulnerabilities for years. It will take more than a handful of exhausted developers to keep us safe

Parts of the internet are going dark. In the Netherlands, government websites, including its digital ID login service, have become unavailable. Finland has taken public services offline, and Wikimedia, the organisation behind Wikipedia, has switched off some of its systems too.

This sounds like the results of a cyber-attack. In most instances, however, the people running the sites deliberately switched them off because the alternative – keeping them online – was too risky. The future is here, and suddenly much of our digital infrastructure is looking very fragile.

The websites were turned off because of two serious security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language that is used by about 70% of websites that we can track. Those vulnerabilities in effect gave hackers an open window through which to climb and loot everything within. That could mean an attacker getting into an online shop, stealing customers’ addresses and passwords, or changing its checkout page to harvest card details. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre advised organisations that were unable to update immediately to consider taking their systems offline.

It’s very tricky to get people to care about something quite so techy. PHP is a tricky abbreviation – even explaining what it stands for (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) is complicated, because it’s recursive. And how it helps the web work is also difficult to explain: a good analogy is it’s like the back-of-house team in a restaurant: your browser puts in an order, and PHP handles the cooking and delivers the meal. In any case, what matters is that you’ve almost certainly used websites powered by it this week.

I’ve been reporting on scares like these in our digital architecture for more than a decade, and the underlying problem barely changes. In 2014, I wrote about Heartbleed, a vulnerability in OpenSSL, the software that helps keep communications across the internet secure. It was up to two men named Steve – working for OpenSSL on a shoestring budget and shouldering an awful lot of responsibility – to keep us from disaster. Twelve years later, it feels like we’re still having the same conversation.

Heartbleed wasn’t the end of it. In 2021 I reported on a dangerous flaw in Log4j, a seemingly mundane tool that records what happens inside computer systems. Then three years later we had XZ Utils, a tool for shrinking file sizes used on Linux computers into which someone had deliberately planted a backdoor. In each of these incidents, small teams working for the public good recognised the problem, acted, and averted disaster. Each one of these incidents underscored how we rely on a handful of under-resourced individuals to keep vital parts of the web secure.

The PHP Foundation made that point itself this week. Its developers first identified the issue that could bring the internet to a halt in 2024, but it was seen as too expensive and too tricky to fix. The foundation has since admitted the delay was a “structural failure” owing to poor resource levels.

This is where AI comes in. In August, researchers working with Calif, OpenAI and Wiz identified how easily the PHP issue could be exploited by using AI tools. And hackers quickly did too. Cloudflare’s chief executive, Matthew Prince, said his company had seen millions of attempts to exploit it already.

Automated systems powered by AI can hammer away at weaknesses in an instant, bombarding their human guards with reports that they have to sift through. Researchers documented about 48,000 vulnerabilities across the internet in 2025. We’ve already passed 84,000 in 2026, with more than two months of the year still to go. That’s one every five minutes. Not every one will be as serious as this latest one, which scored 9.2 on a 10-point scale used to measure these things. But we’re facing an onslaught.

Which all makes for an uncomfortable reality: we’re going to have more days like these. AI makes it inordinately cheaper to find weaknesses in vast volumes of old code, and repairing them is difficult. A 2025 review by the UK government found that about 28% of central government technology was classed as “legacy” – meaning out of date – while some organisations couldn’t even estimate how much old software they had. In April, ministers admitted they couldn’t give a comprehensive account of what had since been fixed or retired.

So we need to fix that. Companies need to know what software they’re using, including the obscure elements they rely on, and who’s responsible for fixing it. That documentation is boring work, which is probably why it’s overlooked. But we’re in a different world now, and it needs to be done. Paradoxically, AI can help with it. But companies and the organisations protecting us also need adequate funding.

There are some things to be optimistic about. The OpenSSL Foundation, the not-for-profit company that fell victim to the Heartbleed vulnerability in 2014, received more than €400,000 from Germany’s sovereign tech fund last year to bolster its resources. The PHP Foundation has hired more staff and is using AI to help triage what’s important and what’s not. And a number of organisations deployed fixes before the current issue went public.

But more is needed. The solution is the same one we keep talking about, but rarely actually do anything about: the big tech companies making billions from software they get for nothing (because of its open-source nature) should contribute properly to maintaining it. Governments ought to do the same, rather than hoping a handful of exhausted developers will keep things ticking over indefinitely.

I’m growing sick of reporting on, and explaining why, the internet repeatedly breaks. I’ve covered Heartbleed, Log4Shell and XZ Utils – and am now documenting the fallout from PHP. I don’t particularly want to keep doing it. Yet I fear unless we start properly valuing those who keep our internet safe, I will be.

Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite App

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Champions League review: PSG take a hit, Man City’s empty seats and teenage hope for Liverpool
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: John Brewin
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The reigning champions must deal with the absence of Khvicha Kvaratskhelia for some time, while fans at Anfield were thrilled by Rio Ngumoha

Paris Saint-Germain beat Barcelona 4-2 on Tuesday, but the reigning champions lost the best player in last season’s tournament, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. This autumn has seen much lobbying for the Ballon d’Or, with the Georgian a popular choice, despite his absence from the World Cup. He is expected to be out for six months, although Rodri’s comeback from serious injury – he was rested by Barcelona on Tuesday until coming off the bench in the 60th minute – shows it can take far longer than that for players to rediscover their highest level.

“Why me?” Kvaratskhelia asked his Instagram followers. The PSG policy of resting players in Ligue 1 to save them for the Champions League failed to protect him. By resting Rodri, Barcelona followed a wider practice among major clubs in European competition of saving stars’ legs for big domestic occasions. Barcelona face Real Madrid this weekend though Lamine Yamal is not being spared; his brilliant goal in Paris made it 10 goals, matched by 10 assists, from 10 matches.

Another heavyweight battle saw Arsenal lose Bukayo Saka to a first-half quad injury in an entertaining 2-2 draw at Bayern Munich. Declan Rice powered in a late equalizer after Harry Kane had put on a show that included a goal and an assist. Does the Ballon d’Or beckon for Kane? The prediction markets suggest so.

Matching Barcelona’s perfect record this season at home and abroad are Manchester City, who continue to thrive amid infamy. A resurgent Phil Foden scored a hat-trick and new signing Allan impressed. The official crowd for their 5-1 defeat of AEK Athens was 40,402, but it looked smaller, and mockery duly descended on the club. There is mitigation for those who stayed away, including high ticket prices for Champions League matches in tough economic times, and a run of five home matches in 17 days. Still, City remain in the crosshairs, and the empty seats raise eyebrows for a club reporting record revenues. Equally, it is fair to point out that Anfield was not full, either, for Liverpool’s 4-3 defeat of Villarreal.

A clean sweep of wins for Serie A, with three of their clubs scoring four goals. Inter let the side down with their 1-0 defeat of Shakhtar Donetsk. Roma defeated Slovan Bratislava 4-0, and Como beat Manchester United 4-1, but the game of the week came in Naples. Scott McTominay scored twice, his first goals since a procedure on a benign heart arrhythmia as Napoli beat Bodø/Glimt 4-3 for their first win of the group stage. “I still need to find my best form, but I am not far away,” said McTominay.

Liverpool were a mess in the first 30 minutes against Villarreal and it was Rio Ngumoha who led the recovery. The 18-year-old played off the right, supplying two assists with his left foot: the long-term replacement for Mohamed Salah may already be at Anfield. Liverpool have nursed Ngumoha along, though this was his fifth start of the season. “Everyone is chipping in but for him to work with Mo [Salah] last year was obviously massive,” Virgil van Dijk said of the teenager.

With traditional Serie A giants Juventus and Milan in the Europa League, Como are enjoying their first season in the Champions League. If Manchester United were dreadful on Wednesday, Como’s rise hit its highest point yet. The club’s success carries echoes of Brighton and Bournemouth’s ascents, although Como’s is even more remarkable. They were a Serie D club in 2008, and the city is now known for something beyond its glorious scenery. Champions League winner Thierry Henry is among the investors in the club as is Como’s coach, Cesc Fàbregas, although the prime financiers are the Indonesian billionaire Hartono brothers.

Jamestown Analytics, the Brighton owner Tony Bloom’s company, has been consulting Como. Arsène Wenger, Pep Guardiola, José Mourinho and Antonio Conte are the elite coaches Fàbregas played under, and he has forged a high-pressing style against Italian orthodoxy. As United labored, they were swarmed by Como’s worker bees. Real Madrid have a buy-back option for Nico Paz, bought by Como in 2024, and the scorer of two fine goals against United. Argentina’s latest Messi replacement is rather beefier than his country’s idol.

As Como deepened Michael Carrick’s plight, thoughts moved to potential replacements. Fàbregas has been mentioned, though United fans will recall the summer of 2013’s unsuccessful chase for him. Had a deal been done, his midfield partner would have been … Carrick.

Another week, another Manchester United PR crisis. This one involved Carrick hitting back at his players, a rarity in his managerial career. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” Bruno Fernandes said.

Carrick’s riposte: “If you don’t run and you don’t run forward and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win.”

On CBS, Jamie Carragher weighed, saying of Fernandes: “They all think he’s working hard. He’s not. He’s killing the rest of the team doing it.”

The Amazon All or Nothing documentary series currently in production for United’s season will be appointment viewing.

After two consecutive weeks of action, we have a fortnight off. Will Carrick still be at United by the time they host Roma on 3 November? Aston Villa, who have three wins from three and are second place in the table, have a glamour trip to Barcelona. Real Madrid, another side on three wins, travel to AEK.

After defeat to Inter, Shakhtar’s adopted home, Stamford Bridge, hosts Sporting Lisbon, who this week were on the wrong end of Lask’s first ever group-stage win.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Iran threatens oil and AI facilities across seven Gulf countries if US and Israel renew attacks
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Iran’s security chiefs say there will be ‘zero red lines’ if Trump and Netanyahu attack again

Iran will strike oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities across as many as seven countries in the Gulf in the event of a fresh US-Israeli attack, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, has said.

Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Mohammad Ghalibaf, the hardliner who led Iran’s negotiations with the US to end the conflict between the two countries, said Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed in principle on an attack, but could not guarantee a successful outcome. He added: “We see the next conflict as an existential threat. The third war in two years means a threat to existence. Our strategy is ‘zero red lines’.”

Mohammadi said: “We break the temporal and spatial dimensions of the conflict. The war will continue longer and in a wider geographical area than the enemy anticipates.”

Iran’s ability to mount such operations, including any unofficial help it receives from China or Russia, will be a key factor in any American decision to restart the war.

Iranian media reported that Rezaei had declared: “In the event of a war, cables, datacentres and artificial intelligence facilities could also be targeted. If the conflict breaks out again, we will have a broader plan.

“There can be no arrangement in which Iran’s economic lifelines come under attack while the economic architecture enabling those attacks is considered untouched and immune.”

According to recent reports in US media, US military advisers have drawn up a detailed list of targets for a fresh joint US-Israel assault on Iran to be implemented after the US midterm elections on 3 November.

Foreign ministers from three European countries, as well as Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt, will meet in Istanbul on Friday to establish agreed policies on the linked Iranian, Yemini and Palestinian crises. There is an alarm that a further war is now the working assumption in Tehran and Washington.

The naval services of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed to have simultaneously struck four commercial ships seeking to navigate through the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The ships were said to be transferring oil from ship to ship.

The IRGC claimed a further three ships had been struck when they hit mines in the strait. There was no independent verification that this number of ships were hit, but Brent crude oil was trading at $113.4 a barrel, a recent high, propelled by US reports of the imminent renewed joint Israeli-Iranian assault on Iran.

Trump has backed away from striking Iran again seven times in the past four months. However, a deadlock in diplomatic negotiations has led US government officials to brief about a potential new military campaign that would target missile sites, oil installations and nuclear sites.

The sabre-rattling by both sides has coincided with extended joint-training manoeuvres by the US and Israel, including practice runs over Iraq. Dozens of Israeli planes also flew close to the Iranian border earlier this week, according to the news site Axios. A big fire at a large aluminium factory in Arak in central Iran suggests sabotage operations may be under way inside the country.

Netanyahu met the US secretary of defence, Pete Hegseth, in Israel on Monday to discuss the timing and purpose of a joint attack, including the possible political implications for Netanyahu’s chances of re-election.

Netanyahu would prefer it if Iran attacked first, he reportedly told Hegseth.

A US military buildup is due to be completed by early November, before a possible newly Democrat-inclined Congress or Senate take their seats in January. Trump intends to have stationed three aircraft carriers, thousands of marines, fighter jets and special operations forces in the Middle East by November.

Reza Nasri, an international lawyer close to the Iranian foreign ministry, said: “A third wave of war would not stay contained. Power grids, desalination plants, refineries and ports across the region would burn. Tens of millions would be left without water or electricity, and a massive wave of refugees would move from Arab countries towards Europe.

“Hormuz would close completely, oil would spike, and the global economy would tip into recession. Israel’s economy, already bled by mobilisation and missile fire, would not survive a prolonged war of attrition. And Trump would be trapped in a crisis that consumes the rest of his presidency and leaves a wreck for his successors,” Nasri said.
