Fars news agency, which is close to the IRGC, said Iran had issued directives to its various military and operational units “stipulating that in the event of a new widespread war, involving the assassination of Iranian officials and the killing of civilians, the Iranian response will not be limited to military targets, but will also include political targets”.

Mediators from Iran and Pakistan this week again explored familiar if reconfigured options for a ceasefire, including proposals that Iran receive billions in frozen assets in return for lifting its blockade of the strait, allowing UN weapons inspectors to view its bombed nuclear sites and to export its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country.

Iran has offered to end the Hormuz blockade within seven days and start talks on its nuclear file, but only if preconditions are met first including lifting US sanctions.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Pete Hegseth’s staff break priceless historic globe he requested for office
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Hegseth’s aides, who attempted to move 30in fragile globe themselves, dropped it during relocation, army officials say

A priceless pre-second world war globe coveted by the US defence secretary Pete Hegseth for his office in the Pentagon was damaged by his staff in a botched attempt to relocate it, army officials have admitted.

Photographs published by the Washington Post on Thursday show the shattered 30-inch Eisenhower globe, said to have been used by Dwight D Eisenhower, the 34th US president, as he plotted the D-day landings as allied supreme commander.

The fragile item was broken when Hegseth’s aides eschewed the services of specialist movers, then dropped it after deciding they would transport it themselves, the Post said, citing sources familiar with the February incident.

A US army spokesperson, in an email to the newspaper, conceded the damage occurred during “an attempted move”.

“The spherical portion of the globe was detached from the metal mounting that allows it to rotate,” the spokesperson said.

One photograph shows fragments of the globe below its wooden frame on a blue hallway carpet. A second shows an inches-wide gash in the bottom of the globe, with its base punched through.

According to the Post’s sources, Hegseth took a liking to the globe, one of two similar artifacts dating to the 1930s and housed in the Pentagon, and asked for it to be placed in his office.

The defence secretary has a well-documented fascination in the history of war, and has boasted of instilling a “warrior ethos” in the US military since his January 2025 confirmation.

The globe’s historical significance was attractive to him, the Post’s report noted, and aides moved quickly to enact the relocation.

Such was their haste, the sources said, that instead of waiting to engage specialist movers who would have packed the globe with precision and care, they dispatched their own team.

“They lost control of the artifact and dropped it, sending the globe crashing on to its base and impaling the fragile shell near Antarctica,” one of the sources said, blaming an “apparent lack of patience”.

Ultimately, the globe was not relocated, and is currently undergoing repair.

An account of a successful 2022 relocation of an Eisenhower globe, between two army facilities in Alabama, appears on the website of specialist moves Craters & Freighters, which highlights the level of expertise and care necessary for such an undertaking.

“Since the globe is considered priceless, we knew its value was much greater than financial, and that our team was heavily relied upon for a safe delivery,” the article said, describing how the company designed and precision-built protective crating.

An spokesperson for the “war department”, as the US Department of Defense has rebranded itself during Donald Trump’s second term, dismissed the significance of the incident in a statement to the Guardian.

“An accident occurred while staff were transporting a replica of the Eisenhower globe as part of its relocation,” the official’s statement said.

“Accidents happen, we are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired. It is unsurprising that the Washington Post is once again dedicating time to another inconsequential non-story.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Republican leader embarrassed by Ali G film says he plans to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Catherine Shoard
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Exclusive: Michael Aboud, whose actions in what he believed to be a documentary are likely to come under considerable scrutiny, has expressed anger at the film-maker

The chair of the El Paso County Republican Party has said he intends to sue Sacha Baron Cohen over footage of the local politician used in new satircal comedy Ali G: Who Iz I?

In the film, Michael Aboud is shown taking part in a training programme with another Cohen character, ex-Mossad terrorist expert Col Erran Morad, who instructs Aboud and fellow Maga sympathisers in self-defence techniques including the wearing, over clothes, of protective plastic buttocks. He also schools them in how to fire bullets from the middle of these buttocks by the repeated up and down manipulation of a rubber penis.

Aboud and a fellow student, former preacher and aspirant actor Joshua Loudermilk, are then recruited by Morad to help in a mission to prevent the birth on US soil of the baby of a fictional South American drugs kingpin, who Mossad has confused for Ali G.

This involves Aboud and Loudermilk helping Morad to abduct Ali G’s girlfriend, Julie (played by the actor Morgana Robinson), while she is apparently in the late stages of labour. They drive her in a kebab van disguised as an ambulance to a remote abandoned medical facility where she gives birth (to a lifelike prosthetic).

They then abandon her at the facility while placing her live baby in a zipped bag and driving it towards Mexico. In the final reel, Loudermilk is seen attempting to discharge fire from his fake buttocks, while Aboud takes the decision to drop the baby – then being dangled from a drone at a considerable height – to the ground to prevent it touching US soil. The actions could not be anything other than extremely serious for a real infant.

Until the Guardian contacted Aboud on Tuesday, the businessman was unaware of his participation in anything other than what he believed to be a nonfiction film. In a statement, Aboud called Baron Cohen “and his entire film crew … a bunch of liars [who] deceive people to benefit themselves. They claimed that this would be a documentary about the illegals crossing the border. Then they said they were adding in this self-defence guy from Israel.”

He added: “It is my opinion that Sasha Cohen [sic] is a pervert. Plus he talked about how Muslims are all gay because they follow the sex practices of Mohamid [sic]. No one should spend one penny watching anything he produces or appears in. I plan to sue him.”

Pressed further on whether he stands by his actions in the film, Aboud declined to comment.

The film repeatedly stresses that neither Aboud nor Loudermilk are “in on it”. Loudermilk has not responded to requests for comment, but his social media feed suggests a level of understanding about the project not shared by most of his fellow participants.

Earlier this week, Loudermilk posted on Facebook that “I got to spend 12 hours one on one with Sasha [sic] and he taught me soooo much about the fun of making others laugh” as well as a link to a video promo for the film, saying, “I am in the trailer.” On 10 January, he also posted a headshot of himself, saying: “Howdy. Done with Sasha Cohen movie and ready for more.”

Representatives for the film have told the Guardian that Loudermilk was unaware of the true nature of the film.

Aboud’s shock at his involvement is particularly surprising given that he, along with Loudermilk, features in the second trailer for the film, which was released a fortnight ago.

That clip alone contains considerable clues to those involved that all is not what it seems. In his address to the recruits, Morad, who was a fixture of Baron Cohen’s 2018 show Who is America?, advises the group that they should not be fooled, for the immigrants they are set against “are not coming here to mow your lawn, trim your trees, rake your leaves, clean your house, care for your babies, bus your tables, wash your cars, paint your houses, build your fences, install your roofs, drywall, plumbing or electric. They are coming to kill you.”

Another section of the film involves Ali G hosting a “free speech” web show in which he is given a questionable script to read by South African producer Dirk Visser, who could not be contacted for comment.

The character also presides over a gameshow of Visser’s invention in which contestants, against the clock, must stuff mannequins depicting “undesirables” including rappers, gay people, Muslims and Mexican babies into pretend shower cubicles, before pressing a button to seemingly activate the release of the poisonous gas Zyklon B. The segment ends with a mass Nazi salute.

One of those who takes part is the disgraced former Republican congressman George Santos, who tells the camera his takeaway from playing the game is that next time he would try to grab more babies, as they’re easier to fit in the shower. In correspondence with the Guardian, Santos also suggested he was unaware of the true nature of the film, “as me and my team had no involvement”, and declined to justify his behaviour.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Miranda Bryant in Muhos and Otanmäki
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push

Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northern Finland. Now they are all gone.

After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River.

“It doesn’t end. It goes on and on,” says Mari Annala, an ecologist from the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation (SLL), looking at drone footage of the former forest from the perimeter.

With 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, Finland has found itself at the forefront of the tech companies’ latest push. As well as its relative geopolitical and geological stability and abundance of land, the cool climate makes it especially attractive for saving on energy costs.

Earlier this month, Google was ordered by the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) to temporarily stop work on Muhos and another site about 100km south-east in the village of Otanmäki after it failed to complete the necessary environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land. The news has prompted widespread outcry and a national reckoning over what role, if any, the country should play in the global rush to build datacentres to keep up with rapid AI development.

Last week, Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted “on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time”.

Muhos and Otanmäki are part of a €13bn AI infrastructure project by Google that has attracted criticism from Donald Trump, who would rather the centres were built in the US and has publicly called for the company to reconsider. It is the biggest ever project of its kind in the Nordic country.

The Finnish government, which has presided over deep spending cuts, has encouraged the investment. Last month, when the Google plans were announced, the country’s prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a “top priority” and “the value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment”. He said the Google deal would “deliver lasting benefits for both parties”.

But the revelations over Google’s misconduct have prompted public concern over what these deals mean for nearby communities, energy prices for Finnish households and Finland’s natural environment, a national source of pride. The datacentre push is likely to become a key election issue when Finns go to the polls in April.

In addition to the 250,000 trees felled at Muhos, Annala estimates that an additional 150,000 trees were felled at Otanmäki. Because the trees have been felled illegally, she says wood from the two sites cannot be sold to wood-processing plants.

The move has also prompted questions over why Finland’s renewable energy sources are being used to power international corporations.

More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding more datacentre regulation and a fee to compensate local communities for environmental damage. Since the scandal broke, Orpo has described what happened in Muhos as a “cold shower”.

Hanna Halmeenpää, chair of SLL’s board, said she had been incredulous when she discovered Google’s law breaking. “At first I couldn’t believe it,” she said. “I have never heard that any company has done anything like this in Finland.” She said the system depended a lot on trust, which she believes Google took advantage of. “They bought the vast land area and they just started to cut it, just like that,” she said. “It’s pure arrogance and it’s amazing.”

The speed of developments had shocked the country, she said. “Many people are just watching the news and asking each other: ‘What’s happening now? What can we do about it? And do we have to take all these datacentre projects in Finland?’”

Jussi Kangasharju, head of computer science at the University of Helsinki, said that while datacentres brought a limited number of jobs, potentially boosting the local economy, the benefits on a national level were minimal. “Really, for Finland, there are no benefits,” he said. “They are international companies serving international customers. Very little corporate taxes go to Finland. Datacentres ultimately have very little benefit for others except the datacentre operator.”

With legislation still playing catchup, there is a rush to get projects under way as fast as possible.

Some are calling for a centralised body to coordinate datacentre projects, rather than leaving so much of the decision-making down to municipalities that are likely to prioritise the immediate needs of the local area.

In Muhos and Otanmäki, there are people who support the projects, along with the jobs and land taxes they will bring into the local area. But many believe they have been sold short by municipalities.

Antti Jakonen, who lives in Muhos, said that, although the trees felled represented a small fraction of Finland’s overall forests, he objected to the manner in which it had been carried out. “It has been done in the wrong way. American style. No sense. No sense at all,” he said. The former entrepreneur and fisher wants Google to compensate by helping to restore the local salmon population destroyed decades ago by hydropower.

In Otanmäki, the disruption to nature and to residents’ daily lives is being vividly felt. When the trees were felled, the wolves who had lived there came to the village, said Anni Ranta, 53, whose family has lived there for generations.

A former mining village, the area is known for its rare earth elements. Ranta’s family live at the centre of the village next to a triangular church spire and a former bar that has been empty for years. The peaceful forest used to extend for miles from the village. Now the sound of building work next to the clearcut Google site reverberates.

“We had wolves coming into the village because all the wild animals moved out of the forest,” said Ranta. “They fled. What worries me about the datacentres is also the noise because this is hardrock soil. Even when we are standing here talking,” she added, stamping her feet, “it’s like a drum.”

Such is her strength of feeling against the arrival of Google that she is thinking of moving out. She also fears the datacentre could make the village a target for Russia, with whom Finland shares a long border. “I don’t want them here,” she said of Google. “I don’t want them in Finland at all. I don’t like the whole idea of AI and the world changing and the way it’s changing. It’s going too fast, too soon.”

Her father, Pentti Korhonen, a retired wilderness guide, said that since the forest was destroyed, the water in the stream has turned brown. “There is no need at all for datacentres in Finland. No need for datacentres at all,” he said.

Vesa Hyyryläinen, chair of the local SLL district, said three-toed woodpeckers nesting in the forest had been pushed out. “All of us nature conservationists are very worried about our Finnish political situation and politics,” said the biologist and osprey expert. “I wonder why we have to sacrifice so much of our nature. They give everything away too easily.”

He said, however, that he understood why authorities were trying to bring in new sources of investment and jobs, given the region’s ageing population. “Young people go to Helsinki and Berlin and Paris,” he said. “There are so few people. We have to sacrifice.”

Veli-Matti Uski, director general of the ministry of environment, said the government was “monitoring the general development of the [datacentre] sector, [and the] application of its legislation, and is prepared to propose legislative amendments as necessary”.

Google said it was working to protect water quality at the Muhos site, and that it planned to plant trees across 130 hectares there. Conservationists say that figure is too low to have any real impact in comparison to the damage done by the tree felling.

A spokesperson said: “We have operated in Finland for 15 years and have always worked to meet or exceed zoning, environmental, health and safety requirements.

“After receiving the LVV letters on 6 October, we stopped preparatory works at Muhos and Kajaani [where the Otanmäki site is located] and have submitted a formal response to LVV confirming this.

“We will fully comply with LVV’s requests in this matter. We look forward to maintaining an active, open dialogue with all authorities to strengthen our partnership with Finland and local organisations.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Alberta welcomed migrant workers. Now, it wants to restrict their rights
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
‘Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living,’ Vanesa Ortiz says

When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico, she found herself in a city gripped by winter. Outside the airport, it was -15C (5F).

“I would come to understand that this was not an extreme cold,” she said. “But in the moment it was terrifying.

But she also found in those first moments an immense warmth. She was welcomed by elderly volunteers in white cowboy hats, and Ortiz soon felt that Calgary was a place she could one day raise a family. And yet when the teacher reflects on that moment a decade ago, she worries that the opportunities she had to put down roots could be soon closed to others.

This week, Alberta held a referendum, asking residents to weigh in on the province’s relationship with Canada – and the extent to which the province should restrict some newcomers’ access to healthcare, education and social support. It also asked about the need for constitutional reforms.

While unofficial results show both the separation and constitutional questions will fail, the ones on immigration are likely to succeed.

“I love Calgary and I love Alberta,” said Ortiz. “But when I hear people asking whether people should get access to these services – I mean, that was my daughter’s education. That was my family’s healthcare.”

The referendum amplified the grievances of fringe separatists, but it also exposed a central tension in Alberta’s approach to immigration. Even as the oil-rich province seeks newcomers to fill shortages in the job market, the provincial government wants to limit services available to some of those same workers.

The governing United Conservative party blames the rapid population growth for overcrowded and underfunded hospitals and schools But critics say the proposed solution – restricting access to healthcare, education and social supports –could leave workers and their families more vulnerable without fully addressing the underlying causes of the crisis.

The referendum asked if the government should introduce a law ensuring only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and “individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” can access healthcare and education. Another asked if newcomers should have lived in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for certain social support programmes and allowing the province to charge some temporary residents fees for healthcare and education.

Earlier in the year, the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, blamed the immigration policy of Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government for the resource strains in classrooms, emergency rooms and social support systems. And in a social media post, Smith said: “For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable.”

Canada’s federal government has since trimmed immigration targets and placed restrictions on its temporary foreign worker program amid criticisms it was being abused by large companies. But the western province’s economy relies on workers from abroad to fill jobs in sectors, like agriculture, food services and tourism, where employers struggle to recruit or retain enough staff.

Ortiz, who works with the non-profit Asociación de Mexicanos en Calgary, worries mounting skepticism towards migrant workers will push workers into the shadows and make them more vulnerable to labor exploitation.

“I can’t imagine the scale of the harm that a policy like this might create,” she said, noting that thousands of farm workers in the province don’t receive healthcare.

Ortiz has seen views shift on immigration in recent years and says the results of the referendum reflect a population that is “squeezed” economically.

“Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living. That’s not going to fix our classrooms. They keep essential services open. In many cases, they are front line workers. And now they’re being treated as disposable.”

For some residents, the proposals represent a sharp reversal from Alberta’s earlier efforts to attract newcomers. The UCP government invested in recruitment and expanded its provincial immigration nomination targets to address labour shortages. But as a growing number of Albertans sour on immigration, the government position has shifted.

Ximena González, a Calgary-based writer, said when the provincial government began its campaign to bring in more people, it “wanted more workers to exploit”, noting that most workers come from abroad on temporary permits.

“Now, the message feels more out in the open: ‘We wanted you to come, to exploit you. And now, we don’t need you anymore – so we will punish you.”

The provincial government has claimed that temporary residents, who make up almost 6% of Alberta’s total population, contribute roughly $150m in tax revenues but cost the province more than $1bn annually in health, education and other social services.

Economist Gillian Petit notes that temporary residents also remit taxes to the federal government, which helps fund Alberta’s healthcare, meaning those residents likely contribute far more than the province acknowledges. If they contribute less in total tax dollars than other Albertans, it is because they earn less than the median resident. They are also less likely to use healthcare and education resources than the average Albertan.

“In all honesty, if I were a temporary resident and had to choose whether or not to stay, I wouldn’t,” said González, who came to Canada 16 year ago as an international student. “I would not feel wanted, and I don’t want to be treated like a third class citizen.”

She says that media fixation on Alberta’s fringe independence movement meant the other questions in the referendum received little scrutiny and left voters uninformed.

“The media failed to help people to make an educated vote – instead of just voting based on racism.”

Economist Jim Stanford said hundreds of thousands of residents skipped over those questions on immigration, choosing to only answer the one on separation.

“This cannot remotely be interpreted as a mandate for the government to crack down on immigration,” he said, adding the province didn’t have the power to “unilaterally” act on these proposals. “This was a symbolic ideological exercise and gives a cast of legitimacy to some of these very right wing nativist sentiments that are bubbling in the far right of Alberta politics.”

During a series of town halls over the years led by the government, more extreme views on immigration were clear. One resident received cheers after suggesting a policy of mass deportations and another said immigrants “harm” children and suggested she might seek asylum in the US.

For Ortiz, the government’s about-face reflects a “betrayal” of the workers who have helped build the province.

“We’re asking people if we should remove the right to access healthcare and education from taxpayers who are, quite literally, building our communities,” she said. “But I also worry that what gets lost in this debate is these people. They are not just labour. They work, study and raise their children here. They need to know they deserve the chance to build a life with dignity and with respect to feel safe and to feel welcome.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Ali G: Who Iz I? review – Sacha Baron Cohen’s high-stakes satire punches up and down with spectacular bad taste
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Peter Bradshaw
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Baron Cohen’s live-ammo prankster is back, 20 years on, but has to battle with his own irrelevance in search of big laughs and the approval of a new generation

Exclusive: Republican leader embarrassed by film says he plays to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’

If you liked Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G the first time around, you’ll like this less; if you disliked it, you’ll dislike this more; if you suspected it was racist, you’ll be more emboldened to say so – especially as Baron Cohen has dreamed up a whole new character apparently to pre-empt and mock precisely that objection. Broad and crass as it often is – in fact always is – this Ali G sequel is sometimes funny: the athletic vigour of our hero’s pranking and punking is like the umpteenth Jackass film at which you might find yourself laughing, and Baron Cohen blunders with the semi-intentional force of an XL bully into the issue of whether jokes are still allowed.

Unlike the first film, Ali G in Da House from 2002, this is not a full written-through narrative. It is basically another live-ammo series of hoaxes with some spectacular bad taste perpetrated upon the deserving and less deserving; it satirises the shamelessness of anti-woke free speech martyrs, punching up and down with grossout cringe, and the targets include some big names who shouldn’t be revealed here. There are two other subordinate characters: Erran Morad, a sinister Mossad/IDF officer turned US security consultant (who appeared in Baron Cohen’s Who Is America? TV series), and a new figure: Dr Nira Cain-N’Degrocello, a grotesquely supercilious white liberal who is the self-appointed scourge of cultural appropriation. The dupes are built into a big silly climax fabricated with body doubles and (presumably) covert reshooting.

The insurmountable problem is that the film keeps having to tell you who is and isn’t “in on it”: at the beginning, over the closing credits at the end and even briefly in the middle of the action. Well, Ali G was from so very long ago, and even the high-water mark of Baron Cohen’s Borat popularity was quite long ago, and the online media scene now so fragmented that … yes … people have forgotten, a whole new generation doesn’t know. People really don’t recognise him.

The high concept is that Ali is now washed up, short of money and unpopular, and old-school media figure that he is, he disapproves of a plan by his heavily pregnant partner Julie (Morgana Robinson) to launch an OnlyFans account. But on trying to sell his fax machine in a Staines high street pawn shop, an old fax chunters out of it with an offer from HBO for a new show. Overexcited, Ali and Julie head off to the US to sucker some people in the traditional style; the smallscreen setup blown up to high-def cinematic proportions. His fictional woke tormentor decides to take him down and, by employing the Israeli hardman, tries to convince credulous and aggressive Republicans that Ali is a Mexican terrorist whose baby must be prevented at all costs from being born on US soil. The movie does make a few people look silly, yes, although Baron Cohen doesn’t land a huge punch on a big name the way he did in the Borat sequel.

So who iz Ali G and what iz the point of trundling him out again? The first film implied he was once a Robert Smith-type goth, but that is now forgotten about. Interestingly, one person who this film doesn’t allude to is Tim Westwood, the BBC Radio 1 hip-hop DJ and son of the Bishop of Peterborough whose speech mannerisms were held to be one influence on Baron Cohen’s great creation, and proof positive that white people did indeed patronisingly ape a street way of speaking. Westwood’s subsequent all-too-unfunny history, perhaps, doesn’t mesh with trying to revive Ali G now as comedy IP. The movie outings of Ricky Gervais’s David Brent and Steve Coogan’s Alan Partridge worked better because they could more plausibly represent the melancholy of getting older and irrelevant. Ali G feels older in the wrong way, and the On-the-Buses humour with Julie is tired. The best bits will be available on TikTok and Instagram reels soon enough.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: The Audacity review – cracking TV packed with even more gloriously awful people than Succession
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Lucy Mangan
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
This Silicon Valley satire follows a CEO in trouble after the collapse of an acquisition deal. Created by Succession writer Jonathan Glatzer, each character is more awful than the next – and it is stuffed with twists and treacheries

What if Mike Judge’s cult hit sitcom Silicon Valley were remade as a dramedy and we had in the meantime come to appreciate tech and its titans as existential threats to humanity, I hear you ask. Well, wonder no more – the answer is here, and it is The Audacity. It comes at you in hour-long episodes, which rush past at breakneck speed and leave you panting and deeply unsettled in their wake. Rather like modern life itself, of course, except for the relief available while the credits roll, before the next chunk of horrors arrives.

The Audacity has a sprawling cast (especially in the opening episodes, which really are frenetic) but the figure around which most of the narratives move is Duncan Park (Billy Magnussen). He is the part-bullish, part-neurotic and wholly unbearable CEO of Hypergnosis, a data brokerage company he founded with a friend, who has since been struck by tragedy.

Duncan, who has not absorbed the key point of the Silicon Valley maxim and spends his time moving fast and breaking his own stuff, is in trouble. Hypergnosis was in acquisition talks with Cupertino (named after the location of Apple’s real-world headquarters and just possibly meant to evoke the behemoth) until Duncan leaked the news to boost his share price before the company valuation. That brought the deal to a screeching halt. He is now on the hunt for a play that will enable him to avoid the humiliation and (relative) poverty that will occur once word of the cancelled acquisition gets out.

Duncan’s wife, Lili (Lucy Punch), and daughters are weary of and maddened by him, and his therapist JoAnne (Sarah Goldberg) even more so. She is almost as gloriously hateful a character as Duncan, and that is before he gets the goods on her with an eye to blackmail. This feels like the right time to note that The Audacity’s creator, Jonathan Glatzer, was one of the writers on the first two seasons of Succession, the show that made “gloriously hateful characters” an art form.

JoAnne is married to Gary (Paul Adelstein), a slightly more ethical member of the same profession, though in the Valley this still means a lot of time spent administering ADHD tests to students in the hope that a diagnosis will buy them extra time on tests, and other such small corruptions. She shares custody of her son, Orson (Everett Blunck), with her equally unlovely ex-husband, and although she uses Orson’s birthday as her computer password, it’s not the right date.

Like most of the younger characters – including the Parks’ older daughter, Jamison (Ava Marie Telek), whose weight and academic results are ceaselessly monitored by her mother – Orson is a sweet child. Heartbreakingly resigned to his fate as an afterthought in his parents’ lives, he forms a growing friendship with Jamison’s little sister, embryonic kleptomaniac Tess (Thailey Roberge). The younger characters’ quiet endurance of, and resistance to, the chaos, greed and narcissism that surrounds them gives emotional heft to the show’s satirical thrust. Is gen z a reservoir of hope, or is youth just a brief period in everyone’s lives before the venality of the world – especially in its tech-aggravated modern iteration – gets to work? The bleakness of the latter gives us pause.

Add to the mix a potent turn from Zach Galifianakis as Carl Bardolph, another self-obsessed tech titan (worshipped for inventing “Bardolph’s Law”, a principle of infinite growth and profit “based on the logic of a cancer cell” that he once scribbled on a napkin while high); a genius coder called Harper (Jess McLeod), whose new algorithm may save Park or destroy the last vestiges of society; Rob Corddry as a rep for the Veterans’ Association, begging for a morsel of aid from billionaires; and about 700 supporting characters, twists, treacheries, good deals, bad deals and ayahuasca trips, with no clear way to distinguish what is satire and what is reportage – and you have The Audacity.

Once you’ve calmed down – and in later episodes, as the show gains confidence, it does too – it will fill both the Succession and Silicon Valley (sitcom)-shaped holes in your life. Unlike Hypergnosis, that’s an acquisition worth making.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: Heartbreak, hope and human imperfection: Leonard Cohen’s greatest songs – ranked!
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Alexis Petridis
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
A decade after his final album, and his death, we rate the best of the Canadian singer-songwriter who brought a deep, spiritual wisdom to love and grief

The synth-heavy production on 1988’s I’m Your Man has always been divisive – even Leonard Cohen’s longtime collaborator Anjani Thomas subsequently expressed misgivings – but on its opening track, it really works. The Pet Shop Boys-ish arrangement chafes against Cohen’s growling vocal, amplifying First We Take Manhattan’s shiver-inducing sense of brooding menace.

Seven years – and a personal financial crisis – after 2004’s half-hearted Dear Heather, Cohen returned to the studio with his powers freshly marshalled. As if to underline the point, Old Ideas opened with the sharply witty Going Home, on which Cohen’s muse addresses the listener directly, disparaging the artist himself as “a lazy bastard in a suit”.

Cohen famously called his 1977 LP Death of a Ladies’ Man “a catastrophe”, which perhaps reflected more on its drug- and booze-soaked recording with dangerously erratic producer Phil Spector than the finished album. It’s an outlier in Cohen’s catalogue, but one with much to commend it. Certainly, he maintained an understandable fondness for the rock’n’roll-influenced Memories, often performing it live.

Cohen’s renaissance continued apace on Popular Problems. Released the day before his 80th birthday, it sounded suspiciously like a masterpiece. Almost Like the Blues found him reflecting sorrowfully on man’s inhumanity to man – not merely torture, killing and war, but “all my bad reviews” – and staring down his own mortality, replete with a jab at Richard Dawkins.

Shruggingly titled, largely recorded in collaborator Sharon Robinson’s garage and packaged in a sleeve featuring a selfie, Ten New Songs was an understated return to recording after Cohen’s five years of Buddhist study. But beneath its unassuming veneer lurked beautiful songs: the chanson-like A Thousand Kisses Deep is an exquisite reflection on regret and time’s passing.

Nowhere else on this album does the cocktail of Cohen’s songwriting and Spector’s more-is-more approach to production gel so perfectly: the title track is a fantastic song. Moreover, the weight of Spector’s arrangement, the way it causes the tempo to drag, seems to complement rather than suffocate its mood.

Other artists have made albums that looked imminent death in the face – Warren Zevon’s The Wind, Queen’s Innuendo – but You Want It Darker, released less than three weeks before the end of Cohen’s life, may be the most poised and affecting. “I’m ready, my Lord,” he sang on its title track, a complex, thorny examination of faith.

In which a brief tryst with Janis Joplin – “We fell into each other’s arms through a process of elimination,” he later recalled – turns into a kind of eulogy, not just for the late singer, but for the era in which they met. It’s haunted by the sense of optimism extinguished.

Rock stars of a certain vintage were wont to write despairing state-of-the-world addresses in the late 80s – Lou Reed’s New York is full of them – but Everybody Knows is a cut above, its relentlessly bleak worldview leavened by black humour: “Everybody’s got this broken feeling, like their father or their dog just died.”

Against stiff competition, Songs of Love and Hate may be Cohen’s darkest album. Avalanche is its claustrophobic heart, a relentless, shimmering guitar figure, a confusing but compelling tumble of imagery, with his voice at its most poisonous. Nick Cave called it one of “the essential pillars that hold up the structure of my artistic world”.

Inspired by the story of the Lagerkapellen – concentration camp orchestras whose music accompanied forced labour and executions – there’s something eerie about Dance Me to the End of Love’s klezmer-inspired melody and lyrical pleas for lifelong fealty. The latter are filled with intimations of darkness; it’s never entirely clear that love will overcome them.

“I’ve seen the future, baby, and it’s murder”: Cohen’s apocalyptic response to the sociopolitical upheavals of the early 90s – most obviously the Los Angeles riots – depicted a world in which “attitudes are all extremist and they’re all defensive”. Thirty-four years on, it sounds grimly prophetic, its upbeat soft-rock backing only serving to amplify the unease.

Cohen found writing a trying experience – lurid stories abound of him beating his head against the floor while working on Hallelujah. He poured it all into the thrillingly vivid, mordantly funny Tower of Song, which has often struck a chord with other artists, covered by everyone from Phoebe Bridgers to Tom Jones to the Jesus and Mary Chain.

Anthem is home to perhaps Cohen’s most-quoted lyric: “There is a crack in everything, that’s how the light gets in.” But in truth, it’s just one among a plethora of memorable lines in the song’s gospel-infused paean to hope and human imperfection, a song he later suggested represented “everything my whole work and life had gathered around”.

Even by the standards of Cohen’s synth era, the backing of I’m Your Man is low-rent and cheesy, but it fits perfectly with a song about abasement. Its emotional tone shifts from lustful to desperate to hopeless: “A man never got a woman back, not by begging on his knees,” he notes in a moment of clarity, then carries on regardless.

Hallelujah’s progress from an album Cohen’s US record label refused to release to his most famous song – via, of all things, a cover by John Cale that appeared on the soundtrack of Shrek – is fascinating. Cohen later proposed a moratorium on its use in films, but, in truth, it has survived ubiquity with its power to move intact.

Cohen’s original intention was to try his luck as a Nashville songwriter. If you squint, you can just about make out the shape of a county song in So Long, Marianne’s beautiful admission of guilt, although it’s hard to imagine the Music Row treatment could improve on its wonderfully ramshackle string accompaniment.

Another Cohen classic with country music in its bones – Kris Kristofferson said he wanted the opening lines on his gravestone – Bird on the Wire was coaxed out of a depressed Cohen by his then girlfriend, Marianne Ihlen. It sounds utterly, authentically defeated, like one long sigh, destined to soundtrack moments of gloomy self-reflection for the rest of time.

There are infinitely worse ways to start your debut album than with a song so good, it immediately becomes a standard, covered by Nina Simone, Neil Diamond, Roberta Flack and Aretha Franklin. Some recompense, perhaps, for the titular lady’s refusal to let Cohen touch her perfect body with anything other than his mind.

Reducing Leonard Cohen’s oeuvre to 20 songs is a thankless task: the compiler is abundantly aware that umpteen deserving songs have been neglected. Similarly, there’s no head-and-shoulders “best” song, merely personal favouritism. Still, you listen to Famous Blue Raincoat’s disconsolate depiction of a love triangle – in the form of a letter to the other male party – and boggle at the idea Cohen was dissatisfied with such an impossibly beautiful song, which so perfectly conjures up an atmosphere of shadowy small-hours reflection, and which comes complete with one of his loveliest melodies (subsequently pinched on – crikey – Leo Sayer’s When I Need You).

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Glee’s pro-LGBTQ+ vision captured 2010s hope. Can a reboot handle Trump’s America? | Alim Kheraj
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Alim Kheraj
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
The beloved high school TV show is returning in a different political climate. I’m skeptical that Ryan Murphy has the nuance this moment needs

For months, Ryan Murphy has been discussing Glee. In July, he expressed his love for the musical comedy drama he created. In September, he said that he had finished writing a pilot for a potential reboot, adding that he had reached out to some of the cast about a reunion. And now it is official: Disney+ and Hulu have commissioned a Glee revival.

Glee, which ran for six seasons between 2009 and 2015, was a cultural juggernaut during its initial tenure. The show won six Emmys, four Golden Globes and made stars of actors including Lea Michele, Jonathan Groff, Chris Colfer, Darren Criss and the late Cory Monteith and Naya Rivera. Centred on the trials of New Directions, a scrappy show choir at the fictional McKinley high school in Ohio, the show became known for its peppy covers of show tunes, 80s power pop hits such as Journey’s Don’t Stop Believin’ (a Glee signature), 2010s chart-toppers and some truly baffling mashups (the amalgamation of Scissor Sisters’ Let’s Have a Kiki and Turkey Lurkey Time from Promises, Promises remains … a choice).

Nevertheless, these musical numbers worked: compilation albums regularly scaled the charts, and the cast even embarked on a US and UK tour, which was recorded and later released in cinemas as Glee: The 3D Concert Movie. Even today, the show’s soundtrack cast generates more than 4 million monthly listeners on Spotify.

It’s this longevity that is probably behind Glee’s return. On social media, videos featuring people recreating the show’s take on I Say a Little Prayer – complete with McKinley cheerleaders’ choreography – continue to rack up views, while over a million videos on TikTok are tagged with “#Glee”. Gen Z audiences, meanwhile, have revisited the show – albeit not always so favourably – thanks to streaming services, with recap podcasts and YouTube videos cropping up in response. “That show is interesting because it’s come back around,” Murphy said in July. “So many young people now watch it.”

Still, this extended shelf life is surprising given Glee’s politics: no show exemplified Obama-era optimism and liberal identity politics more. Murphy utilised Glee as a vehicle for representation, filling the show with characters from marginalised backgrounds. This was particularly apparent with the show’s numerous LGBTQ+ characters. Glee’s arrival on TV in the year after Proposition 8, which banned same-sex marriage in California, provided Murphy with an opportunity to shift public perception of LGBTQ+ people. While its pro-queer messaging was about as tactful as a neon green American Apparel “Legalize Gay” tank top, there’s little doubt that its emphasis on queer representation – even if said queer people were covering the novelty EDM monstrosity The Fox (What Does the Fox Say?) while wielding puppets – was significant.

Glee cleared the path for Lady Gaga’s Born This Way and Dan Savage’s “It Gets Better” campaign, ushering in an age of hopefulness about the trajectory of LGBTQ+ rights. While it would take until the summer of 2015 for same-sex marriage to be legalised in the US – an issue covered in Glee’s final season with the nuptials between queer couples Brittany and Santana, and Kurt and Blaine – the increasingly queernormative world of Glee presented a utopian future for LGBTQ+ people, one where those in high school were no longer bullied for being queer, young trans people could transition without interference and gays could live in harmony alongside their heterosexual counterparts. A post-Glee world suggested that, no matter your differences, everyone would be equal.

The last 11 years, however, have highlighted what a fantasy Murphy’s egalitarian vision for the future was. The pandemic, a second Trump presidency and vast economic disparity have stoked divisions and cemented inequalities. Anti-LGBTQ+ legislation, both in the US and the UK, has created a hostile environment for the queer community, particularly for trans people, with the Institute for Strategic Dialogue reporting an increase in anti-LGBTQ+ hate crimes in the US, the UK and Europe. In this context, the identity politics propagated by Glee 1.0, which prized individual visibility, regularly weaponised victimhood, and made a (literal) song and dance about liberalism to promote a vision of societal equality, feel dated. Despite any good intentions, it is these very values that, some hypothesise, have contributed to the so-called “war on wokeness”.

Since its conclusion, Glee’s legacy has also tarnished. Along with allegations of on-set bullying, racism and favouritism, a number of the cast have died: Monteith, who played football star Finn Hudson, died from an accidental overdose in 2013; Mark Salling, whose character Noah Puckerman was the school’s bad boy, was arrested for possession of child sexual abuse material in 2015 and later died by suicide; and Rivera drowned in 2020. The writing, too, has been criticised, particularly for how it handled its characters of colour, disability, bisexuality, and the dynamics between students and teachers.

It’s this environment in which Glee returns. Some former stars, including Michele, Heather Morris and Chord Overstreet, are already on board. But whether Murphy will be able to produce something that speaks to our current climate is debatable. The prolific showrunner’s allergy to subtlety, as evidenced by recent output The Shards, All’s Fair and his exploitative Monster anthology series, suggests not.

Instead, this reboot feels like a shallow and desperate attempt by a streaming service to reclaim a dwindling gen Z audience. Meanwhile, Murphy’s ham-fisted identity politics feel incongruous at a time where nuance, tact and self-awareness feel more necessary than ever. Personally, when it comes to the Glee revival, I’ve stopped believin’.

https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.title: Gradual decay or sudden destruction? Ancient philosophers on the end of the world
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.author: Christopher Star
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.text:
The feeling that the world is ending is nothing new – Plato, Epicurus and the Stoics all visualized the apocalypse

Do your feelings of existential dread extend beyond your own personal mortality? Do they include fears about the survival of our culture and institutions, our species, nonhuman life and the Earth itself? Do you feel like there’s nothing that can help to wrap your head around the biggest problem we face: the end of the world as we know it?

Apocalyptic expectations are on the rise. According to a 2022 Pew Research Center survey, 39% of Americans believe that we are living in the end times.

Yet the feeling that the world is coming to an end is nothing new. Anticipating and preparing for the end of the world is an ancient practice. In fact, many of the ways in which we envision future catastrophes can be traced back to the ancient Mediterranean world.

Greek and Roman authors set up their accounts of the end of the world as the product of reason rather than divine revelation – the product of the rational study of the laws of nature that govern the universe. They saw the end of the world as an inevitability and typically saw the aftermath, if there was one, as a repeat of the cycle of human development. The main piece of wisdom they seek to provide is how to face catastrophe without fear.

This is particularly true of the Epicureans and Stoics. Their goal is to meet all events up to and including the end of the world with equanimity. The Roman poet Horace offers a summation of this ideal in his Odes: the “righteous and resolute man” will remain “undaunted even if the sky should fall and the ruins strike his head”.

These ancient texts do not explicitly offer solutions or means of avoidance, and as Horace makes clear, they can envision the end of the world as the ultimate test of masculine endurance. Yet they also provide an understanding of the long perspective of human history, and how humanity relates to cosmological and geological history. Unlike our doomsday prepperism, their form of preparation did not require any building projects or financial expenditures; rather, they encouraged preparation that was psychological, epistemological and ecological. This required one to study nature in order to understand its workings and the place of humanity within it.

My new book, How to Face the End of the World, offers several passages from ancient Greek and Roman authors about the end of the world in the original Greek and Latin, along with my translation and introduction. The collection begins with a passage from the archaic Greek poet Hesiod’s Works and Days. The other texts are by ancient philosophers: Plato, Lucretius and Seneca. Each developed different scenarios for how the world could end, but all posited that the end would come from the forces of nature, rather than the wrath of the gods.

Ancient Greek and Roman accounts of world destruction, as well as Jewish and Christian apocalypses, tap into what is likely an underlying psychological truth about these types of stories. They are a means to understand the future, and to realize the hidden natural and divine forces at work in the cosmos. Their power to reveal ultimate truths and to prepare us to face the future may explain why stories about the end of the world are found across cultures and why they have persisted from the ancient world to today.

Hesiod (ca 700BC) is the classical world’s intellectual forefather for envisioning the end of humanity. One of Hesiod’s most famous stories is the myth of the metallic races. It traces the succession of humanity from the ideal time of the primordial “golden race” to the present “iron race”.

Hesiod predicts that at some point in the future, Zeus will destroy the current iron race. He enigmatically makes no mention of what will happen after this destruction. His silence served as an impetus for later authors to imagine different scenarios, ranging from a continuation of the cycle and a return to the Golden Age, to the end of humanity and the world itself.

Also contained in Hesiod’s account is the suggestion that humans can avoid Zeus’s wrath by honoring the gods and living a just and simple life. The prophecy of doom is not a fixed certainty, but rather a warning of what could happen.

Plato (420sBC–347BC) is perhaps most famous today for the portrayal of his hero, Socrates, and for the political philosophy of the Republic. Less well known is that he invented the story of Atlantis, which serves as part of his theory of cyclical global catastrophes.

In his dialogues Timaeus and the Laws, Plato posits that the world will exist for eternity, but that human development will be continually hindered due to periodic terrestrial catastrophes. In short, the world does not end, but advanced societies do.

With his stories, Plato appears to be testing the imagination of his audience. In the Laws, it seems clear that he is engaging in a thought experiment about how human society might rebuild after a global catastrophe. Unlike the violent post-apocalyptic narratives of today, Plato imagines that the survivors would live in peace and work together.

Epicurus (341BC–270BC) believed that the goal of life is pleasure and freedom from disturbance. For Epicurus and his followers, there was a strong connection between ethics and physics. In other words, understanding the nature of the universe was linked to living a good life.

Epicurus theorized that the cosmos consisted of atoms and void, as opposed to the other elements of earth, air, fire and water; that the gods existed, but did not care for humans. As a result, death was nothing to us – simply the dissolution of atoms back into the void. There was no punishment or reward to expect in the afterlife.

Very little of Epicurus’s work survives from the reported 300 volumes he composed, but a brief account of how worlds end is preserved in one of his letters: “A world is an encasement of a heaven, which contains stars and an earth and all phenomena and is separated from the infinite; it ends with a boundary that is either thin or thick and when this boundary breaks apart everything within it will be ruined.”

Epicurus’s most famous disciple was the Roman poet Titus Lucretius Carus (ca 98BC–ca 55BC). One key way in which Lucretius departs from and develops Epicurus’s teachings can be seen in his accounts of the end of the world. Lucretius offers two scenarios: slow, gradual decay, or one sudden day of destruction.

When we come to Stoic cosmology, we seem to leave the realm of plausibility and have to abandon our deep-seated notions of time’s arrow moving in one direction. But if you prefer to think of time as moving in great cycles of creation and destruction, or ever had the feeling of deja vu, the Stoics are for you.

Founded by Zeno of Citium (ca 334BC–ca 262BC) in Athens during the late fourth century BC, the Stoics argued that “creative fire” was the primal building block of the cosmos. Eventually this fire would consume everything and then the cosmos would be reborn, events known as the ekpyrosis (conflagration) and apokatastasis (restoration).

Only brief fragments and reports, some of them hostile, remain of the early Stoics on this theory. Some Stoics even rejected the idea of cyclical conflagrations. There are no detailed accounts of how the conflagration would unfold or how humans should prepare for it in the fragments that survive of the early Stoics. Most likely, it was believed to lie in the distant future.

The Stoic perspective on the end of the world changed during the Roman period. For example, as part of his daily practice of ethical philosophy, the emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote a brief reminder to himself in his Meditations that the end will come very quickly.

The most detailed Stoic accounts of the end of the world survive in the works of Seneca the Younger (ca 4BC–AD65). Among Greek and Roman authors, Seneca had the greatest interest in the end of the world. He wrote about it throughout his career, exploring different apocalyptic scenarios in several of his philosophical works, as well as one of his plays, the Thyestes.

Although Seneca’s descriptions of destruction go into great detail, he is not solely focused on the catastrophe itself. Rather, exploring the end of the world serves a deeper philosophical and therapeutic purpose. Like the Epicureans, the Stoics closely connected the study of ethics and physics. Understanding nature’s cycles could help one to live a better life by understanding that death is a part of nature, both for the individual and for our world.

In his Natural Questions, Seneca also considers how people would react when experiencing a global catastrophe. Seneca states that the destruction is close at hand, so perhaps his interest in human reactions to catastrophe was part of his own psychological preparation for the event.

What is the wisdom provided by these Greek and Roman authors? How might their visions of the end of the world help us today, if at all? On one level, we can see the origins of several narratives and ideas that are still very much alive today: the myth of decline from the Golden Age, Plato’s story of Atlantis, the Epicurean theory of total planetary destruction, as well as the Stoic theory of eternal return. Overall, however, it may simply seem depressing to read account after account of the end of the world.

Nevertheless, there may be value in envisioning the various forms that future global catastrophes could take. In 2020, a group of scholars published a piece arguing that morbid curiosity and exposure to apocalyptic and similarly frightening narratives can provide psychological tools and resilience when real catastrophes hit.

One of the members of the team, the literary scholar Mathias Clasen, wrote that mental time travel, the ability to imagine possible futures, has been important for human development. Apocalyptic narratives serve a key purpose in that they allow humans to imagine and plan for the “worst-case scenario”.

Other scholars, such as philosopher Hans Jonas, have urged us to accept that the odds are high that catastrophe awaits us in the future. We should not only envision the future as catastrophe but wager that the future will be bad rather than good. Yet this is not simply a prediction of doom and despair. As the contemporary philosopher and cultural critic Slavoj Žižek noted in Too Late to Awaken: What Lies Ahead When There Is No Future?, perhaps envisioning the future catastrophe as inevitable is paradoxically the way to avoid it.

Ancient philosophers might be best known for writing lengthy tomes. They did not compose works summarizing their theories of the end of the world but rather included them within larger philosophical arguments on nature, ethics and politics. But there also was the tradition of distilling ideas into a short work, or enchiridion, that one could keep close to hand – the literal meaning of the word. We can perhaps let the ancient Greek and Roman apocalypses discussed here and collected in my book serve as a low-stakes method of doomsday prepping.

Excerpted from How to Face the End of the World: An Ancient Guide for Apocalyptic Times (2026), published by Princeton University Press and reprinted here by permission

Christopher Star is professor of classics and director of the Axinn Center for the Humanities at Middlebury College. His books include Apocalypse and Golden Age: The End of the World in Greek and Roman Thought

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in $10bn lawsuit against BBC
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jeremy Barr in Miami
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Judge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for deposition

Donald Trump has been ordered by a US judge to cooperate with the discovery process mandated for his lawsuit against the BBC and to sit for a deposition by 11 December – or else he could be subject to sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the $10bn lawsuit.

The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together comments made by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. While the broadcast was not readily available to view in Florida, Trump’s team has argued that he was personally damaged by the broadcast under Florida’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

During a lengthy hearing dealing with a variety of discovery issues, federal magistrate judge Enjoliqué Lett on Thursday also rejected a request by Trump’s legal team to prevent the seven-hour-long deposition from being videotaped, though it will only be accessible to attorneys in the case.

Lett agreed with contentions from the BBC’s lawyers that Trump’s team had not been sufficiently forthcoming in handing over internal documents relevant to the case ahead of an 18 December deadline for discovery.

“We still have a completely lopsided [situation] here on discovery. They have produced absolutely nothing of any substance,” attorney Charles Tobin, on behalf of the BBC, argued in a Miami courtroom. The documents that Trump’s team have turned over have primarily been either pulled from the internet or provided by the BBC itself.

“It strains credulity that a thorough search has been done in order to determine that all of these requests have been responded to,” Lett told Alejandro Brito, Trump’s Florida-based attorney. “The court is not satisfied that anyone is doing a thorough job.”

The judge gave the plaintiffs 30 days to produce the relevant documents. While she acknowledged that the discovery process can be “burdensome” on both parties, she said that “failure to do so could result in sanctions, including possible dismissal of the suit for failure to prosecute the case and engage in meaningful discovery process”.

Of the Trump team’s obligation to adequately participate in the discovery process, the judge said: “This is the last opportunity to do so.”

After discussing the discovery process, the judge turned to the BBC’s request to compel the president’s team to agree for a deposition, after a previously scheduled date – 16 October – was cancelled for what Trump’s counsel said were “other matters of national importance”. While the BBC argued that Trump was actually campaigning in Georgia on that day, Brito said the president was “involved in a host of things” on a daily basis that the BBC’s legal team “has no idea” about.

While Lett said she was obligated to adhere to the discovery schedule mandated in the case, that timeline could be extended by district court judge Jeffrey T Kuntz. Tobin, representing the BBC, said his side is willing to push back the timeline for Trump’s deposition if Kuntz adjusted the discovery schedule.

Lett once again threatened sanctions – including dismissal – if Trump’s team did not comply with her deposition order.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Macron bans ‘illegitimate‘ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrest
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Jon Henley in Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
French president will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ regarding demonstrations on Friday as part of tough security response to recent rioting

Angry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases

Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost of living protests at the weekend.

Speaking after a ​meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, the French president said on Thursday that demonstrations organised by recognised groups would be allowed to go ahead, although their routes could be changed.

Protests requested by “individuals or groups with no legitimate authority” would be banned, Macron said. Requests by organisations such as trade unions would be “examined in accordance with the law” but may have to use alternative routes.

The measures were necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, he said, adding: “The rules are simple and I think they’re commonsense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days.”

Macron blamed much of last weekend’s unrest and looting on rioters who came expressly to loot, but said the worst of the violence was due to “political and seditious acts by ultra far-left groups who aimed to bring down the Republic”.

“The priority is a return to calm,” he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide concrete “next steps” for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.

An initial police ban on a student protest planned in Paris for Thursday was later overturned by a court, but marches also scheduled for that day in Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon were halted.

Authorities have already declared a ban on “all protests” on Saturday in the centre of the Lyon, France’s third-biggest city, where between 200 and 300 shops were ransacked and looted last weekend and the tourist office was set ablaze.

Authorities in Nice and Toulon announced similar bans for Saturday. In Paris, a march planned for Saturday to be held in the east of the capital, starting at Place de la Bastille, was authorised but banned from heading into the city centre.

However, a separate march through the capital planned for Saturday by students and some members of the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, whose protests over fuel prices rocked France in 2018 and 2019, would not be permitted, authorities in the capital said.

France’s main student union, UNEF, has also called ‌for rallies on Saturday. Businesses in central Paris and other cities had already begun boarding up their windows and hiring private security in preparation for violence, French media reported.

The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 174 of the 2,500 people arrested since last weekend’s rioting had been remanded in custody and more than 900 were being prosecuted. Two people have been arrested after Limoges town hall was set on fire.

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, was hosting a meeting of key figures from France’s main political parties on Thursday to hear their views and seek cooperation, and was due to meet several big city mayors later in the day.

The tough security response has included partial night-time curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, as well as bans on gatherings in areas such as around the Elysée presidential palace, the parliament and the city’s main train stations.

The demonstrations began last month in a high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings and spread nationwide, with strikes, blockades and demonstrations by high school pupils around the country.

Those demonstrations have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, six months before next year’s presidential elections that will choose Macron’s successor.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Pete Hegseth reportedly authorizes DHS to test ‘heat ray’ at US-Mexico border
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The Pentagon’s Active Denial System shoots energy beam that causes ‘sensation of intense heat on surface of skin’

Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, reportedly signed a memo last month permitting the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to test a non-lethal “heat ray” for potential use at the US southern border.

The “heat ray”, known as the Active Denial System, is a military-grade weapon that shoots an energy beam causing “a sensation of intense heat on the surface of the skin”, according to a 2009 National Defense University case study on the weapon.

The sensation “creates an intolerable sensation and reflexive movement” such as ducking or running.

In a memo, first obtained by CNN, Hegseth authorized a “temporary loan” of the Active Denial System to the DHS for seven months beginning in September. The DHS can request further use of the Pentagon system if needed.

A spokesperson for Customs and Border Protection (CBP) said in a statement it was “continually evaluating new technology, especially technology that can save lives while simultaneously enhancing national security effectiveness”.

When asked for comment, the Pentagon referred the Guardian to the DHS, which shared the CBP statement.

It is unclear what the DHS plans to use the Active Denial System for exactly, but the memo permits the department to use it for potential operations at the US-Mexico border.

The US military initially brought the system to Afghanistan nearly 20 years ago, but it was quickly returned home without ever being used, the Washington Post reported.

Previously, CBP officials reportedly considered using the Active Denial System in areas with a large number of illegal crossings or for crowd dispersal, but it was never deployed.

When used, the Active Denial System can produce an invisible beam of 95 gigahertz that penetrates about 1/64th of an inch into the skin, causing a burning sensation. (The system is technically not a “heat ray” because it uses millimeter waves, not infrared, Forbes reported in 2020.)

Pentagon officials have compared the feeling to a blast of heat when opening a hot oven, according to CNN. The feeling is temporary, lasting between 10 and 15 minutes.

In 2012, the Marine Corps announced that the system was compliant with international legal obligations of the US, and officials said they felt “comfortable” that it was safe.

The new memo, seen by CNN, states that the DHS will be solely responsible for the system’s “employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures”. It also states that no Department of Defense personnel shall operate it.

During the first Trump administration, officials sought to use the Active Denial System, first in 2018 to stop migrants from crossing the border, the New York Times reported. Later, in 2020, the administration also sought it to control protests in Washington DC after the killing of George Floyd, the Washington Post reported.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Trump’s Fifa peace prize was a sham. A reimagined award can still have meaning | Leander Schaerlaeckens
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The first awarding marked the apex of Gianni Infantino’s hubris. A new version could highlight the good in the world of soccer

Poor Fifa peace prize. Unloved, unliked, mocked, tainted by association with its first winner. And now demoted, too, after Fifa president Gianni Infantino dumped the thing on the global governing body’s “social responsibility committee” to look after. To redeem it, rather than to ditch it, to spare Infantino the embarrassment of acknowledging that his fake prize was really just a fake prize all along.

Here is where we should probably acknowledge that, as fake prizes go, and in the context of what it was intended to accomplish, the first awarding of the Fifa peace prize was an unqualified success. It achieved exactly what it was meant to, made by Infantino to flatter Donald Trump, the man he needed to keep on his side to safeguard the riches to be extracted from the North American market in order to consolidate his power base within Fifa. Trump, the gullible buffoon, was pleased as punch – handed a big, golden bauble and a medal he placed around his own neck – and briefly forgot about the Nobel peace prize he desperately covets.

The 22-person social responsibility committee is one of the dozens of standing committees Infantino has created to dole out generous per diems to his allies. It has been charged with recasting the prize into a recognition of social harmony and responsibility, as the Guardian has reported, and will probably seek to depoliticize it – or at least stop awarding it to politicians. There are no aspiring autocrats to placate for the foreseeable future, after all, since Saudi Arabia’s de-facto ruler and host of the 2034 World Cup, Mohammed bin Salman, doesn’t seem to go in for that kind of thing.

That first incarnation of the prize will stand as a monument to Infantino’s folly, as the apex of his hubris and his era of genuflecting to strongmen. That is, of course, assuming he survives the fallout of his attempt to privatize a chunk of the World Cup and re-emerges somewhat chastened and cautious, if either of those behaviors are still within his capacity. And if he makes it through another presidential election in March.

But a second version of the Fifa peace prize holds genuine potential to highlight some of the good the sport occasionally does, to platform and recognize those who leverage soccer’s vast cultural influence to improve the lives of others. The magic of soccer is that it transcends the field and reflects cultures and geopolitics; it becomes anthropological ritual, spoken as the world’s common language. Sometimes, it transforms into a vessel for virtue.

You could give the new prize to Afghan Women United for getting recognized as the official representatives of their country all while playing as refugees in exile. In June, they contested a pair of friendlies against the Cook Islands in New Zealand. They lost both matches, yes, but that’s beside the point. Their mere existence doubles as a towering protest against the Taliban, which has resumed its violent oppression of women since storming back into Kabul in 2021.

You could give it to Ukrainian club Shakhtar Donetsk, for persevering and even thriving in spite of Russia’s invasion – either through proxies or outright – of their Donbas region a dozen years ago, forcing the club to play elsewhere ever since.

Give it to former Spain international Juan Mata, for his work with Common Goal in convincing other players and managers to donate 1% of their earnings to charity; to Marcus Rashford, for shaming the Tory government into feeding children during a pandemic; to Sadio Mané, for bankrolling the construction of a hospital and other infrastructure projects in his native Senegal; to N’Golo Kanté for doing much the same in Mali.

Give it to Scotland’s Tartan Army, for raising money for children’s charities wherever they play. Hell, give it to the England players for donating their match fees to charity causes since 2007, adding up to more than $6.7m (£5m).

How would any of this relate to peace? Fair question. The peace prize could stand to be rebranded, the better to disassociate it from the least peaceful leader of a western nation in generations. It should probably have clearer qualifications and regulations, too, which is to say that it should have qualifications and regulations. And it’s probably best to shy away from the notion of steering entirely clear of politics. You can either have an award that acknowledges social good or you can be apolitical. You cannot do both.

But that needn’t be a bad thing, if this prize is sincere in rewarding one of the sport’s best citizens – and so long as it serves more than the Fifa president’s selfish interests.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Rookie Lendeborg jaws at ‘weak ass’ Dončić and admits he didn’t watch much NBA
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Golden State Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg had an extraordinary NBA debut as he jawed with Luka Dončić and admitted he had largely been exposed to the league through highlights before turning professional.

Lendeborg was given the task of guarding the Los Angeles Lakers star for large parts of Wednesday’s game, which Dončić’s team won 127-105.

However, Lendeborg said he “lost all respect” for Dončić’s quest for foul calls during the game.

“I had a lot of respect for him [because] I didn’t really watch the NBA much,” Lendeborg said. “I just watched highlights and seen him kill people. But being in it firsthand and seeing all the whining and complaining, I lost all respect.”

Lendeborg was the No 11 overall pick by the Warriors in this year’s draft after helping Michigan win the NCAA Tournament. He had early success shutting down Dončić, but the six-time All-Star went on to score 28 points in the Lakers’ victory.

In the second quarter, Dončić was fouled by Lendeborg after a pump fake and celebrated in front of the rookie.

“You get the foul call. Congratulations, bro,” Lendeborg said. “Then you talk to me like you did something great. C’mon, dog. That shit is weak. It kind of threw me off because I have so much respect for him. Gone, man. Gone.”

Lendeborg was given a technical for jawing at Dončić. “I was telling him he sucks,” Lendeborg said. “He can’t score on me. You talk but you can’t score on me. I said it the whole game. I said a couple cuss words, obviously. That’s why I got the technical. But I was letting him know.”

“I guess this is what the NBA is like, man,” Lendeborg said. “A lot of flopping, a lot of foul baiting, a lot of praying to the refs, man. Interesting first game for me.”

Lendeborg had already made an impression before his debut. He admitted he used to hate his new teammate Stephen Curry because he was a fan of one of his playing rivals, Kyrie Irving. Warriors veteran Draymond Green, who is not shy of expressing his own opinions, had no problems with the rookie’s attitude.

“In this league, everybody always says, ‘Oh, there’s certain guys you got to respect,’” Green said after Wednesday’s game. “I ain’t come in the league like that. Everybody will say, ‘Oh, the rookie learned his lesson.’ What’d he learn? The next time he see him, go at his ass again.”

“He was talking crazy,” Dončić said. “But I wasn’t trying to talk back. This season, I’m not trying to get techs.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: CDC denies approval for high volume measles test, ‘prioritizing emerging technologies’
