https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Melody Schreiber
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
California, Oregon, Washington and Hawaii health officials ask CDC, ‘prioritizing emerging technologies’, to reconsider

California and Washington asked the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in May to validate a new way to test for measles – but after waiting two months, the CDC denied the request, citing “other competing priorities”, according to a letter from the West Coast Health Alliance to the CDC director, Erica Schwartz.

The letter, signed by health officials in California, Hawaii, Oregon and Washington, asks Schwartz to reconsider and validate a rapid, high-volume measles test in preparation for major outbreaks. The alliance also asked the CDC to create protocols to test for other high-priority pathogens to prepare for future outbreaks.

The CDC is “ensuring state and local health departments have the support needed to strengthen measles detection and outbreak response”, said Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The agency was “prioritizing emerging technologies” to respond to the measles outbreak, Hilliard said.

The spokesperson did not answer questions about whether the CDC had plans to validate a high-throughput measles assay.

Such a test would “dramatically strengthen” the ability of laboratories to respond quickly to outbreaks, the health officials said – which would help preparedness for known pathogens like Ebola or hantavirus as well as emerging threats.

Right now, laboratories have to rely on lower-volume tests for measles, like individual polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests.

In the Covid pandemic, most public health labs bought high volume equipment, like the Hologic Panther Fusion, a PCR platform for diagnosing illness that can process up to 500 tests in eight hours. That way, labs could process large batches of Covid tests very quickly.

But there is no high-throughput test to diagnose measles – at least, not one that has been published or validated by the CDC.

Texas state laboratories developed such a test during the measles outbreak in west Texas last year, but they have not distributed or published the protocol. The CDC could implement and publish this or another protocol so other public health labs could run laboratory diagnostic tests.

The CDC has reportedly completed studies on the Texas test and another from ARUP Laboratories, “but they were not full validations or a comprehensive comparison”, the officials said in the letter.

The alliance asked Schwartz to develop an assay, or test, for measles diagnostic testing on the Panther Fusion and to publish that protocol so any lab can run the tests. Having tests ready to go is an essential part of preparing, the letter said: “If a large outbreak were to occur in our region, without high-throughput capacity, it would be more difficult to scale up diagnostic testing appropriately, impairing patient care and public health investigation.”

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Haiti move Nations League home clash with USA to Miami amid gang violence crisis
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jeff Rueter
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
On Thursday, Concacaf announced that it had approved Haiti’s request to relocate their Nations League quarter-final first leg on 14 November from Kingston, Jamaica, to Miami in an “exceptional hosting arrangement”. Haiti have been unable to play nominal “home” games within their borders since July 2021, with the United Nations estimating that 90% of Port-au-Prince – including the national stadium – is controlled by violent gangs.

Initially, Haiti’s match, the first leg of a home-and-away series against the United States, had been booked in Kingston. The Grenadiers had previously played their World Cup qualifiers in Curaçao, Aruba and Barbados. However, the Nations League format slated Curaçao and Jamaica to host their matches on the same night as Haiti’s, shunting Haiti to Sabina Park, the home of the Jamaica national team until their current venue opened in 1962. Now a cricket ground, Sabina Park hosted two of Haiti’s Nations League qualifiers.

While the shuffle sends Haiti within their opponents’ borders, they couldn’t have found a more hospitable home away from home. Miami boasts by far the largest population of Haitians and their descendants, with nearly half a million concentrated predominantly in South Florida. They’ll play at Nu Stadium, where they played the venue’s first international friendly – a pre-World Cup clash with Peru – in front of a sold-out crowd of 26,700. That support dwarfed the crowds they drew at Sabina Park, where their two matches attracted an average of 297 fans.

Haiti once dominated their series with the United States, ending the US’s World Cup qualifying run in 1969. The US have won four of their six clashes this century, with the other two matches ending in draws.

This will be Haiti’s first trip back to the United States since the 2026 World Cup, a hero-making turn for the Caribbean nation in their first tournament appearance since 1974. The Grenadiers were handed a difficult group, losing all three games against Morocco, Scotland and Brazil. Nonetheless, they enjoyed fantastic support from Haitian fans at their matches in Massachusetts, Philadelphia and Atlanta.

Although a rebooking, this could give the national team a chance to play in front of a considerable number of compatriots.

Concacaf added that “this flexibility will remain in place for as long as the security situation in Haiti persists”. Haiti, as well as clubs based in Haiti, will need to seek approval from Concacaf for each match they look to play in “the territory of its opponents”, a separate arrangement from the neutral sites they’ve previously booked. The confederation closed by stipulating that the measure “may be amended or withdrawn by the Concacaf Council at any time”.

⚽ Updates from 5.45pm BST kick-offs, then the 8pm games ⚽ Live scores | Table | Read Football Daily | And mail Daniel

Rutter finds Osman at inside-left, a lovely ball arced down the line and inside. Inside the box, he shows the defender too much of the it but bundles through one challenge, only to stumble into the second and lose possession.

These Brighton players have loads to play for. Imagine the atmosphere around their training ground at the moment, and how much those not starting in the league want to force their way in. Given the struggles of various among the rich clubs, they’ve a proper chance of making top five – and who knows what else.

Rutter backs in inside the box and, expertly found by Gross, he controls and spins away from goal, his marker too tight, then lashes a shot just wide of the near post.

Salah watches Reus go right and clips over his legs and into the middle of the net.

31 min Franculino beats one man then another as he weaves into the box, Magnusson steps across him, and that’s an easy call for the ref.

Poznan are second in the Ekstraklasa, with 27 goals in 10 games, easily the most in the league, and they look likely tonight. I’d be shocked if this contest ends 0-1, but Sunderland should be good for at least one more goal too.

In Turkey, Trabzonspor are dominating against Hearts, but they’ve Andre Onana in goal and one can never be sure when he might toss one in: when Man United were last in the Champions League, they scored 12 goals in three matches against Bayern, Galatasaray twice and FCK, earning a single draw, largely because of his work in net.

Back in Poznan, Sunderland find Fofana, left side of the box, he shoots low and hard … hitting the far post! But the ball is then cut back to Xhaka who, eight yards out, should score. He sweeps goalwards … and straight at the keeper.

I guess he’s one of the first of the new guard of manager who had no playing career to speak of, but had a talent for understanding the game and where once, they’d have been a coach if that, now they’re running clubs. I’m certain we’ll see much more of this. Oh, but as I type, Verbruggen has to save sprawlingly at his near post.

Every time I’ve looked at Brighton, who show eight changes from their weekend win, they’ve got Jablonec boxed. The way Fabian Hurzeler has inculcated a style that allows players to come in and out without it changing, is exceptional.

Three against Grazer at the weekend and now, the ball is given away in midfield, Weinhandl, the 17-year-old, wins it back, slides through the centre, and Diakite leans one way to slot confidently the other.

And he’s playing well, pulling wide and crossing to win a corner. Back to the pink kit, given this is its second away outing in Europe, against teams with whom Sunderland’s colours don’t clash, we have to assume someone at the club is doing their best to make it legendary. It’d go nice with Frankfurt in May.

“It’s hard not to root for Timur Tutierov,” writes Kári Tulinius. “He is a Crimean Tatar refugee. He was just nine when Russia invaded and he fled with his family to Spain. Four years later they moved back to Ukraine. He’s never been back to his home.”

Sunderland fans in Poznan. I can only imagine the scenes, given a wild fanbase who feared they’d never get to do this.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
Attorney general says ‘there’s scenarios we could all come up with’ when asked if DoJ would intercede to stop states from certifying election

How will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questions

Asked by a reporter earlier whether there was any scenario in which the Department of Justice would weigh in on states’ certifying process or try to block states from certifying the election, attorney general Todd Blanche did not rule it out.

Blanche replied: “Is there any scenario? Yes, of course there’s scenarios we could all come up with.”

He added: “It is not DOJ’s intention to improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process, but to say that there’s no circumstances that we would ever do that – of course I’m not going to say that.”

And following up from our last post, Calley Means has officially announced his resignation on social media.

He said he was doing so with “tremendous respect” for Donald Trump and Robert F Kennedy Jr, the health secretary.

“They laid out a vision of combatting the entrenched, dark forces in DC that profit from Americans getting sick,” he wrote. “More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history – and I know this movement is just getting started.”

Calley ⁠Means, a ⁠senior ⁠adviser to ​US health secretary ⁠Robert F Kennedy ⁠Jr ​who ‌has also ‌worked ‌in the White House to further his “Make America ‌Healthy Again” policies, has quit ​his role today, ​the Wall ​Street ​Journal (paywall) reports.

According to reports, Means departed his role over frustrations that the White House had stalled progress on Kennedy’s MAHA agenda, but said he would continue working to further the movement.

In a statement to Politico, Means said: “I leave with tremendous respect for President Trump and RFK — two historic figures who are committed to confronting a corrupt DC bureaucracy that is doing everything possible to protect the status quo.

“The past two years have seen historic policy and cultural change to confront the chronic disease crisis and healthcare incentives that profit from us being sick. This movement is in the first inning and just getting started.”

The Department ​of ​Health and ​Human Services did ​not immediately ‌respond to ​a ​Reuters request for comment.

Two administration officials have told Politico that Means’s breaking point came this week after a meeting between Kennedy and White House officials to discuss defining ultra-processed foods (a key MAHA priority) was postponed.

“That was the straw that broke the camel’s back,” said one of the officials. “Calley’s been pushing very, very hard for this, but it’s been a very opaque process and has been just continuously stonewalled.”

Maine Republican senator Susan Collins has distanced herself from a new radio ad attacking her Democratic opponent Troy Jackson as a “freak” and a “creep” because “he has two kids with his cousin”, saying yesterday that the ad should be taken down.

The spot, airing on Maine radio in the form of a country song, is from the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans. Among the lyrics in the jingle: “If he’ll screw his own family, he’ll screw yours too.”

Collins told reporters during a campaign appearance in Lewiston that she “had nothing to do with that ad”. She added that federal law bans her from coordinating with the super PAC, but she has publicly called for it to be removed.

Previously, in a Politico story last month, Collins referenced Jackson’s relationship with a second cousin. “I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin,” Collins said. “I don’t know whether people know that or not.”

In an op-ed published yesterday, Lana Pelletier, Jackson’s partner, criticized the radio ad and other attacks on her family by Collins and her supporters, saying she never thought they “would stoop this low”.

“Senator Collins has been quick to demand respect and decency for herself. My family deserved the same,” Pelletier said. “I am not a helpless woman who needs politicians to tell the world what happened in my own life. And I am not a punchline or a caricature of where I come from.”

Jackson, a former state lawmaker and lumberjack, and Pelletier are longtime partners who have two sons together.

Jackson’s deputy campaign manager, Dan Gottlieb, said yesterday that Collins owes Jackson’s family an apology.

“Susan Collins herself spread these disgusting personal attacks on Troy’s family,” he told the Associated Press. “Now she wants Mainers to believe she’s above the very attacks she helped spread.”

Democrats are hoping for a win by Jackson over the incumbent Collins as the party tries to retake the Senate.

“This race is unique in Maine history in the number of personal attacks,” Collins said yesterday.

The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together comments made by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. While the broadcast was not readily available to view in Florida, Trump’s team has argued that he was personally damaged by the broadcast under Florida’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

During a lengthy hearing dealing with a variety of discovery issues, federal magistrate judge Enjoliqué Lett on Thursday also rejected a request by Trump’s legal team to prevent the seven-hour-long deposition from being videotaped, though it will only be accessible to attorneys in the case.

Lett agreed with contentions from the BBC’s lawyers that Trump’s team had not been sufficiently forthcoming in handing over internal documents relevant to the case ahead of an 18 December deadline for discovery.

“We still have a completely lopsided [situation] here on discovery. They have produced absolutely nothing of any substance,” attorney Charles Tobin, on behalf of the BBC, argued in a Miami courtroom. The documents that Trump’s team have turned over have primarily been either pulled from the internet or provided by the BBC itself.

“It strains credulity that a thorough search has been done in order to determine that all of these requests have been responded to,” Lett told Alejandro Brito, Trump’s Florida-based attorney. “The court is not satisfied that anyone is doing a thorough job.”

Before traveling to Nebraska, JD Vance fielded questions from reporters and expressed confidence in possible negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, following Steve Witkoff’s meetings with leadership of both countries in recent days.

“The reason why we haven’t struck a peace deal is because they’ve just been too apart on some of the details of that negotiation,” Vance said. “So, I think Steve re-engaged the process … He feels optimistic. I mean, the nature of these things is you take a swing at it, you see how much progress you can make, and then you go back at it, and sometimes it works, and sometimes it doesn’t.”

While Witkoff said that trilateral talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv “at the technical level” would follow his discussions this week, Russia still carried out a massive “demonstrative” attack on Ukraine overnight, bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after Putin’s meeting with Witkoff wrapped up.

The latest strikes killed at least two people and wounded 22, including four children.

Democrats lead Republicans 63% to 26% among likely voters aged 18-29, according to a new poll by Harvard’s Institute of Politics.

However, 33% of young Americans say they will definitely vote in the upcoming midterms, down from 40% who said the same ahead of both the 2018 and 2022 cycles.

In 2024, 56% of men between the ages of 18 and 29 voted for Trump while just 40% of their female peers did so. Harvard’s new poll shows that while women still favor Democrats, 66% to 21%, that number is also robust among young men: 58% to 32%.

Another key takeaway from the survey, the last before the November midterms: only 9% of 18- to 29-year-olds say the nation is generally headed in the right direction, while 62% say it is off on the wrong track and 26% say they are unsure.

Following the recent controversy around Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign ad that features Amy Acton’s estranged mother, Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the Center for Politics – a key election forecaster – has shifted the Ohio gubernatorial race from “toss up” to “leans Democratic”.

As I noted earlier, a number of Republicans, including the outgoing governor Mike DeWine, have criticized the ad, which includes Acton’s mother – who she hasn’t seen since she was removed from her care at age 12 – calling her daughter a “liar”.

Mike DeWine, the outgoing Republican governor of Ohio, has called on Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign to take down the recent ad that includes the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

DeWine called the campaign spot “deeply, deeply troubling” and said it was “wrong” to have run it. The governor told reporters today that he would not rescind his endorsement of Ramaswamy in the bitter gubernatorial race against Acton – who served as the health director in DeWine’s administration and guided the state through its Covid-19 pandemic response.

On Wednesday, Acton responded to the recent controversy and told a group of voters said Ramaswamy shouldn’t have “exploited” her mother.

A reminder that Acton and her brother were removed from their mother’s care when Acton was 12, after their stepfather was arrested and charged for raping her. However Arthur remained married to her husband, and they fled the state.

Meanwhile, at an event stumping for Ramaswamy in Cincinnati on Wednesday, JD Vance chided Republicans for their outrage over the ad. The vice-president said he wasn’t going to weigh in on whether the spot was “appropriate or not”. Instead his “message” for fellow elected Republicans was to “stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days”.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on AI safety: the push for global regulation must advance | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The current US administration is an obstacle, but public demand for protection will ultimately prevail

Organisations around the world scrambled on Thursday to fix critical flaws in PHP, the software that powers much of the web. The vulnerabilities could allow attackers to take control of affected servers. Some websites were taken offline as a precaution while fixes were installed. The paradox is that while AI helped researchers uncover the flaw, it also threatens to accelerate the ability to exploit it. Amazon said that it had detected an attempt before the public disclosure of the PHP flaws.

What the episode highlights is AI’s central role in security – and not always for the right reasons. OpenAI’s models have also been responsible for two alarming hacks this year – a security breach of an Australian health department website and a raid by a swarm of AI bots on Hugging Face, an AI services platform. Citing those incidents, the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, warned that a similar cyber-attack on the UK is “likely, if not inevitable”.

Britain is not uniquely vulnerable. In some respects it is more advanced than many countries in grasping the scale of the challenge. The London-based AI Security Institute is internationally recognised as an authority in a rapidly evolving field. A cybersecurity bill to protect critical digital infrastructure is going through parliament.

As Mr Narayan concedes, national governments face limits in protecting their citizens from a global threat. Having Donald Trump in the White House makes the international challenge harder. The US president has rejected calls for international negotiations on AI regulation. He is even dismissive when the bosses of US technology companies recognise the need for external monitoring and ask for statutory guardrails on their own activities.

Mr Trump takes the view that America’s lead at the most advanced frontier of AI is a national strategic asset that would be compromised if other nations, and China in particular, were allowed to set the pace of advancement. In the president’s eyes it is a race for global supremacy and only losers urge caution. “Whoever wins AI, wins,” he has said. That is a disturbingly reckless approach to technology that, in some of the more apocalyptic prognoses, has the potential to destroy humankind. Even in more circumspect scenarios, the risk of some catastrophic incident or severe economic shock caused by the malicious or accidental use of AI is growing at a rate that more responsible leaders than Mr Trump cannot afford to ignore.

Andy Burnham has said that he intends to put AI at the top of the agenda when the UK holds the G20 presidency for the first half of next year. In his speech at the Labour party conference earlier this month, the prime minister compared his role to the global leadership position that Gordon Brown took on as the chair of the G20 in early 2009, coordinating a response to the financial crisis.

But the world looks very different in 2026. Mr Burnham’s convening power will not move a US administration that treats historic allies and multilateral institutions with contempt. That is not a reason to abandon the ambition. The drive to build some global regulatory architecture has to advance. If Mr Trump cannot be moved by care for humanity, this week’s PHP emergency should remind him that America’s technological lead offers no protection from disruption. Shielding US citizens and businesses from such turmoil requires international cooperation that a race for AI supremacy puts at risk.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Christa Pike’s IV team warned vein might be ‘blowing’ before failed execution
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ed Pilkington in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
New account from Pike’s lawyer suggests team was racked by doubts even before pentobarbital began to flow

The Tennessee execution team tasked with setting an intravenous line in the arms of the death row prisoner Christa Pike through which she could be injected with a lethal dose of pentobarbital repeatedly warned that her vein might be “blowing”, before they went ahead with the procedure, her lawyer has revealed.

Members of the intravenous (IV) team used up to 10 needles as they sought to establish a line through which Pike could be killed with a massive dose of the sedative. About 20 minutes into the attempt, they began discussing among themselves whether the prisoner’s vein “might be blowing”.

Two unidentified members of the team began poking the site through which they were trying to set up the line, and both agreed that they couldn’t tell whether they had succeeded in finding the vein. “One of them said something like: ‘It’s either blood or blown, I need to know,’” the lawyer’s new account says.

The potentially critical new details of how Tennessee’s execution team failed to kill Pike, 50, on 30 September are contained in the most detailed account yet given by Pike’s lawyer Randy Spivey.

In a declaration that was released as part of separate legal proceedings, Spivey gave a minute-by-minute chronology of Pike’s ordeal, which he personally witnessed in the death chamber.

The account suggests that the IV team was racked by doubts even before the pentobarbital began to flow, as they struggled to find a vein for almost an hour. The search began at 6.35pm that evening, and was completed at 7.24pm, at which point the team left the chamber assuming everything was going according to plan.

The execution was eventually called off, and after 10 days in hospital Pike was returned to prison in Nashville. She is the only prisoner in modern times to survive a full dose of a lethal injection drug.

Though she can now talk and walk, her long-term prognosis is still unknown. The gruesome events of her failed execution have prompted nationwide soul-searching about the death penalty in the US, and forced the Republican governor of Tennessee, Bill Lee, to call off all executions in the state pending a review.

Spivey’s blow-by-blow chronology gives agonizing new details about the lengths to which the IV team went to find a vein, as well as their profound anxieties about whether they were doing the right thing. A person on the IV team named by Spivey as “member two” first expressed the fear that Pike’s vein might be blown at 6.53pm.

The team then discarded the 20-gauge needle that they had been using, saying: ‘“It’s not long enough. What is the longest you’ve got?”

Three minutes later, at 6.57pm, member two repeated it “might be blowing”. Spivey reported: “Member two and IV team member 3 inspected the insertion site and poked it. Both said that they ‘can’t tell’.”

Despite the uncertainty, the IV team agreed among themselves that they had established a line just two minutes later, only to discover that it was not, in fact, properly working. “I need to work again,” member two said, pulling the needle out of Pike’s left arm. “It appeared to be severely bent,” Spivey records.

At 7.08pm member two called on the team to think again. “Let’s regroup,” he said. They began checking Pike’s right arm again, and poking around the insertion site. At 7.13pm, member two told Pike directly that they “have it”, and the injection of pentobarbital that they thought would kill her was set to begin.

The revelations of so many doubts and foiled efforts to find a line, including the critical fears that her vein might have blown, lend added weight to one of the most prominent theories that have emerged for how the execution failed and Pike survived. Had the drug entered her bloodstream at such a extreme dose she would almost certainly have died, but if her vein burst, the pentobarbital would have been diverted into her arm tissue, causing her severe injuries but falling short of killing her.

As Spivey noted in his chronology, at 7.34pm Pike cried out: “I feel like my arm is about to bust. It burns.”

Spivey’s detailed minute-by-minute account is attached as an exhibit in a new legal motion filed on behalf of Tony Carruthers and other death row prisoners. Tennessee attempted to execute Carruthers on 21 May, but he too survived after the execution team failed to find a vein in more than 30 minutes.

Carruthers’s lawyers have asked permission from the Davidson county chancery court to file a supplemental complaint challenging Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol. They made an initial complaint in March 2025 in which they warned that the prisoner could face a torturous death by pentobarbital poisoning because the team administering the lethal drug were “incompetent, insufficiently trained, insufficiently dedicated to doing their jobs, and/or insufficiently attentive”.

As such, they warned, the execution ran an unacceptable risk of violating constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.

The failed executions in May, and Pike’s subsequent failed execution in September, bear out the lawyer’s advance warnings, the new motion asserts. “The specific failures that Mr Carruthers and Ms Pike endured were predicted, in detail and at length,” the new motion states.

Kit Thomas, an attorney for the death row plaintiffs, said: “Instead of addressing the problems in the 2025 Protocol when we identified them last year, the Tennessee Department of Correction and the Attorney General’s Office doubled down on secrecy and refused to make changes. The result was just as we predicted: extreme pain and suffering for our clients, in botched execution attempts that also inflicted lasting harm on victims’ families, corrections staff, and media witnesses, among others.”

Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of her friend Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 at the time of the murder, and spent the next almost three decades in solitary confinement.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: Super Graphic Spectacular review – Chappell Roan dazzles at her gloriously gay mini-festival
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Emma Madden
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
Shrine Auditorium, Los AngelesWith performances by Christina Aguilera, Lola Young and Tinashe, the pop star brings a colorful vision to life in support of LGBTQ+ charities

At Chappell Roan’s Super Graphic Spectacular, the sincerely camp pop star imagines a world where the most vulnerable among us aren’t wielded as scapegoats, and where life can be good, so long as we are good to one another.

That better world takes the form of a two-night extravaganza at Los Angeles’s Shrine Auditorium, part kiki ball, part fabulous revue, celebrating the first anniversary of the Midwest Princess Project, the nonprofit Roan founded in 2025 to support transgender youth and LGBTQ+ communities.

Named after her breakout album, The Rise and Fall of a Midwest Princess, the nonprofit has raised more than $800,000 and supported more than 60 organizations in its first year. Its work extends the promise at the heart of Roan’s music: that queer people, particularly those who grew up feeling estranged from their surroundings, can find somewhere to belong. For an artist whose rise has been inseparable from the extravagant performance of identity, the event offers a way to translate that feeling of collective recognition into practical support.

The Shrine Auditorium, with a capacity of about 6,300, is at least 10 times smaller than the crowds Roan usually plays to. The bill, however, is hardly modest. Pop stars Lola Young and Tinashe share the stage with drag acts and burlesque performers whose influence on Roan’s gleefully excessive presentation is unmistakable. Hosting the festivities is Caleb Hearon, everyone’s favorite algorithm-touted gay guy. “Why’s a man here? It feels like Chappell doing Make-A-Wish,” he jokes at the beginning of the night.

On the first of the two nights, straight men are in the minority. They dangle from the arms of their fabulous girlfriends, who wear sequins and cowboy hats, like accessories themselves, dressed in black bandanas and Spider-Man tees. Both groups queue for the same bathroom. “Restrooms are non-binary tonight,” a security attendant announces. Roan has not skimped on a single detail.

She has transformed the Shrine into a rococo burlesque ballroom, its gilded scrollwork set against great, swooping red velvet curtains. Blaine Petrovia, the night’s opening act, slides down a tall pole at the center of the stage, executing extravagant, sensual flourishes in a slutty circus routine.

There is hardly a pause between the night’s five acts as Hearon ushers performers on and offstage, vamping about straight men (why are they all fake photographers?) and straight women (ditto, but witches?).

Lola Young, the first of the night’s two guest singers, takes the stage in what might be called normal-people drag, looking a little out of place. She performs just three songs, closing with her hit Messy. An extraordinary vocalist still early in her career, Young has yet to master stage presence or crowd management, though her awkwardness remains charming, much as it did when PinkPantheress used to sheepishly carry a bag on stage.

The house band remains the same throughout, presumably to lend the night some cohesion, but Roan’s two guest singers struggle to distinguish themselves from it. The coherence of Roan’s universe is also its limitation: the show is so thoroughly organized around her sensibility that its glammed-up, exaggerated arrangements don’t quite work for everyone. Tinashe, the night’s second guest singer, is a case in point.

Tinashe’s latest album, for my money one of the best of the year, is supremely chic. Here, the band distorts its sleekness into chintz. It’s a testament to Tinashe’s deftness as a performer that she rises to the occasion, delivering Roan-filtered versions of her songs with ease, but the crowd doesn’t quite respond in kind. When she sings Nobody Wanna Dance Anymore, the audience largely proves her right. Devastatingly, that is one of the only two (two!) songs Tinashe is allotted.

The space made for Roan proves worthwhile when the headliner launches into an extraordinary hour-and-a-half set. It confirms her status as one of the greatest performers in pop, and possibly in any genre, working today. She emerges relatively understated, by her standards, in a gray gown, with a long red fishtail woven into her hair.

Roan’s world is one of ballroom, drag, glam rock, girlhood splendor and sex. She hiccups her way through Midwest Princess hits – Femininomenon, Casual, and Super Graphic Ultra Modern Girl – without a hair out of place.

By now, Roan’s production is so perfected that the cracks that peek through tonight feel graciously illuminating. Several songs into her set, she begins to look noticeably nervous, taking swigs from her lilac Stanley cup, forgetting lyrics, and smiling diffidently. “I have a surprise,” she announces, telling the crowd that she is about to bring out a guest who has “paved the way”. Cyndi Lauper? I think. Madonna, if we’re being incredibly ambitious.

Then Christina Aguilera appears in black lingerie, and Roan, who has spent the evening functioning with the precision of the well-oiled Femininomenon she is, suddenly becomes a giggling fan. Aguilera sings Beautiful, accompanied by piano, while Roan watches from the bench in disbelief.

There is something especially moving about hearing a song you have taken for granted, through sheer ubiquity, suddenly acquire a new resonance. As Aguilera sings Beautiful to a predominantly queer audience, the familiar becomes elemental again. “Words won’t bring you down.”

Roan appears charmingly nervous as the two duet her indie-folk ballad Coffee, forgetting her words again and regaining her composure only after Aguilera leaves the stage. Then she becomes the slick, precise performer again, leading the crowd into the YMCA’s sexier, uncloseted cousin, Hot To Go!

She closes with the song that traces her escape from her conservative Missouri upbringing into a world of her own making. In Los Angeles, surrounded by fabulous gays, Pink Pony Club needs little explanation. Pink confetti bursts overhead, and the fantasy she once sang about is no longer somewhere else. It is here.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump attacks Ohio governor over call for Ramaswamy to drop ‘deeply troubling’ ad
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Republican Mike DeWine says Ramaswamy ‘wrong’ to run controversial ad, drawing swift rebuke from president

Ohio’s Republican governor Mike DeWine on Thursday said gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy was “wrong” to release an ad critical of his Democratic rival Amy Acton that featured her estranged mother, and implored Ramaswamy to take the ad down.

DeWine’s comments drew a swift rebuke from Donald Trump, who urged Ramaswamy to keep the ad up.

Acton, who has led the Republican nominee Ramaswamy in recent polls of the governor’s race, has said she has not seen her mother Donna Arthur for decades, after she married a man who sexually abused her when she was 12 years old and stayed with him even after police stepped in.

Calling the ad “deeply, deeply troubling”, DeWine told reporters at the Ohio state capital. “It’s wrong to run this ad,” the Associated Press reported.

“I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down,” the governor added.

The video, which began circulating on social media earlier this week and Ramaswamy’s campaign later told Ohio media outlets is their work, shows Arthur calling her daughter “a liar” and saying she should not be put in charge of the state. Ramaswamy’s campaign said later in the week it would spend $4m to air the ad across the state.

DeWine noted that “family members have always historically been off limits” and Acton had earlier this year mentioned Ramaswamy’s mother’s involvement in an alleged “pump and dump” scheme, though with less prominence than the Ramaswamy ad.

On Truth Social Thursday afternoon, Trump excoriated DeWine for his comments, saying DeWine was “disloyal to the Republican party”.

“He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn’t want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing,” Trump wrote. “I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!”

Connie Luck, a spokesperson for the Republican’s campaign, said: “We refuse to accept the media’s double standards when Democrats have regularly used family members of President Trump, RFK Jr, and other Republicans in ads. Voters shouldn’t buy it.”

Speaking to reporters in Cincinnati on Wednesday, vice-president JD Vance dismissed criticism of Ramaswamy’s campaign. “Whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern,” Vance said.

“I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America. Politics is a tough business.”

In a statement released by Acton’s campaign, her brother, Philip Stearns, called the ad “a despicable low” for Ramaswamy, and noted that he and his sister were removed from Arthur’s custody after her stepfather was arrested.

Republican US senator Jon Husted, who is facing a election bid that could decide which party controls the chamber in the 3 November midterm elections, joined in the condemnation. “I would not have run that ad,” he told the Associated Press.

His Democratic opponent, former senator Sherrod Brown, has called the video “disgusting”, and said all candidates should denounce it.

Ohio’s Republican secretary of state Frank LaRose also criticized Ramaswamy, telling Columbus-area broadcaster ABC 6: “I probably wouldn’t run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision.”

DeWine nonetheless declined to drop his endorsement of Ramaswamy in the governor’s race, saying he wanted to support the “full ticket” of Republican candidates in the midterms.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.title: ‘It’s all God’s creation’: farmers continue a ‘Jewishly inspired’ agrarian tradition
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.author: Andrea Cooper
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.text:
In the US, a growing number of Jewish people are seeking purpose and community through farming

Wendy Rhein is trying to round up the sheep hanging out among the hazelnut and walnut trees of her Chutzpah Hollow farm in Tryon, North Carolina.

“Hi, Brea. Come on down. I hear you,” Rhein calls to the bleating queen of the flock. If the Barbados black belly ewe moves, the rest will follow.

Brea, a bottle-fed lamb named Hadassah and their flock mates bound down the hill when Rhein rustles a box of kosher tea biscuits. The small treat reveals something different about this farm. Rhein is remarkable for several reasons: she’s a female farmer in a male-dominated industry and a single mother who had no farming experience when she launched her farm at age 52. She’s also Jewish.

Rhein, who also works as vice-president of a faith-based advocacy organization, is part of a renewed interest among Jews in farming as an expression of their religion, culture or values. Shani Mink, co-founder of the Jewish Farmer Network, often hears “Jewish farmer – isn’t that an oxymoron?” Mink’s organization serves about 1,800 farmers, most of them first-generation agriculturalists, and offers conferences, classes and farm-to-table Shabbat dinners.

There is no solid estimate of the number of Jewish farmers in the country; the US Department of Agriculture’s census of the farming workforce doesn’t collect data on religion. But as Mink points out: “Jews have been farmers from time immemorial. The Jewish tradition is an agrarian tradition” – evidenced by how many holidays, such as the autumn harvest celebration Sukkoth, are tied to the agricultural calendar.

The Jewish Agricultural Society, chartered in 1900, helped people facing persecution in eastern Europe relocate to US farmland, where they could gain skills and independence. By 1933, more than 100,000 Jews earned some or all of their living from farming, according to Gary Moore, professor emeritus at North Carolina State University. But as the US population shifted away from agricultural work, many Jewish people moved into cities and suburbs. Some are returning to rural environments and family roots to farm, inspired by principles of their faith and building better food systems.

Rhein grew up in Detroit, the daughter of a man who was raised on a dairy farm he couldn’t wait to leave. In contrast, she loved the idea of raising livestock and being closer to her food sources; she challenged herself to prepare every ingredient she and her two sons consumed, down to the ketchup, while living in a high-rise with a kitchen “the size of a postage stamp” in Washington DC. When the pandemic hit, she started to search for land and research a new venture selling starter flocks of sheep.

Her brother, who lives about 45 minutes away in Asheville, showed her properties for sale over FaceTime. “I did not step foot on to this land or into this house until the day of our closing,” she said. Now she owns a 10-acre property.

Despite rising Jewish interest in land stewardship, Mink noted that most Jewish growers are “the only Jewish person in their farming community or the only farming person in their Jewish community”. In Rhein’s case, the nearest synagogue is almost an hour away. For her, that means “how I practice being a Jew on a day-to-day basis is how I farm and how I am attached to and care for this land”.

Rhein donates 10% of everything she raises to a local food bank, a reflection of pe’ah, a Talmudic concept that describes giving part of the harvest to the needy. She prays over every duck, chicken and sheep she slaughters so her family may eat.

“It’s all God’s creation,” she said. “It is a gift that we get to be part of it. We are stewards. We are not owners.”

But she also differs in her interpretation of some principles. The concept of bal tashchit focuses on limiting waste, so she keeps a pig to eat food scraps – a controversial decision for some Jews who don’t eat pork due to kosher dietary practices, many of whom disagree with her choice online.

“I am very clear this is not a quote-unquote ‘Jewish farm’,” Rhein said, “but I do consider us to be a Jewishly inspired place.”

A number of Jewish farming organizations focus on both community building and skills building. The Sacred Slaughter Institute trains students to become a shochets, ritual slaughterers of kosher meat; the butchering process calls for prayer, a highly sharpened knife and a single clean cut to lessen tza’ar ba’alei chayim, or animal suffering. Elsewhere, at the 20-acre non-profit Adamah Farm in Falls Village, Connecticut, Jewish people in their 20s and 30s come for three-month farming fellowships. Located at the Isabella Freedman Jewish Retreat Center, Adamah sells vegetables and herbs through membership in its community-supported agriculture (CSA) model.

Adamah Farm co-founder Shamu Sadeh said the work “is a process of reinvigorating Judaism and the Jewish community with an ecological perspective, and of reinvigorating the ecological environmental community with people who feel spiritually connected”. Graduates work in food rescue programs, food policy, environmental groups and Jewish social services, among other fields; a small percentage are farmers.

Rabbis Shoshana and Philip Ohriner run the 16-acre Ma’alot Farms in Los Gatos, California, with grants from community organizations and foundations. The farm nurtures hundreds of varieties of produce, from olives and broccolini to marionberries, a type of blackberry. Almost everything is given away to people facing food insecurity, including kids in afterschool programs and seniors with nutritional needs.

Ma’alot’s marketing doesn’t refer to Judaism. Still, “you cannot step on to Ma’alot Farms without feeling our Judaism permeate everything”, Philip Ohriner said, “from the way in which we care for our staff and provide a living wage for them and benefits, to the ways in which we seek to share our abundance to feed the hungry, to seek to bring equity and justice more fully into our world.”

At Ekar Farm, located at an eldercare community in Aurora, Colorado, executive director Jason Plotkin offers intergenerational gardening programs and donates about 20,000lb of organic produce annually to groups including Hope Communities, which serves refugees, and Spirit of the Sun, an Indigenous-led organization. The farm grows epazote, Thai hot chilies and bitter melon among its crops based on requests from recipients. Plotkin grew up Jewish but wasn’t religious. “I actually have learned more about my Jewish identity working for Ekar,” he said, “than what I brought into it.”

Non-profit farms exemplify the idea of tzedakah, or charity, a requirement in Jewish tradition. Small-scale for-profit farms strive to be community partners in their own ways.

Zalman (Robbie) Friedman operates a subscription and delivery service for local kosher meat from Robariah Farms in South Deerfield, Massachusetts. A certified shochet, he tends to about 1,000 birds, including meat chickens, egg layers and turkeys. About a quarter of his customers aren’t Jewish but appreciate Robariah’s regenerative farming practices. His birds have plenty of room to move and dine on fresh pasture every day thanks to mobile coops. “We raise a slower-growing variety that’s very active on the grass,” he said.

The laws of kashrut, or keeping kosher, outline how to slaughter an animal but are less specific about its care, Friedman said. “Why can’t it be done in a way that also honors the life of the animal, which is also a very important Jewish value and Jewish practice?”

Jewish guidance can show up even in crop selection. Ian Yosef Hertzmark grows ancient grains such as emmer, einkorn, spelt and Persian wheats, among other crops, on the 32-acre Migrash Farm in Baltimore county, Maryland. He plants ancient grains in the fall to be yoshon, or “old”, taking root before Passover (the Torah forbids eating chadash, or “new” grain). Hertzmark finds fulfillment in having “a relationship with land in an observant and seasonal context”.

Rhein agrees. She feels “more self-aware, more confident, more alive and whole as a human being here, doing this, than I ever felt living in Manhattan … This way of life – attaching yourself to land and animals and seasonality – is a constant sense of joy.”

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Next in line? Main contenders for the Manchester United hot seat
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Will Unwin
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
With Michael Carrick’s future at Old Trafford a matter of some debate, we examine the credentials of those who could succeed him

The German was of interest to Manchester City while Omar Berrada was part of the hierarchy on the other side of town. He is highly thought of and would come with an impressive CV for a 39-year-old, having taken charge of Bayern Munich and Germany. Nagelsmann is regarded as an innovator who is very demanding of his players and builds teams to press relentlessly, a concept not currently used at United, as Bruno Fernandes will testify. His spell with Germany was underwhelming, concluding with a 2026 World Cup last-32 defeat by Paraguay, and at Bayern – with an exceptional squad – he won the Bundesliga in his only full season and was sacked the following March with the team second and still in the Champions League.

The King of the Europa League is tactically astute and knows about working on a budget. If he is intrigued by the prospect of managing United, it would come down to whether he believes they have more potential than Villa, who are one point and place above them in the Premier League and faring much better in the Champions League, and whether United are willing to pay significant compensation. Emery likes a 4-2-3-1 but has always had a central striker at his disposal, and United lack someone strong in this department. Very calm but with a ruthless edge when required, he has plenty of silverware to back up his credentials. He is regarded as one of the game’s great pragmatists and is happy to play on the counterattack, which would suit the United squad.

The Italian, who left Napoli in the summer, knows the Premier League from spells with Chelsea and Tottenham, winning the title with the former in 2017. A fierce competitor and disciplinarian, he would shake up the dressing room with his high standards. His fiery temper can also result in fascinating interactions with the media, including telling a post-match press conference after losing to Burnley that maybe he was not the right man to manage Spurs. His willingness to speak out when it may not necessarily be wise could put United off. His preference for playing three at the back could be problematic considering the personnel at United, as Ruben Amorim found out.

The Northern Irishman worked within the United academy before stepping up to be part of José Mourinho’s backroom staff alongside Carrick. He stayed when Ole Gunnar Solskjær replaced the Portuguese and was credited with having a strong tactical influence as United secured second place. It is often a strength to have a link to a club but considering the struggles Solskjær and Carrick have endured, an external candidate seems more appropriate. He departed to become a head coach at Ipswich and his work there meant he was linked with a return to United to replace Erik ten Hag. McKenna resigned in June after securing promotion to the Premier League for a second time to take time away from the day-to-day grind of managemen. Would he want to end his sabbatical by jumping into a precarious situation after five or so months?

The English option and a manager with plenty of Premier League experience who took Newcastle to the Champions League. Arguably this makes him the safest pair of hands. A hard worker, Howe was often first in and last out at the Newcastle training ground as he pored over every detail. A lover of wingers and 4-3-3, he would be reliant on a central striker such as Benjamin Sesko to step up. He likes to work closely with his nephew Andy, who held senior roles at Bournemouth and Newcastle, which would create an interesting dynamic if he wanted similar at United. Howe, like others in contention, would not cost anything in compensation – and every penny counts at Old Trafford.

The 33-year-old has a growing reputation, with his Brighton team third after scoring 23 goals in seven games. This could explain why he is not particularly keen on leaving at the moment. His team are outperforming United with a squad that looks stronger. The size of United is alluring for many coaches but moving mid-season to a struggling club is not always advantageous because it means stepping into a firefight.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Teacher wounded in Oregon school shooting played dead after she was shot
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dani Anguiano
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Becky Drury says she was hit by gunfire before she could intervene in attack that killed four, including three children

A teacher wounded in last week’s shooting at a Bend, Oregon, elementary school shared her account of the incident, and how she was shot before she could intervene and “[pretended] to be dead”.

Becky Drury was seriously wounded at Silver Rail elementary when Griffin J John II, a 16-year-old former student at the school armed with a shotgun, broke in and headed toward a special education classroom. He shot six people, killing Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher, and three children, including five-year-old Rhoam Summer.

Drury and Saylor Graham, a seven-year-old student, were also shot. Another teacher threw her phone at John and tackled him before a parent fatally shot the teen gunman.

“Here is what I remember: Once I realized something was happening outside, I ran to see what was going on. I then saw the shooter and immediately ran back into the classroom. I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there. Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground,” Drury said.

Her left hand was almost completely severed, and her other arm was also badly injured, Drury said.

“I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again,” she said. “I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act.”

Drury’s account contradicted some reporting that she had thrown herself on top of a student in an effort to protect her, and the 54-year-old said she wanted to ensure “the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately”.

She described the violence as “unimaginable” and said “my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy.”

Public schools in the central Oregon city began reopening this week. Dozens of officers have welcomed students as they return to their classes.

The shooting remains under investigation. The Bend police department said this week that the shotgun used in the incident was purchased legally.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Aipac halts candidate endorsements amid US backlash against Israel
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Alice Speri
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
‘Political candidates’ once reflexive support for Israel has increasingly become a liability

When the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the most prominent pro-Israel lobby group in the US, announced on Wednesday that it would stop endorsing candidates or make direct contributions to them, its many critics were quick to hail the development as Aipac’s admission of how toxic its brand had become.

The announcement marked a significant reversal that underscored just how profoundly US public opinion of Israel has shifted over the latest war in Gaza, and how political candidates’ once reflexive support for Israel has increasingly become a liability.

But Aipac, which only launched its political action committee and started endorsing candidates three cycles ago, is hardly getting out of US elections. It pledged to maintain the work of its deep-pocketed Super Pac, United Democracy Project, and to continue to funnel millions of dollars to prop up pro-Israel candidates through individual donors and Aipac members. The shift in strategy was a sign it was adapting to a changing political landscape, not that it was giving up its efforts to shape it.

“Historically, AIPAC sustained an aura of invincibility that ensured it won most battles by walkover – if you are perceived as invincible, the other side doesn’t even bother to fight you,” the political analyst Trita Parsi wrote. “Rather than invincibility, AIPAC’s name now carries such toxicity that the group doesn’t want its own name on its political donations.”

Aipac did not respond to a request for comment. On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Aipac, which normally backs Democrats, was planning to give as much as $9m to a Pac supporting Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. The group had already spent $32m seeking to defeat El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of Israel, in the primaries.

But the announcement that it would stop directly backing candidates going forward was seen as tacit recognition that Aipac’s open support risked hurting pro-Israel candidates more than it helped them.

“Through this shift, AIPAC openly admitted that their brand has become toxic in the political world,” Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, one of Aipac’s most vocal critics, said. “Fewer and fewer candidates are willing to be publicly affiliated with this extremist, warmongering group. This is a clear signal: being pro-genocide is bad politics and bad policy.”

In a letter from Aipac to members first reported on by Jewish Insider, the group’s leadership seemed to acknowledge that its once formidable power in US elections had suffered as more candidates openly distanced themselves from Israel and from the group itself. In the letter, they noted that the 2026 election was “one of the most challenging environments in recent memory” for the group and predicted that the “challenges we are confronting will continue to grow in the years ahead.”

“To win the fight for the future of the country and the U.S.-Israel alliance, we must build a more strategic, consequential, and nimble political operation,” they wrote. “The only tactic we’re married to is the most effective one.”

While Aipac boasted that it helped 290 candidates this election cycle, leading to the defeat of 29 candidates it described as “anti-Israel”, the group has also suffered major blows – including in Michigan and New Jersey. More than a dozen candidates who took Aipac contributions in the past have since publicly distanced themselves from the group, and New York congressman Pat Ryan announced last week that he would return nearly $250,000 from the group, the latest of several elected officials to return Aipac funds or say they would turn it down.

Dion Nissenbaum, a journalist whose documentary on Aipac was published this week, featuring interviews with former Aipac insiders, told the Guardian that the announcement appeared to be the “first real admission from Aipac that their campaign strategy has backfired”.

Still, he warned, “if Aipac’s super PAC – the main source of its campaign donations – is going to keep operating, it may be an attempt to reinvent itself without ceding the battlefield.”

Tuesday’s announcement would change little in practice, those who have monitored Aipac’s political funding say. An Aipac spokesperson told Jewish Insider that Aipac members had contributed over $90m to candidates this election cycle – far more than the $3m in donations the group contributed directly through its Pac.

“This is not new,” Hady Amr, a former secretary for Israeli and Palestinian affairs with the US state department, noted. “This is Aipac going back to their tried and true approach.”

Groups like TrackAipac and initiatives like the Reject Aipac campaign, that have in recent years played a growing role in calling out candidates over their ties to the group, are already attuned to the varied avenues through which the pro-Israel lobby funnelled contributions to candidates, some more visible than others.

“[Aipac] has already been experimenting with ways to make their support more untraceable,” said Hamid Bendaas of the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, one of the groups behind the Reject Aipac campaign. By dropping endorsements and direct contributions, Aipac was giving up one tool available to lobby organizations to signal to politically-aligned donors who may not be active members which candidates to back. Aipac had calculated that approach was more risky than worth it, he added, but it had plenty of other tools available.

“It’s akin to an animal that chews its leg off to get out of a bear trap. It’s a last resort choice to survive and stay relevant, which they will on both counts,” Bendaas added. “Aipac is going to continue influencing elections. If you’re someone who wants Aipac out of politics entirely, this is not that.

“We know they’re going to continue driving tens of millions of dollars into our elections to support Israel’s atrocities,” echoed Miller of JVP. “And we will continue to fight to fully get them, and their dirty money, out of our politics and out of Congress.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: James Bond finalists to screen-test for role for this week – reports
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Adrian Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Actors in the mix to play 007 in Denis Villeneuve’s installment include Callum Turner and Jack Lowden

The search for the next James Bond may finally be nearing its end: according to reports, a very select group of actors will screen-test to become the next British agent 007 this weekend.

According to the Hollywood Reporter and Variety, citing several sources, a group of very select actors reportedly including Callum Turner and Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, will appear in front of cameras as the secret agent this weekend in London.

The tests supposedly include three elements: stunts, camera presence and dialogue. Reports vary that between three and five actors are finalists for the role, which was vacated by Daniel Craig after 2021’s No Time to Die. Despite speculation to the contrary, Sinners’ Jack O’Connell and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi are not testing, according to the Hollywood Reporter.

Dune film-maker Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next installment of the Bond franchise for Amazon MGM studios, which bought the series rights as part of an $8.45bn (£6.9bn) deal in 2022. Peaky Blinders scribe Steven Knight will pen the script.

The company, which paid more than $1bn last year to wrest “creative control” from the Broccoli family, has neither confirmed nor denied the reports, and referred the Hollywood Reporter to its earlier statement: “The search for the next James Bond is under way. While we don’t plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we’re excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right.”

In April of this year, Amazon film executives urged fans to exercise patience in waiting for the casting announcement, citing an abundance of caution in making the closely watched decision. “I know you’re all wondering when we’re going to announce who’s playing James Bond,” said Courtenay Valenti, the company’s head of film. “Don’t get too excited. Please know that we’re taking the time to do this with care and deep respect. It is the dream of a lifetime for all of us to bring audiences this next chapter, and it’s a responsibility we don’t take lightly.”

Villeneuve, a “diehard Bond fan”, has said the opportunity to add to the beloved franchise is what drew him away from the Dune franchise that has consumed the better part of a decade of his life.

“I said, ‘Maybe it’s a good idea to go back to this project, not out of nostalgia, not because I miss it, but the opposite – I’m tired of it,’” he told Empire of Dune: Messiah, which will premiere this December. “I want to make sure that I will be severe with the material. That I will not be complacent,” he said. “I thought, ‘When it’s done, I need a very powerful rocket to pull me away from Arrakis.’ When I was asked to do the next Bond, I said: ‘OK, this is what I need.’”

It’s been more than 20 years since the last full screen test for Bond; future Superman Henry Cavill was reported to be a finalist, but the role eventually went to Craig, who first appeared in 2006’s Casino Royale.

Speculation over the new Bond has intensified in the months since Villeneuve was revealed as director in 2025. The film is still reportedly positioned for a 2028 release.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Bournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather storm
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Nick Ames at the Vitality Stadium
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
This was a momentous night in Bournemouth’s history, although the truth is they would have been given a far sterner examination by Coventry or Hull. You can only beat what lies in front of you and Marco Rose’s players never relinquished control against a rotten impersonation of a Milan side. The visitors resembled holograms even before Mike Maignan, their goalkeeper, rendered their task impossible with a deserved sending-off in the first half.

By then Justin Kluivert had given Bournemouth the lead with a penalty and it was another spot-kick from Marcus Tavernier, given after Maignan’s rush of blood, that underlined their overwhelming superiority. Amine Adli applied the garnish with a late free-kick and it meant an abject return to British shores for Ruben Amorim, who would have been excused seeing this particular week as the opportunity to make a point. On this evidence Manchester United, to whom Bournemouth travel on Sunday, share more than a few similarities with the modern version of Milan.

At kick-off the local and broader contexts were impossible to ignore. Bournemouth could hardly have imagined, making their great escape from the fourth-tier trapdoor in 2009, that their modest home would host such a luminous name in a competitive fixture. On the weekend they beat Grimsby, the Rossoneri were overcoming Palermo thanks to goals from Kaká and Filippo Inzaghi. However hard you squinted, seeing the seven-time European champions’ colours on display here felt a trick of the light.

“How did we end up here?” asked the public address announcer, a question repeated on a banner hoisted by the north stand. It was worth posing with a bigger picture in mind too. After all, what has happened in football’s ecosystem to ensure the Premier League’s 15th-placed team, for all their merits, could justifiably be named pre-match favourites against one of the most decorated institutions in Serie A?

Sheets of swirling, driving rain were packaged in the south coast welcome for Amorim. He braved the elements without recourse to hat or hood; England had, perhaps, left him more bedraggled in the past. But within eight minutes he suffered a further dampener when, after a rapid Bournemouth start, Kluivert converted from the spot.

The scorer had been involved in a close call directly beforehand, failing to apply contact after fine work from Evanilson and seeing Ben Gannon-Doak’s strike deflected wide as the ball ran on. Milan did not clear their lines from the resulting corner and were punished when VAR found Koni De Winter had deflected Evanilson’s header wide with his arm. There could be no complaints for Amorim.

Bournemouth, whose colours were derived from those of Milan in 1970, continued to force the pace. Yunus Musah was dispossessed and Ryan Christie forced Maignan into a save. When one of Milan’s three Englishmen, Omari Hutchinson, tried to profit from a loose Gannon-Doak pass he could only run into António Silva.

Unlike most of his teammates, Hutchinson at least looked capable of matching Bournemouth’s intensity. Overall Milan could not cope and before the half-hour they self-destructed dramatically. It was a moment of supreme idiocy from Maignan, who had just clawed James Hill’s deflected strike wide but elected to shove Tyler Adams in the face as the subsequent corner was sent in. The penalty award was clear and so was the red card shown to Maignan.

Hutchinson was sacrificed for the replacement keeper Lorenzo Torriani, who was quickly beaten. This time Tavernier, unfazed by a lengthy wait, did the honours in style. An easing-off of the downpour before half-time was scant comfort for Amorim.

Adrien Rabiot was introduced at the break for Milan, whose best hope now was that Bournemouth fancied keeping something in reserve. Their right wing-back, Diego Moreira, bustled forward in a rare suggestion of appetite but it was Gannon-Doak, on the other side of the pitch, who threatened more consistently with a series of darts to the byline.

The wind had swelled to the extent that an Ardon Jashari free-kick, aimed from just inside Bournemouth’s half, blew back towards him before reaching the box. Bournemouth had no need for such help from the elements. They were hardly assisted in their quest for a third by the referee, Vasilis Fotias, who pulled play back to book a lumbering Fikayo Tomori for a foul when the substitute Lewis Cook was clean through.

Christie sliced wide before Adli, a substitute, curled in delightfully from 22 yards. Bournemouth’s faithful could sing in the rain to their heart’s content.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New York city council votes to ban horse-drawn carriage rides
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
City’s council passed Romanch’s Law, named after teen who died when he was ejected from carriage earlier this year

The New York city council has voted to ban horse-drawn carriage rides in the city by 2028 in a decision that has widespread implications for hundreds of jobs.

The council voted on Thursday on Romanch’s Law, legislation named in memory of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who died this summer after he was ejected from a runaway horse-drawn carriage in Central Park.

Under the measure, carriage operations will cease completely in June 2028. The legislation also called for a plan to help affected employees and business owners transition out of the industry in 2027.

Earlier on Thursday, the city council’s committee on health voted six-three in favor of the ban, clearing the way for the full council vote later in the day.

The final vote came just hours after workers and members of the Transport Workers Union (TWU) Local 100, which represents horse carriage drivers, gathered outside city hall in a last-minute push to stop the legislation.

Protesters called on lawmakers to either vote against the proposal or postpone the decision to allow further negotiations. They rallied and held signs decrying the vote, including one person who raised up an actual bag of horse poop in protest.

At the center of their objections is the uncertainty surrounding what happens to workers once the industry shuts down. Carriage operators maintain that their livelihoods are being taken away without a clearly established path forward.

John Samuelsen, president of TWU, told Spectrum NY it is “utterly false” that the bill includes real plans for retraining the workers. “There’s nothing concrete at all,” he said. “The language says consideration will be given. The language should not say that.”

The measure could also put dozens of carriage medallions in jeopardy, including those belonging to immigrant-run family enterprises that have been passed down through generations.

Industry advocates argue that the carriage trade has significant financial importance, saying operators conduct more than 100,000 rides each year and contribute to the city’s tourism sector.

Some carriage drivers expressed disappointment that Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, who has championed himself as a voice for the working class and unions, would take a stand in favor of the ban.

One longtime driver, Conner McHugh, told Gothamist that the mayor “gets up on his podium and announces that he’s just shutting us all down, putting us out of business, doesn’t even talk to us”, adding, “I think this guy is as phoney as a $3 bill.”

McHugh, a second-generation driver, had previously told the Guardian that he feels there is an ongoing effort to drive people like him off land and buildings in Manhattan that coincides with the rezoning of the area where horse stables are located.

“Intimidation has taken various forms,” he said, including “reporting us to ICE and the IRS, keyboard warriors trashing us on social media, animals rights volunteers who have come to Central Park to harass our drivers and create an unsafe situation”.

But advocates pushing for the ban have repeatedly raised concerns over the years about the dangers associated with the rides and the risks to passengers and pedestrians, with those dangers gaining national attention after Mahajan’s death.

The treatment of the carriage horses has also been controversial. Animal welfare campaigners have questioned conditions in the industry, pointing to several horse deaths since 2020, including incidents in which animals collapsed while pulling carriages.

Before the decision, Donald Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform he is “so sad to see the beloved Central Park Horse-drawn Carriage Industry ending after over a Century, based largely on one tragic accident.

“When there is a car accident in the area, of which there are many, they don’t stop cars from entering the Park,” he wrote. “So why would they stop the Carriages? It was a Great Tradition. Another piece of History that’s gone. It will be missed!”

In a separate post, he added: “The Horse-drawn Carriage in New York City is a quintessential New York experience. So sad that, for political reasons, we will see it go!”

The Transport Workers Union had already informed city officials that it plans to pursue legal action in federal court if the legislation passed. Union officials maintain that the measure would unlawfully deprive carriage owners of their operating licenses, valuable medallions and businesses built over many years.

Thursday’s vote follows an agreement reached earlier this month between mayor Mamdani and the head of the city council to eliminate horse-drawn carriage rides across New York City.

Mamdani previously made clear that the administration intended to move ahead with ending the practice while addressing the consequences for those involved. “The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected and the horses are safe,” Mamdani wrote on X.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Elon Musk reportedly invests $1bn in David Ellison’s Skydance
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Musk’s investment into the new media empire comes after Paramount’s $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery

Elon Musk has reportedly invested approximately $1bn in Skydance, the new media empire led by David Ellison.

The deal comes alongside fresh equity infusions from existing investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs, Steve Jobs’s widow. Semafor first reported the news.

The investment follows Paramount’s recent $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery, a huge acquisition that brought the media companies together under the Skydance name. At the head of the new media empire is David Ellison, the son of billionaire Oracle co-founder and Donald Trump ally Larry Ellison.

The cash infusion solidifies an alliance between two of Trump’s richest monetary backers. In September, Semafor reported that Paramount executives had considered Musk as an equity investor, citing his close ties to Larry Ellison, who invested $1bn in Musk’s acquisition of X in 2022 and also $45m in support of Trump’s re-election bid in 2024. Musk spent more than $290m on Trump’s re-election bid and has spent more than $350m backing Republicans in the current US midterm elections.

After the merger, Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz, who previously led Mattel, informed employees that the integration would involve layoffs, stating: “Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce.”

The company’s leadership – which now oversees Paramount and Warner Bros’s movie studios, HBO Max, CBS News and CNN – has set a target of more than $6bn in cost savings over the next three years, a goal that Los Angeles county officials estimate could lead to the loss of 4,500 film and television jobs in Los Angeles alone.

Prior to the merger, a coalition of 12 states, including California and New York, sued Paramount, arguing that the deal would “extinguish” competition and result in “higher prices, lower quality and less content for film and television”.

In September, a settlement agreement required Skydance to release at least 30 films and more than 180 television shows annually, while ensuring that CBS and CNN maintain editorial independence.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Dollar General agrees to nearly $1.9m settlement for overcharging New York customers
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Hudson
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Government inspections showed overcharges as high as 39% on some items. The discount store giant was the subject of a 2025 investigation by the Guardian

Dollar General, the nation’s largest dollar-store chain, has agreed to a $1.875m deal to settle allegations that it “repeatedly and persistently” overcharged customers across New York state.

The New York attorney general’s office found that Dollar General often charged customers higher prices at checkout than the prices it promised on shelf labels, signs, advertising circulars and its mobile app. The state agency said one check of 114 items across multiple stores revealed overcharges on individual items as high as 26%, 38% and 39%.

Under the settlement, Dollar General will donate $1.875m in food and personal items to a regional food bank in upstate New York. The agreement also requires that the company put in place comprehensive price-accuracy safeguards at its more than 600 stores statewide.

“When New Yorkers see a sale price advertised on the shelf, they should be able to trust that they’ll be charged that same price at the register,” the New York attorney general, Letitia James, said.

The pricing issues at the company – which promotes itself as “a lifeline for affordable, everyday essentials” – are not limited to the state of New York.

A Guardian investigation published in December reported that the chain frequently overcharged customers across the nation for such items as Flintstones vitamins, Peter Pan peanut butter and Prego pasta sauce. Dollar General stores flunked more than 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections in 23 states between 2022 and 2025, the Guardian found.

An inspection at a Dollar General in Port Henry, New York, for example, flagged overcharges on 78% of the items checked.
